title: German C2
description: The sixth and last step in German, from C1 to CEFR level C2, the level of the Goethe-Zertifikat C2: Großes Deutsches Sprachdiplom. Lessons cover precise word choice among near-synonyms and their connotations, deliberate shifts of register from Amtsdeutsch to salopp, the Konjunktiv and modality in their subtle uses, verbs with genitive objects, rewriting between nominal and verbal style, complex periods and fine word order, productive word formation and verb prefixes, argument and rhetoric, academic and journalistic writing, idioms, proverbs, collocations, humour, irony and metaphor, and the specialist German of law, medicine, finance, science and administration. Literary German is read across the periods in public-domain texts, with older German, contemporary language change, mediation at C2 and the Goethe C2 exam. About 1,000 new words build on the roughly 4,450 core words of German A1 to C1 for about 5,450 in all, and a reading list suggests books, newspapers and podcasts at this level. Unlocks when German C1 is complete.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: Raunen, tuscheln, wispern: near-synonyms, connotation and the precise word
topics: Verbs of speaking moving and laughing
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At C1 you learned to tell a word's denotation (what it refers to) from its connotation (what it suggests), and to place words on a ladder of register from *gehoben* to *derb* (C1 lesson 18). At C2 the question is narrower and harder: of five words that all seem to mean "whisper" or "walk", which one is right in *this* sentence? The Goethe-Institut's C2 test description expects you to recognize fine stylistic differences, and the CEFR describes C2 users as expressing themselves precisely, with finer shades of meaning; most of that precision lives in the choice between near-synonyms.

This lesson shows the dimensions along which near-synonyms differ, gives you a test to check a choice, and works through three **[[word fields]]**: verbs of saying, of moving and of laughing and crying. It ends with the confusable pairs that still trip up advanced learners (*scheinbar / anscheinend*, *offenbar / offensichtlich* and others) and with the two free dictionaries that help most.

## A reportage: the last round at the fair

Read this local reportage from an (invented) small-town paper. Almost every verb of saying, moving and laughing in it was chosen from a field of near-synonyms, and each choice tells you something the neutral verb would not.

> **Letzte Runde auf dem Festplatz**
>
> Gegen elf leert sich der Festplatz am Mühlbach. Familien mit Kinderwagen schlendern zum Ausgang, ein Vater trägt seine Tochter, die vor Müdigkeit leise wimmert, auf den Schultern. Wer jetzt noch bleibt, bleibt aus Überzeugung. Am Autoscooter kreischen zwei Mädchen bei jedem Zusammenstoß, aus dem Bierzelt dringt Gegröle: Die Kapelle hat aufgehört, die Gäste singen allein weiter, laut und falsch.
>
> Dass es das letzte Fest dieser Art sein könnte, wird seit Wochen gemunkelt. Offiziell verlautet aus dem Rathaus nur, man prüfe „verschiedene Optionen“. Die Schausteller murren, einige nörgeln über die Standgebühren, und Gerda Lindner, seit vierzig Jahren mit ihrem Mandelstand hier, jammert nicht, sie zetert: „Erst erhöhen sie die Gebühren, dann wundern sie sich, dass keiner mehr kommt!“ Ihr Nachbar beteuert, er habe noch nie so wenig verkauft, und gleich darauf, das Geschäft laufe „eigentlich ganz ordentlich“.
>
> Am Tresen schwadroniert ein Mann von den großen Jahren, als hier noch dreitausend Leute gefeiert hätten; sein Gegenüber stichelt, damals habe er ja auch noch Haare gehabt. Beide feixen. Ein Jüngerer faselt etwas von „Eventkonzepten“, nuschelt dann noch etwas in sein Glas und gibt auf.
>
> Kurz vor Mitternacht schreitet der Schützenkönig mit der Königskette um den Hals durchs Zelt, gefolgt von seinem Hofstaat, der ihm deutlich weniger würdevoll hinterhertorkelt. Draußen stapfen zwei Ordner durch den Matsch neben dem Kettenkarussell, ein Hund trottet hinter ihnen her. Eine Katze huscht unter einen Wohnwagen.
>
> Hinter dem Kinderkarussell, wo kaum noch Licht hinfällt, sitzen drei Teenager auf einer Bierbank und tuscheln. Als ich frage, worüber, kichern sie. Dann sagt eine, sehr ernst: „Wenn das Fest wegkommt, wo sollen wir dann hin?“ Die anderen nicken. Eine Andeutung, mehr nicht – aber an diesem Abend war es der klügste Satz auf dem ganzen Platz.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Last round at the fairground**

By eleven the fairground by the Mühlbach is emptying. Families with prams stroll towards the exit; a father carries his daughter, who is whimpering quietly with tiredness, on his shoulders. Anyone still here now is here by conviction. At the bumper cars two girls shriek at every collision, and drunken bawling comes from the beer tent: the band has stopped, and the guests carry on singing by themselves, loud and out of tune.

For weeks people have been whispering that this might be the last fair of its kind. Officially, all the town hall will say is that it is examining "various options". The showmen grumble, some carp about the pitch fees, and Gerda Lindner, who has had her roasted-almond stall here for forty years, doesn't moan, she rails: "First they put the fees up, then they're surprised nobody comes any more!" Her neighbour protests that he has never sold so little, and straight afterwards that business is "actually going quite well".

At the bar a man holds forth about the great years, when three thousand people used to party here; the man opposite him needles that he still had hair back then. Both of them smirk. A younger man drivels something about "event concepts", mumbles something else into his glass and gives up.

Shortly before midnight the king of the marksmen's club strides through the tent with the royal chain round his neck, followed by his court, which staggers after him with considerably less dignity. Outside, two stewards tramp through the mud next to the chair-o-plane, a dog plodding along behind them. A cat scurries under a caravan.

Behind the children's roundabout, where hardly any light reaches, three teenagers sit on a beer bench whispering. When I ask what about, they giggle. Then one of them says, very seriously: "If the fair goes, where are we supposed to go?" The others nod. A hint, nothing more – but that evening it was the wisest sentence on the whole fairground.

</details>

Look at what the verbs do. *murren* and *nörgeln* both mean complaining, but *murren* is a low, discontented grumble while *nörgeln* is carping about details, and Duden labels it *abwertend*. The writer says Frau Lindner *jammert nicht, sie zetert*: *jammern* is plaintive, *zetern* loud and shrill. *beteuern* (to protest, to insist) prepares the irony of the next clause: someone who has to insist that much is probably exaggerating. *schreitet* and *hinterhertorkelt* contrast dignity and its absence in two verbs.

## Why near-synonyms are never interchangeable

A **[[near-synonym]]** is a word whose meaning overlaps with another's so much that dictionaries list them together, yet which can't replace it in every context. Complete synonyms, words that could be swapped in every sentence without any change, are rare or don't exist; *Samstag* and *Sonnabend* come close, and even they differ by region. Near-synonyms differ along six dimensions:

| Dimension | Example | What differs |
|---|---|---|
| denotation, fine detail | *flüstern / wispern / tuscheln* | *flüstern*: without voice; *wispern*: softly and hastily; *tuscheln*: secretly, with others, so outsiders don't hear |
| collocation | *eine Frage stellen / aufwerfen* | you *stellen* a question you ask; a fact or a case *wirft* a question *auf* (raises it): *Der Fall wirft Fragen auf.* |
| valency | *beginnen / anfangen / einsetzen* | *mit etwas beginnen / anfangen*, also *etwas beginnen / anfangen*; *einsetzen* has no object and is said of processes: *Der Regen setzte ein.* |
| register | *raunen / munkeln* | Duden: *raunen* gehoben, *munkeln* umgangssprachlich |
| region | *die Sahne / der Rahm / das Obers* | standard / southern and Swiss / Austrian |
| evaluation | *erzählen / schwadronieren* | *schwadronieren* is talking volubly and loudly, often boastfully: a judgement, not a description |

Two more differences are less visible. **Frequency**: *schreiten* is much rarer than *gehen*, and rare words are marked: they draw attention to themselves. **Typical subject**: *einsetzen* in this sense takes processes (*die Wehen, die Dämmerung, das Tauwetter*), never people; *glucksen* is said of a laughing baby or of water in a pipe, rarely of a board meeting.

One more collocation trap, because it is everywhere in C2 texts: *eine Rolle spielen*, *Kritik üben*, *einen Beschluss fassen*, *eine Frage aufwerfen*. The verb is not chosen for its meaning but because it belongs to the noun. *Kritik machen* or *eine Frage heben* are not wrong because of what they mean, but because German doesn't say them.

## The test frame: checking a choice

When you hesitate between two words, don't compare their dictionary definitions; put each into a set of short sentences (test frames) and see where one fails. It is a version of the substitution test of school grammar (*Ersatzprobe*).

| Frame | *flüstern* | *tuscheln* | *raunen* | *munkeln* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *Sie ___ mir ins Ohr, dass sie gehen wolle.* | ✓ | possible | ✓ (gehoben) | ✗ |
| *In der letzten Reihe wurde die ganze Stunde ___.* | ✓ | ✓ (best) | ✗ | ✗ |
| *Ein ___ ging durch den Saal.* | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ (*ein Raunen*) | ✗ |
| *Man ___ schon lange, dass die Firma verkauft wird.* | rare | rare | possible (gehoben) | ✓ (best) |

The table shows what definitions hide. *munkeln* is not about volume at all: it is about rumours, so it needs content (*man munkelt, dass …*; *es wird gemunkelt*). *tuscheln* is social: several people, and the suspicion that they are talking about someone. *raunen* lives in two fixed patterns, the murmur of a crowd (*ein Raunen ging durch die Menge*) and the mysterious, prophetic hint (*Man raunte von einem Verrat*). And *flüstern* is the neutral word that fits almost anywhere.

Test frames are also the honest answer to "Is X a synonym of Y?": it depends on the frame. Native speakers disagree at the edges (is *tuscheln* possible in the first frame? Duden's second sense of *tuscheln* is passing something on in a whisper, so it isn't excluded), and that is why the frames say "possible" and "best" rather than right and wrong.

## Verbs of saying

| Verb | What it adds to *sagen / sprechen* | Duden label | Typical frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| *beteuern* | to insist, protest (that something is true) | — | *seine Unschuld beteuern*; *Er beteuerte, nichts gewusst zu haben.* |
| *munkeln* | to rumour, to whisper about | umgangssprachlich | *Man munkelt, dass …*; *es wird gemunkelt* |
| *raunen* | to murmur in a low, mysterious voice | gehoben | *ein Raunen ging durch die Menge* |
| *tuscheln* | to whisper secretly with others | oft abwertend | *hinter jemandes Rücken tuscheln* |
| *wispern* | to whisper softly and hastily; also of leaves, wind (literary) | — | *Die Kinder wisperten unter der Decke.* |
| *nuscheln* | to mumble indistinctly | umgangssprachlich | *Er nuschelt so, dass man ihn kaum versteht.* |
| *stammeln* | to stammer (from embarrassment, shock) | — | *eine Entschuldigung stammeln* |
| *schwadronieren* | to hold forth, volubly and often boastfully | — | *von seinen Heldentaten schwadronieren* |
| *faseln* | to drivel, talk confused nonsense | umgangssprachlich abwertend | *Was faselst du da?* |
| *plappern* | to chatter, prattle (often of children) | umgangssprachlich | *Die Kleine plappert den ganzen Tag.* |
| *sticheln* | to make digs, needle | — | *gegen den Chef sticheln* |
| *prahlen* | to boast, brag | — | *mit seinem Auto prahlen* |
| *verlauten* | to be announced, become known (news style) | — | *wie aus Regierungskreisen verlautet*; *Es verlautete, dass …* |

Notes:

- *stammeln* and *stottern* are different: *stottern* is the speech disorder or a habitual stutter, *stammeln* the halting speech of someone confused or moved. You *stammeln* an apology; you *stottern* if you have a stutter.
- *verlauten* belongs to the press. With the source in a *aus*-phrase it is impersonal or has the news as its subject: *Aus dem Ministerium verlautete, man werde …* In the Perfekt it takes *ist* in this sense. The pattern *etwas / nichts verlauten lassen* (to let something be known) is very common: *Der Verein ließ zunächst nichts verlauten.*
- The B1 word *andeuten* (to hint at) has the noun *die Andeutung*: *eine Andeutung machen*, *in Andeutungen sprechen* (to speak in hints).

## Verbs of moving

| Verb | Manner | Duden label | Perfekt |
|---|---|---|---|
| *schlendern* | to stroll, leisurely, without a goal | — | *ist geschlendert* |
| *schreiten* | to stride with measured, dignified steps | gehoben | *ist geschritten* (strong: *schritt*) |
| *stapfen* | to tramp, with heavy steps sinking in (snow, mud) | — | *ist gestapft* |
| *trotten* | to plod, slowly and dully | — | *ist getrottet* |
| *torkeln* | to stagger, reel (drunk, weak) | umgangssprachlich | *ist / hat getorkelt* |
| *schlurfen* | to shuffle, dragging one's feet | — | *ist geschlurft* |
| *hasten* | to hurry, driven by inner unrest | gehoben | *ist gehastet* |
| *huschen* | to flit, scurry quickly and silently | — | *ist gehuscht* |
| *taumeln* | to reel, sway as if dizzy | — | *ist / hat getaumelt* |

Verbs of moving take *sein* when they describe movement to or through a place: *Er ist über den Platz geschlendert.* For *torkeln* and *taumeln*, Duden allows *haben* when only the swaying itself is meant (*Er hat vor Müdigkeit getaumelt*); once there is a direction, it's *sein*: *Er ist aus der Kneipe getorkelt.*

*schreiten* has a second, very common figurative use: *zur Tat schreiten* (to proceed to action), *zur Wahl schreiten*, *Die Arbeiten schreiten voran* (are progressing). The literal sense is solemn or ironic; in a modern report, *schreitet* about an ordinary person suggests pomposity. *hasten* is gehoben too: in everyday speech you *eilst* or *rennst*.

## Verbs of laughing and crying

| Verb | What it describes | Duden label |
|---|---|---|
| *kichern* | to giggle: high, suppressed laughter | — |
| *feixen* | to smirk, grin broadly and smugly, often at someone's misfortune | umgangssprachlich |
| *glucksen* | to chuckle with dark, suppressed sounds; of water: to gurgle | — |
| *grölen* | to bawl, roar (songs), usually drunk | umgangssprachlich abwertend |
| *kreischen* | to shriek, screech | — |
| *murren* | to grumble, mutter discontentedly | — |
| *nörgeln* | to carp, nag, find fault with everything | abwertend |
| *zetern* | to rail, scold loudly and shrilly | emotional abwertend |
| *jammern* | to moan, wail, lament | — |
| *wimmern* | to whimper | — |
| *schluchzen* | to sob | — |

The B2 word *schmunzeln* (to smile with quiet amusement) belongs here too: it is the warm, benevolent counterpart of *feixen*. Compare: *Der Lehrer schmunzelte über die Ausrede* (amused, indulgent) and *Die Schüler feixten, als der Lehrer stolperte* (gloating). The nouns *das Gekicher, das Gejammer, das Gegröle, das Gezeter* (*Ge-… -e*, usually disapproving) are taught in module 2.

## Confusable pairs at C2

| Pair | Difference | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *scheinbar / anscheinend* | *scheinbar*: it only seems so, but isn't; *anscheinend*: it seems so, and probably is | *Er ist scheinbar ruhig* (but nervous inside); *Er ist anscheinend krank* (he hasn't come in) |
| *offenbar / offensichtlich* | *offenbar*: evidently, as far as one can tell (an inference); *offensichtlich*: obviously, plain for all to see | *Der Zug hat offenbar Verspätung* (the board is blank); *Das ist offensichtlich falsch* |
| *selten / rar* | *selten*: rare, infrequent (also adverb: rarely); *rar*: scarce, in short supply, of things or people in demand | *Er kommt selten*; *Gute Handwerker sind rar*; *sich rar machen* (to make oneself scarce) |
| *erstaunlich / verwunderlich* | *erstaunlich*: astonishing, often admiring; *verwunderlich*: strange, mostly negated or in questions | *eine erstaunliche Leistung*; *Das ist nicht verwunderlich* (no wonder) |
| *zeitig / rechtzeitig* | *zeitig*: early; *rechtzeitig*: in time, before it is too late | *zeitig aufstehen*; *rechtzeitig zum Zug kommen* |

Three of these need a caution. In everyday speech *scheinbar* is often used for *anscheinend*; Duden records this use, but careful writers keep the two apart, and C2 readers notice. *offensichtlich* is also used in the sense of *offenbar* in the press, so the difference is a tendency; *offenbar* never means "plain for all to see", though. And *rar* is mostly predicative (*sind rar*, *machen sich rar*); *ein rares Exemplar* exists but sounds marked or collector's jargon.

## Checking with Duden and the DWDS

Two free online dictionaries do most of the work:

- **Duden online** (duden.de) gives each word's *Gebrauch* label (*gehoben, umgangssprachlich, abwertend* …), its grammar and, on separate pages, groups of synonyms (*Synonyme*). Use the synonym pages to find candidates, never to choose: the list puts *raunen* and *flüstern* side by side without saying that one is gehoben.
- The **DWDS** (dwds.de, the Digital Dictionary of the German Language at the Berlin-Brandenburg Academy) shows each word in real corpus sentences and, in the *Wortprofil*, the words it most typically combines with. If you want to know whether people *stellen* or *aufwerfen* a particular question, or what usually *setzt ein*, the Wortprofil answers from thousands of texts.

A good routine: find candidates in the synonym list, check the label in Duden, check the collocations in the Wortprofil, and then run your own test frames.

## Words of this lesson

The lesson's words are the verbs in the three tables, *die Andeutung*, and three words about words: *das Wortfeld* (word field), *die Bedeutungsnuance* (shade of meaning) and *sinnverwandt* (similar in meaning: *sinnverwandte Wörter*). Notice in the vocabulary which verbs are weak (nearly all), which one is strong (*schreiten: schritt, ist geschritten*) and which take *sein*.

## Pronunciation

- Verbs in *-ieren* are stressed on *-ie-*: *schwadronieren*, schwa-dro-NIE-ren.
- The prefix *be-* is unstressed: *beteuern*, be-TEU-ern.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing from a synonym list without checking the register: ~~Der Minister raunte, er werde zurücktreten~~ in a news report sounds like a fairy tale. Write *Der Minister kündigte an* or *deutete an*.
- Using *munkeln* for volume: ~~Sie munkelte mir ins Ohr~~ → *Sie flüsterte mir ins Ohr.* *munkeln* is about rumours.
- *haben* with a verb of moving that has a direction: ~~Er hat über den Markt geschlendert~~ → *Er ist über den Markt geschlendert.*
- *stottern* for embarrassment: *Er stammelte eine Entschuldigung* (not ~~stotterte~~, unless he has a stutter).
- *verwunderlich* as praise: ~~eine verwunderliche Leistung~~ → *eine erstaunliche Leistung.*
- *scheinbar* where you mean *anscheinend* in careful writing: *Die Firma ist anscheinend insolvent* (it probably is) vs *Die Firma ist scheinbar gesund* (but isn't).
- False precision: piling up rare verbs (*Er hastete, stapfte und schritt …*) to sound advanced. One marked verb in a sentence is a choice; three are a parody.

## Key points

- Near-synonyms differ in fine denotation, collocation, valency, register, region, evaluation, frequency and typical subject; perfect synonyms are rare.
- Check a choice with test frames, not definitions.
- Speaking: *munkeln* (rumours), *raunen* (gehoben, mysterious), *tuscheln* (secretly, with others), *wispern* (softly, hastily), *beteuern* (insist), *schwadronieren* (hold forth), *verlauten* (press).
- Moving: manner verbs (*schlendern, schreiten, stapfen, trotten, torkeln, schlurfen, hasten, huschen, taumeln*) take *sein* with a direction.
- Laughing and complaining: *kichern, feixen, glucksen, grölen, kreischen; murren, nörgeln, zetern, jammern, wimmern, schluchzen*; several carry *abwertend*.
- *scheinbar* (not really) vs *anscheinend* (probably really); *offenbar* (evidently) vs *offensichtlich* (obviously); *selten* vs *rar* (scarce); *erstaunlich* vs *verwunderlich* (mostly negated); *zeitig* (early) vs *rechtzeitig* (in time).
- Use Duden for labels and the DWDS Wortprofil for collocations.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Malochen oder arbeiten: shifting register on purpose
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 01 was about choosing the precise word within one register. This lesson is about moving between registers deliberately. A C2 speaker can say the same thing to a housing office, a newspaper, a neighbour, a friend and a teenager, and knows exactly which words, which grammar and which spellings belong to each. C1 lesson 18 introduced the dictionary labels (*gehoben, umgangssprachlich, salopp, derb* …) and the synonym ladders; here you climb the ladder in both directions and learn to use the clash between registers on purpose, as columnists, comedians and good speakers do.

The words of this lesson are colloquial and salopp German: the vocabulary of work and money, sleep and food, rows and messes, school and prison as people actually talk about them. Each comes with its Duden label, because the label is half of the meaning.

## A Glosse: moving house with your mates

A *Glosse* is a short, ironic newspaper column. This one (invented) is written in colloquial German, which is normal for the genre; watch what happens in the last paragraph.

> **Umzug mit Kumpels**
>
> Jeder kennt den Satz: „Du, am Samstag zieh ich um, hast du Zeit?“ Man sagt zu, weil man ein guter Kumpel ist, und weiß im selben Moment, dass man es bereuen wird.
>
> Samstag, acht Uhr. Die neue Bude liegt im vierten Stock, Altbau, kein Aufzug. Der Umzugswagen ist kleiner als versprochen, die Firma hat Jonas abgezockt, aber das hat er erst kapiert, als er die Rechnung sah. Jetzt ist es ihm schnuppe. Hauptsache, die Klamotten kommen nach oben.
>
> Um zehn geht mir zum ersten Mal die Puste aus. Sebastian, der seit Wochen für eine Prüfung büffelt und dafür sogar Vorlesungen schwänzt, flunkert, er habe „nur die schweren Kisten“ erwischt. Er hat Kissen getragen. Jonas' Schwester quasselt ununterbrochen, der Vermieter steht im Treppenhaus und motzt über die Kratzer im Lack. Ein Spießer, wie er im Buche steht: Er hat sogar eine Liste dabei.
>
> Mittags futtern wir Pizza auf dem Fußboden. Niemand hat Bammel vor dem Kleiderschrank, sagt jedenfalls keiner. Zwei Stunden später sitzen wir im Schlamassel: Der Schrank passt nicht um die Kurve. Es gibt Zoff. Jonas will ihn zersägen, seine Schwester ist baff, Sebastian labert etwas von Hebelgesetzen.
>
> Abends um neun steht alles. Die Glotze läuft, keiner schaut hin. Wir hängen auf dem Sofa rum, zu müde zum Reden, zu stolz zum Gehen. Wir haben malocht wie die Kumpel unter Tage, und die Knete, die Jonas uns fürs Bier hinhält, lehnen wir natürlich ab.
>
> Am Montag kommt der Brief der Hausverwaltung: „Wir weisen darauf hin, dass gemäß § 7 der Hausordnung das Abstellen von Gegenständen im Treppenhaus untersagt ist. Wir bitten um umgehende Beseitigung des Sperrmülls.“ Gemeint ist der Schrank. Er steht immer noch unten. Spießig? Vielleicht. Aber diesmal hat der Spießer recht.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Moving house with your mates**

Everyone knows the line: "Hey, I'm moving on Saturday, are you free?" You say yes because you're a good mate, and in the same moment you know you'll regret it.

Saturday, eight o'clock. The new pad is on the fourth floor, old building, no lift. The removal van is smaller than promised; the company has ripped Jonas off, but he only twigged when he saw the bill. Now he couldn't care less. The main thing is getting the gear upstairs.

At ten I run out of puff for the first time. Sebastian, who has been cramming for an exam for weeks and has even been skipping lectures for it, fibs that he got "only the heavy boxes". He carried cushions. Jonas's sister yaks non-stop, and the landlord stands in the stairwell griping about the scratches in the paintwork. A textbook square: he has even brought a list.

At lunchtime we tuck into pizza on the floor. Nobody has the jitters about the wardrobe, or at least nobody says so. Two hours later we're in a fix: the wardrobe won't go round the corner. A row breaks out. Jonas wants to saw it up, his sister is flabbergasted, Sebastian blathers on about the laws of leverage.

By nine in the evening everything is in place. The telly is on, nobody is watching. We hang around on the sofa, too tired to talk, too proud to leave. We've slaved away like miners at the coalface, and the cash Jonas holds out to us for beer we naturally refuse.

On Monday the letter from the property management arrives: "We would point out that, in accordance with § 7 of the house rules, the placing of objects in the stairwell is prohibited. We request the immediate removal of the bulky waste." What they mean is the wardrobe. It's still standing downstairs. Square? Maybe. But this time the square is right.

</details>

Three things to notice. First, the salopp words cluster around the body, money, conflict and effort, as colloquial vocabulary does in most languages. Second, *wie die Kumpel unter Tage* is a pun: *der Kumpel* (umgangssprachlich: mate) comes from the miners' word for a fellow miner, and *unter Tage* is mining language for "underground". Third, the last paragraph switches into Amtsdeutsch (*gemäß, das Abstellen von Gegenständen, untersagt, um umgehende Beseitigung bitten*). The clash is the joke: a deliberate Stilbruch, the term C1 lesson 18 taught, used here as a device rather than a mistake.

## One message on six levels

Here is one message, "Our heating has been broken for three days; please repair it", in six registers. Read down the column and watch the markers change.

| Level | The message | Markers |
|---|---|---|
| Amtsdeutsch | *Hiermit zeige ich an, dass die Heizungsanlage der von mir angemieteten Wohnung seit dem 12. d. M. außer Betrieb ist. Ich ersuche um umgehende Instandsetzung und behalte mir eine Minderung der Miete vor.* | *hiermit, anzeigen, ersuchen um, Instandsetzung*, abbreviations (*d. M.* = *dieses Monats*), nouns in *-ung*, extended attribute (*der von mir angemieteten Wohnung*) |
| Pressedeutsch | *Seit drei Tagen ohne Heizung: Mieter in der Lindenstraße frieren. Die Hausverwaltung kündigte an, den Schaden bis Freitag beheben zu lassen.* | headline with colon and no verb, Präteritum, reporting verbs (*kündigte an*), source named |
| neutral standard | *Unsere Heizung funktioniert seit drei Tagen nicht. Könnten Sie bitte möglichst bald jemanden schicken?* | complete sentences, Konjunktiv II of politeness, no marked words |
| Umgangssprache | *Bei uns geht seit drei Tagen die Heizung nicht. Ich hab schon zweimal bei der Verwaltung angerufen, aber da tut sich nix.* | *gehen* for "work", *hab, nix*, Perfekt, *da tut sich nichts* |
| salopp | *Die Bude ist seit drei Tagen eiskalt, Heizung im Eimer, und die Verwaltung pennt. Echt ätzend.* | *Bude, im Eimer* (bust), *pennen* (here: to be asleep on the job), ellipsis, *echt* as intensifier, evaluation |
| Jugendsprache *(receptive)* | *Digga, unsere Heizung ist seit drei Tagen tot, ich frier hier voll. Safe kommt da vor Freitag keiner.* | address *Digga*, English loans (*safe* = surely), *voll* as intensifier, dropped endings |

Two warnings about the last line. Youth language is not one variety: it differs by city, group and year, and its words age fast (lesson 28 takes it further). And it is used mostly in speech and chat among young people; an adult who imitates it usually sounds ridiculous. Recognize it, and leave it there.

## The markers of register

Register is a bundle of choices, not just words. At C2 you should be able to name the marker that places a sentence.

**Vocabulary.** The clearest marker. Many everyday meanings have a word at each level: *arbeiten* (neutral), *schuften* (umgangssprachlich), *malochen* (salopp); *das Geld*, *die Kohle* (B1), *die Knete*, *der Zaster* (both salopp); *schlafen*, *pennen* (umgangssprachlich); *sich streiten*, *Zoff haben* (umgangssprachlich); *das Gefängnis*, *der Knast* (umgangssprachlich). Notice that Duden labels differ in strength: *Zoff* and *Knast* are only umgangssprachlich, *Knete, Zaster, malochen, Abzocke, baff* are salopp.

**Grammar.** C1 lesson 18 gave the main points; in one line each:

- genitive (*das Auto meines Bruders*) vs *von* (*das Auto von meinem Bruder*) vs the possessive dative of speech (*meinem Bruder sein Auto*);
- Präteritum in written narration vs Perfekt in speech (especially in the south);
- *weil* with the verb at the end in writing vs *weil* + verb second in speech: *…, weil ich hab keine Zeit*;
- ellipsis in salopp speech: *Heizung im Eimer* (no article, no verb);
- *würde*-forms and Konjunktiv II of politeness in neutral and formal requests, the indicative or the imperative in speech.

**Spellings of speech.** Informal writing (chats, Glossen, dialogue in fiction) imitates the spoken forms. The official rules, as Duden presents them, are: a dropped final *-e* needs no apostrophe (*ich hab, ich geh, lass das*); an apostrophe may mark other left-out letters where it helps reading (*gibt's, wie geht's, so 'n Zufall, 'nen Kaffee*), and *gibts, gehts* without it are also accepted. Don't use the apostrophe for the genitive *s* of ordinary nouns (*des Kumpels*, not ~~des Kumpel's~~).

**Clitics.** In speech, short words lean on their neighbours (clitics, *Klitika*). Some fused forms are standard written German and fine in any text: *am, im, ins, zum, zur, beim, vom*, and also *aufs, durchs, fürs, übers, ums*. Others belong to speech and informal writing only: *aufm* (*auf dem*), *ausm*, *mitm*, *haste* (*hast du*), *willste, kannste, isses* (*ist es*). Writing *Ich war aufm Amt* in a complaint letter is a register slip, not a typo.

## Stilfärbung and the deliberate Stilbruch

Every word that isn't neutral carries a **[[stylistic colouring]]** (*Stilfärbung*): the register, region, attitude or period it brings with it. *Knete* is salopp; *Amtsdeutsch* is labelled *abwertend*, because the word itself judges the bureaucratic style it names. Two neutral sentences side by side read smoothly; one coloured word in a neutral text stands out, which is exactly what makes it useful.

A Stilbruch is a clash of colourings. In a job application or a report, it is a mistake: *Die Kosten sind leider durch die Decke gegangen* (idiomatic, umgangssprachlich) in a financial report reads as careless. As a device it is everywhere:

- for humour, as in the Glosse above, where the house rules arrive in Amtsdeutsch;
- for irony, when a speaker uses a pompous word for something trivial: *Er geruhte, den Müll hinauszutragen* (*geruhen*, old-fashioned and today mostly ironic: to deign);
- for closeness and authenticity, when a politician or a manager suddenly drops into colloquial speech: *Da muss man jetzt mal ran* (that's something we've got to tackle now);
- for emphasis at the end of a formal argument: a single salopp word as the punchline.

The test for a deliberate Stilbruch: it is rare, it is placed (usually at the end of a paragraph or as a quotation), and the reader can see that the writer knows the neutral word.

## derb and vulgär: recognize, don't produce

Below *salopp* come *derb* (coarse) and *vulgär* (vulgar, often sexual). You need to recognize them in films, novels, football stadiums and comment sections, and to know how strong they are, but this course doesn't practise them, and you shouldn't use them until you have a native speaker's feel for when they work. Two examples of *derb*: *Das ist zum Kotzen* (it makes you sick, literally "it makes you vomit") and *die Fresse* for the face (also in *Halt die Fresse!*, an aggressive "shut up"). *fressen* is neutral for animals and derb for people (C1 lesson 18). Vulgar words are not listed here; a good dictionary marks them *vulgär*, and that label is a warning.

## Choosing a register for the reader

| Situation | Register | Typical choices |
|---|---|---|
| chat with a friend | umgangssprachlich to salopp | *hab, nix, echt, Bude, pennen*; ellipsis; emojis are optional, apostrophes too |
| note to a neighbour | neutral, friendly | *Liebe Nachbarn, …*; *Könnten Sie …*; no salopp words; the Perfekt is fine |
| complaint to a landlord | neutral to formal | *Sehr geehrte …*; facts with dates; *Ich bitte Sie, … bis zum … zu beheben*; no Amtsdeutsch padding, no colloquialisms |
| statement to the press | formal, Pressedeutsch | short, quotable sentences; names and dates; *Wir bedauern …*; no particles |

Most C2 errors are not in the extremes but at the edges: a *nix* in the neighbour's note, an *ersuchen* in the chat, a *Kohle* in the complaint letter. When in doubt, choose the neutral word: it is never wrong, only sometimes colourless.

## The words of this lesson

Each word in the vocabulary has its Duden label in the note. A few points:

- *rumhängen* is the colloquial short form of *herumhängen* (Duden: umgangssprachlich): *Er hängt den ganzen Tag vor der Glotze rum.* It is strong: *hing rum, hat rumgehangen*.
- *abhauen* (to clear off, umgangssprachlich) takes *sein* and a weak Präteritum: *Sie haute ab, sie ist abgehauen.* In the sense "to chop off" it takes *haben*, and Duden gives *hieb ab* (gehoben) besides *haute ab*.
- *baff* and *schnuppe* don't decline: they are used only after *sein* (*Ich war baff. Das ist mir schnuppe.*).
- *die Klamotten* (clothes) is plural only in this sense; *der Kumpel* has the plural *die Kumpel*, colloquially *die Kumpels*.
- *der Schlamassel* can also be *das Schlamassel*; in Austria only the neuter is used.
- *abgefahren* (far out, amazing) is the participle of *abfahren*; Duden labels the adjective umgangssprachlich and notes that it is becoming dated.
- *ätzend* literally means "corrosive" (*ätzende Säure*); in speech it means "awful": *Montags ist es echt ätzend.*
- *schnorren* means to cadge small things regularly without giving anything back (*eine Zigarette schnorren*), *abzocken* to rip someone off, usually for money.

Several of these words came into German from Yiddish or Rotwelsch (the old secret language of travellers and thieves), according to Duden's etymologies: *malochen* (Yiddish, from Hebrew), *Knast* and *Zaster* (thieves' cant; *Zaster* via Romani *sáster*, iron). That is part of their colouring: they were never the words of offices.

## Pronunciation

- *malochen*: stress on the second syllable, [maˈloːxn̩] (Duden also gives a short *o*).
- *der Schlamassel*: stress on *-mas-*.
- *futtern*: short *u*, stress on the first syllable, [ˈfʊtɐn].
- In colloquial speech, endings and unstressed words shrink: *haste* [ˈhastə], *hab ich nich gesehn*. Recognize these forms when you listen; in careful speech, say the full words.

## Common mistakes

- Overusing salopp words to sound fluent. Native speakers mix one or two into neutral speech; a sentence full of *Knete, Bude* and *pennen* sounds like a parody of youth speech from decades ago.
- Mixing levels by accident: ~~Sehr geehrter Herr Krause, die Heizung ist im Eimer.~~ → *Sehr geehrter Herr Krause, die Heizung ist seit Montag defekt.*
- Writing speech clitics in formal texts: ~~aufm Bürgeramt~~ → *auf dem Bürgeramt*.
- Thinking *umgangssprachlich* means "wrong". *Zoff, Knast, kapieren* are good German in the right place, and Duden lists them without disapproval.
- Declining *baff* or *schnuppe*: ~~ein baffer Kollege~~ → *ein verblüffter Kollege*.
- False precision in Amtsdeutsch: writing *betreffs* and *Instandsetzungsmaßnahme* in a complaint does not make it more effective, just harder to read.
- Taking *derb* words from films into conversation with people you don't know well.

## Key points

- Register is a bundle of markers: vocabulary, grammar (genitive vs *von*, Präteritum vs Perfekt, *weil* + verb second), spellings of speech (*hab, gibt's*) and clitics (*aufm, haste*).
- The six levels of this lesson: Amtsdeutsch, Pressedeutsch, neutral standard, Umgangssprache, salopp, Jugendsprache (recognize only).
- Duden labels are part of the meaning: *Knete, Zaster, malochen, abzocken, baff* are salopp; *pennen, Zoff, Knast, kapieren, Glotze* umgangssprachlich; *Spießer, spießig* umgangssprachlich abwertend; *Amtsdeutsch* abwertend.
- Every non-neutral word has a Stilfärbung; a Stilbruch is a mistake by accident and a device on purpose.
- *derb* and *vulgär*: recognize, don't produce.
- Choose the register for the reader; when in doubt, use the neutral word.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Komme, was wolle: the Konjunktiv in its subtle uses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You know the Konjunktiv's main jobs: Konjunktiv I for reported speech, extended over whole paragraphs in academic writing (C1 lesson 04), and Konjunktiv II for unreal conditions, wishes and comparisons, also in the past with modal verbs (C1 lesson 03). At C2 the Konjunktiv turns up in places where it doesn't report and isn't unreal: in fixed formulas (*Gott sei Dank, koste es, was es wolle*), in concessions (*sei es aus Angst, sei es aus Gier*), in the "summing-up" phrases of everyday speech (*Das wär's*), and as a professional tool of distance in crime and court reporting, where a single indicative can turn a suspect into a culprit.

The theme is crime, investigation and the courts. The core words of German criminal procedure (*der Staatsanwalt, das Alibi, festnehmen, der Freispruch, der Täter, die Bewährung*) are already yours; this lesson adds the vocabulary of suspicion, evidence and custody that court reports are made of.

## A court report

Read this report from an (invented) regional paper. The trial is in progress, so every claim belongs to someone. Mark who says what, and how the grammar shows it.

> **„Ich habe keinen Cent genommen“**
>
> Seit drei Verhandlungstagen sitzt Markus T. im Saal 4 des Justizzentrums, als ginge ihn das alles nichts an. Der 46-Jährige, bis zu seiner Festnahme im vergangenen Herbst Leiter einer Tankstelle am Stadtrand, soll über zwei Jahre hinweg Bareinnahmen von insgesamt rund 180.000 Euro unterschlagen haben. So jedenfalls sieht es die Staatsanwaltschaft. T. bestreitet das. Er habe „keinen Cent genommen“, ließ er über seinen Strafverteidiger erklären; das Geld sei bei der Abholung durch einen Sicherheitsdienst verschwunden, mit dem er nichts zu tun habe.
>
> Ein Geständnis gibt es nicht, die Beweislage ist dünn: Es ist ein klassischer Indizienprozess. Die Spurensicherung fand T.s Fingerabdrücke am Tresor – was wenig besagt, denn er hatte als Filialleiter jeden Tag damit zu tun. Schwerer wiegt die Zeugenaussage einer Kollegin. Sie habe ihn mehrfach nach Feierabend mit einer Sporttasche aus dem Büro kommen sehen, sagte sie in ihrer Vernehmung. Die Verteidigung hält dagegen, die Zeugin sei mit T. seit Langem zerstritten.
>
> Und dann ist da noch die Geschichte, die T. am zweiten Tag selbst erzählte. Ein früherer Bekannter habe ihn erpresst; er habe zahlen müssen, „koste es, was es wolle“. Belege legte er nicht vor. Wie dem auch sei: In diese Richtung ermittelt wurde offenbar nie. Eine Strafanzeige wegen Erpressung, so der Verteidiger, werde man nachreichen.
>
> Gut zwei Monate saß T. in Untersuchungshaft, weil das Gericht Fluchtgefahr annahm; inzwischen ist der Haftbefehl gegen Auflagen außer Vollzug gesetzt. Für die Berichterstattung gilt, was für das Gericht gilt: Bis zu einem rechtskräftigen Urteil ist Markus T. ein Angeklagter, kein Täter. Ob er das Geld genommen hat oder ob, wie er sagt, ein Dritter dahintersteckt, wird die Kammer entscheiden müssen. Das Urteil soll Ende des Monats fallen. Eines immerhin ließ sich beobachten: Am Ende des dritten Tages wirkte T. zum ersten Mal nervös.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**"I didn't take a cent"**

For three days of hearings Markus T. has been sitting in courtroom 4 of the Justice Centre as if none of it had anything to do with him. The 46-year-old, who until his arrest last autumn managed a petrol station on the edge of town, is alleged to have embezzled cash takings totalling around 180,000 euros over two years. That, at least, is how the prosecution sees it. T. denies it. He "didn't take a cent", he had his defence lawyer declare; the money, he says, disappeared when it was collected by a security firm he had nothing to do with.

There is no confession, and the evidence is thin: it is a classic trial on circumstantial evidence. Forensics found T.'s fingerprints on the safe – which says little, since as branch manager he handled it every day. A colleague's witness statement weighs more heavily. She said in her questioning that she had several times seen him leave the office after closing time with a sports bag. The defence counters that the witness fell out with T. long ago.

And then there is the story T. told himself on the second day. A former acquaintance, he said, had blackmailed him; he had had to pay, "whatever the cost". He produced no evidence of this. Be that as it may: apparently no one ever investigated in that direction. A criminal complaint for blackmail will be filed later, according to the defence lawyer.

T. spent just over two months in custody on remand because the court assumed he might abscond; the arrest warrant has since been suspended subject to conditions. For the reporting, what applies to the court applies too: until a final judgment, Markus T. is a defendant, not a culprit. Whether he took the money or whether, as he says, a third party is behind it is for the chamber to decide. The verdict is expected at the end of the month. One thing, at least, could be observed: at the end of the third day, T. looked nervous for the first time.

</details>

Every verb form in this text has a job:

| Form | Example | Job |
|---|---|---|
| *soll* + perfect infinitive | *soll … unterschlagen haben* | the accusation, attributed to someone else ("is alleged to have") |
| Konjunktiv I | *Er habe …, das Geld sei … verschwunden*; *so der Verteidiger, werde man …* | the defendant's, the witness's and the lawyer's statements, not the reporter's |
| indicative | *T. bestreitet das. Die Spurensicherung fand …* | facts the reporter vouches for |
| *als* + Konjunktiv II | *als ginge ihn das alles nichts an* | an unreal comparison: the reporter's impression |
| KI formula | *koste es, was es wolle*; *Wie dem auch sei* | fixed expressions, quoted or used by the reporter |

## Distance in crime reporting

German court and crime reporting has a grammar of caution. Four tools, from strongest to weakest:

1. Konjunktiv I for everything the police, the prosecution, witnesses or the defence say: *Der Angeklagte habe das Geld nicht genommen. Die Zeugin sei sich sicher.* With a named source in the paragraph, the Konjunktiv I can run on over several sentences (C1 lesson 04).
2. soll / sollen + perfect infinitive for an accusation or a report from others: *Er soll die Kasse geleert haben* (he is alleged to have …). Unlike the Konjunktiv I, *soll* doesn't name a source; it only says "not my claim".
3. Adjectives and nouns of suspicion: *mutmaßlich* (B2: alleged, presumed), *tatverdächtig*, *der Tatverdächtige*, *der Beschuldigte*. *der mutmaßliche Täter* is the standard press phrase; *der Täter* without it is a judgement.
4. Verbs of attribution: *wirft ihm vor, legt ihm zur Last* (charges him with), *nach Angaben der Polizei*, *laut Anklage*.

The terms for the person also follow the stages of the procedure. The Code of Criminal Procedure (StPO, § 157) distinguishes the *Beschuldigte* (during the investigation), the *Angeschuldigte* (once the charge has been filed) and the *Angeklagte* (once the court has opened the main proceedings). The police and the press add *der Tatverdächtige* (the suspect), which isn't a procedural term. Careful reporting normally calls someone *der Täter* only after a final conviction (*rechtskräftig verurteilt*); the Pressekodex (guideline 13.1) also allows it when the person has confessed and there is further evidence, or committed the act in public view.

This is not just style. The Pressekodex of the Deutscher Presserat, the self-regulatory code of the German press (version of 19 March 2025), says in Ziffer 13, "Unschuldsvermutung":

> „Die Berichterstattung über Ermittlungsverfahren, Strafverfahren und sonstige förmliche Verfahren muss frei von Vorurteilen erfolgen. Der Grundsatz der Unschuldsvermutung gilt auch für die Presse.“

— "Reporting on investigations, criminal trials and other formal proceedings must be free of prejudice. The principle of the presumption of innocence also applies to the press." Its guideline 13.1 adds: „Zwischen Verdacht und erwiesener Schuld ist in der Sprache der Berichterstattung deutlich zu unterscheiden.“ (In the language of reporting, a clear distinction must be made between suspicion and proven guilt.) The Konjunktiv is one of the ways German does that.

Compare two headlines: *Tankstellenleiter unterschlug 180.000 Euro* (a verdict before the verdict) and *Tankstellenleiter soll 180.000 Euro unterschlagen haben* (an accusation, correctly reported).

## Konjunktiv I formulas: wishes and exhortations

Outside reported speech, Konjunktiv I survives in fixed expressions. The **[[optative]]** expresses a wish in the third person:

- *Es lebe die Freiheit!* — Long live freedom! (also *Hoch lebe …*)
- *Gott sei Dank!* — Thank God! (originally "thanks be to God")
- *Gott behüte!* / *Gott bewahre!* — God forbid!
- *Möge das neue Jahr Ihnen Glück bringen.* — May the new year bring you luck.
- *Er ruhe in Frieden.* — May he rest in peace.

Only *Gott sei Dank* and *Es lebe …* are everyday German; *Möge …* belongs to speeches, greeting cards and solemn writing, where it can also sound ironic (*Möge die Macht mit dir sein*, the German version of a famous film line).

The **[[hortative subjunctive]]** (*Adhortativ*) urges a group that includes the speaker. It is formed with *wir* and the verb first: *Gehen wir! Fangen wir an! Nehmen wir an, …* For most verbs this form looks like the indicative; only *sein* shows the Konjunktiv I clearly: *Seien wir ehrlich.* — Let's be honest. In formal writing *Nehmen wir an …* and *Halten wir fest: …* are common ways to structure an argument.

## Concessive formulas

Concessive formulas say "whatever the circumstances, it makes no difference". They are fixed, and the Konjunktiv I is obligatory in them:

| Formula | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *Koste es, was es wolle* | whatever the cost | *Er will den Posten, koste es, was es wolle.* |
| *Komme, was wolle* | come what may | *Komme, was wolle, wir halten zusammen.* |
| *Wie dem auch sei* | be that as it may | *Wie dem auch sei, die Frist ist abgelaufen.* |
| *Dem sei, wie ihm wolle* (more formal) | be that as it may | *Dem sei, wie ihm wolle: Die Entscheidung steht.* |
| *sei es …, sei es …* | whether … or … | *Sei es aus Angst, sei es aus Gier – er schwieg.* |
| *Es sei denn, …* | unless | *Wir fangen um acht an, es sei denn, der Zeuge verspätet sich.* |

*sei es … oder …* is also possible (*sei es aus Angst oder aus Gier*). *Es sei denn* (B1) is the one you will use most; it is followed by a main-clause order or a *dass*-clause: *…, es sei denn, dass der Zeuge sich verspätet.*

Older and literary German has more: *Was er auch sage, man glaubt ihm nicht* (whatever he may say) and *er sei, wer er wolle* (whoever he may be). Recognize them; today you would write *Was er auch sagt*.

## als ob, als wenn, als: KI or KII?

Unreal comparisons (C1 lesson 03) allow both Konjunktivs:

- *Er tut, als ob er unschuldig wäre.* (KII: the most common in speech and writing)
- *Er tut, als ob er unschuldig sei.* (KI: more formal, typical of newspapers)
- *Er tut, als wäre er unschuldig. / …, als sei er unschuldig.* (*als* with the verb straight after it)
- *Er tut, als wenn er unschuldig wäre.* (*als wenn* is a little more colloquial than *als ob*)

There is no difference in meaning between KI and KII here: both say "as if". The choice is register. With *als* alone, the finite verb comes directly after *als*: ~~als er wäre unschuldig~~. In casual speech you will also hear the indicative, *Er tut so, als ob er nichts weiß*; it is colloquial, and in writing the Konjunktiv is expected.

## Purpose clauses: damit er es wisse *(receptive)*

In older and very formal texts, *damit*-clauses sometimes have a Konjunktiv I: *Man schrieb ihm, damit er es wisse.* Today the indicative is normal: *…, damit er es weiß.* You will meet the old form in nineteenth-century prose and occasionally in legal commentary; don't use it in your own writing.

## The "summing-up" Konjunktiv II

In everyday speech the Konjunktiv II often marks neither an unreal situation nor a polite request, but a summing-up: something has just been completed, and the speaker draws a line under it. German grammars sometimes call it the *bilanzierende* Konjunktiv.

- *So, das hätten wir.* — Right, that's done.
- *Da hätten wir's.* — There we are. (often: so that's the problem)
- *Das wär's.* — That's it. / That's all. (at the end of a shopping list, a meeting, a speech)
- *Wäre das also geklärt.* — So that's settled.
- *Das wäre alles für heute.* — That's all for today.

The Konjunktiv makes the close softer than the indicative (*Das ist alles*), and in a shop *Das wär's* is simply the normal way to say you have everything. Nothing in these sentences is unreal.

## Three Konjunktiv IIs in one text

The same form can do three different jobs. In this exchange at a police station, each Konjunktiv II is labelled.

> **Beamter:** Sie wollen also Strafanzeige erstatten. Hätten Sie Ihren Ausweis dabei? *(politeness)*
>
> **Frau Berger:** Ja, hier. Wenn ich den Mann gestern nicht gesehen hätte, wüsste ich gar nicht, dass jemand im Keller war. *(irrealis, unreal past and present)*
>
> **Beamter:** Könnte es auch ein Nachbar gewesen sein? *(potentialis: a real possibility)*
>
> **Frau Berger:** Das glaube ich kaum. – So, das wär's, oder? *(summing-up)*

The test: does the sentence describe something contrary to fact (irrealis)? Then it is unreal. Does it present a real possibility cautiously (*Es könnte regnen*, *Das dürfte stimmen*)? Then it is potential. Is it a request or question you could also make in the indicative? Then it is politeness.

## Look-alikes in listening

In speech you can't see the context that writing gives you, so listen for these pairs:

- *sie hätten* in reported speech (the replacement form for *sie haben*: *Die Zeugen sagten, sie hätten nichts gesehen*) vs *sie hätten* as an unreal past (*Sie hätten das melden müssen*: you should have reported it).
- *sei* as Konjunktiv I (*Er sagt, er sei unschuldig*) vs *sei* as the imperative (*Sei still!*).
- *habe, werde* as Konjunktiv I of *er* (*er habe, er werde*) vs the indicative of *ich* (*ich habe, ich werde*): the subject decides.
- *soll* + perfect infinitive (hearsay: *Er soll es getan haben*) vs *sollte* + perfect infinitive (*Er sollte bis Montag alles erledigt haben*: he was supposed to have finished everything by Monday).

## Words: suspicion, evidence and custody

- *der Tatverdacht* (suspicion of an offence; *dringender Tatverdacht*, strong suspicion, is one condition for remand), *tatverdächtig*, *der/die Tatverdächtige* (declined like an adjective: *ein Tatverdächtiger*).
- *die Staatsanwaltschaft* is the prosecutor's office; *der Staatsanwalt* (B2) the person.
- *das Indiz* (plural *die Indizien*) is a piece of circumstantial evidence; a trial that rests on such evidence is an *Indizienprozess*. *der Beweis* is proof.
- *die Spurensicherung* is both the securing of evidence and the team that does it.
- *die Vernehmung* and *vernehmen* (strong: *vernahm, hat vernommen*) are the official words for questioning; in gehoben style *vernehmen* also means "to hear": *Man vernahm ein Klopfen.*
- *die Untersuchungshaft* (often *U-Haft*: remand), *der Haftbefehl* (arrest warrant), *die Festnahme* (arrest; the verb *festnehmen* is B1).
- *unterschlagen* (inseparable, strong: *unterschlug, hat unterschlagen*) is to embezzle something entrusted to you, and also to withhold information: *Er hat diese Tatsache unterschlagen.* The separable *unterschlagen* (*die Beine unterschlagen*, to cross one's legs under oneself) is a different verb.
- *die Bestechung* (bribery) and *bestechlich* (corruptible); *die Erpressung* and *erpressen* (blackmail, extortion); *die Hehlerei* and *der Hehler* (handling stolen goods, the fence).
- *die Strafanzeige* (*Strafanzeige erstatten gegen*: to report someone to the police), *das Strafmaß* (the sentence, how much punishment), *das Delikt* (an offence), *die Fahndung* and *fahnden nach* (police search, to search for a wanted person), *das Geständnis* (confession; *ein Geständnis ablegen*).

## Common mistakes

- Indicative where the accusation is someone else's: ~~Der Angeklagte nahm das Geld aus dem Tresor~~ → *Der Angeklagte soll das Geld aus dem Tresor genommen haben* / *Laut Anklage nahm er …*
- *Täter* before the verdict: write *der mutmaßliche Täter*, *der Angeklagte* or *der Tatverdächtige*.
- *muss* for hearsay: ~~Er muss das Geld genommen haben~~ is the reporter's own conclusion ("he must have"), the opposite of distance. Use *soll*.
- Indicative in fixed formulas: ~~Koste es, was es will~~ is heard, but the formula is *koste es, was es wolle*.
- Word order after *als*: ~~als er wäre unschuldig~~ → *als wäre er unschuldig*.
- Reading *Das wär's* as unreal: it means "that's it", nothing more.
- *Beweis* for an indication: an *Indiz* points in a direction; a *Beweis* proves. Calling fingerprints on a safe the manager used daily a *Beweis* is false precision.

## Key points

- Court and crime reports keep distance with Konjunktiv I, *soll* + perfect infinitive, *mutmaßlich / tatverdächtig*, and verbs of attribution; the Pressekodex (Ziffer 13) makes the presumption of innocence a rule of writing.
- *Beschuldigter → Angeschuldigter → Angeklagter* follow the stages of the procedure; *Täter* only after a final conviction.
- Optative and hortative formulas: *Es lebe …, Gott sei Dank, Möge …*; *Seien wir ehrlich, Nehmen wir an*.
- Concessive formulas with obligatory KI: *koste es, was es wolle; komme, was wolle; wie dem auch sei; dem sei, wie ihm wolle; sei es …, sei es …; es sei denn*.
- *als ob / als wenn / als* + KI (formal) or KII (more common); *als* takes the verb straight after it.
- The summing-up KII: *Das wär's. Da hätten wir's. So, das hätten wir.*
- Tell KII politeness, irrealis and potentialis apart by asking what the sentence claims about reality.

lessons.title: Dürfte, schwerlich, droht zu: modality beyond the modal verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At C1 you learned to grade certainty with the modal verbs in their subjective use, from *muss* (I'm sure) through *dürfte* and *könnte* to *kann nicht* (impossible), also about the past (C1 lesson 02). But modal verbs are only one of the ways German expresses how sure a speaker is, whether something is necessary, or what a situation is likely to turn into. Modal words (*zweifelsohne, schwerlich, womöglich*), a small group of verbs with *zu* (*scheinen, drohen, versprechen, pflegen, vermögen*) and verbs of evidence (*legt nahe, deutet darauf hin*) do the same work, often more precisely. A C2 writer chooses among all of them.

The theme is psychology and personality, a field in which careful hedging is not decoration but honesty: a magazine article can't diagnose its readers. The C1 and B2 words of the field (*die Resilienz, das Selbstwertgefühl, die Psychotherapie, die Angststörung, das Persönlichkeitsmerkmal, verdrängen*) are taken for granted.

## A magazine article on introverts

Read this article from an (invented) popular-science magazine. Underline every word that tells you how certain the writer is.

> **Still, aber nicht schwach**
>
> Wer auf Partys früh nach Hause geht, gilt schnell als schüchtern, mitunter sogar als arrogant. Dabei dürfte die Sache komplizierter sein. Introvertierte Menschen, so die gängige Beschreibung, schöpfen ihre Energie eher aus dem Alleinsein, extrovertierte aus der Gesellschaft anderer. Eine Persönlichkeitsstörung ist das zweifelsohne nicht, sondern eine Spielart des Normalen; die meisten Menschen liegen ohnehin irgendwo dazwischen.
>
> Woher die Neigung kommt, ist schwerlich mit einem Satz zu beantworten. Zwillingsstudien legen nahe, dass die Veranlagung eine erhebliche Rolle spielt, und das Temperament eines Kindes lässt mitunter schon früh vermuten, wie es sich später verhalten wird. Festgelegt ist damit nichts. Erziehung, Kultur und Erfahrungen vermögen viel zu verändern, und wer als Kind still war, sucht als Erwachsener nicht zwangsläufig die Stille.
>
> Vorsicht ist geboten, wo aus Beobachtungen Diagnosen werden. Dass jemand ungern telefoniert, deutet nicht auf eine Phobie hin, und wer lieber allein arbeitet, ist nicht automatisch antriebslos. „Viele Befindlichkeiten werden heute vorschnell zur Krankheit erklärt“, sagt die Psychotherapeutin Lena Hartwig, eine ausgewiesene Expertin für Verhaltenstherapie. Echte Angststörungen gebe es, und sie seien gut behandelbar – aber sie seien eben selten das, was man auf Partys beobachte.
>
> Bleibt die Frage nach dem Beruf. Introvertierte, heißt es oft, seien gewissenhafter und hörten besser zu. Ganz so einfach ist es nicht: Gewissenhaftigkeit gilt in der Forschung als eigenes Persönlichkeitsmerkmal, das mit Introversion wenig zu tun haben dürfte. Wer verstehen will, wie ein Mensch tickt, muss also mehr als eine Eigenschaft betrachten.
>
> Und das Bauchgefühl, das uns sagt, jemand sei „eben so“? Es verspricht ein verlässlicher Kompass zu sein, droht aber gerade hier in die Irre zu führen. Intuition ist nützlich, wo wir viel Erfahrung haben; über einen Menschen, den wir seit zehn Minuten kennen, weiß sie wenig. Zweifelsfrei belegt ist nur eines: Wer still ist, hat deshalb noch lange nicht nichts zu sagen.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Quiet, but not weak**

Anyone who leaves a party early is quickly thought shy, sometimes even arrogant. Yet the matter is probably more complicated. Introverted people, according to the usual description, draw their energy more from being alone, extroverted people from the company of others. This is undoubtedly not a personality disorder but a variety of the normal; most people fall somewhere in between anyway.

Where the tendency comes from can hardly be answered in a sentence. Twin studies suggest that innate disposition plays a considerable part, and a child's temperament sometimes hints early on at how it will behave later. Nothing is fixed by that. Upbringing, culture and experience can change a great deal, and someone who was quiet as a child doesn't necessarily seek quiet as an adult.

Caution is needed where observations turn into diagnoses. If someone dislikes phoning, that doesn't point to a phobia, and someone who prefers to work alone isn't automatically listless. "Many sensitivities are declared an illness too quickly these days," says the psychotherapist Lena Hartwig, a recognized expert in behaviour therapy. Real anxiety disorders exist, she says, and they can be treated well – but they are rarely what you observe at parties.

That leaves the question of work. Introverts, it is often said, are more conscientious and better listeners. It isn't quite that simple: researchers treat conscientiousness as a personality trait of its own, which probably has little to do with introversion. Anyone who wants to understand what makes a person tick has to look at more than one trait.

And the gut feeling that tells us someone is "just like that"? It promises to be a reliable compass, but here of all places it threatens to lead us astray. Intuition is useful where we have a lot of experience; about a person we have known for ten minutes, it knows little. Only one thing is proven beyond doubt: being quiet is far from meaning you have nothing to say.

</details>

The writer is certain only twice: *zweifelsohne* (it isn't a disorder) and *zweifelsfrei belegt* (the final point). Everything else is graded: *dürfte* (probable), *schwerlich* (hardly possible), *legen nahe* (suggest), *lässt vermuten* (hints), *mitunter* (sometimes, not always), *nicht zwangsläufig* (not necessarily), *deutet nicht … hin* (doesn't point to). The expert's statements are in Konjunktiv I (lesson 03). That is what responsible popular science sounds like.

## The certainty scale across word classes

| Degree | modal verb (subjective) | modal word | other expressions |
|---|---|---|---|
| certain | *muss* | *zweifelsohne, zweifellos, gewiss, sicher* | *es steht fest, dass*; *zweifelsfrei belegt* |
| probable | *dürfte*, *wird (wohl)* | *wahrscheinlich, vermutlich, wohl* | *es spricht viel dafür, dass*; *legt nahe* |
| possible | *kann, könnte*, *mag* (conceding) | *vielleicht, möglicherweise, womöglich* | *es ist denkbar*; *lässt vermuten*; *deutet darauf hin* |
| improbable | *dürfte kaum* | *kaum, schwerlich* | *es ist fraglich, ob* |
| excluded | *kann nicht* | *keinesfalls, auf keinen Fall* | *es ist ausgeschlossen, dass* |

**[[Modal words]]** are adverbs that express the speaker's attitude to the whole statement. You can test for one: it can answer a yes/no question on its own (*Kommt sie? — Vermutlich. / Sicher. / Kaum.*), which ordinary adverbs of manner can't. Some notes on the C2 ones:

- *zweifelsohne* means the same as *zweifellos* (B2) but is more formal and a little old-fashioned; it suits essays and speeches. Both are stronger than *sicher*.
- *gewiss* and *sicherlich* are interesting: in argument they are often concessive and so weaker than they look. *Das ist sicherlich richtig, aber …* grants a point in order to move past it, like *zwar … aber*. *Gewiss, die Kosten sind hoch. Allein …* does the same in a more elevated register.
- *schwerlich* (hardly, scarcely likely) is formal: *Das wird sich schwerlich beweisen lassen.* In everyday speech, *kaum* or *wohl kaum*.
- *womöglich* (B2) means "possibly", often with a hint that the possibility is unwelcome or surprising: *Er hat womöglich recht.* (He may even be right.)
- *mitunter* (at times, now and then) is a frequency adverb, not a modal word, but in academic and journalistic writing it works as a hedge: *Introvertierte wirken mitunter abweisend* is defensible; *Introvertierte wirken abweisend* is a stereotype. *bisweilen* is a more elevated synonym.

## Modalitätsverben: scheinen, drohen, versprechen …

A handful of verbs combine with *zu* + infinitive to modify another verb the way modal verbs do. German grammars call them **[[modality verbs]]** (*Modalitätsverben*); English grammars speak of semi-modals.

| Verb | Meaning with *zu* + infinitive | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *scheinen* | seems to (an impression) | *Sie scheint die Antwort zu kennen.* |
| *drohen* | threatens to: something bad looks likely | *Die Lage droht zu kippen.* |
| *versprechen* | promises to: something good looks likely | *Der Abend verspricht spannend zu werden.* |
| *pflegen* | usually does (formal) | *Er pflegte nach dem Essen eine Stunde zu lesen.* |
| *vermögen* | is able to (gehoben) | *Niemand vermag zu sagen, wie es weitergeht.* |
| *wissen* | knows how to | *Sie weiß sich zu helfen. Der Film weiß zu überzeugen.* |
| *verstehen* (often with *es*) | knows how to, is skilled at | *Er versteht es, Menschen zu begeistern.* |

Three things set them apart from ordinary verbs with an infinitive:

1. **With *scheinen, drohen* and *versprechen*, the subject doesn't act.** In *Die Lage droht zu kippen*, the situation threatens nobody; the speaker judges that it may tip over. Compare the ordinary verb: *Der Chef droht, ihn zu entlassen* (the boss threatens to fire him: a real threat by a person). The same holds for *versprechen*: *Sie verspricht, pünktlich zu sein* (a real promise) vs *Der Sommer verspricht heiß zu werden* (it looks as if it will be hot).
2. **No comma.** The Modalitätsverb and the infinitive form one verbal unit, so no comma separates them: *Die Lage droht zu kippen.* The ordinary verb takes an infinitive clause, which may have a comma: *Er drohte, die Polizei zu rufen.* (*verstehen* with *es* is the exception among the verbs above: *es* points forward to the infinitive, so the comma is required: *Er versteht es, Menschen zu begeistern.*)
3. **They mostly occur in the present and Präteritum.** *Die Lage hat zu kippen gedroht* is grammatical but rare; you will meet *drohte zu kippen*.

*scheinen* is the most frequent of them and also the most useful hedge: *Die Therapie scheint zu wirken* (it seems to be working) commits you less than *Die Therapie wirkt*. In the past: *Er scheint es gewusst zu haben* (he seems to have known).

Recap from earlier courses, because they belong to the same family: *haben … zu* (must: *Sie haben das Formular auszufüllen*), *sein … zu* (can or must be done: *Das ist nicht zu ändern*), *nicht brauchen zu* (needn't), and *es gilt zu* (the task is to: *Jetzt gilt es, Ruhe zu bewahren*, C1 lesson 09).

## Subtle uses of the modal verbs

Some modal-verb uses have nothing to do with ability or obligation in the usual sense:

- *Das will gelernt sein.* — That takes practice. (*wollen* + passive infinitive: something requires it). Also *Das will gut überlegt sein.*
- *Was soll das?* — What's the point of that? / What's that supposed to mean? (annoyed); *Was soll ich dort?* — What would I do there?
- *Er mag kommen.* (formal) — Let him come, I don't mind; *Mag sein, dass …* — It may be that … (conceding). This concessive *mögen* is the present counterpart of C1's *Er mag es gewusst haben, aber …*.
- *Das dürfte reichen.* — That should be enough (probably).
- *Sie müsste längst da sein.* — She ought to be here by now (expectation based on reasoning).
- *Das kann ja heiter werden!* — Well, this is going to be fun! (ironic: things look bad).

## Hedging in psychological and medical reporting

Research results are about probabilities and groups, not about individuals; good reporting says so. These verbs and phrases let you present a finding with exactly the strength the evidence has:

| Expression | Strength | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *X belegt / zeigt, dass …* | strong (use sparingly) | *Mehrere Studien belegen, dass …* |
| *X spricht dafür, dass …* | fairly strong | *Vieles spricht dafür, dass Bewegung hilft.* |
| *X legt nahe, dass …* | moderate: suggests | *Die Daten legen nahe, dass Schlaf eine Rolle spielt.* |
| *X deutet darauf hin, dass …* / *weist auf … hin* | moderate: points to | *Das deutet auf einen Zusammenhang hin.* |
| *X lässt vermuten, dass …* | weak: gives reason to suspect | *Die Befunde lassen vermuten, dass …* |
| *X geht mit Y einher* / *ist mit Y assoziiert* | correlation only | *Perfektionismus geht häufig mit Erschöpfung einher.* |
| *Es gibt Hinweise auf …* | weak | *Es gibt Hinweise auf eine genetische Komponente.* |

Two rules of thumb. First, correlation is not causation: *Wer viel grübelt, schläft schlechter* reports a correlation; *Grübeln verursacht Schlafstörungen* claims a cause. Second, a magazine can describe symptoms but not diagnose: *Wenn Sie sich in dieser Beschreibung wiedererkennen, kann ein Gespräch mit einer Fachperson sinnvoll sein* is responsible; *Sie leiden an einer Zwangsstörung* is not, however sure the writer feels.

## ausgewiesen: two senses

*ausgewiesen* has a sense that learners often miss. As an adjective before an expert noun it means "proven, recognized": *eine ausgewiesene Expertin für Verhaltenstherapie*, *ein ausgewiesener Kenner der Szene*. That sense is a vocabulary item of this lesson.

As the participle of *ausweisen* it means "shown, designated" in official and financial language: *Im Haushalt ist ein Überschuss ausgewiesen* (the budget shows a surplus); *Die Fläche ist als Bauland ausgewiesen* (designated as building land). And *ausweisen* also means "to expel, deport": *Der Diplomat wurde ausgewiesen.* Context decides.

## Words: psychology and personality

- *introvertiert* and *extrovertiert* are the everyday forms; in psychological writing you will also meet *extravertiert* and *die Extraversion*. Neither is a diagnosis.
- *die Persönlichkeitsstörung* is a clinical term (*die narzisstische Persönlichkeitsstörung*); *der Narzissmus* and *narzisstisch* are also used loosely in everyday speech, often too loosely.
- *zwanghaft* (compulsive) and *die Zwangsstörung* (obsessive-compulsive disorder); *die Phobie* (*eine Phobie vor Spinnen*); *traumatisch*.
- *die Neurose* and *neurotisch* come from psychoanalysis; current diagnostic manuals have largely replaced the term with more specific diagnoses, but it lives on in everyday speech.
- *das Unterbewusstsein* (the subconscious; psychoanalysis prefers *das Unbewusste*), *die Psychoanalyse*, *die Verhaltenstherapie* (behaviour therapy). *der Psychotherapeut / die Psychotherapeutin* is a protected professional title in Germany.
- *gewissenhaft* and *die Gewissenhaftigkeit* (conscientious, conscientiousness: one of the "Big Five" personality traits), *die Selbstwirksamkeit* (self-efficacy: the belief that you can cope), *die Veranlagung* (innate disposition), *das Temperament*, *die Verhaltensweise* (a way of behaving; *das Verhalten*, B1, is behaviour in general).
- *labil* and *die Labilität* (unstable, instability, emotionally or of health), *antriebslos* and *die Antriebslosigkeit* (listless, lack of drive, a common symptom term), *die Befindlichkeit* (state of mind; in the plural often ironic: *Befindlichkeiten*, touchy feelings), *der Perfektionismus*.
- *die Intuition, intuitiv, das Bauchgefühl* (gut feeling, everyday word).

## Pronunciation

- In *Psychologie, Psychotherapeut, Psychoanalyse*, the *p* is pronounced: [ps-], not [s-] as in English.

## Common mistakes

- Treating *drohen* as neutral: ~~Das Wetter droht schön zu werden~~ (only as a joke). For good prospects, *versprechen*.
- A comma with the Modalitätsverb: ~~Die Lage droht, zu kippen~~ → *Die Lage droht zu kippen.*
- *pflegen zu* in everyday speech: *Er pflegt um sieben aufzustehen* sounds stilted; say *Er steht normalerweise um sieben auf.*
- Overconfident modal words: *zweifelsohne* and *zweifelsfrei* only for what is really beyond doubt; three of them in one paragraph read as false precision.
- Reading concessive *sicherlich* as certainty: *Das ist sicherlich richtig, aber …* is a polite disagreement.
- Confusing *dürfte* (probably) and *darf* (is allowed): *Das dürfte reichen* ≠ *Das darf reichen*.
- Diagnosing: ~~Er ist ein Narzisst~~ in a report about someone's behaviour. Describe the behaviour: *Er stellt sich gern in den Mittelpunkt.*

## Key points

- Certainty is graded by modal verbs, modal words and verbs of evidence; choose the strength the evidence supports.
- Modal words: *zweifelsohne* (formal, certain), *gewiss / sicherlich* (often concessive), *schwerlich* (formal: hardly), *womöglich* (possibly, unwelcome); *mitunter* as a frequency hedge.
- Modalitätsverben *scheinen, drohen, versprechen, pflegen, vermögen, wissen zu, verstehen zu*: with *scheinen, drohen, versprechen* the subject doesn't act; no comma (except *verstehen es, …*).
- Subtle modal uses: *Das will gelernt sein; Was soll das?; Er mag kommen; Das dürfte reichen.*
- Research reporting: *belegt > spricht dafür > legt nahe > deutet darauf hin > lässt vermuten*; correlation is not causation; describe, don't diagnose.
- *ausgewiesen*: "recognized" before an expert noun; "shown, designated" as a participle in official texts.

lessons.title: Er bedarf keiner Hilfe: genitive objects and the government of verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Every verb comes with slots: a subject, perhaps an object in the accusative or dative, perhaps a prepositional object. Which slots a word opens is its **[[valency]]**; which case or preposition it demands is its **[[government]]** (*Rektion*). Most of the time you don't think about either, because you have learned *helfen* + dative and *warten auf* + accusative as chunks. At C2 three things make valency worth a lesson of its own: a small group of verbs and adjectives that take a genitive object, which is rare in speech but frequent in formal, legal and moral language; pairs in which the genitive and a prepositional alternative differ in register; and prefixes such as *be-* that change a verb's valency.

A genitive object is an object in the genitive case that the verb itself requires: *Er bedarf keiner Hilfe* (he needs no help), *Wir gedenken der Opfer* (we commemorate the victims). It is not a genitive attribute (*das Haus meines Vaters*) and not the object of a preposition (*wegen des Regens*).

The theme is ethics and morality: virtue and vice, honesty and hypocrisy. *die Ethik, die Moral, das Gewissen, gedenken* and *sich enthalten* are earlier words.

## An essay: Von der Redlichkeit

Read this essay from the (invented) weekend supplement of a newspaper. It is written in an elevated register, and that is where genitive objects live.

> **Von der Redlichkeit**
>
> Es gibt Tugenden, die niemand mehr beim Namen nennt. Die Redlichkeit gehört dazu. Das Wort klingt nach Großvaters Zeiten, nach Handschlag und Ladenkasse, und doch bedarf kaum eine Gesellschaft ihrer so sehr wie eine, in der jeder jeden der Lüge bezichtigt.
>
> Redlich ist, wer nicht mehr behauptet, als er weiß, und nicht weniger zugibt, als er getan hat. Das klingt bescheiden. Es ist aber schwer, denn die Versuchung ist groß, sich der eigenen Fehler stillschweigend zu entledigen und sich der Verdienste anderer zu rühmen. Wer sich so verhält, muss nicht niederträchtig sein; meist ist er nur bequem.
>
> Gefährlicher ist die Heuchelei. Der Heuchler predigt Demut und lebt Hochmut, er verurteilt die Laster und die Gier der anderen und erfreut sich selbst eines beträchtlichen Vermögens. Seine Doppelmoral fällt selten sofort auf, weil sie sich der Sprache der Tugend bemächtigt hat. Wird er schließlich der Lüge überführt, ist die Empörung groß, und mitunter wird er seines Amtes enthoben. Geläutert ist er dadurch noch lange nicht.
>
> Die Rechtschaffenheit, das ältere Wort für dieselbe Haltung, hat einen schlechten Ruf: Man denkt an Kleinbürger, die sich ihres Rechts sicher sind und der Nachbarn wegen die Hecke schneiden. Das ist ungerecht. Rechtschaffene Menschen sind sich ihrer Grenzen bewusst. Sie vergewissern sich der Fakten, bevor sie urteilen, und enthalten sich des Urteils, wo sie nichts wissen.
>
> Bleibt die Frage, ob man Redlichkeit lernen kann. Wer der Läuterung durch Skandale harrt, wird lange warten. Doch gewissenlos ist kaum jemand von Geburt an. Die meisten machen sich kleiner Unredlichkeiten schuldig, ohne es zu merken, und sie könnten es merken, wenn jemand sie darauf hinwiese. Eine Behauptung, die jeder Grundlage entbehrt, sollte niemand stehen lassen – auch die eigene nicht.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**On integrity**

There are virtues that nobody calls by their name any more. Integrity is one of them. The word sounds like grandfather's day, of handshakes and the shop till, and yet hardly any society needs it as much as one in which everyone accuses everyone else of lying.

A person of integrity is someone who claims no more than they know and admits no less than they have done. That sounds modest. But it is hard, because the temptation is great to quietly rid oneself of one's own mistakes and to boast of other people's merits. Someone who behaves like this needn't be vile; usually they are just lazy.

Hypocrisy is more dangerous. The hypocrite preaches humility and lives arrogance; he condemns the vices and the greed of others and himself enjoys a considerable fortune. His double standards are seldom noticed at once, because they have taken over the language of virtue. When he is finally proven to have lied, the outrage is great, and sometimes he is removed from office. That doesn't mean he has been purified by it, far from it.

Rectitude, the older word for the same attitude, has a bad reputation: people think of petty bourgeois who are sure of their rights and trim the hedge for the neighbours' sake. That is unfair. Upright people are aware of their limits. They make sure of the facts before they judge, and they refrain from judging where they know nothing.

That leaves the question of whether integrity can be learned. Anyone who waits for scandals to bring moral purification will wait a long time. Yet hardly anyone is unscrupulous from birth. Most people are guilty of small dishonesties without noticing, and they could notice if someone pointed it out to them. A claim that lacks any foundation shouldn't be left standing by anyone – not even one's own.

</details>

The essay has fifteen genitive objects: thirteen with verbs (*bedürfen, bezichtigen, sich entledigen, sich rühmen, sich erfreuen, sich bemächtigen, überführen, entheben, sich vergewissern, sich enthalten, harren, sich schuldig machen, entbehren*) and two with adjectives (*sich ihres Rechts sicher*, *sich ihrer Grenzen bewusst*). *der Nachbarn wegen* is not a genitive object: it is the preposition *wegen* placed after its noun, which is formal.

## Verbs with a genitive object

| Verb | Meaning | Example | Everyday alternative |
|---|---|---|---|
| *bedürfen* | to require | *Das bedarf einer Erklärung.* | *Das braucht eine Erklärung.* |
| *gedenken* | to commemorate | *Wir gedenken der Toten.* | *Wir erinnern an die Toten.* |
| *harren* (gehoben) | to await | *Viele Fragen harren noch einer Antwort.* | *warten auf* |
| *entbehren* | to lack (formal) | *Die Behauptung entbehrt jeder Grundlage.* | *Es gibt keine Grundlage für …* |
| *sich bemächtigen* | to seize | *Die Rebellen bemächtigten sich des Senders.* | *den Sender unter ihre Kontrolle bringen* |
| *sich entledigen* | to rid oneself of | *Er entledigte sich seiner Jacke.* | *Er zog seine Jacke aus; etwas loswerden* |
| *sich enthalten* | to abstain from | *sich der Stimme enthalten* | *nicht abstimmen* |
| *sich erfreuen* | to enjoy (have) | *Sie erfreut sich bester Gesundheit.* | *Sie ist sehr gesund.* |
| *sich rühmen* | to boast of, pride oneself on | *Die Stadt rühmt sich ihrer Altstadt.* | *ist stolz auf* |
| *sich vergewissern* | to make sure of | *Vergewissern Sie sich der Fakten.* | *sich vergewissern, dass / ob …*; *prüfen* |
| *sich bedienen* | to make use of | *sich eines Tricks bedienen* | *einen Trick benutzen* |
| *sich annehmen* | to take care of, take up | *Der Ausschuss nimmt sich des Problems an.* | *sich um etwas kümmern* |

Notes:

- *entbehren* has two valencies with two meanings. With a genitive it means "to lack" and usually has *jeder* or *jeglicher*: *Der Vorwurf entbehrt jeglicher Grundlage.* With an accusative it means "to do without, miss": *Wir können ihn nicht länger entbehren* (we can't spare him any longer). The adjective *entbehrlich* (dispensable) belongs to the second.
- *bedürfen* is conjugated like a modal verb: *ich bedarf, du bedarfst, er bedarf; bedurfte; hat bedurft*. In the present it is most often impersonal or has a thing as its subject: *Es bedarf keiner weiteren Worte.* (No more words are needed.)
- *harren* is gehoben and appears mostly in fixed patterns: *der Dinge harren, die da kommen* (to wait and see what happens), *einer Lösung harren*.
