- *sich vergewissern* with a genitive is formal; with a clause it is neutral and common: *Vergewissern Sie sich, dass die Tür verschlossen ist.*
- *sich rühmen* also takes a *zu*-infinitive: *Er rühmt sich, nie krank gewesen zu sein.*

## Accusative and genitive: accusing, convicting, depriving

A second group has two objects: a person in the accusative and a thing in the genitive. Most belong to the language of law and accusation.

| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *jemanden einer Sache bezichtigen* | to accuse someone of | *Man bezichtigte ihn des Betrugs.* |
| *jemanden einer Sache beschuldigen* | to accuse | *Sie wird des Diebstahls beschuldigt.* |
| *jemanden einer Sache anklagen* | to charge (in court) | *Er wurde des Mordes angeklagt.* (also *wegen Mordes*) |
| *jemanden einer Sache überführen* | to prove someone guilty of | *Die DNA-Spur überführte ihn der Tat.* |
| *jemanden einer Sache berauben* | to rob someone of | *Man beraubte sie ihrer Freiheit.* |
| *jemanden einer Sache entheben* | to relieve someone of (an office, a duty) | *Der Minister wurde seines Amtes enthoben.* |
| *jemanden des Landes verweisen* | to expel from the country | *Er wurde des Landes verwiesen.* |

*bezichtigen* is more formal and more often used for an unproven or unfair accusation than *beschuldigen*. *überführen* means to prove guilt with evidence; it is not the court's verdict (*verurteilen*, to convict and sentence). In the passive these verbs keep their genitive: *Er wurde der Tat überführt.*

## Adjectives with a genitive

| Adjective | Example | Alternative |
|---|---|---|
| *sich einer Sache bewusst sein* | *Sie ist sich der Gefahr bewusst.* | (no common alternative) |
| *sich einer Sache sicher sein* | *Er ist sich seiner Sache sicher.* | *sicher sein, dass …* |
| *einer Sache würdig sein* | *Das ist eines Ministers nicht würdig.* | (negative: *unwürdig*) |
| *einer Sache schuldig sein* | *Er ist des Mordes schuldig.* | *schuldig an* + dat. |
| *einer Sache mächtig sein* (gehoben) | *Sie ist der deutschen Sprache mächtig.* | *spricht Deutsch* |
| *einer Sache fähig sein* | *Ich halte ihn einer solchen Tat nicht für fähig.* | *zu etwas fähig sein* |
| *einer Sache überdrüssig sein* (formal) | *Sie war des ewigen Streits überdrüssig.* | *hatte genug von …* |
| *einer Sache müde sein* (formal) | *Er war des Wartens müde.* | *hatte es satt zu warten* |

*sich einer Sache bewusst sein* is the one you will use in everyday writing: it is neutral, and the genitive is obligatory. *der Sprache mächtig* is a fixed formula, mostly in job ads and official texts (*Bewerber sollten der deutschen Sprache in Wort und Schrift mächtig sein*).

## Genitive or preposition: a question of register

For many of these verbs there is an alternative, and the alternative is the normal word. The genitive is not wrong; it is formal, literary or official.

| gehoben / formal | neutral |
|---|---|
| *sich einer Sache erinnern* | *sich an etwas erinnern* |
| *sich einer Sache schämen* | *sich für etwas schämen* / *wegen etwas* |
| *einer Sache harren* | *auf etwas warten* |
| *einer Sache bedürfen* | *etwas brauchen* |
| *sich einer Sache entledigen* | *etwas loswerden* |
| *sich einer Sache bemächtigen* | *etwas an sich reißen* |
| *jemanden einer Sache bezichtigen* | *jemandem etwas vorwerfen* |

*Ich erinnere mich dieses Tages genau* is correct, elevated German (and common in older literature: *Ich erinnere mich seiner* = I remember him). In conversation it sounds bookish; *Ich erinnere mich genau an diesen Tag* is the normal sentence. Don't correct either one: they differ in register, not in correctness.

## Fixed genitives

Some genitives are adverbials in fixed phrases. They are frozen: you can't change the noun or add an article.

- *guter Dinge sein* (to be in good spirits), *unverrichteter Dinge* (without having achieved anything): *Die Ermittler mussten unverrichteter Dinge abziehen.*
- *meines Erachtens* (in my view, formal; abbreviated *m. E.*), *meines Wissens* (to my knowledge)
- *eines Tages, eines Abends* (one day, one evening), *letzten Endes* (in the end), *allen Ernstes* (in all seriousness), *des Weiteren* (furthermore)
- *schweren Herzens* (with a heavy heart), *gesenkten Kopfes* (with head bowed), *stehenden Fußes* (immediately, formal)

## How be- changes valency

The prefix *be-* often turns a verb with a prepositional or dative object into a verb with an accusative object. The meaning stays close, but the thing affected becomes the direct object, and the verb can form a normal passive.

| Without *be-* | With *be-* |
|---|---|
| *auf eine Frage antworten* | *eine Frage beantworten* |
| *an etwas zweifeln* | *etwas bezweifeln* |
| *über etwas urteilen* | *etwas beurteilen* |
| *in einem Haus wohnen* | *ein Haus bewohnen* |
| *jemandem drohen* | *jemanden bedrohen* |
| *jemandem etwas rauben* | *jemanden einer Sache berauben* |

The last pair shows a complete change of valency. *rauben* has the thing as accusative and the victim as dative: *Man raubte ihr die Handtasche.* *berauben* makes the victim the accusative and the thing a genitive: *Man beraubte sie ihrer Handtasche.* The second is more formal, and it is the one used figuratively: *jemanden seiner Hoffnung berauben*.

*be-* verbs are often more formal and more "affected" than the base verb. *Er hat die Frage beantwortet* focuses on the question as dealt with; *Er hat auf die Frage geantwortet* only says that he reacted.

## Genitive objects in moral and legal language

The genitive object survives where language is solemn or precise: in law, in judgments of guilt, in commemoration and in the moral essay. Typical phrases:

- *sich einer Straftat schuldig machen* (to be guilty of a criminal offence), *sich der Beihilfe schuldig machen* (to aid and abet)
- *der Tat überführt*, *des Mordes angeklagt*, *seines Amtes enthoben*
- *der Opfer gedenken*; neutral: *im Gedenken an die Opfer*
- *Die Behauptung entbehrt jeder Grundlage.* (a classic denial in press statements)
- *Es bedarf einer Lösung.* (official style)

## Words: virtue and vice

- *die Tugend* (virtue) and *tugendhaft*; *das Laster* (vice) and *lasterhaft* (depraved). Don't confuse *das Laster* with *der Laster*, the colloquial word for a lorry.
- *die Redlichkeit* and *redlich* (honest, upright; also of effort: *sich redlich bemühen*, to try one's honest best), *die Rechtschaffenheit* and *rechtschaffen* (upright, decent; Duden: veraltend). *ehrlich* (A2) and *die Ehrlichkeit* (B1) are the everyday words.
- *die Niedertracht* and *niederträchtig* (vile, base, malicious): strong words.
- *die Heuchelei, heucheln* (to feign: *Interesse heucheln*), *der Heuchler / die Heuchlerin*, *die Doppelmoral* (double standards).
- *die Gier* (greed, craving; compounds *die Habgier, die Geldgier*), *die Demut* and *demütig* (humility, humble), *der Hochmut* and *hochmütig* (haughtiness, arrogance; proverb: *Hochmut kommt vor dem Fall*).
- *die Läuterung* (moral purification, often through suffering; verb *läutern*), *gewissenlos* (unscrupulous).

## Common mistakes

- A dative or accusative where the genitive is required: ~~Das bedarf eine Erklärung~~ → *Das bedarf einer Erklärung.* ~~Sie ist sich die Gefahr bewusst~~ → *Sie ist sich der Gefahr bewusst.*
- Mixing two constructions: ~~sich an etwas bewusst sein~~; ~~sich einer Sache vergewissern, dass …~~ (choose one: *sich der Sache vergewissern* or *sich vergewissern, dass …*).
- Using a genitive object in everyday speech and sounding like a nineteenth-century novel: *Ich bedarf eines Kaffees* is a joke, not a request.
- Starring the genitive alternative as wrong: *Ich erinnere mich seiner* is correct, only gehoben.
- *überführen* for "convict": a court *verurteilt*; evidence *überführt*.
- *entbehren* with the wrong meaning: *Die Firma kann ihn nicht entbehren* (can't do without him) vs *Die Kritik entbehrt jeder Grundlage* (lacks).
- Forgetting the article on a genitive object: ~~Er wurde Mordes angeklagt~~ → *des Mordes* (*wegen Mordes* has no article).

## Key points

- Valency is the set of slots a word opens; government is the case or preposition it requires. A genitive object is required by the verb or adjective itself.
- Genitive verbs: *bedürfen, gedenken, harren, entbehren, sich bemächtigen, sich entledigen, sich enthalten, sich erfreuen, sich rühmen, sich vergewissern, sich bedienen, sich annehmen.*
- Accusative + genitive: *bezichtigen, beschuldigen, anklagen, überführen, berauben, entheben, des Landes verweisen.*
- Adjectives: *sich bewusst, sicher, würdig, schuldig, mächtig, fähig, überdrüssig, müde.*
- The genitive is formal; the prepositional or simple alternative is neutral; both are correct.
- Fixed genitives: *guter Dinge, unverrichteter Dinge, meines Erachtens, letzten Endes, schweren Herzens.*
- *be-* turns prepositional and dative objects into accusatives (*antworten auf → beantworten*); *rauben → berauben* swaps the objects completely.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Übersetzen: English ↔ German and where it goes wrong
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At C2 you will often move between English and German: summarizing an English source in German, explaining a German text to English speakers, checking a translation at work. This module has been about precision, register and nuance, and translation tests all three at once, because a translation has to be right in meaning, in register and in what it leaves unsaid.

This honors lesson looks at the structural shifts that every English–German translation needs, at false friends that still catch advanced learners, at loan translations, idioms, titles and puns, and finally at two translations of one short passage from Mark Twain (public domain), to see what a word-for-word version gains and loses against a free one.

## Translation shifts

A **[[translation shift]]** is a change of grammatical form between the source and the target text: a verb becomes a noun, an active becomes a *man*-sentence, a particle becomes an intonation. The term goes back to the linguist J. C. Catford (1965). Shifts are not errors; a translation without them is usually bad German or bad English.

From English into German, the typical shifts are:

| English | German | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *-ing* clause | subordinate clause or nominal phrase | *After leaving the house, she …* → *Nachdem sie das Haus verlassen hatte, …* / *Nach dem Verlassen des Hauses …* (formal) |
| gerund as subject | infinitive or nominalized infinitive | *Smoking is not allowed.* → *Rauchen verboten.* / *Das Rauchen ist nicht gestattet.* |
| progressive | simple tense, often with *gerade* | *I'm reading.* → *Ich lese gerade.* |
| passive with *it* | *man*, a passive, or *sollen* | *It is believed that …* → *Man nimmt an, dass …*; *He is said to be rich.* → *Er soll reich sein.* |
| noun as adjective | compound | *a climate protection law* → *ein Klimaschutzgesetz* |
| *there is / there are* | *es gibt*, or a verb of position | *There's a book on the table.* → *Auf dem Tisch liegt ein Buch.* |
| tag question | particle | *You've met her, haven't you?* → *Du kennst sie doch?* |

The last two rows are where translations most often sound translated. German prefers verbs of position (*liegen, stehen, hängen*) to a general *es gibt*, and it expresses with a particle (*doch, ja, wohl*) what English does with a tag question or intonation.

From German into English, the shifts go the other way:

- Modal particles usually disappear or become intonation, a tag, or a word such as *after all, just, really*: *Das ist ja interessant!* — Oh, that's interesting! *Komm doch mit!* — Why don't you come along?
- Konjunktiv I in reports becomes a reporting verb or *reportedly, allegedly*: *Der Minister sei nicht informiert gewesen* — The minister had not been informed, he said.
- Nominal style often becomes verbs: *nach Abschluss der Prüfung* — once the review is complete.
- Long attributes become relative clauses: *die von der Kommission vorgeschlagenen Maßnahmen* — the measures proposed by the commission.

## False friends at C2

The beginners' false friends (*bekommen*, *Gift*, *also*) are behind you. These are the ones that still slip into the writing of advanced learners, often because the English sense also exists in German, but only as a minor one:

| German | Means | Not | English word in German |
|---|---|---|---|
| *eventuell* | possibly, perhaps | eventually | *schließlich, irgendwann* |
| *konsequent* | consistent, rigorous, single-minded | consequent | *daraus folgend* |
| *sensibel* | sensitive | sensible | *vernünftig* |
| *aktuell* | current, up to date | actual | *tatsächlich, eigentlich* |
| *prinzipiell* | in principle, basically | principled | *grundsatztreu, mit Prinzipien* |
| *die Kompetenz* | competence; also authority, jurisdiction | (only skill) | *die Zuständigkeit* (jurisdiction) |
| *seriös* | respectable, trustworthy | serious | *ernst, ernsthaft* |
| *sympathisch* | likeable, pleasant | sympathetic | *mitfühlend, verständnisvoll* |
| *die Konkurrenz* | competition, competitors | concurrence | *die Übereinstimmung* |

Two need comment. *Kompetenz* in official German often means "power to decide": *Das liegt nicht in der Kompetenz des Landes* (that is not within the Land's jurisdiction). An English translator who writes "competence" there isn't wrong in EU English, but a general reader will think of ability. And *prinzipiell* is a hedge as often as not: *Prinzipiell bin ich einverstanden* means "In principle I agree", which in German, as in English, usually announces a *but*.

## Loan translations and the Sinn machen debate

A loan translation (German C1's honors module defined the term) translates a foreign word part by part: *der Wolkenkratzer* is usually given as a loan translation of *skyscraper*, *das Flutlicht* of *floodlight*, and *die Gehirnwäsche* of *brainwashing*. Once established, they don't feel foreign at all.

The best-known current case is *Sinn machen*, which most commentators trace to English *make sense*. Language critics have objected for decades that German *Sinn* is not "made" but "has" or "results": *Das ergibt Sinn, das hat Sinn, das ist sinnvoll*. Others reply that the phrase is now everywhere in speech and in much of the press, and that languages borrow patterns all the time. Both positions are respectable; the practical advice for a C2 writer is simple. In speech, *Das macht Sinn* is normal. In formal writing or for a conservative reader, *Das ist sinnvoll* or *Das ergibt Sinn* avoids the discussion.

Other patterns of the same kind, which some readers notice: *in 2025* (German: *2025* or *im Jahr 2025*), *einmal mehr* (*once more*; German has *wieder einmal*), *Ich erinnere das* without *mich an* (heard especially in the north and often criticized as an Anglicism). Note them; don't panic about them.

## Idioms, register and puns

An idiom is translated by an idiom of the same register, not by its words. *It's raining cats and dogs* (colloquial) is *Es gießt in Strömen* or *Es schüttet*, not a sentence about animals. *To kick the bucket* (salopp) is *den Löffel abgeben* (salopp), not the neutral *sterben*. When no equivalent exists, translators either explain (*He's a lame duck* → *Er ist ein Präsident auf Abruf*, "a president on his way out") or move the colour elsewhere in the sentence, a strategy called compensation.

Puns are the hardest case. *Time flies like an arrow; fruit flies like a banana* depends on *flies* being both a verb and a noun, and *like* both a preposition and a verb. No German sentence does both; a translator either writes a new joke on another double meaning, explains the original in a footnote, or leaves it out. Calling a pun *unübersetzbar* usually means "not translatable word for word", not "impossible to replace".

Titles are a small craft of their own. Publishers and film distributors translate for the market, not for the words: *Die Hard* became *Stirb langsam* in Germany, and many English films keep their English title or get a new English one. When you mention a work in German, use the German title if there is an established one, and give the original in brackets if your reader may know it.

## Two translations of one passage

Here is the opening of Mark Twain's *The Adventures of Tom Sawyer* (1876), quoted from Project Gutenberg (eBook no. 74). Aunt Polly is looking for Tom.

> "Tom!"
>
> No answer.
>
> "TOM!"
>
> No answer.
>
> "What's gone with that boy, I wonder? You TOM!"
>
> No answer.
>
> The old lady pulled her spectacles down and looked over them about the room; then she put them up and looked out under them. She seldom or never looked *through* them for so small a thing as a boy; they were her state pair, the pride of her heart, and were built for "style," not service—she could have seen through a pair of stove-lids just as well. She looked perplexed for a moment, and then said, not fiercely, but still loud enough for the furniture to hear:
>
> "Well, I lay if I get hold of you I'll—"

Two German versions, both written for this lesson. Version A stays close to the words:

> „Tom!“ – Keine Antwort. – „TOM!“ – Keine Antwort. – „Was ist mit diesem Jungen los, frage ich mich? Du TOM!“ – Keine Antwort.
>
> Die alte Dame zog ihre Brille herunter und blickte über sie hinweg im Zimmer umher; dann schob sie sie hinauf und blickte unter ihr hervor. Sie blickte selten oder nie *durch* sie hindurch nach etwas so Kleinem wie einem Jungen; sie war ihre Staatsbrille, der Stolz ihres Herzens, und war für den „Stil“ gebaut, nicht für den Dienst – sie hätte ebenso gut durch ein Paar Herdringe sehen können. Sie blickte einen Moment verwirrt drein und sagte dann, nicht heftig, aber doch laut genug, dass die Möbel es hören konnten: „Nun, ich wette, wenn ich dich zu fassen bekomme, werde ich –“

Version B is free:

> „Tom!“ – Nichts. – „TOM!“ – Nichts. – „Wo steckt der Bengel bloß? Tom, du!“ – Nichts.
>
> Die alte Dame schob die Brille auf die Nasenspitze und spähte darüber hinweg durchs Zimmer, dann schob sie sie hoch und spähte darunter hervor. *Durch* die Gläser sah sie selten oder nie, schon gar nicht nach etwas so Geringem wie einem Jungen: Es war ihre Sonntagsbrille, ihr ganzer Stolz, gemacht zum Staat und nicht zum Gebrauch – durch zwei Herdringe hätte sie genauso viel gesehen. Einen Augenblick stand sie ratlos da, dann sagte sie, nicht scharf, aber immerhin so laut, dass die Möbel es hören konnten: „Na warte, wenn ich dich erwische, dann …“

What each version does:

| Passage | Version A | Version B | Comment |
|---|---|---|---|
| *What's gone with that boy, I wonder?* | *Was ist mit diesem Jungen los, frage ich mich?* | *Wo steckt der Bengel bloß?* | A translates the words, but *frage ich mich* tacked on is stiff; B moves "I wonder" into the particle *bloß* and the colloquial *Bengel*. |
| *No answer.* | *Keine Antwort.* | *Nichts.* | Both are fine; B is more spoken. |
| *her state pair* | *ihre Staatsbrille* | *ihre Sonntagsbrille* | *Staatsbrille* is not a German word; *Sonntagsbrille* gives the sense "best pair". |
| *built for "style," not service* | *für den „Stil“ gebaut, nicht für den Dienst* | *gemacht zum Staat und nicht zum Gebrauch* | A is a calque. B uses old *der Staat* "finery, show" (as in *mit etwas Staat machen*) and so even echoes Twain's *state pair*. |
| *Well, I lay if I get hold of you I'll—* | *Nun, ich wette, wenn ich dich zu fassen bekomme, werde ich –* | *Na warte, wenn ich dich erwische, dann …* | *I lay* is dialect for "I bet". A keeps the bet but sounds like a written threat; B finds the spoken German threat formula *Na warte*. |

Version A is useful as a study aid: you can see the English through it. As a text it fails, because its German is unidiomatic and its register is too high for an old lady's exasperated shout. Version B reads like German, but it takes decisions a reader can't check: *Bengel* adds a judgement, *spähte* is more vivid than *looked*. That is the classic trade-off between a *wortgetreue* and a free translation. For a literary text most translators aim at B and argue about each decision; for a contract or a medical leaflet, accuracy wins and style comes second.

## Words of this lesson

- *wortgetreu* (word-for-word, faithful to the wording) vs *sinngemäß* (B2: in substance).
- *die Ausgangssprache / die Zielsprache* (source / target language), *der Ausgangstext / der Zieltext*.
- *die Entsprechung* (a corresponding expression, a counterpart) and *das Äquivalent* (an equivalent, a little more technical).
- *die Übertragung* is a more literary word for a translation (*in der Übertragung von …*), and also a transmission (of data, of a broadcast, of a disease) and, in psychoanalysis, transference. *die Nachdichtung* is a free verse translation that recreates a poem.
- *die Wiedergabe* (rendering, reproduction: *die Wiedergabe eines Gesprächs*; also playback), *unübersetzbar*, *der Übersetzungsfehler*, *das Simultandolmetschen* (simultaneous interpreting), *verdeutschen* (to put into German, often of foreign words: *ein Fremdwort verdeutschen*).

## Common mistakes

- *eventuell* for "eventually": ~~Eventuell hat er zugestimmt~~ means "perhaps he agreed". "Eventually he agreed" is *Schließlich stimmte er zu.*
- *sensibel* for "sensible": ~~eine sensible Entscheidung~~ → *eine vernünftige Entscheidung*.
- Translating the progressive literally: ~~Ich bin lesend~~ → *Ich lese gerade.*
- Keeping English word order and *es gibt* where German has a verb of position.
- Translating an idiom word for word into the wrong register: a salopp English phrase into neutral German loses the joke; a neutral one into salopp German adds one.
- Calling something *unübersetzbar* when it is only hard.

## Key points

- Translation shifts are normal: *-ing* forms become clauses or nouns, passives become *man* or *sollen*, tag questions become particles; German particles and Konjunktiv I become intonation, words or reporting verbs in English.
- C2 false friends: *eventuell, konsequent, sensibel, aktuell, prinzipiell, Kompetenz, seriös, sympathisch, Konkurrenz*.
- Loan translations (*Wolkenkratzer*) become invisible; *Sinn machen* is normal in speech and debated in formal writing.
- Translate idioms by idioms of the same register; puns and titles are recreated, not translated.
- A wortgetreue translation shows the source; a free one reads like the target language. Choose according to the text's purpose.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Schwulst und Prägnanz: Lichtenberg, Schopenhauer and Kraus on style
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

German has a long tradition of writers who wrote about bad writing, and three of them are still quoted in every style guide: the Göttingen physicist Georg Christoph Lichtenberg (1742–1799), the philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) and the Viennese satirist Karl Kraus (1874–1936). All three are in the public domain. This honors lesson reads them for two reasons: what they attack (padding, pomp, nested sentences, fashionable words) is still what a C2 writer has to avoid, and how they write (antithesis, the **[[aphorism]]**, irony) shows what precision looks like at its sharpest. At the end you will rewrite a padded paragraph, and we will take a fair look at where these critics were snobbish or are now simply dated.

## Lichtenberg: the notebook as a laboratory

Lichtenberg taught experimental physics at Göttingen and was famous in his lifetime as a scientist and a wit. His notebooks, which he called *Sudelbücher*, were not meant for publication; selections appeared after his death, from 1800 on. He explained the name himself, with a merchant's comparison: „Die Kaufleute haben ihr Waste book (Sudelbuch, Klitterbuch glaube ich im Deutschen)“ (merchants have their waste book … I believe in German it's called a *Sudelbuch*, a *Klitterbuch*): a rough book in which everything is written down first, before it is put in order.

The quotations below follow the text of the *Aphorismen (Sudelbücher)* on Projekt Gutenberg-DE (which names Carl Hanser Verlag as its source); it keeps Lichtenberg's spelling (*läßt, daß*).

> „Wenn ein Buch und ein Kopf zusammenstoßen und es klingt hohl, ist das allemal im Buch?“ (Sudelbuch D)

— If a book and a head collide and there's a hollow sound, is it always in the book? The sentence is built as a question, and the question is the joke: the reader has to supply the answer (no, it may be the reader's head), and in doing so turns the joke on himself.

> „Ein Buch ist ein Spiegel, wenn ein Affe hineinguckt, so kann freilich kein Apostel heraus sehen.“ (Sudelbuch E)

— A book is a mirror: if an ape looks into it, no apostle can look out, of course. The same thought as the first, with an image instead of a question. *freilich* (of course, admittedly) is a little old-fashioned now; *heraus sehen* would be written *heraussehen* today.

> „Heutzutage machen drei Pointen und eine Lüge einen Schriftsteller.“ (Sudelbuch D)

— Nowadays three punchlines and a lie make a writer. A complaint about the literary market that sounds remarkably modern.

> „Es läßt sich ohne sonderlich viel Witz so schreiben, daß ein anderer sehr vielen haben muß es zu verstehen.“ (Sudelbuch D)

— You can write without any great wit in such a way that someone else needs a great deal of it to understand you. *Witz* here has its older sense of "intelligence, wit" (as in *Mutterwitz*), not "joke". This is Lichtenberg's attack on obscurity: difficult writing is not proof of a difficult thought.

Notice how short these are, and how each ends on its strongest word (*Buch, sehen, Schriftsteller, verstehen*). That is the aphorism: a single sentence, or two, that states a thought so compactly and pointedly that it can stand alone.

## Schopenhauer: "Über Schriftstellerei und Stil"

Schopenhauer's essay on authorship and style is a chapter of the second volume of *Parerga und Paralipomena* (1851), a collection of essays that made him famous late in life. It is long, polemical and often very funny. Its main targets, in summary:

- **Writing without thinking.** Schopenhauer divides authors into those who write because they have something to say and those who write in order to write (and, he adds, to be paid). Style, for him, is the physiognomy of the mind: a muddled style shows a muddled thinker.
- **Obscurity as a pose.** He attacks the philosophers of his day, above all Hegel (as in much of his work), for hiding a lack of ideas behind impenetrable language.
- **Nested sentences.** He mocks periods in which one clause is boxed inside another until the reader has to hold half a page in memory before the verb arrives; the German name for these is *Schachtelsätze*.
- **Damage to the language.** He rages against writers and journalists who, to save a syllable, mangle words and grammar.

The best-known sentence of the essay (chapter XXIII, § 283) is usually quoted shortened and rearranged (*Die erste … Regel des guten Stils ist diese, daß man etwas zu sagen habe*). In full, in the spelling of the nineteenth-century editions, it reads:

> „Daher nun ist die erste, ja, schon für sich allein beinahe ausreichende Regel des guten Stils diese, daß man etwas zu sagen habe: o, damit kommt man weit!“

— Hence the first rule of good style, and indeed one that is almost sufficient on its own, is to have something to say: oh, that gets you a long way! Notice that Schopenhauer, too, writes a long sentence here, but a transparent one: the long subject comes first, *diese* points forward, and the rule itself, *daß man etwas zu sagen habe* (Konjunktiv I, a normal choice in a definition in his time), comes at the end. The ironic afterthought *o, damit kommt man weit!* is aimed at all the writers who ignore it.

## Kraus: language as the mother of thought

Karl Kraus wrote and, for most of its life, alone filled the Viennese journal *Die Fackel* (The Torch), from 1899 until his death in 1936. His enemy was the newspaper phrase: the ready-made formula that lets a writer produce sentences without thinking and lets readers consume them without noticing what they mean. In the First World War he made this a moral argument: the phrases of the press, he believed, had made the killing sayable.

Two of his aphorisms:

> „Die Sprache ist die Mutter, nicht die Magd des Gedankens.“

— Language is the mother, not the handmaid, of thought. (First printed in *Die Fackel* no. 288, 11 October 1909, p. 14; reprinted in the collection *Pro domo et mundo*, 1912.) The sentence is an antithesis in its tightest form: two nouns of the same shape (*Mutter, Magd*), one denied, one asserted. It also states Kraus's whole programme: you don't first think and then find words; working on the words is working on the thought.

> „Der Aphorismus deckt sich nie mit der Wahrheit; er ist entweder eine halbe Wahrheit oder anderthalb.“

— The aphorism never coincides with the truth; it is either half a truth or one and a half. (Quoted from the selection of his *Aphorismen* on Projekt Gutenberg-DE, based on an edition by Volk und Welt, 1971.) An aphorism about aphorisms, and an honest one: the form is built to exaggerate.

## What they attack, in today's terms

| Fault | German term | What it looks like |
|---|---|---|
| padding | *Füllwörter, Weitschweifigkeit* | *eigentlich, quasi, im Grunde genommen, sozusagen*; saying the same thing twice |
| pomp | *Schwulst, schwülstig* | *im Rahmen der stattgefundenen Maßnahmen*; heavy compounds and nouns where a verb would do |
| affectation | *geschraubt, gestelzt* | *Es darf seitens der Leitung darauf hingewiesen werden, dass …* |
| boxes inside boxes | *Schachtelsatz* | a relative clause inside a *dass*-clause inside a parenthesis, with the verb at the end of it all |
| fashionable words | *Modewörter* | the word everyone uses this year (and nobody next year) |
| the ready-made phrase | *die Phrase, die Floskel* | *in trockenen Tüchern, auf den Weg bringen, ein Stück weit*, used without thought |

The opposite of all of this is *die Prägnanz*: saying exactly what you mean, in as few words as the thought needs. *prägnant* (C1: concise and to the point) is the adjective.

## Rewriting a padded paragraph

Here is a paragraph from an (invented) company newsletter. Every sentence is grammatical; almost every sentence is padded.

> Im Rahmen der im vergangenen Quartal durchgeführten Umstrukturierungsmaßnahmen ist es seitens der Geschäftsleitung als sinnvoll erachtet worden, die bisher bestehenden Abteilungen Vertrieb und Marketing im Grunde genommen zu einer einzigen Einheit zusammenzuführen. Dies erfolgte vor dem Hintergrund der Tatsache, dass es in der Vergangenheit eigentlich immer wieder zu gewissen Abstimmungsproblemen gekommen war, die sozusagen die Effizienz beeinträchtigt hatten.

A prägnant version:

> Im letzten Quartal hat die Geschäftsleitung Vertrieb und Marketing zu einer Abteilung zusammengelegt. Die beiden Abteilungen hatten sich immer wieder schlecht abgestimmt, und das hatte Zeit gekostet.

What changed:

- *Im Rahmen der … durchgeführten Umstrukturierungsmaßnahmen* → *Im letzten Quartal*: the frame adds nothing that the verb *zusammenlegen* doesn't say.
- *ist es seitens der Geschäftsleitung als sinnvoll erachtet worden, … zusammenzuführen* → *hat die Geschäftsleitung … zusammengelegt*: active voice, the agent as subject, a simple verb.
- *die bisher bestehenden*: if they are merged, they existed. Deleted.
- *im Grunde genommen, eigentlich, sozusagen, gewisse*: fillers that weaken without adding. Deleted.
- *Dies erfolgte vor dem Hintergrund der Tatsache, dass …* → a second main clause: the reason is stated, not announced.
- *die Effizienz beeinträchtigt* → *Zeit gekostet*: concrete instead of abstract. (If the newsletter needs the abstract word, keep it; prägnant doesn't mean colloquial.)

From 58 words to 27, with no information lost. That is the practical lesson of all three critics.

## A fair word

These critics were brilliant, and they were not always fair.

- **Snobbery.** Schopenhauer's contempt extends to whole groups: journalists, professors, the public, and, in other essays, women, about whom he wrote things no one would defend today. His judgements on style are worth reading; his judgements on people are worth noting as evidence of his prejudices.
- **Polemic.** Kraus's attacks on individual journalists and writers could be merciless and personal, and later readers have found some of them unjust. His method, the close reading of a single phrase until it gives itself away, remains a model.
- **Dated rules.** Some of what they condemned is now standard German: words they disliked as new have become normal, and spellings they defended have been reformed. A rule of style is a rule for a particular time and readership, not a law of nature.
- **Long sentences are not always bad.** German can handle long periods well (Kleist and Thomas Mann wrote them masterfully), and lesson 07 in module 2 teaches you to read and build them. The fault the critics attack is not length but opacity: a sentence the reader can't follow on first reading.

Lichtenberg comes off best: his irony is aimed at books and minds, his own included.

## Words of this lesson

- *die Stilkritik* (criticism of style), *der Stilist / die Stilistin* (a writer with a fine style: *ein glänzender Stilist*), *der Sprachkritiker / die Sprachkritikerin*.
- *der Aphorismus* (plural *die Aphorismen*) and *aphoristisch*.
- *weitschweifig* and *die Weitschweifigkeit* (long-winded, long-windedness); *schwülstig* and *der Schwulst* (bombastic, bombast); *geschraubt* (convoluted, affected) and *gestelzt* (stilted, stiff); both describe unnatural, over-formal language.
- *die Prägnanz* (conciseness, pithiness), *das Sprachgefühl* (feel for language: *ein gutes Sprachgefühl haben*), *das Füllwort* (filler word; plural *die Füllwörter*).

## Common mistakes

- Confusing *prägnant* with "pregnant": it means concise and to the point.
- Believing that formal means padded: a formal text can be prägnant. *Wir haben Ihren Antrag abgelehnt, weil …* is formal and clear.
- Cutting so hard that the tone becomes curt: in a letter of condolence or an apology, a little ceremony is part of the message (German C1's honors lesson on solemn occasions was about this).
- Quoting the critics as authorities on today's German: they are witnesses of their time.

## Key points

- Lichtenberg's *Sudelbücher* (published after his death, from 1800 on), Schopenhauer's "Über Schriftstellerei und Stil" (*Parerga und Paralipomena* II, 1851) and Kraus's *Die Fackel* (1899–1936) are the classics of German style criticism.
- They attack padding (*Füllwörter, Weitschweifigkeit*), pomp (*Schwulst*), affectation (*geschraubt, gestelzt*), nested periods (*Schachtelsätze*), fashionable words and the ready-made phrase.
- Their own prose works through the aphorism, antithesis (*Mutter / Magd*) and irony.
- Prägnanz means the fewest words the thought needs: active verbs, agents as subjects, concrete words, no fillers.
- Read them critically: much of their snobbery and some of their rules are dated.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Umformulieren: Nominalstil and Verbalstil in both directions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 2 is about building sentences and words: rewriting, long periods, fine word order, word formation and verb prefixes. It starts with the skill the Goethe-Zertifikat C2 tests directly. In Schreiben Teil 1 you get a short text (a presentation of about 200 words) with marked passages; you rewrite each passage using a word that is given and may not be changed, and the meaning must stay the same. The Goethe-Institut's test description gives 2 points for a correct item and 1 for an item with minor errors.

At C1 (lesson 06) you turned clauses into noun phrases: *weil → wegen, obwohl → trotz, um … zu → zur*. That is half of what C2 asks. This lesson goes in both directions and covers every kind of **[[reformulation]]** the task uses: clause ↔ phrase, connector ↔ preposition ↔ adverb, relative clause ↔ participle, modal verb ↔ its substitutes, Funktionsverbgefüge ↔ simple verb, active ↔ passive substitutes, direct ↔ indirect speech. It also asks the question the exam doesn't: which version is better for this reader?

The theme is urban planning and housing: how a city turns an old railway site into a new neighbourhood.

## A planning document

German planning documents are written in a dense nominal style. Read this excerpt from the (invented) justification of a development plan, the *Begründung zum Bebauungsplan*.

> **Bebauungsplan Nr. 214 „Am alten Güterbahnhof“ – Auszug aus der Begründung**
>
> **1. Anlass und Ziel der Planung.** Mit der Aufgabe des Güterbahnhofs im Jahr 2019 ist im Osten der Stadt eine rund elf Hektar große Brachfläche entstanden. Mit dem vorliegenden Bebauungsplan macht die Stadt von ihrer Planungshoheit Gebrauch: Ziel ist die Entwicklung eines gemischt genutzten Wohnquartiers mit etwa 900 Wohnungen, von denen mindestens 30 Prozent im Sozialwohnungsbau zu errichten sind. Die Umwidmung der bisherigen Bahnfläche in Bauland erfordert eine Änderung des Flächennutzungsplans, die im Parallelverfahren erfolgt.
>
> **2. Städtebauliches Konzept.** Angesichts des anhaltenden Flächenverbrauchs am Stadtrand setzt die Stadt auf die Nachverdichtung bereits erschlossener Flächen. Die Bebauung erfolgt in vier- bis sechsgeschossigen Blöcken, deren Höhe zur angrenzenden Altbebauung hin abnimmt, damit das gewachsene Stadtbild nicht beeinträchtigt wird. Erhaltenswerte Bausubstanz, insbesondere die ehemalige Lokhalle, wird einer Umnutzung als Quartierszentrum zugeführt.
>
> **3. Freiflächen und Verkehr.** Zur Minderung der Flächenversiegelung werden die Innenhöfe teilweise entsiegelt; für Flachdächer wird eine Dachbegrünung festgesetzt. Durch die Anbindung an die geplante Ortsumgehung sowie eine konsequente Verkehrsberuhigung im Inneren des Gebiets soll Durchgangsverkehr weitgehend vermieden werden. Stellplätze sind vorrangig in Quartiersgaragen nachzuweisen.
>
> **4. Bodenordnung.** Ein Teil der Grundstücke wird nicht verkauft, sondern im Erbbaurecht an Genossenschaften und die städtische Wohnungsbaugesellschaft vergeben, um der Bodenspekulation vorzubeugen. Die Ermittlung der Grundstückswerte erfolgt auf Grundlage der aktuellen Bodenrichtwerte. Nach Abschluss der Prüfung aller eingegangenen Stellungnahmen ist eine erneute Beteiligung der Öffentlichkeit vorgesehen.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Development plan no. 214 "At the old goods station": excerpt from the justification**

**1. Reason for and aim of the plan.** When the goods station was given up in 2019, a derelict site of about eleven hectares was left in the east of the city. With this development plan the city exercises its planning authority: the aim is to develop a mixed-use residential neighbourhood with about 900 flats, at least 30 percent of which are to be built as social housing. Rezoning the former railway land as building land requires an amendment to the land-use plan, which is being carried out in a parallel procedure.

**2. Urban design concept.** In view of the continuing consumption of land on the outskirts, the city is relying on the densification of sites that already have roads and services. The buildings will be blocks of four to six storeys whose height decreases towards the adjacent older buildings so that the established townscape is not impaired. Buildings worth preserving, in particular the former locomotive shed, will be converted into a neighbourhood centre.

**3. Open spaces and traffic.** To reduce the sealing of the ground, some of the inner courtyards will be unsealed; green roofs are prescribed for flat roofs. The connection to the planned bypass and consistent traffic calming inside the area are intended to keep through traffic out as far as possible. Parking spaces are to be provided mainly in neighbourhood car parks.

**4. Land arrangements.** Some of the plots will not be sold but granted on long leasehold to cooperatives and the municipal housing company, to prevent land speculation. Land values will be determined on the basis of the current standard land values. Once all comments received have been examined, the public will be consulted again.

</details>

Count the verbs that carry meaning: *entstanden, macht Gebrauch, erfordert, setzt, abnimmt, vergeben*. Almost everything else is in verbal nouns, most of them ending in *-ung* (*Aufgabe, Entwicklung, Umwidmung, Änderung, Nachverdichtung, Bebauung, Minderung, Anbindung, Ermittlung, Prüfung, Beteiligung*) and in empty verbs (*erfolgt, wird zugeführt, ist vorgesehen*). That is normal for the text type. It is precise, it hides who acts, and residents find it hard to read. Every sentence can be rewritten in verbal style, and the rest of the lesson shows how.

## Clause ↔ phrase: the hard cases

The C1 table (temporal, causal, conditional, concessive, final and modal relations) is in the reference sheet. These are the conversions that trip up advanced learners:

| Clause | Phrase | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *Ohne dass die Anwohner beteiligt wurden, …* | *Ohne Beteiligung der Anwohner …* | *ohne dass* → *ohne* + noun; no article is usual |
| *Je dichter ein Quartier bebaut wird, desto wichtiger werden Freiflächen.* | *Mit zunehmender Bebauungsdichte gewinnen Freiflächen an Bedeutung.* | *je … desto* → *mit zunehmendem / steigendem / wachsendem* + noun |
| *Dadurch, dass die Höfe entsiegelt werden, …* | *Durch die Entsiegelung der Höfe …* | *dadurch, dass* and *indem* → *durch* + acc. |
| *Wenn kein Bebauungsplan vorliegt, …* | *Mangels eines Bebauungsplans …* / *Ohne Bebauungsplan …* | missing condition → *mangels* + gen. (formal) or *ohne* |
| *Statt dass neue Flächen versiegelt werden, …* | *Statt einer Versiegelung neuer Flächen …* | *statt dass* → *statt* + gen. |
| *Solange das Verfahren läuft, …* | *Für die Dauer des Verfahrens …* / *Während des Verfahrens …* | *für die Dauer* stresses the whole period |
| *Sobald der Plan in Kraft tritt, …* | *Mit Inkrafttreten des Plans …* | *mit* + noun for "at the moment when" |
| *Soweit es das Baurecht zulässt, …* | *Im Rahmen des baurechtlich Zulässigen …* | *im Rahmen* + gen. for limits |
| *Wie erwartet, …* / *Wie vereinbart, …* | *Erwartungsgemäß …* / *Vereinbarungsgemäß …* | comparison clause → adverb in *-gemäß* |

Three things to watch in the noun phrase:

1. **Who acts.** The object of the verb becomes the genitive, the doer goes into *durch* or (formal) *seitens*: *Die Stadt prüft die Einwände* → *die Prüfung der Einwände durch die Stadt*. Intransitive verbs keep the subject as the genitive: *Die Mieten steigen* → *der Anstieg der Mieten*.
2. **Tense and modality are lost.** *Nachdem der Plan beschlossen worden war* and *nachdem der Plan beschlossen worden ist* both become *nach Beschluss des Plans*. If the time relation matters, keep the clause or add an adverb (*nach dem bereits erfolgten Beschluss*).
3. **Negation changes form.** *weil kein Geld da ist* → *aus Geldmangel* / *mangels finanzieller Mittel*; *wenn die Anwohner nicht zustimmen* → *ohne Zustimmung der Anwohner*.

And in the reverse direction, give the clause a subject. *Bei Nichteinhaltung der Frist* is not *Wenn nicht eingehalten*: it is *Wenn die Frist nicht eingehalten wird, …* (or *Wenn Sie die Frist nicht einhalten, …* in a letter to a person).

## Connector ↔ preposition ↔ adverb

Many logical relations exist in three word classes. Each one has its own word order, and the exam often gives you the word from another class than the one in the text.

| Relation | Subordinating conjunction (verb last) | Preposition (+ case) | Adverb (verb second, or in the Mittelfeld) |
|---|---|---|---|
| concession | *obwohl, obgleich* | *trotz* + gen., *ungeachtet* + gen. | *trotzdem, dennoch, gleichwohl* |
| cause | *weil, da* | *wegen, aufgrund* + gen. | *deshalb, daher, deswegen* |
| consequence | *sodass, so … dass* | *infolge* + gen. | *folglich, infolgedessen* |
| time: after | *nachdem* | *nach* + dat. | *danach, anschließend* |
| time: before | *bevor, ehe* | *vor* + dat. | *zuvor, vorher* |
| time: during | *während* | *während* + gen. | *währenddessen, unterdessen* |
| condition | *wenn, falls, sofern* | *bei, im Fall(e)* + gen. | *dann, in diesem Fall* |
| purpose | *damit, um … zu* | *zu, zwecks* + gen. | *dazu, zu diesem Zweck* |
| means | *indem, dadurch, dass* | *durch* + acc., *mittels* + gen. | *dadurch, damit* |
| contrast | *während, wohingegen* | *im Gegensatz zu* + dat. | *dagegen, hingegen* |

The adverb refers back to the previous sentence, so the rewrite needs two main clauses:

- *Obwohl die Nachverdichtung umstritten ist, hält der Rat daran fest.*
- *Trotz der umstrittenen Nachverdichtung hält der Rat daran fest.* (Or *Trotz der Kritik an der Nachverdichtung …*, if the controversy is the point.)
- *Die Nachverdichtung ist umstritten. Dennoch hält der Rat daran fest.* / *Der Rat hält dennoch daran fest.*

Notice what the middle version does: *umstritten* has become an attribute, which shifts the emphasis from the dispute to the measure. In the exam, the safest phrase is the one closest to the clause. A noun made from *umstritten* would be clumsy, so most writers choose *trotz der Kritik an der Nachverdichtung* or *trotz aller Bedenken gegen die Nachverdichtung*. Check that such a paraphrase adds nothing: *Kritik* is what makes a measure *umstritten*, so it keeps the meaning; *trotz heftiger Kritik* would not.

## Relative clause ↔ participle

This is C1 lesson 08 in reverse and forward:

- *die Flächen, die bereits versiegelt worden sind* → *die bereits versiegelten Flächen* (passive, completed: Partizip II)
- *die Familien, die neu zugezogen sind* → *die neu zugezogenen Familien* (verbs with *sein*: Partizip II is active)
- *der Verkehr, der ständig zunimmt* → *der ständig zunehmende Verkehr* (active, simultaneous: Partizip I)
- *der Plan, der noch beschlossen werden muss* → *der noch zu beschließende Plan* (modal passive: *zu* + Partizip I)

Going back from participle to clause, choose the tense from the context: *die geplante Ortsumgehung* is *die Ortsumgehung, die geplant ist* (state) or *die man plant*, not *die geplant wurde*, which suggests the planning is over.

## Modal verbs and their substitutes

Each line says the same thing; they differ in register and emphasis.

| Modal verb | Substitutes |
|---|---|
| *Das kann man nicht vorhersagen.* | *Das ist nicht vorherzusagen.* / *Das lässt sich nicht vorhersagen.* / *Das ist nicht vorhersagbar.* |
| *Bauherren müssen einen Lageplan vorlegen.* | *Bauherren haben einen Lageplan vorzulegen.* / *Ein Lageplan ist vorzulegen.* / *Es ist ein Lageplan vorzulegen.* |
| *Die Mieten werden wahrscheinlich steigen.* | *Die Mieten dürften steigen.* / *Die Mieten werden voraussichtlich steigen.* |
| (fear) *Es ist zu befürchten, dass das Quartier zu teuer wird.* | *Das Quartier droht zu teuer zu werden.* |
| (expectation) *Man kann erwarten, dass das Projekt gelingt.* | *Das Projekt verspricht ein Erfolg zu werden.* |
| *Man muss jetzt handeln.* | *Jetzt gilt es zu handeln.* |

Two traps. *sein + zu* can mean "can" or "must", and only the context decides: *Der Plan ist im Rathaus einzusehen* (can be inspected), *Stellplätze sind nachzuweisen* (must). If the given word is *lässt*, you need the "can" reading. And *drohen zu* is only for things the speaker fears; the neutral alternatives are modal words (*voraussichtlich, vermutlich*: m1 lesson 04).

## Funktionsverbgefüge, passive and reported speech

**FVG ↔ simple verb.** The FVG is more formal and often marks a phase (C1 07): *Der Plan tritt im Mai in Kraft* = *gilt ab Mai*; *Die Stadt stellt Flächen zur Verfügung* = *stellt Flächen bereit*; *eine Entscheidung treffen* = *entscheiden*; *in Erwägung ziehen* = *erwägen*. When rewriting into verbal style, the noun often becomes the verb (*Die Stadt hat Kritik am Investor geübt* → *Die Stadt hat den Investor kritisiert*); check that the object's case changes with it.

**Active ↔ passive substitutes.** *Man wird den Plan im Mai beschließen* can become *Der Plan soll im Mai beschlossen werden*, *Der Plan steht im Mai zur Abstimmung* or, in the planning style of the text, *Die Beschlussfassung erfolgt im Mai*. Only the werden-passive keeps an agent comfortably (*vom Stadtrat*).

**Direct ↔ indirect speech.** *„Wir werden die Bürger erneut beteiligen“, sagte die Baudezernentin.* becomes *Die Baudezernentin sagte, man werde die Bürger erneut beteiligen* (Konjunktiv I; *wir* → *man* or *die Stadt*), or without a reporting verb: *Nach Angaben der Baudezernentin sollen die Bürger erneut beteiligt werden* / *Der Baudezernentin zufolge …*. *zufolge* follows its noun (dative); *laut* precedes it.

## Doing the exam task

The task gives you a sentence with a marked passage and a word, for example:

> *Die Stadt will die Brachfläche bebauen, **obwohl viele Anwohner protestiert haben**.* — TROTZ

1. **Name the relation** (concession) and the class of the given word (preposition + genitive).
2. **Build the phrase** around a noun from the clause: *protestieren → der Protest*. Who protested becomes the genitive: *trotz der Proteste vieler Anwohner*.
3. **Reattach it** and fix the word order: *Die Stadt will die Brachfläche trotz der Proteste vieler Anwohner bebauen.*
4. **Check meaning**: nothing added (*heftige Proteste* would add), nothing lost (*viele*), the given word unchanged (*trotz*, not *trotzdem*).

The same in the other direction:

> *Die Entscheidung fällt erst **nach Abschluss der Bürgerbeteiligung**.* — NACHDEM

→ *Die Entscheidung fällt erst, nachdem die Bürgerbeteiligung abgeschlossen ist.* (With a dated past event: *… abgeschlossen worden ist*.)

One more with an adverb:

> ***Wegen der hohen Bodenpreise** verkauft die Stadt keine Grundstücke mehr.* — DESHALB

→ *Die Bodenpreise sind hoch. Deshalb verkauft die Stadt keine Grundstücke mehr.* In a single sentence: *Die Bodenpreise sind hoch, deshalb verkauft die Stadt …* (*deshalb* is an adverb, so the verb comes straight after it).

## When verbal style is better

The planning text was written for lawyers and the planning committee. For residents, the city publishes a *Bürgerinformation*. Here is section 3 rewritten:

> *Was passiert mit den Höfen und Dächern? Viele Höfe sind heute asphaltiert. Wir reißen einen Teil davon auf, damit dort wieder Rasen und Bäume wachsen können. Flache Dächer müssen begrünt werden. Autos sollen nicht quer durch das Viertel fahren: Die neue Ortsumgehung führt den Verkehr außen herum, und in den Straßen im Quartier wird nur langsam gefahren. Parkplätze gibt es vor allem in Sammelgaragen am Rand.*

What changed: *wir* names the actor; nouns became verbs (*Entsiegelung → aufreißen*, *Begrünung → begrünt werden*); the technical *Stellplätze nachweisen* became an everyday statement; sentences got shorter. What was lost: precision (*teilweise entsiegelt* is a legal statement; *einen Teil aufreißen* is not). A good Bürgerinformation says where the binding text can be read. Neither style is "better" in general: the nominal one is right for a document that has legal effect, the verbal one for people who are affected by it.

## The words of this lesson

- **Planning levels.** The *Bauleitplanung* has two stages: the *Flächennutzungsplan* (land-use plan) covers a whole municipality and is preparatory; the *Bebauungsplan* (development plan, colloquially *B-Plan*) covers one area and is binding. Municipalities draw them up under their *Planungshoheit*, which follows from their right to self-government (Art. 28 Abs. 2 GG). What may be built and how is also governed by each Land's *Bauordnung*.
- **Land.** *das Bauland* (building land), *das Baugebiet* (an area designated for building), *die Baulücke* (a gap between buildings). *Umwidmen* and *die Umwidmung* change the legal designation of land; *die Umnutzung* changes the use of a building (a factory becomes flats). *Die Nachverdichtung* builds more on land that is already developed; *der Flächenverbrauch* is the take-up of new land for building and roads.
- **Sealing.** *versiegeln* (B2) covers ground with asphalt or concrete; *entsiegeln* removes it; *die Flächenversiegelung* is the result. *Begrünen* and *die Begrünung* mean planting greenery; *die Dachbegrünung* is a green roof.
- **Money and ownership.** *das Erbbaurecht* is a long leasehold (often 60–99 years): the city keeps the land and grants the right to build on it. *Der Bodenrichtwert* is an average land value per square metre, set by the local *Gutachterausschuss*. *Die Grundsteuer* (property tax) has been levied under new rules since 1 January 2025; eleven Länder use the federal model, which takes the Bodenrichtwert into account, and five use models of their own (as of early 2026, Haufe overview; court challenges were still pending).
- **Areas.** *das Sanierungsgebiet* is a formally designated redevelopment area; *die Quartiersentwicklung* the development of a neighbourhood; *das Wohnquartier* a residential neighbourhood; *das Stadtbild* the townscape. *Die Bausubstanz* is the fabric of existing buildings (*gute / marode Bausubstanz*).
- **Traffic.** *die Ortsumgehung* (bypass), *die Verkehrsberuhigung* (traffic calming), *die Verkehrsplanung* (transport planning). *Die Bodenspekulation* is buying land in the hope that its value rises.

## Common mistakes

- Changing the given word: the exam gives *trotz*, you write *trotzdem*. The item is wrong even if the sentence is good.
- Adding meaning in the noun phrase: *obwohl sie protestierten* → ~~*trotz ihrer heftigen Proteste*~~. Keep to what was there.
- Losing the agent or the negation: *wenn die Stadt nicht zustimmt* → ~~*bei Zustimmung der Stadt*~~ (meaning reversed) → *ohne Zustimmung der Stadt*.
- The wrong case after the preposition: *trotz* and *wegen* take the genitive in standard written German (*trotz des Protests*); the dative is colloquial and loses points in a formal text.
- Verb second after an adverb: ~~*Deshalb die Stadt verkauft*~~ → *Deshalb verkauft die Stadt*.
- Reading *sein + zu* the wrong way: *Der Plan ist einzusehen* is "can be inspected", not "must".
- False precision in Verbalstil: turning *teilweise* into *alle* or dropping *voraussichtlich*. A simpler sentence must still say the same thing.
- Substantivitis: *zur Sicherstellung der Durchführung der Prüfung* (three nouns in a chain, two of them genitives). Two at most; give the sentence a verb.

## Key points

- Goethe C2 Schreiben Teil 1: rewrite the marked passage with the given word, unchanged, keeping the meaning.
- Every relation exists as conjunction, preposition and often adverb: *obwohl / trotz / dennoch*, *weil / wegen / deshalb*, *nachdem / nach / danach*. Each has its own word order.
- Hard nominal cases: *ohne dass → ohne*, *je … desto → mit zunehmendem*, *dadurch, dass / indem → durch*, missing condition → *mangels*, *sobald → mit*.
- Relative clauses ↔ participles; modal verbs ↔ *sein/haben + zu*, *sich lassen*, *-bar*, *drohen/versprechen zu*; FVG ↔ simple verb; direct ↔ indirect speech with KI, *zufolge*, *nach Angaben*.
- Nominal style hides tense, modality and agents; verbal style shows who does what. Choose by reader and purpose.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Satzperioden: reading and building complex sentences
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 06 rewrote clauses as phrases. This lesson goes the other way: sentences built from many clauses, the kind you meet in science journalism, in the Feuilleton and in older literature. A long, carefully built sentence of this kind is a **[[period]]** (*Satzperiode*). Reading one at C2 means never losing the thread: you know which verb belongs to which subject, where an insertion begins and ends, and what a pronoun refers to. Writing at C2 means knowing when a period helps and when it should be split.

You will learn to take a 60-word sentence apart, to recognize **[[parenthesis]]** (*Parenthese*), stacked insertions and coordination ellipsis, to spot attachment and scope ambiguity, and to decide when a period has to go.

The theme is astronomy and space flight.

## A science feature

Read this (invented) feature from a popular science magazine. The first sentence has about 70 words. Don't translate as you go: look for the finite verbs first.

> **Staub vom Anfang der Welt**
>
> Dass ein Gramm grauer Staub, den eine Kapsel nach sechs Jahren im All zur Erde gebracht hat, Forscherinnen und Forscher in mehreren Ländern in Aufregung versetzt, versteht nur, wer weiß, dass Asteroiden wie jener, den die Raumsonde *Ariadne* angeflogen hat, als nahezu unveränderte Überreste aus der Entstehungszeit des Sonnensystems gelten, das sich – so die gängige Annahme – vor rund 4,6 Milliarden Jahren aus einer Wolke aus Gas und Staub bildete.
>
> Die Reise begann mit einem Start, bei dem nichts schiefgehen durfte. Die Trägerrakete, deren drei Raketenstufen nacheinander gezündet und abgeworfen wurden, brachte die rund 600 Kilogramm schwere Nutzlast in einen Orbit um die Sonne, von dem aus die Sonde – nach einem Vorbeiflug an der Erde, der ihr zusätzlichen Schwung verlieh – Kurs auf den Asteroiden nahm.
>
> Dort angekommen, kartierte sie die Oberfläche des Himmelskörpers, die – anders als in den Modellen vorhergesagt – nicht von feinem Staub bedeckt, sondern mit Geröll und Kratern übersät war, und schoss ein kleines Projektil in den Boden, um Material aus tieferen Schichten aufzuwirbeln, das nicht wie die oberste Schicht über Jahrmilliarden dem Sonnenwind ausgesetzt gewesen war.
>
> Der heikelste Teil der Mission war der Wiedereintritt. Die Raumkapsel trat mit etwa zwölf Kilometern pro Sekunde in die Atmosphäre ein, wurde von ihrem Hitzeschild geschützt und schwebte schließlich an einem Fallschirm zu Boden, wo ein Team, das die Signale der Bodenstation ausgewertet hatte, sie binnen weniger Stunden fand.
>
> Was die Proben verraten, wird man erst in einigen Jahren wissen. Schon jetzt aber ist klar, warum man sich nicht mit Meteoriten begnügt, die auf der Erde gefunden werden: Sie haben den Sturz durch die Atmosphäre überstanden und lagen oft jahrelang im Regen, bevor jemand sie aufhob. Die Körner von *Ariadne* dagegen hat nie ein irdischer Wassertropfen berührt.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Dust from the beginning of the world**

Why one gram of grey dust, brought to Earth by a capsule after six years in space, has researchers in several countries in a state of excitement is understood only by those who know that asteroids like the one the space probe *Ariadne* visited are considered almost unchanged remnants from the time when the solar system formed, which, according to the usual assumption, happened about 4.6 billion years ago out of a cloud of gas and dust.

The journey began with a launch at which nothing could go wrong. The launch vehicle, whose three rocket stages were ignited and jettisoned one after the other, put the payload of about 600 kilograms into an orbit around the Sun, from which the probe, after a flyby of Earth that gave it extra momentum, set course for the asteroid.

Once there, it mapped the surface of the body, which, unlike what the models had predicted, was not covered with fine dust but strewn with rubble and craters, and fired a small projectile into the ground to stir up material from deeper layers that, unlike the top layer, had not been exposed to the solar wind for billions of years.

The trickiest part of the mission was re-entry. The capsule entered the atmosphere at about twelve kilometres per second, was protected by its heat shield and finally floated to the ground on a parachute, where a team that had analysed the ground station's signals found it within a few hours.

What the samples reveal will only be known in a few years. But it is already clear why scientists are not content with meteorites found on Earth: they have survived the fall through the atmosphere and often lay in the rain for years before someone picked them up. The grains from *Ariadne*, on the other hand, have never been touched by a drop of water from Earth.

</details>

## Taking a period apart

**Step 1: find the finite verbs** and count them. In the first sentence there are seven: *gebracht hat, versetzt, versteht, weiß, angeflogen hat, gelten, bildete*. Seven finite verbs, seven clauses.

**Step 2: find the main clause.** Only one finite verb stands in second position after a complete first constituent: *versteht*. Everything before it is the Vorfeld (here a whole *dass*-clause); *nur* belongs to the main clause.

**Step 3: bracket the clauses**, using the conjunctions and relative pronouns as left brackets and the finite verbs as right brackets. Indentation shows the depth:

> [*Dass ein Gramm grauer Staub* … *Forscherinnen und Forscher … in Aufregung versetzt*,]  ← object clause in the Vorfeld (what is understood)
>     [*den eine Kapsel … zur Erde gebracht hat*,]  ← relative clause on *Staub*
> **versteht nur,**  ← main clause
> [*wer weiß,*]  ← the real subject of *versteht*: "whoever knows"
>     [*dass Asteroiden wie jener* … *als … Überreste … gelten*,]  ← object of *weiß*
>         [*den die Raumsonde … angeflogen hat*,]  ← relative clause on *jener*
>         [*das sich – … – vor rund 4,6 Milliarden Jahren … bildete*.]  ← relative clause on *Sonnensystem*

**Step 4: check every reference.** *den* (masculine accusative) can only be *Staub*; the second *den* only *jener* (= *Asteroid*). The last *das* is neuter, so it refers to *das Sonnensystem*, although *gelten* stands between them: the relative clause has been moved to the right of its clause, which German allows when the clause would otherwise be stranded in the middle.

**Step 5: paraphrase the core.** *Wer weiß, dass Asteroiden Überreste aus der Frühzeit sind, versteht die Aufregung.* Now the rest falls into place.

This is the depth C2 texts reach: a main clause, a subject clause, an object clause and relative clauses on two levels. Readers can follow it because each clause is closed before the next one opens, except the two relative clauses that sit inside their *dass*-clauses, and those are short.

## Centre embedding and where it breaks

When a clause is placed inside another clause, before that clause's verb, the reader has to keep every open bracket in mind. One level is normal, two are hard work, three are practically unreadable:

- *Die Sonde, die das Team gebaut hat, startet im Mai.* (one level: fine)
- *Die Sonde, die das Team, das die Agentur beauftragt hat, gebaut hat, startet im Mai.* (two levels: grammatical, but you have to read it twice)
- *Die Sonde, die das Team, das die Agentur, die der Bund finanziert, beauftragt hat, gebaut hat, startet im Mai.* (three levels: grammatical, unusable)

The repair is always the same: move material out of the middle. Put the relative clause at the end of its clause (the Nachfeld: *Die Sonde startet im Mai. Gebaut hat sie ein Team, das die Agentur beauftragt hat*), turn a clause into a participial attribute (*das von der Agentur beauftragte Team*), or start a new sentence.

## The Satzklammer with a long Mittelfeld

A main clause can be long without containing any subordinate clause. The finite verb and the rest of the verb (participle, infinitive, separable prefix) form a bracket, and everything between them waits for the end:

> *Die Kapsel **ist** nach einer sechsjährigen Reise und einem Wiedereintritt mit zwölf Kilometern pro Sekunde wenige Stunden nach der Landung von einem Team der Bodenstation in der australischen Wüste **gefunden worden**.*

Read it as: *ist … gefunden worden*: the capsule was found. The rest answers when, by whom and where. Science writers often take one element out of the bracket to lighten it (*… gefunden worden, und zwar in der australischen Wüste*), and in speech, comparisons and long prepositional phrases go to the Nachfeld (C1 lesson 20).

## Parenthesis: dashes, brackets, commas

A **[[parenthesis]]** interrupts a sentence with an insertion that is grammatically independent of it: a comment, an explanation, an aside. German marks it in three ways:

- **Dashes** are the most noticeable: *Das Sonnensystem bildete sich – so die gängige Annahme – vor rund 4,6 Milliarden Jahren.*
- **Brackets** make the insertion look like a side note: *Der Zwergplanet Pluto (bis 2006 als Planet gezählt) hat eine Umlaufzeit von etwa 248 Jahren.*
- **Commas** are the weakest: *Die Mission, das war allen klar, durfte nicht scheitern.*

In the Amtliches Regelwerk (2024 version), commas that set off insertions and supplements are covered by § 72, dashes by § 77. Two details of § 77 matter:

1. If the sentence itself needs a comma where the dashes end, the comma comes after the second dash: *Als die Kapsel landete – es war kurz nach Mitternacht –, jubelte das Team.* The comma closes the *als*-clause.
2. A question or exclamation inside the dashes keeps its own mark: *Die Sonde – wer hätte das gedacht? – funktionierte noch nach zwölf Jahren.*

**Stacked appositions** are a related device: *Ariadne, die erste europäische Probenrückführungsmission, ein Projekt von zwölf Ländern, startete …* Two appositions in a row are possible; a third usually means the sentence should be split.

## Coordination ellipsis

When two clauses are joined by *und*, *oder* or *aber*, words they share are usually left out the second time:

- **Shared subject**: *Die Kapsel trat in die Atmosphäre ein, wurde vom Hitzeschild geschützt und schwebte zu Boden.* (One subject, three verbs, even across active and passive.)
- **Shared finite verb** (gapping): *Die erste Stufe brannte zwei Minuten, die zweite sechs.*
- **Shared verb at the end of subordinate clauses**: *weil die Rakete zu schwer und der Treibstoff zu knapp war.*

Ellipsis is only clean when the omitted word would have the same form and the same function in both parts. Careful writers avoid it when the forms differ:

- ~~*Die Agentur unterstützt und hilft den Teams.*~~ *unterstützen* takes the accusative, *helfen* the dative: *Die Agentur unterstützt die Teams und hilft ihnen.*
- ~~*weil die Rakete zu schwer und die Tanks zu klein waren*~~: the omitted verb would be *war*, the one that is there is *waren*. Many speakers accept such a number mismatch in speech; in careful writing, give each part its own verb: *weil die Rakete zu schwer war und die Tanks zu klein waren.*
- A subject in the nominative can't be shared with a clause that needs the same person in another case: ~~*Die Astronautin landete und wurde sofort gratuliert.*~~ (*gratulieren* takes the dative) → *Die Astronautin landete, und ihr wurde sofort gratuliert.*

## Attachment ambiguity

A phrase can sometimes attach to two different words, and the sentence has two meanings:

- *Die Astronomin beobachtete den Kollegen mit dem Fernglas.* Who has the binoculars: she (she used them to watch him) or he (she watched the colleague who had them)?
- *die Beobachtung des Astronomen*: did the astronomer observe something (subjective genitive) or was he observed (objective genitive)?
- *Die Bilder der Sonde, die gestern veröffentlicht wurden, …*: here the verb number settles it (*wurden*: *die Bilder*); with *wurde* it would be *die Sonde*.

Context usually resolves the ambiguity, but in a precise text the writer should resolve it: *Mit dem Fernglas beobachtete die Astronomin den Kollegen* (fronting makes the instrument reading clear), *den Kollegen, der ein Fernglas hatte*.

## Scope ambiguity of nicht and nur

Negation and focus particles affect the part of the sentence they have in their scope, and the scope is not always visible in writing.

- *Die Mission wurde nicht abgebrochen, weil der Treibstoff knapp war.* Reading 1: it wasn't aborted, and the reason was the fuel shortage (odd, but possible). Reading 2: it was aborted, but not because of the fuel. In speech, the stress (*nicht ABgebrochen* vs *nicht, WEIL …*) decides. In writing, make reading 2 explicit: *Die Mission wurde nicht deshalb abgebrochen, weil der Treibstoff knapp war, sondern …*
- *Die Sonde hat nur Bilder vom Krater geschickt.* Only pictures (no measurements), or pictures only of the crater? Move *nur* before the constituent you mean, or front it: *Nur vom Krater hat die Sonde Bilder geschickt.*
- *Alle Sonden haben ihr Ziel nicht erreicht* is heard as "none did" by some speakers and as "not all did" by others. Say *Keine Sonde hat ihr Ziel erreicht* or *Nicht alle Sonden haben ihr Ziel erreicht.*

## The writer's side: when to split

A period earns its length when its parts are logically subordinate to one another and the reader is led from the known to the new: the first sentence of the feature delays its point on purpose, as an opening hook. A period is too long when:

- the reader has to hold more than two open brackets (centre embedding);
- the main clause comes only after 25 words and nothing prepares for it;
- one relative clause refers to a noun in another relative clause, and the pronouns could point to two nouns;
- the sentence contains two main ideas.

Split at the main idea. The first sentence of the feature could be: *Ein Gramm grauer Staub versetzt Forscher in mehreren Ländern in Aufregung. Eine Kapsel hat ihn nach sechs Jahren im All zur Erde gebracht. Der Grund für die Aufregung: Asteroiden wie dieser gelten als nahezu unveränderte Überreste aus der Entstehungszeit des Sonnensystems.* Clearer, but the suspense is gone. Neither is wrong; choose by genre and reader.

## The words of this lesson

- **Bodies and phenomena.** *der Himmelskörper* (celestial body) covers stars, planets, moons and asteroids. *der Meteorit* is a rock from space that reaches the ground; the glowing streak it makes in the air is *der Meteor*, popularly *die Sternschnuppe*. *der Zwergplanet* (dwarf planet), *der Krater*, *der Sternhaufen* (star cluster), *das Sternbild* (constellation), *die Milchstraße* (the Milky Way, also our galaxy), *das Schwarze Loch* (Duden: *schwarzes* or *Schwarzes Loch*), *der Urknall* (the Big Bang). *der Sonnenwind* is the stream of charged particles from the Sun; where it meets the Earth's magnetic field near the poles, it produces *das Polarlicht* (aurora).
- **Eclipses.** In *die Sonnenfinsternis* the Moon covers the Sun; in *die Mondfinsternis* the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
- **Space flight.** *die Raumsonde* (uncrewed probe), *die Trägerrakete* (launch vehicle) with its *Raketenstufen*, *die Nutzlast* (payload), *der Weltraumbahnhof* (spaceport), *die Bodenstation* (ground station), *der Orbit* (also *die Umlaufbahn*, B2), *die Umlaufzeit* (orbital period), *der Wiedereintritt* (re-entry), *die Raumkapsel*, *die Mondfähre* (lunar module), *andocken* (to dock: *an der Raumstation andocken*), *der Raumflug*, *die Raumfahrtagentur*, *die Erdbeobachtung* (Earth observation from satellites). *der Raumfahrer / die Raumfahrerin* is the general German word; *Astronaut* and *Kosmonaut* are also used.
- **The science.** *die Astronomie* is the science of the stars, *der Astronom / die Astronomin* the scientist; *astronomisch* also means "enormous" in everyday German: *astronomische Preise*. Don't confuse *Astronomie* with *Astrologie*.
- **Grammar talk.** *die Parenthese* and *die Mehrdeutigkeit* (ambiguity; *mehrdeutig* is the adjective).

## Common mistakes

- Reading the first finite verb as the main verb. In a period that opens with a subordinate clause, the main clause's verb comes later: find the verb in second position after a complete first constituent.
- Losing the reference of a relative pronoun: check gender and number (*das* → *Sonnensystem*, not *Staub*).
- Forgetting the comma after a closing dash when the clause ends there: ~~*Als die Kapsel landete – es war kurz nach Mitternacht – jubelte das Team.*~~
- Sharing a word in ellipsis that would need another case or form: ~~*Sie unterstützt und hilft den Teams.*~~
- Placing *nur* or *nicht* where it takes the wrong scope, and assuming the reader will hear the stress you have in mind.
- False sophistication: writing periods because "C2 is complex". A C2 writer can build a long sentence and chooses to when it helps.

## Key points

- A period can be taken apart: count the finite verbs, find the main clause, bracket the clauses, check every reference, paraphrase the core.
- Centre embedding becomes unreadable beyond two levels; move material to the Nachfeld, into an attribute or into a new sentence.
- Parenthesis with dashes, brackets or commas; a comma required by the sentence comes after the second dash.
- Coordination ellipsis requires the same form and function in both parts.
- Attachment and scope ambiguity (*mit dem Fernglas*; *nicht …, weil*; *nur*) must be resolved by word order or rewording in precise writing.
- Split a period at its main idea when the reader has to hold too many open brackets.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Kühe hat er drei: fine word order in the Mittelfeld and Vorfeld
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You have known the basic rules since A1: verb second, verb last in subordinate clauses, one constituent before the verb. At C1 (lessons 05, 16, 20) you learned where focus particles, modal particles and *nicht* go, and how the Vorfeld and the Nachfeld carry emphasis. What still gives advanced learners away is the fine order: *Er hat es ihm gegeben* or *Er hat ihm es gegeben*? *Den Weizen verkauft er an die Genossenschaft* or *Er verkauft den Weizen an die Genossenschaft*? Both orders in the second pair are correct, but they don't say the same thing.

This lesson collects the tendencies of **[[Mittelfeld order]]** (pronouns, definiteness, animacy, length, adverbials), shows what can stand in the Vorfeld and why a writer puts it there (**[[topicalization]]**), and covers **[[split topicalization]]** (*Kühe hat er drei*), the placeholder *es* and the empty Vorfeld of speech.

The theme is agriculture.

## A reportage

Read this (invented) reportage from a regional newspaper. Watch the beginnings of the sentences.

> **„Kühe hat er noch drei“ – Besuch auf einem Hof im Wandel**
>
> Den Hof am Ortsrand von Kirchbrunn bewirtschaftet die Familie Haller seit fünf Generationen. Milchkühe gab es hier früher sechzig, heute stehen noch drei im Stall – „für die Enkel“, sagt Georg Haller und lacht. Die Milchwirtschaft hat er vor zwölf Jahren aufgegeben; der Preis, den die Molkerei zahlte, deckte die Kosten nicht mehr. Seitdem setzt er auf Ackerbau: Weizen, Raps, Zuckerrüben und, seit drei Jahren, Erbsen.
>
> „Die Fruchtfolge ist das A und O“, erklärt er, während wir über einen Acker gehen, auf dem gerade die Aussaat begonnen hat. „Wer jedes Jahr dasselbe anbaut, laugt den Boden aus.“ Monokulturen, wie man sie aus anderen Regionen kennt, hält er für einen Irrweg. Gepflügt wird auf seinen Feldern seit Jahren nicht mehr; das schone die Bodenfruchtbarkeit und schütze vor Erosion, sagt er. Ertragreicher sei der Boden dadurch nicht geworden, aber stabiler.
>
> Ob einer seiner beiden Söhne den Hof einmal übernimmt, weiß er nicht. Die Hofnachfolge ist in der Region ein Dauerthema: Viele Agrarbetriebe finden niemanden, der weitermachen will. „Zeit für Urlaub hat man keine, und reich wird man auch nicht“, sagt Haller. „Kommt drauf an, wie man rechnet“, wirft seine Frau ein, die die Buchhaltung macht.
>
> Mit der Agrarpolitik hadert er. Die Regeln für Dünger und Pflanzenschutz seien strenger geworden, und das sei grundsätzlich richtig – die Nitratwerte im Grundwasser seien in manchen Gegenden einfach zu hoch. „Aber es fehlt die Verlässlichkeit. Kaum hat man investiert, ändern sich die Vorgaben.“ Die Gülle, die er für seine Felder braucht, bezieht er inzwischen von einem Nachbarn, der noch Viehzucht betreibt.
>
> Am Ende des Rundgangs zeigt er auf den Mähdrescher in der Halle, gemeinsam angeschafft mit drei anderen Landwirten. Allein hätte sich keiner von ihnen so eine Maschine leisten können. Einer Genossenschaft, wie sie sein Großvater mitgegründet hat, gehört sie nicht – aber das Prinzip, sagt Haller, sei dasselbe.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**"He has three cows left": a visit to a farm in transition**

The farm on the edge of Kirchbrunn has been run by the Haller family for five generations. There used to be sixty dairy cows here; today three are left in the barn, "for the grandchildren", says Georg Haller with a laugh. He gave up dairy farming twelve years ago; the price the dairy paid no longer covered the costs. Since then he has concentrated on arable farming: wheat, rapeseed, sugar beet and, for the last three years, peas.

"Crop rotation is the be-all and end-all," he explains as we walk across a field where sowing has just begun. "If you grow the same thing every year, you exhaust the soil." He considers monocultures of the kind found in other regions a wrong turn. His fields haven't been ploughed for years; that protects the fertility of the soil and prevents erosion, he says. The soil hasn't become more productive as a result, but it has become more stable.

He doesn't know whether one of his two sons will take over the farm one day. Farm succession is a constant topic in the region: many farms can't find anyone who wants to carry on. "You have no time for holidays, and you don't get rich either," says Haller. "Depends how you count," his wife puts in; she does the accounts.

He is at odds with agricultural policy. The rules on fertilizer and crop protection have become stricter, he says, and that is right in principle: nitrate levels in the groundwater are simply too high in some areas. "But there's no reliability. You've hardly invested before the requirements change." He now gets the liquid manure he needs for his fields from a neighbour who still keeps livestock.

At the end of the tour he points at the combine harvester in the shed, bought jointly with three other farmers. None of them could have afforded such a machine alone. It doesn't belong to a cooperative like the one his grandfather helped to found, but the principle, says Haller, is the same.

</details>

Few of the reportage's sentences start with the subject. Most start with an object (*Den Hof*, *Monokulturen*, *Die Gülle*), a participle (*Gepflügt*), a predicative (*Ertragreicher*), a prepositional object (*Mit der Agrarpolitik*), a dative (*Einer Genossenschaft*) or a noun split off from its numeral (*Milchkühe … sechzig*, *Zeit … keine*). None of these is a stylistic oddity; each links the sentence to what came before or sets up a contrast.

## The Mittelfeld: tendencies, not laws

The Mittelfeld is everything between the finite verb (or the conjunction) and the end of the clause. Its order follows tendencies that can be overridden by emphasis. The stronger the tendency, the higher it stands in this list:

1. **Unstressed personal pronouns come first**, in the order nominative – accusative – dative: *Gestern hat er es ihm verkauft.* *Hat sie es dir gezeigt?* The reverse ~~*er ihm es*~~ is not standard (only with a stressed *ihm*, and even then it sounds odd; use a full noun instead). An unstressed object pronoun usually comes before a full-noun subject: *Dann hat ihn der Bauer verkauft* is more natural than *Dann hat der Bauer ihn verkauft*, though both are correct.
2. **The reflexive *sich*** comes early as well, before or after a full-noun subject: *Dann hat sich der Betrieb vergrößert* / *Dann hat der Betrieb sich vergrößert*.
