3. **Known before new.** Definite noun phrases (things already mentioned or known) precede indefinite ones (new information): *Er hat den Mähdrescher einem Nachbarn geliehen* (the machine is the topic, the neighbour is new) vs *Er hat dem Nachbarn einen Mähdrescher geliehen* (now the machine is new).
4. **Dative before accusative** when both are full nouns with the same status: *Der Bauer hat dem Nachbarn das Saatgut verkauft.* This is the default because the dative usually names a person and the accusative a thing: **animate before inanimate**.
5. **Short before long.** A long object goes later, or its relative clause goes to the Nachfeld: *Er hat die Gülle einem Nachbarn abgekauft, der noch Viehzucht betreibt.*

These tendencies interact. When they point in different directions, information structure (known before new) usually wins: *Den Weizen hat er der Genossenschaft verkauft, die Gerste einem Händler.*

## Adverbials

For adverbials, the textbooks give the order temporal – causal – modal – local, often remembered as *te-ka-mo-lo*:

> *Er fährt morgen (te) wegen des Regens (ka) mit dem Traktor (mo) aufs Feld (lo).*

Use it as a starting point, not a rule. Three things refine it:

- **Sentence adverbials** that comment on the whole statement (*leider, vermutlich, glücklicherweise*) come early, often right after the pronouns: *Er hat es leider nicht geschafft.*
- **Complements of place and direction** (*aufs Feld, in den Stall*) are part of the predicate and stay at the end, next to the verb: *Er hat die Kühe gestern in den Stall gebracht*, not ~~*… in den Stall gestern gebracht*~~.
- **Known adverbials precede new objects.** *Er hat gestern einen neuen Pflug gekauft* (the purchase is the news) vs *Er hat den Pflug gestern gekauft* (the time is the news).

## Where nicht and the particles go

A recap from C1, because these placements interact with everything above:

- **Sentence negation**: *nicht* follows the pronouns, definite objects and most adverbials, and precedes the predicative, a complement of place or direction, and the verbal end of the clause: *Er pflügt den Acker nicht.* *Er fährt heute nicht aufs Feld.* *Der Boden ist nicht ertragreicher geworden.*
- **Negation of one constituent** puts *nicht* directly before it, usually with *sondern*: *Er fährt nicht heute, sondern morgen aufs Feld.*
- **Modal particles** follow pronouns and known definite noun phrases and precede new information and *nicht*: *Das hat er ja damals nicht gewusst.* *Das ist doch der Mähdrescher vom Nachbarn.*
- **Focus particles** stand before their focus: *Nur der Weizen ist verkauft* (nothing else) vs *Der Weizen ist nur verkauft* (sold, not yet delivered).

## The Vorfeld at C2

The Vorfeld holds exactly one constituent. The subject is the neutral choice. Anything else in the Vorfeld does one of three jobs: it **links** to the previous sentence, it **sets a frame** (time, place, topic), or it **contrasts**. This is topicalization.

| What stands first | Example from the text or theme | Job |
|---|---|---|
| object (accusative) | *Den Hof … bewirtschaftet die Familie Haller seit fünf Generationen.* | links to the title |
| object with relative clause | *Die Gülle, die er braucht, bezieht er von einem Nachbarn.* | topic of the sentence |
| prepositional object | *Mit der Agrarpolitik hadert er.* | new topic, set up as the frame |
| dative object | *Einer Genossenschaft gehört sie nicht.* | contrast (a cooperative vs a private arrangement) |
| predicative | *Ertragreicher sei der Boden nicht geworden, aber stabiler.* | contrast |
| participle | *Gepflügt wird auf seinen Feldern nicht mehr.* | puts the action first, here in an impersonal passive |
| infinitive with object | *Den Hof übernehmen will keiner der Söhne.* | contrast: they might do other things |
| part of an FVG | *Zur Sprache kamen auch die neuen Düngeregeln.* | frame for a new topic |
| subordinate clause | *Ob einer seiner Söhne den Hof übernimmt, weiß er nicht.* | the open question is the topic |

When a participle, an infinitive or a predicative stands first, the rest of the sentence usually carries contrast or new information, and in speech the first element gets a rising accent. Don't overdo it: a text in which every sentence starts with a fronted object reads like a parody of a news magazine.

## Split topicalization: Kühe hat er drei

German can split a noun phrase: the noun (with any adjectives) goes to the Vorfeld, and the quantifier stays in the Mittelfeld. This is split topicalization.

- *Milchkühe gab es hier früher sechzig.* (= *Es gab hier früher sechzig Milchkühe.*)
- *Zeit für Urlaub hat man keine.* (= *Man hat keine Zeit für Urlaub.*)
- *Neue Maschinen kauft er keine mehr.*
- *Geld haben wir keins.* (spoken; written also *keines*)
- *Gute Böden gibt es hier nur wenige.*

The conditions:

- The part left behind is a numeral or an indefinite quantifier: *drei, keine, viele, wenige, einige, genug, welche*. With *kein*, the left-behind word takes the pronoun form: *keine, keinen, keins/keines*.
- It doesn't work with the definite article or a possessive: ~~*Kühe hat er die*~~, ~~*Kühe hat er seine*~~.
- It is typical with objects (including the object of *es gibt*) and with the subject of verbs like *fehlen*: *Helfer fehlen uns noch zwei.*

The effect is contrast or a summing-up: the noun is the topic (*Kühe*: as for cows …), the quantity is the news (*drei*). It is common in speech and in lively written styles (reportage, interviews, columns), less so in academic prose.

## Placeholder es and the empty Vorfeld

**The placeholder *es*** (C1 lesson 10) holds the Vorfeld when nothing else should stand there and disappears as soon as something else does: *Es fehlt die Verlässlichkeit* → *Verlässlichkeit fehlt*; *Es wird hier nicht mehr gepflügt* → *Hier wird nicht mehr gepflügt* → *Gepflügt wird hier nicht mehr*.

**The empty Vorfeld** is a feature of speech. A pronoun that refers to something obvious (*das, es*, sometimes *ich*) can be left out of the Vorfeld, and the sentence starts with the verb:

- *Kommt drauf an.* (*Das kommt darauf an.*)
- *Weiß ich nicht.* (*Das weiß ich nicht.*)
- *Hab ich doch gesagt.* (*Das habe ich doch gesagt.*)
- *Muss los.* (*Ich muss los.*, very informal)

This is not a yes/no question: the intonation falls. In writing, use it only in quoted speech, chats and informal messages; in a report it is a register slip.

## The Nachfeld, briefly

What comes after the closing verb is the Nachfeld (C1 lesson 20): comparisons with *als* and *wie* (*Er verdient heute weniger als sein Vater damals*), relative clauses (*… von einem Nachbarn bezogen, der noch Viehzucht betreibt*) and, in speech and journalism, long prepositional phrases (*Er hat lange gezögert mit der Entscheidung*). It relieves the Mittelfeld and puts weight on the last element.

## Word order and emphasis in two text types

In the reportage, the Vorfeld mostly carries **links and frames**: the farm, the slurry, agricultural policy. The reader moves from topic to topic. In the farmer's quoted speech, the Vorfeld carries **contrast**: *Zeit für Urlaub hat man keine, und reich wird man auch nicht*: time is denied, wealth is denied, and the fronted elements make the two complaints parallel. *Kaum hat man investiert, ändern sich die Vorgaben* is a fixed pattern of its own: *kaum* + verb second, then the main clause with the verb first.

## The words of this lesson

- **Farming.** *der Ackerbau* (arable farming, on *das Ackerland*) and *die Viehzucht* (livestock breeding) are the two branches; *das Grünland* is grassland and pasture. *Der Agrarbetrieb* is a farm as a business; *der Hof* (A2) is the everyday word. *Die Hofnachfolge* is who takes over the farm.
- **The soil.** *die Fruchtfolge* (crop rotation) as opposed to *die Monokultur*; *die Brache* is land left fallow; *die Bodenfruchtbarkeit* (soil fertility), *die Erosion*. *Ertragreich* means high-yielding.
- **Sowing and harvesting.** *säen* and *die Aussaat* (sowing), *das Saatgut* (seed for sowing), *pflügen* with *der Pflug* (plough), *der Mähdrescher* (combine harvester), *der Ernteausfall* (crop failure, loss of harvest). *Das Getreide* is grain or cereals; *der Weizen* wheat, *der Raps* rapeseed, *die Zuckerrübe* sugar beet.
- **Inputs.** *der Dünger* and *düngen* (fertilizer, to fertilize); *die Gülle* is liquid manure; *das Nitrat* gets into groundwater from too much of it. *der Pflanzenschutz* covers crop protection, including pesticides (*das Pestizid*, earlier). *die Bewässerung* and *bewässern* (irrigation, to irrigate).
- **Structures and policy.** *die Molkerei* (dairy, the plant), *die Genossenschaft* (cooperative), *die Agrarpolitik*, *die Agrarwende* (the transition to a more sustainable farming model, by analogy with *Energiewende*), *die Flurbereinigung* (land consolidation: the reorganization of scattered plots into larger ones). *Artgerecht* (appropriate to the species) describes animal husbandry: *artgerechte Tierhaltung*.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the dative pronoun before the accusative pronoun: ~~*Ich habe ihm es gesagt*~~ → *Ich habe es ihm gesagt.*
- Placing a place or direction complement in the middle: ~~*Er hat die Kühe in den Stall gestern gebracht*~~ → *Er hat die Kühe gestern in den Stall gebracht.*
- Reading every fronted object as passive. *Den Hof bewirtschaftet die Familie Haller*: the family runs the farm; the case endings, not the position, tell you who does what.
- Splitting with a definite article: ~~*Kühe hat er die*~~.
- Putting two constituents in the Vorfeld: ~~*Gestern der Bauer hat gepflügt*~~. English-style "Yesterday the farmer …" is the most persistent advanced error.
- Overusing fronting for "style": a C2 writer fronts for a reason (link, frame, contrast).
- Using the empty Vorfeld in formal writing: ~~*Ist bekannt, dass …*~~ → *Es ist bekannt, dass …*

## Key points

- Mittelfeld: unstressed pronouns first (nominative – accusative – dative), then known before new, animate before inanimate, short before long; *te-ka-mo-lo* is a tendency for adverbials; place and direction complements stay next to the verb.
- *nicht* follows definite objects and most adverbials, precedes predicatives and directional complements; modal particles precede new information.
- The Vorfeld holds one constituent: subject (neutral) or anything else to link, frame or contrast, including participles, infinitives, predicatives and parts of FVG.
- Split topicalization: noun in the Vorfeld, quantifier left behind (*Kühe hat er drei*, *Zeit hat man keine*); not with definite determiners.
- Placeholder *es* disappears when something else takes the Vorfeld; the empty Vorfeld (*Kommt drauf an*) belongs to speech.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Gerede, Schreiberling, notlanden: productive word formation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At C1 (lesson 19) you met intensifying compounds (*blitzschnell, spottbillig*), augmentative prefixes (*Riesen-, Mords-*) and conversion (*das Für und Wider*). This lesson is about the finer tools: suffixes that look alike but judge differently (*kindlich* or *kindisch*?), formations that sound annoyed (*das Gerede, die Warterei, der Schreiberling*), feminine forms of job titles, and two odd corners of German morphology, the **[[back-formation]]** (*notlanden* from *Notlandung*) and the **[[Zusammenrückung]]** (*das Vergissmeinnicht*). A C2 reader hears the attitude in a word's form; a C2 writer chooses the form that carries the attitude they mean.

The theme is crafts and trades, an old and very transparent part of the German vocabulary.

## A reportage from a workshop

Read this (invented) reportage. Look at how the words are built.

> **Drei Jahre und ein Tag**
>
> Das Erste, was man von Lena Brückner sieht, ist der schwarze Hut. Dann die Kluft: weite Hose aus Cord, Weste, weißes Hemd. Die 24-jährige Zimmerin ist seit vierzehn Monaten auf der Walz, und drei Wochen lang arbeitet sie nun in der Werkstatt von Herbert Kling, einem der letzten Drechsler im Landkreis.
>
> „Gesellen auf Wanderschaft sind bei uns immer willkommen“, sagt Kling, während auf der Drehbank eine Schale aus Kirschholz Form annimmt. Er ist 67 und hat seinen Meisterbrief vor über vierzig Jahren gemacht. Drechseln, sagt er, sei kein Hexenwerk, aber eine Sache der Geduld. „Wer hier nach zehn Minuten fertig sein will, ist ein Pfuscher, kein Handwerker.“
>
> Die Regeln der Walz sind alt und je nach Gesellenvereinigung etwas verschieden. In der Regel muss, wer losgeht, die Gesellenprüfung bestanden haben, ledig und schuldenfrei sein. Drei Jahre und einen Tag lang darf er sich seinem Heimatort nicht auf weniger als fünfzig Kilometer nähern. Das Handy bleibt meist zu Hause. „Am Anfang dachte ich, das halte ich keine zwei Wochen durch“, erzählt Brückner. „Inzwischen vermisse ich das ständige Gepiepe überhaupt nicht.“
>
> Von dem Gerede, die Walz sei ein romantisches Relikt, hält sie wenig. Gelernt hat sie in diesen Monaten mehr als in der ganzen Ausbildung: Dachstühle in Tirol, eine Werkbank für eine Schreinerei in der Schweiz, nun das Hobeln und Drechseln bei Kling. Feiglinge, sagt sie lachend, hielten es auf der Walz nicht lange aus. Wer im Regen an der Landstraße steht und nicht weiß, wo er schlafen wird, lernt schnell, Leute anzusprechen.
>
> Dass die Innungen heute vor allem um Nachwuchs kämpfen, wissen beide. Kling hat in diesem Jahr keinen einzigen Lehrling gefunden. „Die jungen Leute wollen alle studieren“, brummt er, und dann, nach einer Pause: „Kann ich ihnen auch nicht verdenken.“ Brückner weiß schon, wo sie nach der Walz arbeiten will: in einem kleinen Betrieb, der Häuser aus Holz baut. „Handwerklich“, sagt sie, „ist das das Zünftigste, was man machen kann.“

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Three years and a day**

The first thing you see of Lena Brückner is the black hat. Then the outfit: wide corduroy trousers, waistcoat, white shirt. The 24-year-old carpenter has been on her journeyman's travels for fourteen months, and for three weeks now she is working in the workshop of Herbert Kling, one of the last wood turners in the district.

"Journeymen on their travels are always welcome here," says Kling, while a bowl of cherry wood takes shape on the lathe. He is 67 and got his master craftsman's certificate more than forty years ago. Wood turning, he says, isn't witchcraft, but it takes patience. "Anyone who wants to be finished here after ten minutes is a bungler, not a craftsman."

The rules of the Walz are old and differ slightly from one journeymen's association to the next. As a rule, anyone who sets off must have passed the journeyman's examination and be single and free of debt. For three years and a day they may not come within fifty kilometres of their home town. The mobile phone usually stays at home. "At first I thought I wouldn't last two weeks," says Brückner. "Now I don't miss the constant beeping at all."

She doesn't think much of the talk that the Walz is a romantic relic. She has learned more in these months than in her whole apprenticeship: roof trusses in Tyrol, a workbench for a joinery in Switzerland, now planing and turning with Kling. Cowards, she says with a laugh, wouldn't last long on the Walz. If you stand by a country road in the rain and don't know where you'll sleep, you quickly learn to talk to people.

Both know that today the guilds are fighting above all for new recruits. Kling hasn't found a single apprentice this year. "Young people all want to go to university," he growls, and then, after a pause: "Can't blame them, either." Brückner already knows where she wants to work after the Walz: in a small firm that builds wooden houses. "In terms of craft," she says, "that's the most proper thing you can do."

</details>

Almost every noun in the text is a transparent formation: *Drechsler* (from *drechseln*), *Meisterbrief*, *Wanderschaft*, *Handwerker*, *Schreinerei*, *Lehrling*, *Feigling*. Two of them carry an attitude: *das Gepiepe* (the annoying beeping) and *das Gerede* (idle talk). And *das Zünftigste* plays on two senses of *zünftig*: "proper, real" and "belonging to a guild (*Zunft*)".

## Suffix pairs that judge differently

Some adjectives from the same base differ only in the suffix, and the suffix carries the judgment. Learners who pick the wrong one say something they don't mean.

| Pair | Neutral or positive | Critical or different |
|---|---|---|
| *kindlich / kindisch* | *kindlich*: like a child, appropriate to a child: *kindliche Neugier* | *kindisch*: childish, said of adults who behave like children: *Sei nicht so kindisch!* |
| *geschäftlich / geschäftig* | *geschäftlich*: concerning business: *ein geschäftlicher Termin* | *geschäftig*: busy, bustling: *geschäftiges Treiben in der Werkstatt* |
| *sinnlich / sinnig* | *sinnlich*: of the senses, sensual: *ein sinnliches Erlebnis* | *sinnig*: well thought out, in current use often ironic: *Sehr sinnig, die Leiter vor die Tür zu stellen.* |
| *ehrlich / ehrbar / ehrenhaft* | *ehrlich*: honest; *ehrenhaft*: honourable (motives, conduct): *ein ehrenhafter Rücktritt* | *ehrbar*: respectable in the eyes of society (Duden: gehoben): *ein ehrbares Handwerk* |
| *furchtbar / fürchterlich / furchtsam* | *furchtbar, fürchterlich*: terrible; both also colloquial intensifiers (*furchtbar nett*) | *furchtsam*: timid, fearful (no register label in Duden): *ein furchtsames Kind* |
| *herrlich / herrisch* | *herrlich*: wonderful | *herrisch*: domineering, imperious |
| *geistig / geistlich* | *geistig*: mental, intellectual: *geistige Arbeit* | *geistlich*: religious, of the church: *ein geistliches Amt* |
| *launig / launisch* | *launig*: witty and good-humoured: *eine launige Rede* | *launisch*: moody |

A rough pattern, with many exceptions: with words for people and character, *-isch* is often critical (*kindisch, herrisch, launisch*), while *-lich* describes neutrally (*kindlich, herrlich*). Don't apply it to new words without checking: *künstlerisch, politisch* and *praktisch* are entirely neutral.

## Formations that sound annoyed

German has several productive patterns for "a lot of this, and it gets on my nerves".

**Ge- + verb stem + -e** forms neuter nouns for a repeated, usually irritating activity. After stems in *-el* and *-er*, the final *-e* is dropped:

- *das Gerede* (idle talk, gossip), *das Gerenne* (running about), *das Gehupe* (honking), *das Gepiepe* (beeping), *das Getue* (fuss, airs)
- *das Gejammer* (moaning), *das Gemecker* (grumbling), *das Gezeter* (shrieking, scolding)

Compare *das Reden* (talking, neutral), *die Rede* (a speech) and *das Gerede* (talk you don't take seriously). Older *Ge-* words are no longer felt as formations and are neutral: *das Gebirge, das Gebäude, das Gemälde, das Getreide*.

**-erei** makes feminine nouns for an activity that goes on too long: *die Schreiberei* (paperwork, scribbling), *die Fahrerei* (all that driving), *die Warterei* (all that waiting), *die Raserei* (speeding). The same suffix forms neutral names for businesses and their premises: *die Schreinerei, die Bäckerei, die Druckerei, die Molkerei* (lesson 08). The context decides.

**-ling** forms masculine nouns for people. Several are critical: *der Feigling* (coward, from *feige*), *der Schreiberling* (hack writer), *der Emporkömmling* (upstart). Others are neutral or affectionate: *der Lehrling* (apprentice), *der Liebling*, *der Säugling*. Whether *der Flüchtling* sounds belittling is debated; some institutions prefer *die Geflüchteten*, others keep *Flüchtling* as the neutral standard word.

**-ler** forms people nouns that are often slightly disparaging: *der Abweichler* (dissenter, in party politics), *der Hinterbänkler* (backbencher), *der Provinzler* (provincial). But *der Künstler, der Sportler* and *der Wissenschaftler* are neutral, and in *der Drechsler* the *-l-* belongs to the verb (*drechseln*).

## Agent nouns and feminine forms

Most trades form the person noun with **-er**, the feminine with **-erin**: *der Dachdecker / die Dachdeckerin, der Klempner / die Klempnerin, der Maurer / die Maurerin, der Schweißer / die Schweißerin, der Drechsler / die Drechslerin.*

Some need care:

- *der Geselle* is a weak noun (*des Gesellen, dem Gesellen*), feminine *die Gesellin*.
- *der Schmied / die Schmiedin*; *der Steinmetz / die Steinmetzin* (Duden lists *Steinmetzin*).
- *der Zimmermann*: Duden gives the plural *die Zimmerleute* and no feminine. The official name of the training occupation is *Zimmerer/Zimmerin*, which is how the reportage can call Lena Brückner *Zimmerin*.
- *-mann* compounds usually pair with *-frau* (*der Kaufmann / die Kauffrau, der Fachmann / die Fachfrau*), and their plurals in *-leute* include everyone: *Kaufleute, Fachleute, Zimmerleute*.

Before you form a feminine you haven't seen, check Duden or DWDS: most exist, a few are new or still unusual, and some are avoided in favour of a neutral form.

## Infinitives as nouns

Any infinitive can become a neuter noun for the activity: *das Hobeln, das Drechseln, das Löten*. It is the natural form after *beim* and *zum*: *Beim Schweißen trägt man eine Schutzmaske. Zum Leimen braucht man Zwingen.* The *-ung* noun, where there is one, names a process or result and is often more technical: *die Lötung* (a soldered joint), *die Verputzung* (rare; one says *der Putz*). Three degrees of attitude, from one verb:

- *das Reden* (the activity), *die Rede* (the result, a speech), *das Gerede* (the activity, judged).

## Back-formation: notlanden

A **[[back-formation]]** is a word formed by removing what looks like a suffix. German has many verbs formed back from nouns: *notlanden* (from *Notlandung*), *staubsaugen* (from *Staubsauger*), *uraufführen* (from *Uraufführung*), *bausparen* (from *Bausparer, Bausparkasse*), *bergsteigen* (from *Bergsteiger*).

These verbs are awkward because the language can't decide whether their first part is a separable prefix. Duden settles them one by one:

- *staubsaugen*: *er staubsaugt, staubsaugte, hat gestaubsaugt* (inseparable, with *ge-* in front).
- *uraufführen*: used mostly in the infinitive and the participle: *Das Stück wird im Mai uraufgeführt.* Finite forms (*~~es uraufführt~~, ~~es führt urauf~~*) are avoided.
- *notlanden*: Duden lists it as a weak verb; its sibling *notwassern* (to ditch, of an aircraft) is given as *notwasserte, notgewassert, notzuwassern*, with *ge-* and *zu* inside as if the verb were separable but the finite form unseparated. In practice, speakers and journalists prefer constructions that avoid the finite main-clause form: *Die Maschine musste notlanden. Die Maschine ist notgelandet.*
- *bergsteigen* is used mostly in the infinitive: *Wir gehen bergsteigen.*

When you are unsure, do what native speakers do: use the infinitive with a modal verb or the participle.

## Zusammenrückung: das Vergissmeinnicht

A **[[Zusammenrückung]]** is a word made from a phrase or sentence that is simply written together, keeping its internal grammar:

- *das Vergissmeinnicht* (forget-me-not; *mein* is an old genitive of *ich*)
- *der Taugenichts* (good-for-nothing: *taugt nichts*), *der Habenichts* (have-not), *der Tunichtgut* (ne'er-do-well)
- *das Stelldichein* (rendezvous, old-fashioned), *der Springinsfeld* (a young hothead)

Words for people are masculine; others vary. The type is no longer very productive, but writers coin new ones for effect: *ein ewiges Hin-und-Her*, *das Rundum-sorglos-Paket*.

## Ad-hoc compounds

C1 lesson 19 covered how to read long compounds: from the right, the last part is the head, the parts before it narrow it down. Journalists coin them freely: *die Gesellenwanderschaftstradition* is *die Tradition der Wanderschaft von Gesellen*. In your own writing, three parts are usually the limit; beyond that, use a genitive or a preposition.

## The crafts as a museum of word formation

Many trade names are old but still transparent:

- *der Dachdecker* covers roofs (*Dach + decken + -er*); *der Maurer* builds walls (*mauern*, from *die Mauer*); *der Schweißer* welds (*schweißen*).
- *der Zimmermann* works in timber: *Zimmer* is usually explained as originally meaning building timber or a timber structure, a sense lost in the everyday word but kept in the verb *zimmern* (to build from wood).
- *der Drechsler* turns wood on a lathe (*drechseln*); *der Schmied* forges (*schmieden*).
- *der Steinmetz*: the second part is usually traced to a Romance word for mason (compare French *maçon*); scholars differ on the details.
- *der Klempner* is the word in the north; in the south and in Austria and Switzerland the trade is *der Spengler*, in Swabia *der Flaschner*. Officially, *Klempner* is now the training occupation for sheet-metal work on roofs and façades, while plumbing belongs to the *Anlagenmechaniker/in für Sanitär-, Heizungs- und Klimatechnik*; in everyday speech the plumber is still *der Klempner*.

## The words of this lesson

- **Training and status.** The path is *Lehrling* (or *Auszubildender*) → *die Gesellenprüfung* → *der Geselle / die Gesellin* → *der Meisterbrief* (master craftsman's certificate). *Die Walz* is the traditional journeymen's travels (Duden: "besonders früher"; *auf der Walz sein, auf die Walz gehen*).
- **Organizations.** *Die Zunft* (guild) is the historical word; today's local trade associations are *die Innungen*. *Zünftig* has three senses in Duden: proper and hearty (*eine zünftige Brotzeit*), professional (*veraltend*), and belonging to a guild. *Handwerklich* means relating to a craft or to manual skill: *handwerkliches Können*.
- **Tools and materials.** *die Werkbank* (workbench), *die Zange* (pliers, tongs), *der Hobel* (plane) and *hobeln*, *die Kreissäge* (circular saw), *der Leim* (glue for wood) and *leimen*.
- **Work.** *verputzen* is to plaster a wall, *der Putz* the plaster (not the same as *putzen*, to clean); *mauern* (to lay bricks), *löten* (to solder), *schweißen* (to weld), *lackieren* (to varnish, to paint with lacquer), *schmieden* (to forge), *drechseln* (to turn wood).
- **Attitude.** *das Gerede*: talk not worth listening to; also gossip that damages someone: *ins Gerede kommen* (to become the subject of gossip).

## Common mistakes

- Calling an adult's behaviour *kindlich* when you mean *kindisch*, or praising someone as *ehrbar* when you mean *ehrlich*.
- Reading *-erei* always as pejorative: *die Schreinerei* is a joiner's workshop, not "too much joinery".
- Forming a finite main-clause form of a back-formation as if it were an ordinary separable verb: ~~*Die Maschine landete not*~~ is rare; say *Die Maschine musste notlanden* or *Die Maschine ist notgelandet*.
- Using *Gerede* for neutral "talk": *Das Gerede über die Fusion* already says you don't believe it.
- Inventing feminine forms without checking: most exist, but *Zimmermann* has no feminine in Duden (*Zimmerin* comes from *Zimmerer*).
- Treating *zünftig* as only "guild-related": in everyday German it usually means proper, hearty or rustic.

## Key points

- Suffix pairs differ in judgment: *kindlich/kindisch, geschäftlich/geschäftig, sinnlich/sinnig, ehrlich/ehrbar/ehrenhaft, herrlich/herrisch, geistig/geistlich, launig/launisch*.
- *Ge-…-e* (*Gerede, Gejammer*), *-erei* (*Warterei*), *-ling* (*Feigling, Schreiberling*) and *-ler* (*Abweichler*) can carry irritation or contempt; each also has neutral members.
- Feminine forms: *-er/-erin* is regular; check irregular ones (*Gesellin, Steinmetzin, Zimmerin*); *-leute* plurals include everyone.
- Back-formations (*notlanden, staubsaugen, uraufführen*) have unsettled forms; prefer infinitive and participle.
- Zusammenrückungen (*Vergissmeinnicht, Taugenichts*) are phrases written as one word.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Umschiffen oder umschiffen: verb prefixes and particle verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Since A1 you have separated *aufstehen* and *anrufen* and kept *verstehen* and *bekommen* together. At C2 the interesting verbs are the ones that can do both. *Umfahren* means "to knock down" when the stress is on *um* and "to drive around" when it is on *fahren*; *übersetzen* means "to translate" or "to ferry across". The difference shows in speech (stress), in writing (where *ge-* and *zu* go) and in the sentence (separated or not). This lesson sorts the **[[particle verbs]]** (*Partikelverben*, separable) from the **[[prefix verbs]]** (*Präfixverben*, inseparable), goes through the seven prefixes that can be both, and recaps what *be-, ent-, er-, ver-* and *zer-* do, with verbs from the sea.

The theme is the sea and sailing.

## A sailing trip

Read this (invented) reportage. Notice the verbs with *um-, über-, durch-* and *auf-*.

> **Gegen den Wind**
>
> Um sieben Uhr morgens legen wir in Stralsund ab. Die „Möwe“, ein alter Kutter, den drei Freunde vor zehn Jahren vor dem Abwracken bewahrt haben, ist kein schnelles Schiff, aber ein gutmütiges. Skipperin Anke Rauh steht am Ruder, der Rest der Crew lehnt an der Reling und beobachtet die Brandung an der Sandbank.
>
> Der Plan klingt einfach: die Insel Rügen umsegeln, das Kap im Norden umschiffen und am Abend in einer Bucht auf der Ostseite ankern. Doch die See hat andere Pläne. Kaum haben wir die Meerenge hinter uns, schläft der Wind ein. Flaute. Das Großsegel hängt schlaff am Mast, und an Deck wird es still.
>
> „Früher hätte man jetzt gewartet“, sagt Rauh. „Heute wirft man den Motor an und tut so, als sei das selbstverständlich.“ Sie erzählt von den Gezeiten an der Nordsee, wo man ohne Gezeitenkalender schnell auf einer Sandbank aufläuft, und von einem Freund, dessen Boot vor Jahren in einem Sturm gekentert ist. Die Seenotretter haben ihn nach zwei Stunden aus dem Wasser gezogen. „Seitdem fährt er nur noch mit Rettungsweste. Und er übersetzt Bücher über die Seefahrt – vom Schreibtisch aus.“
>
> Am Nachmittag kommt der Wind zurück, erst zögernd, dann kräftig aus Nordwest. Wir kreuzen gegen die Wellen, der Bug taucht tief ein, Gischt fliegt über das Deck bis zum Heck. Den Leuchtturm am Kap sehen wir lange, bevor wir ihn erreichen. Als wir ihn endlich umrundet haben, jubelt die Crew, als hätten wir den Atlantik durchquert.
>
> Abends, vor Anker in einer stillen Bucht, sitzen wir an Deck. Schiffbruch, sagt Rauh, erleide man selten auf hoher See, sondern meistens in Küstennähe, wo man sich sicher fühlt. Dann lacht sie: „Aber das ist kein Grund, an Land zu bleiben.“

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Against the wind**

At seven in the morning we cast off in Stralsund. The *Möwe* ("Gull"), an old cutter that three friends saved from the scrapyard ten years ago, isn't a fast boat, but a good-natured one. Skipper Anke Rauh is at the helm; the rest of the crew lean on the rail and watch the surf on the sandbank.

The plan sounds simple: sail around the island of Rügen, round the cape in the north and anchor in a bay on the east side in the evening. But the sea has other plans. We have hardly left the strait behind us when the wind dies. Calm. The mainsail hangs limp on the mast, and on deck it goes quiet.

"In the old days you would have waited now," says Rauh. "Today you start the engine and act as if that were the most natural thing in the world." She tells us about the tides in the North Sea, where without a tide table you soon run aground on a sandbank, and about a friend whose boat capsized in a storm years ago. The sea rescuers pulled him out of the water after two hours. "Since then he only sails in a life jacket. And he translates books about seafaring – from his desk."

In the afternoon the wind comes back, hesitantly at first, then strongly from the north-west. We beat against the waves, the bow dips deep, spray flies across the deck to the stern. We see the lighthouse on the cape long before we reach it. When we have finally rounded it, the crew cheers as if we had crossed the Atlantic.

In the evening, at anchor in a quiet bay, we sit on deck. Shipwreck, says Rauh, rarely happens on the high seas, but mostly near the coast, where you feel safe. Then she laughs: "But that's no reason to stay on land."

</details>

*Umsegeln, umschiffen, umrunden* and *durchqueren* are inseparable here: the stress is on the verb stem, the participle has no *ge-* (*umrundet, durchquert*), and each has an accusative object (*die Insel, das Kap, ihn, den Atlantik*). *Ablegen, einschlafen, anwerfen, auflaufen* are separable: *legen … ab, schläft … ein, wirft … an, aufläuft* (verb last in the subordinate clause). And *übersetzt* is the inseparable "translates", which the skipper uses as a joke: the friend no longer *setzt über* (ferries across) but *übersetzt* (translates).

## Separable or inseparable: the tests

| Test | Particle verb (separable) | Prefix verb (inseparable) |
|---|---|---|
| stress | on the particle: *'umfahren* | on the stem: *um'fahren* |
| main clause | particle at the end: *Er fährt das Schild um.* | stays together: *Er umfährt das Hindernis.* |
| participle | *ge-* inside: *umgefahren* | no *ge-*: *umfahren* |
| zu-infinitive | *zu* inside: *umzufahren* | *zu* in front: *zu umfahren* |
| typical meaning | literal, spatial, often a change of position | figurative or "all around / all through", often with an accusative object |

The written tests (participle and zu-infinitive) are the reliable ones. Stress is how you tell them apart in listening.

## The seven two-way prefixes

*durch-, über-, um-, unter-, wider-, hinter-* and *voll-* can be separable particles or inseparable prefixes. The general pattern: as a particle the word keeps its spatial meaning; as a prefix it covers or passes through its object, often figuratively.

| Verb | Separable (stress on the particle) | Inseparable (stress on the stem) |
|---|---|---|
| *umfahren* | to knock down: *Er hat das Verkehrsschild umgefahren.* | to drive round: *Wir haben den Stau umfahren.* |
| *umschiffen* | to transfer to another ship (rare): *Die Fracht wurde umgeschifft.* | to sail round; to get round a problem: *Sie hat die heikle Frage elegant umschifft.* |
| *übersetzen* | to ferry across: *Wir sind ans andere Ufer übergesetzt.* | to translate: *Sie hat den Roman übersetzt.* |
| *überziehen* | to put on over: *Zieh dir eine Jacke über!* | to overdraw, to overrun: *Er hat sein Konto überzogen. Die Rednerin hat überzogen.* |
| *unterhalten* | to hold underneath (colloquial): *Halt mal den Eimer unter!* | to entertain, to maintain, (*sich*) to talk: *Wir haben uns lange unterhalten.* |
| *durchschauen* | to look through (colloquial): *Schau mal hier durch!* | to see through someone: *Ich habe ihn sofort durchschaut.* |
| *umgehen* | to deal with: *Sie ist gut mit der Kritik umgegangen.* | to circumvent: *Er hat die Vorschrift umgangen.* |
| *unterstellen* | to take shelter: *Wir haben uns unter der Brücke untergestellt.* | to insinuate: *Sie unterstellt mir böse Absicht.* |
| *durchbrechen* | to break in two: *Der Mast ist durchgebrochen.* | to break through: *Die Wellen durchbrachen den Deich.* |
| *wiederholen* | to fetch back: *Er hat sich sein Werkzeug wiedergeholt.* | to repeat: *Können Sie das wiederholen?* |

*wieder-* is not one of the seven (it is almost always separable), but *wiederholen* is the best-known pair of all.

The remaining three prefixes lean to one side:

- **wider-** is inseparable in most verbs (*widersprechen, widerstehen, widerlegen*: *Er widersprach*); it is separable in *widerspiegeln* and *widerhallen* (*Das Ergebnis spiegelt die Stimmung wider*).
- **hinter-** is inseparable in standard German (*hinterlassen, hinterfragen, hintergehen*, C1 *hinterziehen*). Separable uses (*Geh mal hinter!*, "go to the back") are colloquial and regional.
- **voll-** is inseparable in a few old verbs with abstract meaning (*vollenden, vollbringen, vollziehen*: *Er hat das Werk vollendet*) and separable when it means "full" (*volltanken, vollschreiben, volllaufen*: *Das Boot ist vollgelaufen*).

## Valency and auxiliary

The inseparable verbs of this lesson take an accusative object, the thing that is surrounded, crossed or passed under, and form the Perfekt with *haben*, even though they describe movement:

- *Sie hat die Insel umsegelt.* (*segeln* alone: *Sie ist nach Rügen gesegelt.*)
- *Er hat den Atlantik durchquert.*
- *Der Tunnel unterquert den Fluss; die Bahn hat den Fluss unterquert.*

The separable verbs of movement often have no object and take *sein*: *Wir sind übergesetzt. Das Boot ist aufgelaufen.* With an object they take *haben*: *Der Fährmann hat uns übergesetzt.*

## Hearing the difference

Stress is the only clue in speech when the form is ambiguous:

- *Er hat den Pfosten 'umgefahren.* — He knocked the post over. *Er hat den Pfosten um'fahren.* — He drove round the post. Here the participles differ (*umgefahren / umfahren*), but in a subordinate clause the forms are spelled alike: *…, wenn du den Pfosten 'umfährst* (knock it over) vs *…, wenn du den Pfosten um'fährst* (drive round it).
- *Wir wollen bei Sassnitz 'übersetzen.* — We want to cross over at Sassnitz. *Wir wollen den Text über'setzen.* — We want to translate the text.

Listen for which syllable is loud and long, and check whether the verb has an object that could be "gone round".

## Nouns from the two kinds

The two verbs behind one spelling often produce different nouns, and the noun tells you which verb is meant. Lesson 06's *Ortsumgehung* is a good example: a bypass goes round a town, so it comes from inseparable *um'gehen*.

| Separable verb | Its noun | Inseparable verb | Its noun |
|---|---|---|---|
| *'umgehen mit* (to deal with) | *der Umgang* (*der Umgang mit Kritik*) | *um'gehen* (to circumvent) | *die Umgehung* (*die Umgehung des Gesetzes, die Ortsumgehung*) |
| *'übersetzen* (to ferry across) | *die Überfahrt*, *das Übersetzen* | *über'setzen* (to translate) | *die Übersetzung* |
| *'unterhalten* (to hold under) | none in use | *unter'halten* (to entertain; to maintain) | *die Unterhaltung* (conversation; entertainment), *der Unterhalt* (upkeep; maintenance payments) |
| *'unterstellen* (to shelter) | *der Unterstand* (shelter) | *unter'stellen* (to insinuate) | *die Unterstellung* (insinuation) |
| *'überziehen* (to put on) | *der Überzieher* (old-fashioned: overcoat) | *über'ziehen* (to overdraw) | *die Überziehung* (*der Überziehungszins*) |

The *-ung* nouns usually keep the stress where the verb has it: *Über'setzung, Um'gehung, Unter'stellung*. Nouns without *-ung* tend to stress the first syllable: *'Umgang, 'Überfahrt, 'Unterhalt*. In listening, this is one more clue to which verb lies behind a noun.

Don't build an *-ung* noun from a separable verb just because the inseparable one has one: *die Übersetzung* is always a translation, never a crossing.

## be-, ent-, er-, ver-, zer- at sea

The inseparable prefixes from C1 have recognizable patterns. None is a strict rule, but each helps you guess a new verb.

| Prefix | Typical effect | Sea verbs |
|---|---|---|
| *be-* | makes a verb transitive: the object is covered or reached | *ein Gewässer befahren* (to navigate), *das Schiff beladen* (to load) |
| *ent-* | removal, away from | *entladen* (to unload), *entkommen* (to escape) |
| *er-* | result, often a final one | *ertrinken* (to drown, die in water), *erreichen* (to reach) |
| *ver-* | away, wrong, or completely | *verschiffen* (to ship off), *versenken* (to sink something), *sich verfahren* (to lose one's way) |
| *zer-* | destruction, into pieces | *zerschellen* (to be smashed): *Das Schiff zerschellte an den Klippen.* |

One trap: *entern* (to board a ship by force) has no prefix at all. It is usually traced to a Dutch verb, ultimately from Spanish *entrar*: *Die Piraten enterten das Schiff* (weak, regular).

## The words of this lesson

- **The ship.** *der Bug* (bow) and *das Heck* (stern); *das Deck*; *die Reling* (rail); *der Mast*; *die Takelage* (rigging); *das Ruder* (rudder or helm; also the oar of a rowing boat); *der Anker* and *ankern*. Left and right are *das Backbord* and *das Steuerbord* (Duden: Seewesen, Flugwesen; Austria also *der*); as adverbs *backbord(s)* and *steuerbord(s)*: *Land backbord voraus!*
- **Boats and people.** *der Kutter* (cutter, a small fishing or sailing vessel), *der Segler / die Seglerin* (sailor in the sporting sense; also a sailing ship), *der Seemann* (seaman; plural *die Seeleute*), *die Seefahrt* (seafaring, navigation).
- **The sea.** *die Gezeiten* (plural: tides; Ebbe und Flut), *die Brandung* (surf), *die Meerenge* (strait), *die Flaute* (calm; figuratively a slack period: *Flaute auf dem Arbeitsmarkt*), *der Leuchtturm* (lighthouse).
- **Trouble.** *kentern* (to capsize), *auflaufen* (to run aground), *stranden* (to be stranded, of ships and of people: *in Paris gestrandet*), *der Schiffbruch* (shipwreck; *Schiffbruch erleiden*, also figuratively: a plan fails), *schiffbrüchig* (shipwrecked), *die Seenot* (distress at sea: *in Seenot geraten*), *der Seenotretter* (sea rescuer). All three verbs take *sein*.
- **Crossing and going round.** *umschiffen, umsegeln, durchqueren, unterqueren* (inseparable, with *haben*).
- **Grammar talk.** *das Partikelverb, das Präfixverb, untrennbar* (inseparable; the opposite of *trennbar*).

## Common mistakes

- Using the wrong participle: ~~*Wir haben die Insel umgesegelt*~~ → *Wir haben die Insel umsegelt.* ~~*Er hat das Schild umfahren*~~ when you mean he knocked it over → *umgefahren*.
- Choosing *sein* for an inseparable transitive verb of motion: ~~*Sie ist den Atlantik durchquert*~~ → *Sie hat den Atlantik durchquert.*
- Splitting an inseparable verb: ~~*Er setzt den Text über*~~ → *Er übersetzt den Text.*
- Treating every *wider-* verb as separable (~~*Er sprach mir wider*~~ → *Er widersprach mir*) or every *voll-* verb as inseparable (~~*Ich habe vollgeendet*~~ / ~~*Ich habe den Tank volltankt*~~ → *vollendet*, *vollgetankt*).
- Reading *entern* as *ent-* + *ern*.
- Stressing the wrong syllable when reading aloud: *über'setzen* (translate) said as *'übersetzen* means "ferry across".

## Key points

- Particle verbs (separable): stressed particle, *ge-* and *zu* inside, particle at the end in main clauses; prefix verbs (inseparable): stressed stem, no *ge-*, *zu* in front.
- *durch-, über-, um-, unter-* can be both: literal and spatial as particles, figurative or "all round / all through" as prefixes; *wider-* and *hinter-* are mostly inseparable, *voll-* is separable except in *vollenden, vollbringen, vollziehen*.
- Inseparable verbs of crossing and going round take an accusative object and *haben*: *die Insel umsegeln, den Fluss unterqueren*.
- *be-* transitivizes, *ent-* removes, *er-* marks a result, *ver-* away/wrong/completely, *zer-* destruction; *entern* is not *ent-*.
- In listening, stress decides: *'umfahren* (knock down) vs *um'fahren* (go round).

lessons.title: "The Awful German Language": Mark Twain's complaints, checked
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In 1880 Mark Twain published *A Tramp Abroad*, an account of his travels through Germany, Switzerland and Italy; he had spent several months of 1878 in Germany, much of it in Heidelberg, and tried hard to learn the language. Appendix D of the book, "The Awful German Language", is the most famous complaint ever written about German. It is very funny, and it is also a tour of exactly the grammar this module has been about: gender and case, the sentence bracket and separable verbs, compounds and adjective endings.

This lesson reads Twain's complaints the way a C2 learner can: for each one, what is true, what is exaggerated and what he got wrong. Then it turns the tables with a reply in German, written in his ironic tone.

Quotations are from Appendix D of *A Tramp Abroad* (first published by the American Publishing Company, Hartford, 1880; public domain), as transcribed by Project Gutenberg (eBook #119, also issued in parts as #5782–5788). Twain's English is easy; his German examples follow the spelling of his time.

## The verdict

Near the end of the appendix, after his proposals for reform, Twain sums up with a calculation:

> "My philological studies have satisfied me that a gifted person ought to learn English (barring spelling and pronouncing) in thirty hours, French in thirty days, and German in thirty years."

**True:** German has more inflection than English or French: four cases, three genders, adjective endings, strong verbs, and word order that depends on clause type. **Exaggerated:** obviously. And note his own exception in brackets: English spelling and pronunciation are among the least regular of any European language, which German speakers learning English find just as awful.

## Gender

> "Every noun has a gender, and there is no sense or system in the distribution; so the gender of each must be learned separately and by heart."

> "In German, a young lady has no sex, while a turnip has."

**True:** grammatical gender (*das Genus*) is not natural sex, and for many simple nouns nothing predicts it: *der Löffel, die Gabel, das Messer*. Learners do have to learn the article with the noun.

**Exaggerated:** "no sense or system" ignores the suffixes, which settle the gender of a large part of the vocabulary. Nouns formed with the suffixes *-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft* and the Latin *-tion/-sion* are feminine; diminutives in *-chen* and *-lein* are neuter (*der Kuchen* doesn't count: its *-chen* is no suffix); nouns in *-ismus* and *-ling* are masculine. *Das Mädchen* is neuter because it is a diminutive in *-chen*, without exception, which is far more system than Twain admits. *Die Rübe* (turnip) is feminine like most nouns in *-e* that aren't people or animals.

There is one real wrinkle he could have exploited: what pronoun refers back to *das Mädchen*? Grammatically *es*, and that is usual right after the noun; further away, *sie* is common and accepted (*Das Mädchen kam herein. Sie setzte sich ans Fenster.*). German, too, lets natural gender win over grammar at a distance.

**Wrong:** in another passage Twain lists genders:

> "a tree is male, its buds are female, its leaves are neuter; horses are sexless, dogs are male, cats are female—tomcats included, of course"

*Der Baum, die Knospe, das Blatt, das Pferd, der Hund, die Katze*: all correct. But the tomcat is *der Kater*, masculine. Twain either didn't know or couldn't resist the joke. (*Der Hengst* and *die Stute* give horses their sexes back, and the female dog is *die Hündin*.)

## Cases and adjective endings

> "When a German gets his hands on an adjective, he declines it, and keeps on declining it until the common sense is all declined out of it."

**True:** an attributive adjective has different endings after *der*-words, after *ein*-words and with no article, in four cases and three genders plus the plural. Learners see a lot of *-e, -en, -er, -es, -em*.

**Exaggerated:** behind the tables is one principle: the noun phrase shows its case and gender once, clearly. If the article does it (*der, dem, des*), the adjective takes a weak ending (*-e* or *-en*); if there is no article or the article shows nothing (*ein* in the nominative masculine and the nominative and accusative neuter), the adjective takes the strong ending: *ein alter Mann, mit frischem Wasser*. Once you see that, the "declining" is a signal system, not madness.

Twain also had a proposal:

> "In the first place, I would leave out the Dative case."

This is where history is ironic. Of the three oblique cases, the dative is the one that is spreading: in colloquial German it competes with the genitive after *wegen, trotz* and other prepositions (*wegen dem Wetter*), while the genitive is retreating from speech (honors lesson 10h2). Twain picked the wrong case to abolish.

## The sentence bracket and separable verbs

> "The Germans have another kind of parenthesis, which they make by splitting a verb in two and putting half of it at the beginning of an exciting chapter and the OTHER HALF at the end of it." (capitals as in the Project Gutenberg text)

His favourite example is *reiste ab* ("departed"), with *ab* arriving many lines after *reiste*.

**True:** this is the *Satzklammer* (also *Verbklammer*): finite verb in second position, the rest at the end, and everything else in between (lessons 07 and 08). A long Mittelfeld does make readers wait.

**Exaggerated:** no German writer puts the particle a chapter away; style guides warn against long brackets, journalists move material into the Nachfeld, and speakers do it constantly (*Er reiste ab, nachdem …*). And the bracket has a use Twain doesn't mention: the closing part tells you that the clause is complete and what kind of action it was. *Er fuhr das Schild …* could still become *um* (knocked it down) or something else; the end of the bracket resolves it, much as a closing bracket does in mathematics.

He also mocks verb-final subordinate clauses with a sentence from a German novel he had been reading (Twain names it as *The Old Mamselle's Secret*, by Mrs. Marlitt). As the Project Gutenberg text prints it, in a footnote:

> *Wenn er aber auf der Strasse der in Sammt und Seide gehuellten jetz sehr ungenirt nach der neusten mode gekleideten Regierungsrathin begegnet.*

Read it like a period from lesson 07. The frame is *Wenn er aber auf der Strasse der … Regierungsrathin begegnet*: "But when he meets the wife of the government official in the street". Between *der* and *Regierungsrathin* stand two participial attributes: *in Sammt und Seide gehuellten* (today *gehüllten*: wrapped in velvet and silk) and *jetz(t) sehr ungenirt nach der neusten Mode gekleideten* (now dressed very freely in the latest fashion). It is a hard sentence, but it is a legitimate German noun phrase with stacked attributes (C1 lesson 08), not chaos.

The spellings are of their time:

| Twain's text | Today | Why |
|---|---|---|
| *Strasse* | *Straße* | English printers often set the German *ß* as *ss*; *ss* is standard in Switzerland today |
| *Sammt* | *Samt* | older spelling with double consonant |
| *ungenirt* | *ungeniert* | loanwords in *-iren* were later standardized as *-ieren* |
| *Regierungsrathin* | *Regierungsrätin* | *th* in native words (*Rath, Thür*) was dropped in the standardized spelling of 1901; the transcription prints no umlaut |
| *jetz*, *mode* | *jetzt*, *Mode* | probably slips in the source or in printing |
| *gehuellten* | *gehüllten* | *ue* for *ü* is a typewriter-style spelling, probably the transcription's; the 1880 print could not be checked |

In Twain's time, a title like *Regierungsrätin* usually named the wife of a *Regierungsrat*; today it is a woman who holds the office herself.

## Compounds

> "These things are not words, they are alphabetical processions."

His examples: *Freundschaftsbezeigungen, Dilettantenaufdringlichkeiten, Stadtverordnetenversammlungen*.

**True:** German writes compounds as one word (*die Zusammenschreibung*), and a compound can be as long as the speaker likes. Some are real monsters, *Wortungetüme*, as Germans themselves call them.

**Exaggerated:** the difference from English is largely one of spelling. *City council meetings* is also a compound of three nouns; English just writes it with spaces. *Stadtverordnetenversammlung* is still the official name of the town council in Hesse and Brandenburg, and to a German reader it is one transparent word: assembly of the city's deputies. *Dilettantenaufdringlichkeiten* (the importunities of amateurs), on the other hand, is a rare and rather comic word.

**What he got right without saying it:** the capital letters (*die Großschreibung*) that mark every noun make these processions much easier to parse than they would be in lower case.

## A reply in Twain's tone

Irony works by keeping a straight face. Here is an original reply, written as if German grammar itself had answered him, in the formal register of an 1880s letter.

> Sehr geehrter Mr. Twain,
>
> mit großem Vergnügen und einer gewissen Kränkung habe ich Ihre Abhandlung über die schreckliche deutsche Sprache gelesen. Erlauben Sie mir, im Namen der Rübe, des Mädchens und aller übrigen Hauptwörter, die Sie so ungerecht behandelt haben, einige Richtigstellungen vorzunehmen.
>
> Zunächst das Geschlecht. Sie klagen, ein Mädchen habe bei uns keines, eine Rübe dagegen schon. Das ist wahr. Aber ist es unsere Schuld, dass das Mädchen auf -chen endet? Jede Verkleinerungsform auf -chen ist sächlich, ausnahmslos, und mehr Ordnung kann man von einer Sprache billigerweise nicht verlangen. Ihr Kater übrigens ist männlich, wie es sich gehört; Sie haben ihn offenbar mit seiner Gattin verwechselt.
>
> Dann das Verb, das Sie so ungern am Ende des Satzes suchen. Wir stellen es dorthin, damit der Leser bis zum Schluss aufmerksam bleibt – eine Höflichkeit, die man im Englischen, wo alles Wichtige gleich am Anfang verraten wird, schmerzlich vermisst. Wer einen deutschen Satz liest, erlebt Spannung; wer einen englischen liest, kennt das Ende, bevor er Platz genommen hat.
>
> Was die Zusammensetzungen angeht, so schreiben wir nur zusammen, was zusammengehört. Sie schreiben „city council meeting“ in drei Wörtern und glauben, es seien drei Dinge. Es ist aber eine einzige Versammlung, und sie verdient ein einziges Wort.
>
> Ihren Vorschlag, den Dativ abzuschaffen, haben wir sorgfältig geprüft. Er ist abgelehnt worden. Der Dativ erfreut sich seither bester Gesundheit und hat sogar begonnen, dem Genitiv seine Präpositionen abspenstig zu machen.
>
> In vorzüglicher Hochachtung und mit nachgestellten Verben verbleibe ich
>
> Ihre ergebene deutsche Grammatik

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

Dear Mr Twain,

It was with great pleasure and a certain sense of injury that I read your treatise on the awful German language. Allow me, in the name of the turnip, the maiden and all the other nouns you have treated so unjustly, to make a few corrections.

First, gender. You complain that with us a maiden has none, whereas a turnip does. That is true. But is it our fault that *Mädchen* ends in *-chen*? Every diminutive in *-chen* is neuter, without exception, and one can hardly in fairness ask more order of a language. Your tomcat, by the way, is masculine, as is only proper; you have evidently mistaken him for his wife.

Next, the verb, which you so dislike having to look for at the end of the sentence. We put it there so that the reader stays attentive to the very end, a courtesy sorely missed in English, where everything important is given away at the start. Whoever reads a German sentence experiences suspense; whoever reads an English one knows the ending before he has sat down.

As for compounds, we only write together what belongs together. You write "city council meeting" in three words and believe they are three things. But it is one single meeting, and it deserves one single word.

We have carefully examined your proposal to abolish the dative. It has been rejected. Since then the dative has been enjoying the best of health and has even begun to lure the genitive's prepositions away from it.

With the highest esteem and with verbs placed last, I remain

Your devoted German Grammar

</details>

How the irony works: the writer agrees with Twain's facts (*Das ist wahr*) and then reinterprets them as virtues (the verb at the end as a courtesy, the long compound as precision). The formal register (*Erlauben Sie mir, billigerweise, In vorzüglicher Hochachtung … verbleibe ich*) is exaggerated just enough to show that the writer isn't entirely serious. And the last joke returns Twain's dative proposal to him with the fact he couldn't know: the dative won.

## The words of this lesson

- **Grammar talk.** *das Genus* (grammatical gender; plural *die Genera*), *der Kasus* (case; plural *die Kasus*, with a long *u*), *die Satzklammer* and *die Verbklammer* (the sentence bracket and the bracket formed by the two parts of the verb), *nachgestellt* (placed after: *ein nachgestelltes Adjektiv, nachgestellte Verben*), *die Zusammenschreibung* (writing as one word; the opposite is *die Getrenntschreibung*), *die Großschreibung* (capitalization).
- **Monsters.** *das Ungetüm* is a monster or a monstrously big thing (*ein Ungetüm von einem Schrank*); *das Wortungetüm* is a monster word, usually a long compound.
- **Mockery.** *der Spötter / die Spötterin* (mocker, scoffer), *spöttisch* (mocking, derisive); *der Humorist / die Humoristin* (humorist, a writer of comic prose; also a comic performer); *das Reisebuch* (travel book).
- **Despair.** *verzweifeln* (to despair: *an der deutschen Grammatik verzweifeln*), with *sein* (Duden: *haben* is veraltet): *Er ist fast verzweifelt.*

## Common mistakes

- Taking Twain literally. His essay is affectionate exaggeration by a writer who kept working at German and later in life spoke it in public.
- Thinking that German gender is completely arbitrary: for derived nouns, the suffix decides.
- Believing that the verb-final rule makes German "harder to understand": in speech, native speakers routinely use the Nachfeld and short brackets.
- Reading old spellings as mistakes: *Strasse, Sammt, ungenirt* reflect the conventions of their time and the habits of English printers (and *gehuellten* probably those of a later transcriber).
- Writing an ironic reply that is merely rude. Irony needs a straight face: agree, then reinterpret.

## Key points

- Twain's complaints point at real features: gender, case and adjective endings, the sentence bracket and separable verbs, and compounds.
- What he exaggerated: the system behind gender suffixes and adjective endings, the length of real brackets, the "strangeness" of compounds (English has them too, written with spaces).
- What he got wrong: *der Kater* is masculine; and the dative he wanted to abolish is the case that is spreading.
- His German examples show the spelling of his time (*Strasse, Sammt, ungenirt, Regierungsrathin*).
- An ironic reply agrees with the facts and reinterprets them; the register does the rest.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Gewinkt oder gewunken? Doubtful cases of German grammar
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At C2 you will sometimes hear two forms where your textbooks taught one: *gewinkt* and *gewunken*, *wegen des Regens* and *wegen dem Regen*, *ich habe gesessen* and *ich bin gesessen*. Native speakers argue about such pairs, and language columns answer letters about them every week. These are **[[doubtful cases]]** (*Zweifelsfälle*): places where two forms compete, both are in use, and the reference works either allow both or describe a difference in region, register or meaning.

This lesson sorts the main types (gender **[[doublets]]**, plurals with different meanings, verbs and nouns in flux, *wegen*, *haben* or *sein*, the dative *-e*), explains who decides what in German, and distinguishes the **[[prescriptive]]** view (how one should write) from the **[[descriptive]]** view (how people do write). The facts come from the dictionaries; the examples and explanations are this course's own.

## A language column

Read this (invented) reader's question and the answer from a newspaper's language advice service.

> **Leserfrage: Gewinkt oder gewunken?**
>
> „Meine Kollegin behauptet, ‚gewunken‘ sei falsch. Ich sage das seit Jahrzehnten so. Wer hat recht?“ – Martina H., Kassel
>
> **Antwort der Redaktion**
>
> Liebe Frau H., Sie dürfen aufatmen – und Ihre Kollegin auch. Beide Formen sind in Gebrauch, und die großen Wörterbücher verzeichnen beide: ‚gewinkt‘ als die ältere, schwache Form, ‚gewunken‘ als Nebenform, die sich nach dem Muster von ‚trinken – getrunken‘ oder ‚sinken – gesunken‘ gebildet hat. Dass ein schwaches Verb ein starkes Partizip annimmt, ist ungewöhnlich. Meist verläuft der Wandel umgekehrt, von stark zu schwach: Das Präteritum ‚buk‘ etwa ist heute weitgehend durch ‚backte‘ ersetzt.
>
> Ist ‚gewunken‘ also ein Fehler? Wer vorschreiben möchte, wie man zu sprechen hat, wird das bejahen. Wer beschreibt, wie tatsächlich gesprochen und geschrieben wird, kommt zu einem anderen Ergebnis: In der Alltagssprache ist ‚gewunken‘ weit verbreitet, und auch in Zeitungen findet man es. Für eine Bewerbung oder einen Bericht an die Geschäftsleitung würden wir Ihnen trotzdem zu ‚gewinkt‘ raten – nicht, weil die andere Form falsch wäre, sondern weil manche Leser sie dafür halten.
>
> Übrigens: Eine Behörde, die solche Fragen verbindlich entscheidet, gibt es für die Grammatik nicht. Der Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung ist, wie sein Name sagt, für die Rechtschreibung zuständig. Ob man ‚gewinkt‘ oder ‚gewunken‘ sagt, ‚wegen des Regens‘ oder ‚wegen dem Regen‘, ‚ich habe gesessen‘ oder ‚ich bin gesessen‘, entscheiden am Ende die Sprecherinnen und Sprecher – und im Zweifel die Erwartungen Ihrer Leser.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen, Ihre Sprachberatung

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Reader's question: gewinkt or gewunken?**

"My colleague claims that 'gewunken' is wrong. I've been saying it for decades. Who is right?" – Martina H., Kassel

**The editors' reply**

Dear Ms H., you can breathe a sigh of relief, and so can your colleague. Both forms are in use, and the major dictionaries list both: 'gewinkt' as the older, weak form, 'gewunken' as a variant formed on the pattern of 'trinken – getrunken' or 'sinken – gesunken'. It is unusual for a weak verb to take on a strong participle. Change usually goes the other way, from strong to weak: the past tense 'buk', for example, has today largely been replaced by 'backte'.

So is 'gewunken' a mistake? Anyone who wants to prescribe how people should speak will say yes. Anyone who describes how people actually speak and write comes to a different conclusion: in everyday language 'gewunken' is widespread, and you find it in newspapers too. For a job application or a report to the management, we would still advise you to use 'gewinkt': not because the other form is wrong, but because some readers think it is.

By the way, there is no authority that decides such questions with binding force for grammar. The Council for German Orthography is, as its name says, responsible for spelling. Whether you say 'gewinkt' or 'gewunken', 'wegen des Regens' or 'wegen dem Regen', 'ich habe gesessen' or 'ich bin gesessen' is in the end decided by the speakers, and, when in doubt, by what your readers expect.

Kind regards, your language advice service

</details>

The column takes a position that is typical of today's language advice: describe the facts, then advise by register. Duden, too, gives *gewinkt* first and adds *auch: gewunken*, noting that the second form is frequent.

## Who decides?

**Spelling** has an official norm: the *Amtliches Regelwerk* with its word list, maintained by the **Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung**. Its statute (2005, amended 2015) gives it the tasks of observing how people write, clarifying doubtful cases of spelling and proposing adjustments where language changes. Its members come from Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, South Tyrol and the German-speaking Community of Belgium. Its proposals become binding for schools and public administration only when the state authorities adopt them; for everyone else, the rules are a standard, not a law.

**Duden** had a special role from 1955, when the education ministers of the West German Länder declared it authoritative in doubtful cases of spelling. That ended with the reform of 1996: since then the official rules decide, and Duden is one dictionary among several (with Wahrig and the online DWDS), although still the best known.

**Grammar** has no official body at all. Grammars and usage dictionaries (Duden's volumes on grammar and on doubtful cases, the grammars of the Leibniz-Institut für Deutsche Sprache, the DWDS) describe usage, mark forms as regional, colloquial or old-fashioned, and recommend. That is the background to every case below: "Duden says" means "the dictionary records", not "the law requires".

## Gender doublets

Some nouns have two genders in standard German, sometimes with a regional distribution, sometimes with a difference in meaning.

| Noun | What Duden records |
|---|---|
| *Joghurt* | *der* or (especially in Austria and Switzerland) *das*; *die* only in eastern Austrian dialect |
| *Virus* | *das* (in medicine and biology); outside technical language also *der*; the computer virus is mostly *der* |
| *Teil* | *der Teil*: a portion of a whole (*der größte Teil der Strecke*); *das Teil*: a separate piece (*das Ersatzteil*; colloquially "thing": *Was ist das für ein Teil?*); in some phrases both occur (*ich für mein[en] Teil*) |

The lesson for writers: in a formal text, use the gender your reader's region expects; in a technical text, use the technical gender (*das Virus*).

## Plurals that mean different things

Some nouns have two plurals with different meanings. These are not free variants:

- *die Banken* (financial institutions) / *die Bänke* (benches)
- *die Wörter* (individual words, as in a list or a dictionary: *ein Text mit 500 Wörtern*) / *die Worte* (connected words, utterances: *Worte des Dankes, mit anderen Worten*). The distinction is a strong tendency; in some fixed uses either is found.
- *die Mütter* (mothers) / *die Muttern* (nuts, for bolts)
- *die Sträuße* (bouquets) / *die Strauße* (ostriches)

## Forms in flux

Some verbs and nouns are moving from one inflection pattern to another, and both forms are in use:

- **winken**: *gewinkt*, also *gewunken* (Duden; frequent in speech). The unusual direction: weak to strong.
- **senden**: in the sense "to send", *sandte, gesandt* are the more common forms, *sendete, gesendet* less common; in the sense "to broadcast" and in technology *sendete, gesendet*, except in Switzerland, where Duden gives *sandte, gesandt* for broadcasting too.
- **backen**: the old Präteritum *buk* has largely given way to *backte*; the participle stays *gebacken*.
- **weak masculine nouns**: *der Präsident, den Präsidenten, dem Präsidenten*. In colloquial speech the ending is often dropped (*mit dem Präsident*); in standard written German it is required.

## wegen + genitive or dative

In standard written German, *wegen* takes the genitive: *wegen des Regens*. The dative (*wegen dem Regen*) is colloquial and in the south also regional; in a formal text it reads as a register slip. Two cases where the dative is standard:

- when the genitive would not be visible, as with plural nouns without an article: *wegen Geschäften* (not ~~*wegen Geschäfte*~~);
- with personal pronouns, where *meinetwegen, deinetwegen* are the standard forms and *wegen mir* is colloquial.

## haben or sein with sitzen, liegen, stehen

In northern and central Germany, *sitzen, liegen* and *stehen* form the Perfekt with *haben*; in southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland with *sein*. Duden records both as standard in their regions: *ich habe gesessen* / (südd., österr., schweiz.) *ich bin gesessen*, and *liegen* and *stehen* follow the same regional pattern. A text for an Austrian newspaper that writes *ich habe gesessen* is as correct as a text for a Hamburg paper that writes it.

## The dative -e

Masculine and neuter nouns could once take *-e* in the dative singular: *dem Kinde, im Hause, auf dem Lande*. Today the ending is optional and sounds elevated or old-fashioned (*in diesem Sinne*). It survives in fixed phrases where leaving it out would sound wrong: *zu Hause, nach Hause, im Grunde genommen, zu Tode, im Zuge*.

## Ersteres and Letzteres

To refer back to the first and the last of two things just mentioned, German uses *der/die/das Erstere* and *der/die/das Letztere*, capitalized since the 1996 reform because they are used as nouns: *Man kann den Zug oder das Auto nehmen; Letzteres ist teurer.* They sound formal; in speech one would say *das Auto ist teurer*. Don't use them with three or more items, where they become unclear.

## Prescriptive and descriptive

The two views answer different questions. **[[Prescriptive]]** advice (*Sprachpflege*, the tradition of "caring for" the language, and popular *Sprachratgeber*) tells you which form to use and often warns against change; Bastian Sick's bestseller *Der Dativ ist dem Genitiv sein Tod* (2004) is the best-known recent example of the genre. **[[Descriptive]]** linguistics records what speakers do, how forms are distributed by region and register, and how they change; it does not call widespread forms "wrong", but it notes where they are not *standardsprachlich* (standard).

For a C2 writer, the practical rule combines both: know the form that careful readers expect in formal writing (the *Hauptform*), know the variants (*Nebenformen*) and where they are normal, and choose by text type and reader. A *Normabweichung* in a chat is style; in a job application it is a risk.

## The words of this lesson

- *der Zweifelsfall* (doubtful case), *die Dublette* (doublet: two forms of one word, also a duplicate in a collection), *die Schwankung* and *schwanken* (variation, to vary or fluctuate: *Die Form schwankt zwischen stark und schwach*).
- *die Sprachnorm* (linguistic norm), *die Normabweichung* (deviation from the norm), *normgerecht* (conforming to the norm), *standardsprachlich* (standard, in standard language).
- *die Hauptform* and *die Nebenform* (main and variant form).
- *präskriptiv* and *deskriptiv*; *die Sprachpflege* (cultivation of the language, the prescriptive tradition); *der Sprachratgeber* (usage guide).
- *kodifizieren* and *die Kodifizierung* (to codify, codification: recording a norm in dictionaries and rule books).

## Common mistakes

- Calling every variant a mistake: *gewunken, ich bin gesessen, das Joghurt* are standard forms in Duden.
- Calling every variant equal: *wegen dem Regen* is colloquial in a formal text, and *dem Präsident* is not standard written German.
- Confusing the plurals: *die Wörter* in a word count, *die Worte* for a speech.
- Thinking the Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung rules on grammar. It deals with spelling.
- Quoting Duden as law. It records and recommends; for spelling, the Amtliches Regelwerk is the reference.

## Key points

- Zweifelsfälle are forms in competition; reference works record both and say where and when each is normal.
- Spelling has an official norm (Amtliches Regelwerk, Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung); grammar has dictionaries and grammars, not an authority.
- Main types: gender doublets (*der/das Joghurt, das/der Virus, der/das Teil*), plurals with different meanings (*Banken/Bänke, Wörter/Worte*), forms in flux (*gewinkt/gewunken, sandte/sendete*), *wegen* + genitive or dative, *haben/sein* with *sitzen*, dative *-e*.
- Prescriptive advice says what you should write; descriptive linguistics says what people write. Choose the Hauptform for formal texts, and know the variants.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Das greift zu kurz: argument structure and fallacies
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 3 is about texts that want something from their readers: agreement, a vote, a grade, a click. It covers argument (this lesson), rhetoric and the C2 speaking exam (12), academic German (13), the press (14) and the C2 writing exam (15). The honors lessons apply the same tools to historic speeches and to science communication.

You already know how to build an Erörterung and a Stellungnahme (C1 lesson 14) and how to concede and push back in a discussion (C1 lesson 28). At C2 the question is no longer whether you can produce an argument, but whether you can take one apart: find the claim, the evidence and the unspoken rule that connects them, see where the reasoning breaks, and say so precisely, in a register that keeps the conversation going. The theme is logic and argument itself.

## The parts of an argument

A useful model comes from the philosopher Stephen Toulmin (*The Uses of Argument*, 1958). German textbooks on argument use it in a simplified form, with German names. An argument has a **[[premise]]** or several, and it moves from them to a claim.

| Part | German name | What it does | Typical markers |
|---|---|---|---|
| claim | *die These, die Behauptung* | what the speaker wants you to accept | *Ich bin der Auffassung, dass …; Es ist an der Zeit, …* |
| reason | *die Begründung, das Argument* | why the claim should be accepted | *denn, weil, da; nämlich; schließlich* |
| evidence | *der Beleg, das Beispiel* | facts, figures, cases that support the reason | *So zeigt …; Belegt wird dies durch …* |
| warrant | *die Schlussregel* | the general rule that links evidence and claim, often unspoken | *Bekanntlich …; In der Regel …* |
| qualification | *die Einschränkung* | how far the claim holds; possible exceptions | *sofern, soweit; in der Regel; zumindest* |
| conclusion | *die Folgerung, die Schlussfolgerung* | what follows | *folglich, also, somit, mithin* |

*der Beleg* is a new sense for a word you know from B1 (*der Beleg* "receipt, proof of payment"): in an argument it is the piece of evidence. *Die These belegen* means to back the claim with evidence; *etwas mit Zahlen untermauern* means to underpin it with figures, and the noun is *die Untermauerung*.

The *Schlussregel* is the part people forget, and it is where most bad arguments hide. *Die Notaufnahmen sind an Silvester voll, also sollte man Feuerwerk verbieten* only works if you accept the rule "what causes many injuries should be banned". Said aloud, that rule needs its own Einschränkung: we don't ban cycling or skiing. Making the hidden rule explicit is often the quickest *Widerlegung* (refutation).

### Three small words with a big job

- *denn* gives a reason in a main clause (verb second, the clause follows the claim): *Wir sollten abwarten, denn die Zahlen sind noch vorläufig.*
- *nämlich* explains or specifies what was just said; it never stands first: *Die Zahlen sind vorläufig, sie stammen nämlich aus nur drei Städten.*
- *schließlich* as a particle gives a reason that the listener ought to know already, often with a touch of reproach: *Du musst es ja wissen, du bist schließlich Ärztin.* As an adverb at the start of a sentence it means "finally": *Schließlich stimmte der Rat zu.*

## Text: a commentary on a ritual debate

Read this commentary from the opinion page of a (fictitious) regional paper. It argues about arguments.

> **Das greift zu kurz**
>
> Jedes Jahr im Dezember wiederholt sich dasselbe Ritual. Kaum liegen die ersten Feuerwerksbatterien im Supermarkt, fordern die einen ein Verbot privater Böller, während die anderen das Ende der Freiheit kommen sehen. Man könnte über die Frage durchaus vernünftig streiten, allein man tut es selten.
>
> Nehmen wir die Befürworter eines Verbots. Ihre These ist klar: Privates Feuerwerk richtet mehr Schaden an, als es Freude bereitet. Als Belege führen sie die Verletzten in den Notaufnahmen ins Feld, den Feinstaub, die verstörten Haustiere. Das ist nicht fadenscheinig, sondern triftig. Doch dann folgt allzu oft der Satz: „Wer heute noch böllert, dem ist das Leid anderer egal.“ Damit verlässt man den Boden der Argumentation. Aus einer Gewohnheit wird ein Charakterfehler, aus dem Gegenüber ein Egoist – ein Argument ad hominem, das niemanden überzeugt, der nicht ohnehin überzeugt ist.
>
> Die Gegenseite macht es nicht besser. „Heute verbieten sie die Raketen, morgen den Grill und übermorgen das Auto“, heißt es dann. Für dieses Dammbruchargument fehlt jeder Beleg; die Beweislast liegt bei dem, der die Lawine kommen sieht. Ebenso beliebt ist der Hinweis, man habe „schon immer“ geknallt. Das mag stimmen, beweist aber nichts: Dass etwas Tradition ist, sagt über seine Berechtigung so wenig aus wie sein Alter über seine Qualität.
>
> Zugegeben, die Abwägung ist schwierig. Gewiss gibt es Städte, in denen ein zentrales Feuerwerk gut funktioniert; daraus folgt jedoch nicht zwingend, dass es überall die bessere Lösung ist. Wer aus drei gelungenen Beispielen ein Gesetz für das ganze Land ableitet, verallgemeinert vorschnell. Und wer jeden Einwand mit dem Satz „Sicherheit geht vor“ vom Tisch wischt, benutzt ein Totschlagargument: Man kann ihm kaum widersprechen, aber es beendet das Gespräch, statt es zu führen.
>
> Was also wäre zu tun? Zunächst sollte jede Seite die stärkste Fassung des gegnerischen Arguments ernst nehmen statt eines bequemen Strohmanns. Die Befürworter eines Verbots wollen niemandem den Spaß verderben; die Gegner verteidigen nicht die Verletzungen. Erst wenn beide das einräumen, lässt sich über das eigentliche Problem reden: Wie viel Risiko für andere ist ein Vergnügen wert? Auf diese Frage gibt es keine schlüssige Antwort, die für alle gilt. Aber es gibt bessere und schlechtere Begründungen. Und darauf käme es an.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**That falls short**

Every December the same ritual repeats itself. No sooner are the first fireworks batteries in the supermarket than some people demand a ban on private firecrackers, while others see the end of freedom coming. One could argue about the question perfectly reasonably, but people seldom do.

Take those in favour of a ban. Their thesis is clear: private fireworks do more harm than they give pleasure. As evidence they cite the injured in the emergency departments, the fine dust, the frightened pets. That is not flimsy but cogent. But then, all too often, comes the sentence: "Anyone who still sets off firecrackers doesn't care about other people's suffering." With that, one leaves the ground of argument. A habit becomes a character flaw, the other person an egoist: an ad hominem argument that convinces no one who isn't convinced already.

The other side does no better. "Today they ban rockets, tomorrow the barbecue and the day after the car," they say. There is no evidence at all for this slippery-slope argument; the burden of proof lies with whoever sees the avalanche coming. Just as popular is the remark that people have "always" set off fireworks. That may be true, but it proves nothing: that something is a tradition says as little about whether it is justified as its age says about its quality.

Admittedly, weighing it up is difficult. Certainly there are cities in which a central fireworks display works well; it does not necessarily follow, however, that it is the better solution everywhere. Anyone who derives a law for the whole country from three successful examples is generalizing hastily. And anyone who sweeps every objection off the table with the sentence "Safety comes first" is using a conversation-killer: you can hardly contradict it, but it ends the conversation instead of conducting it.

So what should be done? First, each side should take the strongest version of the opposing argument seriously instead of a convenient straw man. Those in favour of a ban don't want to spoil anyone's fun; their opponents are not defending the injuries. Only when both concede that can the real problem be discussed: how much risk to others is a pleasure worth? There is no conclusive answer to that question that holds for everyone. But there are better and worse justifications. And that is what it would come down to.
</details>

The headline is a stock phrase for refuting: *Das greift zu kurz* — that falls short (the reasoning doesn't reach far enough). Notice how the writer argues: each paragraph names one weakness, gives it its German name, and says *why* it is a weakness. The text itself has a clear thesis (both sides argue badly), evidence (the quoted sentences), a warrant (good arguments engage with the other side's best case) and a conclusion with a concession.
