**Context.** At the end of the First World War, with revolution spreading from the naval ports, the Social Democrat Philipp Scheidemann proclaimed the republic from the Reichstag building in Berlin on 9 November 1918, the day the Kaiser's abdication was announced. Later the same day Karl Liebknecht proclaimed a "free socialist republic" at the Berlin Palace. *proklamieren* and *ausrufen* (*die Republik ausrufen*) are the verbs for this act; *die Proklamation* is the noun.

**Which words?** No recording exists, and the wording survives in differing versions. A paper of the Bundestag's research service (Wissenschaftliche Dienste, WD 1 - 034/18, 2018) compares them. Scheidemann's own memoirs (*Memoiren eines Sozialdemokraten*, 1928) give the famous ending:

> „Das Alte und Morsche, die Monarchie ist zusammengebrochen. Es lebe das Neue! Es lebe die Deutsche Republik!“

"The old and rotten, the monarchy, has collapsed. Long live the new! Long live the German Republic!"

Citing historical research, the paper says that Scheidemann wrote this text down afterwards and treats it as unreliable. The other versions differ: the evening edition of the *Vossische Zeitung* of 9 November gives a shorter text with *Wir haben auf der ganzen Linie gesiegt; das Alte ist nicht mehr* and ends with *Es lebe die deutsche Republik*; Eduard Bernstein (1921) has *Das monarchische System ist zusammengebrochen* instead of the memoir's sentence and ends with *Es lebe die freie deutsche Republik!* The research service concludes that no single wording can be verified. When you quote the proclamation, say which version you quote.

**Analysis.** Even in the memoir version the rhetoric is plain: *Es lebe …* (Konjunktiv I, the optative of lesson 03) twice, a contrast of *das Alte und Morsche* with *das Neue*, and the apposition *die Monarchie* naming what is meant. A speech from a window or balcony (the sources differ on that too) to a crowd has to work in short, shoutable units.

## Otto Wels, 23 March 1933: against the Enabling Act

**Context.** After the Reichstag fire, the Reichstag met in the Kroll Opera House in Berlin to vote on the *Ermächtigungsgesetz* (Enabling Act), which gave Hitler's government the power to pass laws without parliament (*die Ermächtigung*: authorization). SA and SS men stood in and around the building. The Communist deputies could not take part; many had been arrested or had fled. Otto Wels, chairman of the SPD, spoke against the bill for his party. The SPD's 94 deputies who were present voted against it; it was passed with the required two-thirds majority.

The passages below follow the text on GHDI (reprinted from Paul Meier-Benneckenstein, ed., *Dokumente der deutschen Politik*, vol. 1, Berlin 1935, pp. 36–38); the key sentences are given in the same wording by the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung. The official record is in the Reichstag's stenographic reports (*Verhandlungen des Reichstags*).

> „Das mag geschehen, wenn es nach allen Seiten gleichmäßig und unparteiisch geschieht, und wenn man es unterläßt, besiegte Gegner zu behandeln, als seien sie vogelfrei. Freiheit und Leben kann man uns nehmen, die Ehre nicht. Nach den Verfolgungen, die die Sozialdemokratische Partei in der letzten Zeit erfahren hat, wird billigerweise niemand von ihr verlangen oder erwarten können, daß sie für das hier eingebrachte Ermächtigungsgesetz stimmt.“

"That may happen, if it happens equally and impartially on all sides, and if one refrains from treating defeated opponents as if they were outlaws. Freedom and life they can take from us, but not our honour. After the persecution the Social Democratic Party has suffered recently, no one can fairly demand or expect it to vote for the Enabling Act introduced here."

And from the end of the speech:

> „Wir deutschen Sozialdemokraten bekennen uns in dieser geschichtlichen Stunde feierlich zu den Grundsätzen der Menschlichkeit und der Gerechtigkeit, der Freiheit und des Sozialismus.“

"We German Social Democrats solemnly pledge ourselves in this historic hour to the principles of humanity and justice, of freedom and socialism."

**Analysis.**

- *Freiheit und Leben kann man uns nehmen, die Ehre nicht.* The objects are fronted (lesson 08 in module 2: fronting for contrast), the second half is an ellipsis (*die Ehre [kann man uns] nicht [nehmen]*). The short sentence stands out between two long ones. *man* names no one, and everyone in the hall knew who was meant.
- *als seien sie vogelfrei*: *als* + Konjunktiv I, the formal comparison of lesson 03; *vogelfrei* (outlawed, free to be killed) is a word from medieval law.
- *billigerweise* (in fairness) and *eingebracht* (introduced, of a bill) are parliamentary register: Wels speaks as a member of a parliament that still claims its rules.
- The *Bekenntnis* (pledge) lists four values as genitives in two pairs, *der Menschlichkeit und der Gerechtigkeit, der Freiheit und des Sozialismus*: a parallelism that moves from universal values to the party's own.
- *unterläßt, daß*: old spellings (*unterlässt, dass*).

## Tucholsky, "Ratschläge für einen schlechten Redner" (1930)

Kurt Tucholsky published this piece under his pseudonym Peter Panter in the *Vossische Zeitung* of 16 November 1930. It is quoted here from Projekt Gutenberg-DE, which follows the edition *Panter, Tiger und andere* (Berlin: Volk und Welt, 1957). It is a manual in reverse: every piece of advice describes a mistake, in the *du* imperative of a well-meaning teacher. It opens:

> „Fang nie mit dem Anfang an, sondern immer drei Meilen vor dem Anfang!“

"Never begin at the beginning, but always three miles before the beginning!"

Later: *„Sprich nicht frei – das macht einen so unruhigen Eindruck.“* ("Don't speak without notes – it makes such a restless impression.") The advice on long sentences is itself one long, deliberately tangled sentence that starts *„Sprich mit langen, langen Sätzen – solchen, bei denen du, der du dich zu Hause, wo du ja die Ruhe, …“* and keeps nesting clauses: the form performs the mistake. The short companion piece for good speakers puts the opposite in three words: *„Hauptsätze. Hauptsätze. Hauptsätze.“*

The irony works because the reader recognizes every "rule" from speeches they have suffered through. As a checklist for your own C2 talk (lesson 12), read it backwards: begin at the beginning, speak without reading from a script, use main clauses.

## A later speech: Weizsäcker, 8 May 1985

Richard von Weizsäcker died in 2015, so his speeches are not in the public domain. German copyright allows short quotations for the purpose of analysis (*das Zitierrecht*, § 51 UrhG), with the source named. In a commemoration in the Bundestag on the 40th anniversary of the end of the Second World War in Europe, the Federal President said (text: bundestag.de):

> „Der 8. Mai war ein Tag der Befreiung.“

"The 8th of May was a day of liberation."

The force of the sentence is in its plainness and in its noun. Many Germans had remembered 8 May 1945 as defeat or collapse; *Befreiung* named it, for the whole country, as liberation from the Nazi regime. A *Gedenkrede* (commemorative speech) like this one needs no figure: the choice of one word is the rhetoric.

## Words for speeches and parliaments

- *die Regierungserklärung*: a formal statement of government policy in parliament, often after an election. *die Thronrede*: a monarch's speech opening a parliament (Prussia, the German Empire; today the British King's Speech).
- *das Plenum*: the full assembly (*im Plenum sprechen*, as opposed to a committee); *die Redezeit*: the speaking time allotted; *die Reichstagsrede*: a speech in the Reichstag.
- *die Paulskirche*: the church in Frankfurt where the first German National Assembly met in 1848–49; *die Nationalversammlung* also names the assembly of 1919 in Weimar.
- *die Redekultur*: the culture of public speaking and debate in a society or parliament.

## Key points

- Analyse a speech by occasion, speaker and audience, aim, structure, language and effect.
- Bismarck's "Eisen und Blut" survives as a report in indirect speech; the period is framed by two *nicht … sondern* antitheses.
- Scheidemann's proclamation survives in several versions; say which one you quote.
- Wels's speech uses fronting, ellipsis and parliamentary register to keep dignity under threat.
- Tucholsky teaches good speaking by ironic bad advice; later speeches (Weizsäcker) are quoted briefly, with source, under § 51 UrhG.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Verständlich erklären: science communication
lessons.body:
## From the journal to the public

Lesson 13 was about writing for specialists. This honors lesson is about the opposite direction: taking a specialist text and rewriting it for people who don't share the specialists' training. *die Wissenschaftskommunikation* (science communication) covers everything from a university press release to a children's page, a podcast or an *Erklärvideo* (explainer video). Journalists who specialize in it are *Wissenschaftsjournalistinnen und -journalisten*; the book shelf for it in a shop says *Sachbuch* (non-fiction) or *populärwissenschaftlich* (popular science).

The skill is mediation within one language: you keep the content and change everything else. The hard part is not to simplify, but to simplify without saying something false. The words for the goal are *verständlich*, *allgemeinverständlich* (understandable for everyone) and *laienverständlich* (understandable for lay people); the opposite is *Fachchinesisch* (Duden: umgangssprachlich, abwertend), jargon that outsiders can't follow.

## The source: a specialist abstract

Here is the abstract of a (fictitious) study in an ornithology journal.

> Anthropogener Lärm beeinflusst die akustische Kommunikation zahlreicher Singvogelarten. In der vorliegenden Studie wurde untersucht, ob Kohlmeisen (*Parus major*) die Frequenz ihres Gesangs an Verkehrslärm anpassen. An 24 Standorten mit unterschiedlicher Lärmbelastung wurden über zwei Brutperioden Gesangsaufnahmen von 186 Männchen ausgewertet. Mit zunehmendem Lärmpegel stieg die Mindestfrequenz des Gesangs signifikant an (im Mittel um 210 Hz je 10 dB). Die Effektstärke war moderat; ein Zusammenhang mit dem Bruterfolg ließ sich nicht nachweisen. Die Befunde stützen die Annahme einer kurzfristigen Verhaltensanpassung, lassen jedoch offen, ob diese mit Fitnesskosten verbunden ist.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

Anthropogenic noise affects the acoustic communication of numerous songbird species. The present study investigated whether great tits (*Parus major*) adjust the frequency of their song to traffic noise. Song recordings of 186 males were analysed at 24 sites with different levels of noise pollution over two breeding seasons. As the noise level increased, the minimum frequency of the song rose significantly (on average by 210 Hz per 10 dB). The effect size was moderate; no connection with breeding success could be demonstrated. The findings support the assumption of a short-term behavioural adjustment, but leave open whether it comes with fitness costs.
</details>

Before rewriting, list what must survive any version:

1. **The claim**: great tits sing higher where traffic is louder.
2. **The size and certainty**: the effect is statistically clear but moderate.
3. **The limits**: no effect on breeding success was found; whether the birds pay a price is open.
4. **The method in one line**: many birds, many places, two seasons.

Everything else can change: the terms (*anthropogen, Mindestfrequenz, Effektstärke, Fitnesskosten*), the nominal style (*mit zunehmendem Lärmpegel*), the passive, the sentence length.

## Version 1: the newspaper

> **Meisen singen gegen den Verkehr an**
>
> Wo Autos lärmen, singen Kohlmeisen höher. Das zeigt eine Studie, für die Forschende in zwei Frühjahren den Gesang von 186 Meisenmännchen an 24 unterschiedlich lauten Orten aufgenommen haben. Je lauter der Verkehr, desto höher setzten die Vögel die tiefsten Töne ihres Gesangs an – vermutlich, weil sich hohe Töne besser vom tiefen Brummen der Straße abheben. Der Effekt ist eindeutig, aber nicht groß. Ob den Tieren die Anpassung schadet, ist noch unklar: Die Meisen an lauten Orten zogen jedenfalls nicht erkennbar weniger Junge groß als die an ruhigen. Ob sie auf Dauer einen Preis zahlen, etwa weil Weibchen tiefe Gesänge attraktiver finden, müssen weitere Untersuchungen klären.

What changed: *je … desto* replaces *mit zunehmendem Lärmpegel* (lesson 06 in module 2, in the other direction); *die tiefsten Töne ihres Gesangs* replaces *Mindestfrequenz*; *Bruterfolg* becomes *Junge großziehen*, and *ließ sich nicht nachweisen* becomes *nicht erkennbar weniger*, which keeps the hedge (not "just as many"). What was added: a likely reason, marked *vermutlich*, and an example of a possible cost, marked *etwa* and attached to an open question. The figure *210 Hz je 10 dB* was dropped, because most readers can't interpret it; *eindeutig, aber nicht groß* passes on its meaning. That is a judgment call: a science section aimed at an educated readership might keep it with a gloss.

## Version 2: the children's page

> **Warum Meisen in der Stadt anders singen**
>
> Kohlmeisen singen, um anderen Meisen etwas mitzuteilen: „Das ist mein Revier!“ oder „Hier bin ich!“ In der Stadt ist das gar nicht so leicht, denn Autos und Lastwagen machen viel Lärm. Forscher haben herausgefunden: Wo es laut ist, singen die Meisen ein bisschen höher. Das kennst du vielleicht selbst. Wenn neben dir ein lauter Staubsauger brummt, versuchst du auch, anders zu sprechen, damit man dich versteht. Ob das Höhersingen den Meisen schadet, wissen die Forscher noch nicht.

What changed: short main clauses, *du*, a concrete situation from the child's world. The analogy (*der Staubsauger*) makes the mechanism *anschaulich* (vivid, concrete), but it has a limit: children shout louder, while the birds change pitch. The text says *anders sprechen*, not *lauter*, so the analogy doesn't teach something false. The open question survives in the last sentence.

## Version 3: the podcast

> „Stellen Sie sich vor, Sie wollen jemandem etwas zurufen – und direkt neben Ihnen fährt ein Lkw vorbei. Genau dieses Problem haben Kohlmeisen in der Stadt. Eine neue Studie hat jetzt gemessen, wie sie damit umgehen: Sie singen höher. Und zwar umso höher, je lauter es ist. Wichtig dabei: Der Effekt ist messbar, aber nicht riesig. Und ob das für die Vögel ein Problem ist, das wissen wir noch nicht. In der Studie hatten die Meisen an lauten Straßen jedenfalls nicht erkennbar weniger Nachwuchs. Ich frage gleich mal die Biologin, die das untersucht hat, was sie als Nächstes herausfinden will.“

What changed: spoken syntax (*Und zwar …; Wichtig dabei: …*), a scene to start with, repetition of the key point, and the speaker's voice (*das wissen wir noch nicht*). In audio, the listener can't reread, so each sentence carries one idea, and numbers are kept to a minimum.

## What makes a good popular version

| Keep | Change | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| the claim | technical terms → everyday words or a short gloss | turning *korreliert* into *verursacht* |
| the strength of the evidence (*eindeutig, aber klein*) | nominal style → verbs; passive → active | dropping the hedge in the headline |
| the limits and open questions | long periods → one idea per sentence | analogies that imply the wrong mechanism |
| who found it, with how much data | abstract → scene or example | numbers without a reference point |

The core value is *die Faktentreue* (faithfulness to the facts). *die Vereinfachung* (simplification) is the method, not a vice; but a *vereinfachende* (simplifying, often: oversimplifying) account that changes the claim is a failure of *Verständlichkeit* (understandability) in the wrong direction: it is understandable, and wrong.

### Hedging that survives simplification

Specialist hedges (*Die Befunde stützen die Annahme …; lassen offen, ob …*) can't simply be deleted. Translate them into everyday hedges:

- *signifikant, aber moderat* → *eindeutig, aber nicht groß*
- *ließ sich nicht nachweisen* → *Die Forscher haben keinen Hinweis darauf gefunden, dass …*
- *lassen offen, ob …* → *Ob …, ist noch unklar / wissen die Forschenden noch nicht.*
- *stützen die Annahme* → *spricht dafür, dass …*

Note what *ließ sich nicht nachweisen* does not mean: it does not mean "was shown not to exist". *Kein Hinweis auf einen Schaden* is not *kein Schaden*.

### Analogies and their limits

An analogy borrows understanding from something familiar. Every analogy is wrong somewhere; the question is whether the reader will notice where. Good practice: use the analogy for the mechanism you want to explain and say, if it matters, where it stops: *Anders als wir werden die Meisen dabei nicht lauter, sondern höher.*

## Hype: the press-release problem

Many popular versions are not written by journalists but start from a university's or a company's press release (*die Pressemitteilung*, B1). Press offices want attention, and attention words creep in. A C2 reader recognizes them and asks what is behind them:

| Hype word | What to ask |
|---|---|
| *ein Durchbruch* (a breakthrough) | Compared with what? Has anyone reproduced it? |
| *erstmals* (for the first time) | First in the world, or first in this group, species, country? |
| *Forscher beweisen, dass …* | Did they prove it, or find a correlation (lesson 13)? |
| *könnte bald …* (could soon …) | Who says so: the study, or the press office? |
| *Wundermittel, Sensation* | These are hardly ever the scientists' words. |

The abstract above makes none of these claims, and a faithful popular version shouldn't add them. A headline like *Lärm macht Meisen krank* would be catchier than *Meisen singen gegen den Verkehr an*, and false: the study found no harm. The headline is the part most people read, so it is where *Faktentreue* matters most.

A useful test for your own rewrite: give it to someone who knows the original and ask whether they would sign it. If a researcher says *So habe ich das nicht gemeint*, the simplification has gone too far. Many scientists now take part in the process themselves; universities and research organizations train them for interviews, podcasts and videos, and *Wissenschaftskommunikation* has become a field of research and a profession of its own.

## Anschaulich, verständlich, allgemeinverständlich

These adjectives overlap but differ in focus:

- *anschaulich*: vivid, made concrete through examples or images (*eine anschauliche Darstellung*; noun *die Anschaulichkeit*). *veranschaulichen* (B2) is the verb.
- *verständlich*: understandable (to whoever reads it).
- *allgemeinverständlich*: understandable for a general public, without prior knowledge.
- *laienverständlich*: understandable for lay people, as opposed to experts; common in medicine and law.
- *populärwissenschaftlich*: written to popularize science; sometimes used critically, as in *bloß populärwissenschaftlich*.

## Key points

- Science communication keeps the claim, the strength of the evidence and the limits; it changes terms, style, sentence length and examples.
- Rewrite nominal style into verbs (*mit zunehmendem Lärm → je lauter …, desto …*) and specialist hedges into everyday ones (*lassen offen → ist noch unklar*).
- Analogies explain a mechanism; check that they don't imply a wrong one.
- "No evidence of harm" is not "no harm".
- Newspaper, children's page and podcast need different syntax: compact and attributed, short and personal, spoken and repetitive.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Den Bogen überspannen: idioms at depth
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 is about the parts of German that a dictionary lists but cannot really teach: idioms, proverbs, collocations, humour and imagery. A C2 speaker doesn't just know that *den Bogen überspannen* means "to go too far". They know that it can be put in the passive and *ins Gras beißen* can't, that *jemandem nicht das Wasser reichen können* never appears without a negation, that a headline writer may twist it on purpose, and that it belongs in a commentary but not in a court ruling.

German C1 lesson 17 introduced idioms by their images (the body, animals, food, old crafts), the slots for *jemandem* and *etwas*, and the difference between idioms and proverbs. This lesson goes further: how fixed an idiom really is, which idioms only live in negative sentences, how journalists and advertisers modify idioms, what happens when two idioms collide, how idioms with the same meaning differ in register, and where an English look-alike means something else.

## A commentary from the local paper

Read this commentary from an (invented) regional newspaper. Commentaries are where idioms are most at home in written German: the writer has an opinion and wants to sound lively. Count the idioms as you read; there are more than fifteen.

> **Seilbahn-Pläne: Der Bürgermeister hat den Bogen überspannt**
>
> Nennen wir das Kind beim Namen: Die Seilbahn über den Main war von Anfang an ein Prestigeprojekt. Monatelang hatte Bürgermeister Krämer die Pläne unter Verschluss gehalten. Am Dienstag ließ er endlich die Katze aus dem Sack – und die Katze ist mit 84 Millionen Euro deutlich teurer, als im Rathaus jemals jemand zugeben wollte.
>
> Dass eine Stadt, die ihre Schultoiletten nicht saniert bekommt, plötzlich auf so großem Fuß leben will, ist schwer zu vermitteln. Kein Wunder, dass Krämer den Wind aus den Segeln der Kritiker nehmen wollte, bevor sie sich formieren konnten. Gelungen ist ihm das nicht. Mit seiner Bemerkung, die Gegner seien „ewige Bedenkenträger“, hat er vielmehr Öl ins Feuer gegossen.
>
> Man muss nicht gleich den Teufel an die Wand malen. Seilbahnen funktionieren in vielen Städten, und wer jedes Großprojekt verhindert, schüttet das Kind mit dem Bade aus. Aber man sollte auf dem Teppich bleiben. Dass Kostenschätzungen sich bei solchen Vorhaben verdoppeln, ist leider gang und gäbe.
>
> Die Opposition wiederum macht es sich zu leicht. Sie hat dem Projekt jahrelang Steine in den Weg gelegt, ohne je eine Alternative vorzulegen. Mit ihrer Kampagne, die aus jeder Mücke einen Elefanten macht, erweist sie der Verkehrswende einen Bärendienst.
>
> Wie geht es weiter? Die Fraktion des Bürgermeisters stärkt ihm noch demonstrativ den Rücken, doch hinter vorgehaltener Hand heißt es, man werde sich für die Seilbahn kein Bein mehr ausreißen. Krämer ist mit allen Wassern gewaschen; die Flinte ins Korn werfen wird er so schnell nicht. Sollte das Projekt aber ins Wasser fallen, wird er nicht der Einzige sein, der das Handtuch wirft. Auf einen grünen Zweig kommt so jedenfalls niemand.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Cable car plans: the mayor has gone too far**

Let's call a spade a spade: the cable car over the Main was a prestige project from the start. For months Mayor Krämer had kept the plans under wraps. On Tuesday he finally came out with it, and at 84 million euros it is considerably more expensive than anyone in the town hall was ever willing to admit.

That a city which can't get its school toilets renovated suddenly wants to live in such grand style is hard to sell. No wonder Krämer wanted to take the wind out of his critics' sails before they could get organized. He didn't manage it. On the contrary, with his remark that his opponents were "eternal worriers" he added fuel to the fire.

There's no need to imagine the worst straight away. Cable cars work in many cities, and anyone who blocks every large project throws the baby out with the bathwater. But we should keep our feet on the ground. That cost estimates double in projects like this is, unfortunately, common practice.

The opposition, for its part, is making things too easy for itself. For years it has put obstacles in the project's way without ever presenting an alternative. With its campaign, which makes a mountain out of every molehill, it is doing the transport transition a disservice.

What happens next? The mayor's group in the council is still pointedly backing him, but behind closed doors people say they won't bust a gut for the cable car any more. Krämer knows every trick in the book; he won't give up in a hurry. But if the project falls through, he won't be the only one to throw in the towel. Either way, this gets nobody anywhere.

</details>

Two things in the text are not standard idioms but plays on them. *Die Katze ist mit 84 Millionen Euro deutlich teurer* takes the cat out of the idiom and treats it as a real animal with a price. *den Wind aus den Segeln der Kritiker nehmen* moves the dative person (*den Kritikern*) into a genitive after *Segel*. Both are typical of commentaries, and both are explained below.

## How fixed is an idiom?

An idiom is fixed in its words, not in its grammar. The verb inside it is conjugated, moves to second or final position, and takes tense and mood like any other verb: *Er hat den Bogen überspannt. Hätte sie doch nicht den Bogen überspannt! Wer den Bogen überspannt, …*. What you normally cannot do is swap a word, even for a synonym, or change the article or number:

| Change | Possible? | Example |
|---|---|---|
| tense, mood, person | yes | *Sie warf die Flinte ins Korn. Würde er die Flinte ins Korn werfen?* |
| inserting an adverb or particle | yes | *Er hat den Bogen diesmal wirklich überspannt.* |
| a word replaced by a synonym | no (unless it is a deliberate play) | ~~*den Bogen überdehnen*~~, ~~*das Gewehr ins Korn werfen*~~ |
| article or number changed | no | ~~*einen Bogen überspannen*~~ (that is a literal bow) |
| adjective added to a noun | sometimes, as a modification | *Öl ins ohnehin lodernde Feuer gießen* |
| passive | only some idioms | see below |

### Passive: who can be "done to"?

Idioms that describe an action done to someone often have a passive: *Der Opposition wurde der Wind aus den Segeln genommen. Dem Team wurden nach dem Spiel gehörig die Leviten gelesen. Ihm wurde ein Korb gegeben* is grammatical but unusual: German says *Er hat einen Korb bekommen*, a different idiom for the same scene.

Idioms in which the noun is not a real object of the action have no passive: ~~*Der Löffel wurde von Opa abgegeben*~~ can only be a joke about a literal spoon, ~~*Das Gras wurde gebissen*~~ is nonsense, and ~~*Die Flinte wurde ins Korn geworfen*~~ sounds like a report about a lost gun. *ins Gras beißen* has no accusative object at all, so it has nothing to turn into a subject. A useful test: if the noun in the idiom could never be the subject of a normal sentence about the situation, the passive will sound literal.

The same test explains why *einen Korb geben* prefers *einen Korb bekommen* over the passive. German often has a pair of active idioms for the two sides of a scene: *jemandem einen Korb geben / einen Korb bekommen*, *jemandem die Leviten lesen / sich die Leviten lesen lassen müssen*.

## Polarity idioms: only with a negation

Some idioms exist only in negative sentences. Linguists call them negative-polarity items. Without the negation they don't mean the opposite; they simply sound wrong.

- *Als Pianist kann er seinem Lehrer nicht das Wasser reichen.* — As a pianist he can't hold a candle to his teacher. Not ~~*Er kann seinem Lehrer das Wasser reichen*~~ to mean "he is as good as his teacher".
- *Mit diesen Ideen kommt er auf keinen grünen Zweig.* — With these ideas he'll get nowhere.
- *Dass wir uns getrennt haben, musst du nicht an die große Glocke hängen.* — Mostly negated, or in a reproach: *Musstest du das gleich an die große Glocke hängen?*

"Negative" is wider than *nicht*. These idioms also live in sentences with *kein, nie, kaum, niemand*, in questions that expect "no", and after comparatives that imply a negation:

- *Niemand kann ihr in diesem Fach das Wasser reichen.*
- *Wer kann ihr schon das Wasser reichen?* (= nobody)
- *Er ist nie auf einen grünen Zweig gekommen.*

*sich kein Bein ausreißen* (not to make much effort) is mostly negative too, but the positive *sich ein Bein ausreißen* (to go to great lengths) also exists: *Sie hat sich für das Projekt ein Bein ausgerissen.* So it is a strong tendency, not a strict polarity idiom. Check the dictionary before you un-negate an idiom.

## Modification: idioms twisted on purpose

Writers of headlines, advertising and commentaries like to change an idiom so that the reader recognizes it and notices the change. This is called **[[idiom modification]]** (*Modifikation*). It works only because the idiom is fixed: the twist is a deliberate break of the rule in the table above. The main techniques:

| Technique | How it works | Example (original) |
|---|---|---|
| Expansion | an adjective, genitive or clause is added | *Öl ins Feuer der Haushaltsdebatte gießen*; *den Wind aus den Segeln der Kritiker nehmen* |
| Substitution | one word is replaced, keeping the frame | *Er hat den Bogen nicht überspannt, sondern gleich zerbrochen.* |
| Literalization | the literal meaning is reactivated by the context | *Das Sommerfest ist buchstäblich ins Wasser gefallen.* (it rained) |
| Polarity reversal | a negative idiom is made positive | an energy cooperative's slogan: *Mit uns kommen Sie endlich auf einen grünen Zweig.* |
| Continuation | the image is carried further | *Die Katze ist aus dem Sack – und sie hat Krallen.* |

The cooperative's slogan is a good example of a C2 text. It reverses the polarity (the idiom is negative), and it reactivates *grün*, which now also means "environmentally friendly". The commentary above does the same thing with the cat: once the cat costs 84 million euros, it is no longer only an idiom.

Modification has its limits in serious writing. One twisted idiom in a headline is witty; three in a paragraph look like trying too hard.

## Contamination: two idioms in one

**[[Contamination]]** (*Kontamination*) is the blending of two idioms into one. It happens by mistake in speech, especially under pressure, and on purpose in comedy. Original examples:

- ~~*Wir sollten nicht das Kind mit dem Feuer ausschütten.*~~ (*das Kind mit dem Bade ausschütten* + *mit dem Feuer spielen*)
- ~~*Da hat er wohl den Bogen ins Korn geworfen.*~~ (*den Bogen überspannen* + *die Flinte ins Korn werfen*)
- ~~*Er hat sich mit allen Wassern die Finger verbrannt.*~~ (*mit allen Wassern gewaschen* + *sich die Finger verbrennen*)

A learner's contamination is simply an error. A native speaker's may be a slip (and gets quoted in the press), or it may be a joke told with a straight face. In your own writing, contamination is never safe: the reader can't tell whether you meant it.

## Same meaning, different register

C1 lesson 17 showed that idioms are often more colloquial than the plain word. At C2 you choose among several idioms for the same thing. Dying is the classic case (labels as in Duden):

| Expression | Register | Where you'd find it |
|---|---|---|
| *sterben* | neutral | everywhere |
| *das Ableben* (noun, C1) | gehoben | an obituary, a will |
| *entschlafen* | gehoben, verhüllend (euphemistic) | a death notice: *Sanft entschlafen ist …* |
| *ins Gras beißen* | salopp | an adventure film, a joke about soldiers |
| *den Löffel abgeben* | salopp | banter among friends |
| *abkratzen* | derb | only explained here; offensive about a real death |

*ins Gras beißen* and *den Löffel abgeben* are both salopp, but they are not interchangeable. *ins Gras beißen* calls up a violent death in battle or in a film (*In der letzten Szene beißt der Schurke ins Gras*); *den Löffel abgeben* is the joke an old man makes about his own death (*Bevor ich den Löffel abgebe, will ich noch nach Neuseeland*). Neither belongs anywhere near a real bereavement.

Giving up works the same way: *aufgeben* (neutral), *die Flinte ins Korn werfen* (umgangssprachlich: giving up too early, losing heart), *das Handtuch werfen* (umgangssprachlich in this sense: officially quitting, often a job or a fight). A minister who resigns *wirft das Handtuch*; a student who stops revising after one bad mark *wirft die Flinte ins Korn*.

## Idioms in a story and in a formal text

Idioms belong to texts with a voice: narrative, conversation, commentary, columns, interviews, speeches. In a news report they appear mostly inside quotations or in a slightly lighter last paragraph. In a court ruling, an official letter, a contract or a scientific article they are almost absent, and an idiom there is a Stilbruch (C1). Compare:

- Commentary: *Mit der dritten Preiserhöhung hat der Vermieter den Bogen überspannt.*
- Letter to the landlord: *Die dritte Mieterhöhung innerhalb eines Jahres halte ich für unangemessen.*
- Court: *Die Erhöhung übersteigt die ortsübliche Vergleichsmiete.*

In narrative, idioms often characterize the speaker. A figure who says *Wir müssen keine Haare spalten* sounds practical, perhaps impatient; one who says *Nennen wir das Kind beim Namen* is about to say something unpleasant clearly.

## Where idioms come from

The usual explanations are given in Duden and in Röhrich's *Lexikon der sprichwörtlichen Redensarten*. For many idioms the origin is uncertain or disputed, so say "is usually explained by …", not "comes from …".

- *jemandem die Leviten lesen*: usually explained by reading aloud from Leviticus, the book of the Bible with the rules for priests.
- *jemandem auf den Leim gehen*: usually traced to birdlime, glue once spread on twigs to catch birds.
- *die Flinte ins Korn werfen*: usually explained by a soldier who throws his gun into the field in a hopeless fight.
- *aus der Haut fahren*: one common explanation is a snake shedding its skin.
- *in die Bresche springen*: a breach in a fortress wall (French *brèche*) that someone has to fill.
- *jemandem einen Bärendienst erweisen*: usually traced to a fable, best known in La Fontaine's version, in which a bear throws a stone at a fly on his sleeping friend's face and kills the friend.
- *den Löffel abgeben* and *ins Gras beißen*: *ins Gras beißen* is cautiously explained by a dying fighter biting the earth; for *den Löffel abgeben* there are several competing stories and no agreement.

## False friends with English idioms

Many German and English idioms match exactly, because both languages drew on the Bible, Latin and each other: *mit dem Feuer spielen* (to play with fire), *Haare spalten* (to split hairs), *in die Bresche springen* (to step into the breach), *das Handtuch werfen* (to throw in the towel), *jemandem den Wind aus den Segeln nehmen* (to take the wind out of someone's sails). Others look the same and are not:

| German | Looks like | But means |
|---|---|---|
| *Öl ins Feuer gießen* | (pour oil on troubled waters) | the opposite: to make things worse. Calming is *Öl auf die Wogen gießen*. |
| *die Katze aus dem Sack lassen* | to let the cat out of the bag | often deliberate: to reveal one's plans at last, not only a slip |
| *auf dem Teppich bleiben* | (sweep under the carpet) | to stay realistic; hiding is *unter den Teppich kehren* |
| *auf großem Fuß leben* | (big feet) | to live extravagantly |
| *jemandem einen Korb geben* | (give someone a basket) | to turn someone down |

## The words of this lesson

All the new items are idioms, listed in their dictionary form with their slot (*jemandem, jemanden, etwas*). Learn the slot with the idiom: *jemandem* den Rücken stärken (dative), *jemanden* über den Tisch ziehen (accusative). In idioms with *sich*, check the case: *sich (dat.) die Finger verbrennen* → *Ich habe mir die Finger verbrannt*; *sich (dat.) kein Bein ausreißen* → *Ich reiße mir kein Bein aus*; but *sich (acc.) aus dem Staub machen* → *Ich mache mich aus dem Staub*.

Several take *sein* in the perfect because the verb inside does: *ist aus der Haut gefahren, ist ins Wasser gefallen, ist auf den Leim gegangen, ist in die Bresche gesprungen, ist auf dem Teppich geblieben*. *gang und gäbe* is predicative only (*Das ist hier gang und gäbe*), and it is spelled with *ä*; *gang und gebe* is a misspelling. The linguist's word for all fixed multi-word units is *der Phraseologismus* (plural *die Phraseologismen*).

## Common mistakes

- Swapping a word for a synonym: ~~*Er hat den Bogen überdehnt*~~, ~~*das Kind beim Vornamen nennen*~~. Only the dictionary form is the idiom (unless you are deliberately playing with it, and the reader can tell).
- Making a polarity idiom positive: ~~*Sie kann ihrem Chef das Wasser reichen*~~ to mean "she is as good as her boss". Say *Sie steht ihrem Chef in nichts nach*.
- A passive where the idiom has none: ~~*Von dem Schurken wurde ins Gras gebissen.*~~
- Contamination in writing: ~~*Das schüttet das Fass mit dem Bade aus.*~~ In speech it may pass as a slip; on paper it looks like a gap in your German.
- Register clash: *den Löffel abgeben* in a condolence card, *jemandem die Leviten lesen* in a formal complaint. A higher-register paraphrase is usually there: *verstorben*, *scharf kritisieren*.
- Reading *Öl ins Feuer gießen* through English: it never calms anything down.
- False precision about origins: "This idiom comes from the Middle Ages" is rarely provable. Say "is usually explained by …".
- Too many idioms: a C2 text uses them where they add something. A paragraph with five idioms reads like a parody.

## Key points

- An idiom's words are fixed; its grammar is not. Tense, mood and word order change; synonyms, articles and number don't.
- Only idioms whose noun is really affected by the action have a natural passive (*Ihm wurde der Wind aus den Segeln genommen*); *ins Gras beißen* and *den Löffel abgeben* have none.
- Polarity idioms need a negative context: *nicht das Wasser reichen können, auf keinen grünen Zweig kommen*; *sich kein Bein ausreißen* is mostly negative but has a positive twin.
- **[[Idiom modification]]** (expansion, substitution, literalization, polarity reversal, continuation) is a deliberate twist for headlines and ads; **[[contamination]]** blends two idioms and is an error unless it is clearly a joke.
- Idioms with the same meaning differ in register and image: *entschlafen* (gehoben), *ins Gras beißen* and *den Löffel abgeben* (salopp), *abkratzen* (derb).
- Idioms belong to texts with a voice; in rulings, contracts and scientific prose they are a Stilbruch.
- Give origins as "usually explained by …"; many are disputed.
- Watch English look-alikes: *Öl ins Feuer gießen* inflames, *die Katze aus dem Sack lassen* is often deliberate, *auf dem Teppich bleiben* means staying realistic.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Des Pudels Kern: proverbs and geflügelte Worte
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 16 was about idioms: fixed phrases that fit into a sentence. This lesson is about fixed sentences: proverbs that state a general truth (*Übung macht den Meister*) and quotations from literature and the Bible that have become common property (*des Pudels Kern*, *die Gretchenfrage*). German C1 introduced proverbs briefly (*Lügen haben kurze Beine*, *Wer A sagt, muss auch B sagen*). At C2 you need three more things: telling a proverb from a Redensart and a geflügeltes Wort, recognizing where the most quoted lines come from, and handling the way native speakers actually use proverbs: cut short, twisted, quoted ironically or avoided because they sound trite.

## A column on proverbs

Read this column from the (invented) culture pages of a weekly paper. The columnist writes about her grandmother's proverbs. Notice how rarely a proverb appears whole.

> **Wer rastet, der postet**
>
> Meine Großmutter hatte für jede Lebenslage ein Sprichwort. Kam ich verschlafen zum Frühstück, hieß es „Morgenstund hat Gold im Mund“. Hatte ich mich beim Radfahren blamiert, tröstete sie mich mit „Übung macht den Meister“. Und als mein Bruder seine erste Freundin vorstellte, eine stille Medizinstudentin, murmelte sie nur: „Stille Wasser …“ Den Rest musste sie nicht aussprechen.
>
> Das ist das Erstaunliche an Sprichwörtern: Man muss sie selten zu Ende sagen. „Wer anderen eine Grube gräbt …“ reicht, und jeder weiß, wer am Ende im Loch sitzt. Sprichwörter sind gespeicherte Urteile, die man nur noch aufrufen muss. Gerade deshalb haben sie einen schlechten Ruf. Wer in einer Diskussion „Aller Anfang ist schwer“ sagt, hat meist kein Argument, sondern einen Kalenderspruch.
>
> Und doch sterben sie nicht aus. Sie wandern nur. Was früher auf Wandtellern stand, steht heute auf Tassen und in Werbeslogans, und oft wird es dabei verdreht. „Wer rastet, der postet“, las ich neulich auf einem Plakat für ein Fitnessstudio. Das Antisprichwort funktioniert nur, weil alle das Original kennen. Es ist also eher ein Beweis für die Lebenskraft der alten Volksweisheit als für ihren Untergang.
>
> Noch zäher sind die geflügelten Worte. Kaum jemand hat den „Faust“ ganz gelesen, aber jeder Zweite fragt nach des Pudels Kern oder stellt einer Partei die Gretchenfrage. Schiller hat dem Baumarkt den Werbespruch geschenkt: „Die Axt im Haus erspart den Zimmermann.“ Dass der Satz im Stück mehr über Tell verrät als über Heimwerkerei, weiß kaum noch jemand.
>
> Meine Großmutter hätte zu alldem nur gesagt: „Ende gut, alles gut.“ Ganz so einfach ist es nicht. Aber eine Binsenweisheit ist eben nicht deshalb falsch, weil sie jeder kennt.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**If you rest, you post**

My grandmother had a proverb for every situation in life. If I came down to breakfast half asleep, it was "The early bird catches the worm". If I'd made a fool of myself on my bike, she consoled me with "Practice makes perfect". And when my brother introduced his first girlfriend, a quiet medical student, she only murmured: "Still waters …" She didn't need to say the rest.

That is the astonishing thing about proverbs: you rarely need to finish them. "He who digs a pit for others …" is enough, and everyone knows who ends up in the hole. Proverbs are stored judgements that you only have to call up. That is exactly why they have a bad reputation. Anyone who says "Every beginning is hard" in a discussion usually has no argument, only a calendar motto.

And yet they don't die out. They just move. What used to be written on decorative plates is now on mugs and in advertising slogans, and it is often twisted on the way. "If you rest, you post," I recently read on a poster for a gym. The anti-proverb only works because everyone knows the original. So it is proof of the old folk wisdom's vitality rather than of its decline.

Familiar quotations are even tougher. Hardly anyone has read the whole of *Faust*, but every other person asks about "the poodle's core" or puts "Gretchen's question" to a political party. Schiller gave the DIY store its slogan: "The axe in the house saves the carpenter." Hardly anyone still knows that in the play the line says more about Tell than about DIY.

My grandmother would have said only one thing about all this: "All's well that ends well." It's not quite that simple. But a truism isn't wrong just because everyone knows it.

</details>

## Sprichwort, Redensart, geflügeltes Wort, Zitat

German distinguishes four kinds of fixed or borrowed language. The boundaries are not sharp, but the core cases are clear.

| Term | What it is | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *das Sprichwort* (proverb) | a complete sentence, anonymous, stating a general truth or advice | *Viele Köche verderben den Brei.* |
| *die Redensart* | a fixed expression that is not a full sentence and states no general truth (in linguistics mostly called an idiom, lesson 16) | *jemandem einen Bärendienst erweisen* |
| *das geflügelte Wort* | a quotation that has become common property; its source is known or knowable | *des Pudels Kern* (Goethe), *Zeit ist Geld* (usually traced to Benjamin Franklin) |
| *das Zitat* | a quotation used as such, with its source in mind | *„Wir schaffen das“, sagte Angela Merkel im August 2015.* |

The term **[[winged word]]** (*geflügeltes Wort*) goes back to Homer's "winged words" (words that fly from mouth to mouth); it became the German term for familiar quotations through Georg Büchmann's collection *Geflügelte Worte* (1864), which has been revised and reissued many times since. The plural is *geflügelte Worte*, because these are sayings, not single words (*Wörter*).

A geflügeltes Wort can turn into a proverb when people forget its source: many speakers who say *Die Axt im Haus erspart den Zimmermann* don't know it is Schiller. *Zeit ist Geld* is also often heard as an anonymous proverb.

## Where geflügelte Worte come from

The richest sources of German geflügelte Worte are Luther's Bible, Goethe and Schiller, and later operetta, film and advertising. The quotations below are the forms in common use; the editions differ slightly in spelling and punctuation, so quote from a named edition when you quote exactly. Here *Faust I* is quoted from the Projekt Gutenberg-DE text (Reclam, 1971) and *Wilhelm Tell* from the Cotta edition of 1862 (Project Gutenberg eBook 77182).

**The Bible in Luther's translation** gave German dozens of sayings. Many are so ordinary that they no longer feel like quotations:

- *Hochmut kommt vor dem Fall* (Proverbs 16:18): *Vor dem Spiel prahlte er mit einem Kantersieg. Hochmut kommt vor dem Fall.*
- *Wer anderen eine Grube gräbt, fällt selbst hinein* (after Proverbs 26:27; the modern wording varies).
- *sein Licht unter den Scheffel stellen* (Matthew 5:15), to hide one's talents, and *Perlen vor die Säue werfen* (after Matthew 7:6), to waste something good on people who can't appreciate it.

**Goethe's** *Faust I* (1808) is the most quoted German book. Two quotations have become nouns or noun phrases:

- *des Pudels Kern*: in the scene *Studierzimmer*, the black poodle that has followed Faust home turns into Mephisto, and Faust exclaims: *„Das also war des Pudels Kern!“* (line 1323). Today *des Pudels Kern* means the real heart of a matter that was hidden: *Des Pudels Kern ist nicht der Preis, sondern die fehlende Wartung.* Notice the old word order: the genitive *des Pudels* stands before its noun, as in *Gottes Wille*. With a common noun this is gehoben or archaic today.
- *die Gretchenfrage*: in the scene *Marthens Garten*, Gretchen asks Faust: *„Nun sag, wie hast du's mit der Religion?“* (line 3415). He evades the answer. *Die Gretchenfrage* is now any direct question about someone's real convictions, which they would rather not answer, often in the pattern *Wie hältst du es / Wie hält es die Partei mit …?*: *Die Gretchenfrage dieser Koalition lautet: Wie hält sie es mit der Schuldenbremse?*

**Schiller** gave German many lines, above all from *Wilhelm Tell* (1804) and the *Wallenstein* trilogy. In *Wilhelm Tell* (Act III, Scene 1) Tell has just mended the gate of his house with his carpenter's axe, while his wife Hedwig worries about his dangerous life as a hunter. He puts the tools away, remarks that the gate will now hold for a good while, and adds: *„Die Axt im Haus erspart den Zimmermann.“* In the play it is part of Tell's character, a man who relies on himself and not on others, which matters for the plot. Today it is a jokey motto for DIY.

## Proverbs in use: cut short, twisted, ironic

Native speakers rarely recite a proverb in full. Three habits are typical.

**Cutting short.** Because everyone knows the ending, the first half is enough, often with a knowing pause or three dots: *Wer anderen eine Grube gräbt …*; *Stille Wasser …*; *Was Hänschen nicht lernt …*. The shortened form is more ironic than the full one: it assumes complicity.

**Twisting.** An *Antisprichwort* (anti-proverb; the term is from the paremiologist Wolfgang Mieder) keeps the frame of a proverb and changes its content. It is a kind of modification (lesson 16) at sentence level. Original examples:

- *Wer rastet, der postet.* (a gym poster: if you take a break, you just scroll your phone)
- *Viele Köche verderben den Lieferdienst.* (a restaurant review)
- *Übung macht den Meister, aber der Meisterbrief kostet trotzdem Gebühren.* (a craftsman's complaint)

An Antisprichwort only works if the original is instantly recognizable, which is why the same thirty or forty proverbs are twisted again and again.

**Irony.** A proverb can be said with the opposite intention. After the third failed attempt to put up a shelf, *Na ja, Übung macht den Meister* means "I'm hopeless". *Ende gut, alles gut*, said through clenched teeth after a disastrous holiday, means that it was anything but good. The irony signals are the usual ones (lesson 19): tone, *na ja*, *tja*, a pause, a raised eyebrow.

## The grammar of proverbs

Proverbs preserve older German, and they follow a few patterns that make them memorable.

| Pattern | Examples | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *wer …, (der) …* | *Wer rastet, der rostet. Wer zuletzt lacht, lacht am besten. Wer die Wahl hat, hat die Qual.* | a free relative clause; the *der* that takes it up can be dropped when the case is the same |
| *was …, (das) …* | *Was Hänschen nicht lernt, lernt Hans nimmermehr.* | same pattern with *was* |
| no verb | *Ende gut, alles gut.* | ellipsis; the proverb is a judgement, not a narrative |
| imperative | *Eile mit Weile.* | an old piece of advice addressed to anyone |
| generic present, no article | *Not macht erfinderisch. Kleider machen Leute. Zeit ist Geld.* | general truths in the present, often with bare nouns |
| older forms | *Morgenstund* (for *Morgenstunde*), *gut Ding* (uninflected adjective), *aller Anfang* (*all-* without an article = *jeder*), *nimmermehr*, *stet* | apocope and archaic inflection survive because the proverb is fixed |
| sound | *Eile mit Weile; Wahl – Qual; rastet – rostet; Morgenstund – Mund* | rhyme, assonance and alliteration hold the sentence together |

The dropped *-e* in *Morgenstund* is apocope, typical of older and southern German; it is kept here for the rhyme with *Mund*. *Gut Ding will Weile haben* uses an uninflected adjective before a neuter noun, normal in older German and fossilized in proverbs; today you would say *ein gutes Ding*. Don't imitate these forms outside the proverb.

## English equivalents that aren't quite equivalent

Many proverbs have a direct English partner (*Übung macht den Meister* = Practice makes perfect; *Stille Wasser sind tief* = Still waters run deep). Others have a functional equivalent with a different image:

- *Morgenstund hat Gold im Mund* (the morning hour has gold in its mouth) = The early bird catches the worm.
- *Viele Köche verderben den Brei* (porridge) = Too many cooks spoil the broth.
- *Was Hänschen nicht lernt, lernt Hans nimmermehr* (what little Hans doesn't learn, big Hans never learns) ≈ You can't teach an old dog new tricks. The German is about learning young; the English about the old being unteachable.
- *Wer die Wahl hat, hat die Qual* ≈ to be spoilt for choice, but the German stresses the agony of choosing.
- *Durch Schaden wird man klug* ≈ You learn the hard way (Once bitten, twice shy is narrower: it is about caution).

In translation, look for the functional equivalent; a literal translation of *Morgenstund hat Gold im Mund* sounds charmingly foreign, which is sometimes exactly what you want and usually not.

## When a proverb sounds trite

A proverb is a ready-made judgement. In conversation that is its strength; in an argument it can be a weakness. German has a rich vocabulary for language that is true but empty:

- *der Gemeinplatz*: a commonplace that everyone has heard (*Die Rede bestand aus Gemeinplätzen*).
- *die Binsenweisheit*: a truism, so obvious that saying it adds nothing (*Dass Bildung sich lohnt, ist eine Binsenweisheit*).
- *der Kalenderspruch*: wisdom of the kind printed on tear-off calendars, a little mocking.
- *die Plattitüde* (Duden: gehoben): a banal remark presented as if it were deep.
- *abgedroschen* (umgangssprachlich): worn out by overuse, like grain threshed too often (*eine abgedroschene Phrase*).

In a C2 essay or a Leserbrief, don't open or close with a proverb as if it settled the matter. If you use one, do something with it: question it (*„Aller Anfang ist schwer“, heißt es. Für die Reform gilt eher: Das Ende ist schwer.*), twist it, or quote it as the view you are arguing against. That is how the column above uses *Ende gut, alles gut*: as the grandmother's view, which the writer then qualifies.

## The words of this lesson

The proverbs are listed in their usual form; most are for recognition (German → English only), because typing a whole proverb from an English prompt makes little sense. Learn them as whole units, including their old forms (*Morgenstund*, *gut Ding*). *das geflügelte Wort* is a noun with an adjective, so it declines: *ein geflügeltes Wort, die geflügelten Worte, eines der bekanntesten geflügelten Worte*. *des Pudels Kern* keeps its genitive in every position: *Das ist des Pudels Kern*, *Sie kam des Pudels Kern sehr nahe*. *sprichwörtlich* means proverbial both literally (*eine sprichwörtliche Redewendung*) and in the sense of "famous, legendary" (*die sprichwörtliche Pünktlichkeit der Bahn*, often ironic).

## Common mistakes

- Calling every fixed phrase a *Sprichwort*: *jemandem die Leviten lesen* is a Redensart (idiom); a Sprichwort is a complete sentence with a general truth.
- *geflügelte Wörter*: the plural is *Worte*.
- Inflecting the archaic forms: ~~*Morgenstunde hat Gold im Mund*~~, ~~*Gutes Ding will Weile haben*~~. The proverb keeps its old shape.
- Translating word for word: *The axe in the house saves the carpenter* means nothing to an English reader.
- Using a proverb as an argument in a formal text. It reads as a Gemeinplatz unless you work with it.
- Twisting a proverb your reader may not know. Antisprichwörter work with the famous ones only.
- Attributing quotations from memory: *Zeit ist Geld* is usually traced to Franklin, *Hochmut kommt vor dem Fall* to the Bible; when in doubt, write *wie es heißt* or *wie man so sagt*, and check the source before quoting it exactly.

## Key points

- A Sprichwort is an anonymous full sentence with a general truth; a Redensart is a fixed phrase; a **[[winged word]]** (*geflügeltes Wort*) is a quotation that became common property (Büchmann, 1864); a Zitat is quoted with its source in mind.
- Major sources: Luther's Bible (*Hochmut kommt vor dem Fall*), Goethe's *Faust I* (*des Pudels Kern*, *die Gretchenfrage*), Schiller's *Wilhelm Tell* (*Die Axt im Haus erspart den Zimmermann*).
- Proverbs are cut short (*Wer anderen eine Grube gräbt …*), twisted into Antisprichwörter (*Wer rastet, der postet*) and used ironically.
- Their grammar: *wer …, (der) …*; verbless judgements; imperatives; bare nouns in the present; fossilized old forms (*Morgenstund, gut Ding, aller Anfang, nimmermehr*); rhyme and alliteration.
- Equivalents in English are often functional, with another image.
- A proverb used as an argument sounds like a Gemeinplatz, Binsenweisheit or Kalenderspruch; at C2, question it, twist it or quote it as the view you argue against.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Bedenken äußern, Zweifel hegen: collocations
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At C2, most of your remaining "mistakes" are not mistakes of grammar. They are combinations that are understandable but not what a native speaker would write: ~~*eine Entscheidung machen*~~, ~~*ein Risiko nehmen*~~, ~~*starke Bedenken sagen*~~. Every word is correct, the grammar is correct, and the sentence still sounds translated. The missing piece is the **[[collocation]]** (*Kollokation*): the preferred combination of two words.

Lesson 16 was about idioms, whose meaning you can't work out from the parts. Collocations are transparent: *einen Beschluss fassen* obviously means "to pass a resolution". What you can't work out is the verb: why *fassen* and not *machen*? This lesson shows the types of collocation, how they differ from Funktionsverbgefüge (C1 lesson 07), which collocations are a matter of register rather than right and wrong, where English leads you astray, and how to find the right partner in a corpus.

## A press release

Read this press release from an (invented) municipal theatre after a turbulent season. Press releases are a good place to study collocations: the writer wants to sound competent, so every noun gets its standard verb.

> **Stadttheater Neuwarthe: Intendantin zieht positive Bilanz – und nimmt Abschied**
>
> Nach acht Spielzeiten verlässt Intendantin Dr. Petra Hollweg das Stadttheater. Bei der Pressekonferenz am Montag zog sie eine überwiegend positive Bilanz. Ihr wichtigstes Ziel habe sie konsequent verfolgt: neue Zuschauergruppen zu gewinnen, ohne die eingefleischten Abonnenten zu verlieren. Vor allem das Jugendprogramm habe großen Anklang gefunden.
>
> Hollweg verschwieg auch die schwierigen Momente nicht. Als der Stadtrat 2023 den Beschluss fasste, den Zuschuss um zwölf Prozent zu kürzen, habe sie eine schwere Entscheidung treffen müssen: Statt das Ensemble zu verkleinern, habe man eine Spielstätte geschlossen und die längeren Wege für das Publikum in Kauf genommen. Für diesen Schritt übernehme sie bis heute die volle Verantwortung.
>
> Auch an Konflikten fehlte es nicht. Gegen die Inszenierung des „Woyzeck“ erhob der Kulturausschuss im vergangenen Jahr schwere Vorwürfe; einige Ratsmitglieder nahmen Anstoß an den Nacktszenen. Hollweg ergriff damals öffentlich Partei für den Regisseur. „Ich hege keinen Zweifel daran, dass ein Theater auch provozieren darf“, sagte sie. Mit ihren Argumenten fand sie schließlich Gehör: Im Ausschuss wurde ein Kompromiss geschlossen, der die künstlerische Freiheit wahrte, aber auf das junge Publikum Rücksicht nahm.
>
> Die Sanierung des Haupthauses ist nach Hollwegs Worten „bitter nötig“. Mehrere Gutachter hatten Bedenken gegen den Brandschutz geäußert; der Feueralarm, der im Frühjahr eine Premiere unterbrach, war zwar blinder Alarm, gilt aber als Warnung. Die Stadt hat dem Theater eine Frist bis Ende 2027 gesetzt, um ein Sanierungskonzept vorzulegen.
>
> Hollwegs Nachfolger, der aus Graz kommende Jonas Wendt, will in Neuwarthe „schnell Fuß fassen und lange Wurzeln schlagen“. Er lege großen Wert darauf, zunächst mit allen Abteilungen Gespräche zu führen.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Neuwarthe Municipal Theatre: director takes stock positively – and says farewell**

After eight seasons, artistic director Dr Petra Hollweg is leaving the municipal theatre. At Monday's press conference she gave a largely positive review of her time. She said she had consistently pursued her most important aim: to win new groups of theatregoers without losing the die-hard subscribers. Above all, the youth programme had been very well received.

Hollweg didn't conceal the difficult moments either. When the city council passed a resolution in 2023 to cut the subsidy by twelve per cent, she said, she had had to make a hard decision: instead of reducing the ensemble, they had closed one venue and accepted the longer journeys for the audience. She still takes full responsibility for this step today.

There was no lack of conflict either. Last year the culture committee levelled serious accusations against the production of *Woyzeck*; some council members took offence at the nude scenes. Hollweg publicly took the director's side at the time. "I have no doubt that a theatre is allowed to provoke," she said. In the end her arguments were heard: the committee agreed on a compromise that preserved artistic freedom but showed consideration for the young audience.

According to Hollweg, renovation of the main building is "badly needed". Several experts had voiced concerns about fire safety; the fire alarm that interrupted a premiere in the spring was a false alarm, but is seen as a warning. The city has set the theatre a deadline of the end of 2027 to present a renovation plan.

Hollweg's successor, Jonas Wendt, who comes from Graz, wants "to gain a foothold quickly and put down roots for a long time" in Neuwarthe. He said he attaches great importance to first holding talks with all departments.

</details>

Nearly every noun in the text comes with a verb or adjective that is typical for it: *Bilanz ziehen, ein Ziel verfolgen, Anklang finden, einen Beschluss fassen, eine Entscheidung treffen, in Kauf nehmen, Verantwortung übernehmen, Vorwürfe erheben, Anstoß nehmen, Partei ergreifen, Zweifel hegen, Gehör finden, einen Kompromiss schließen, Rücksicht nehmen, Bedenken äußern, eine Frist setzen, Fuß fassen, Wurzeln schlagen, Wert legen, Gespräche führen*, and on the adjective side *eingefleischte Abonnenten, bitter nötig, blinder Alarm*. Replace any of these verbs with *machen* or *haben* and the text immediately sounds like a learner wrote it.

## What a collocation is

A collocation is a combination of words that occur together far more often than chance would predict, and whose choice is conventional. Its meaning is transparent, but its form is not predictable. In *einen Beschluss fassen*, the noun *Beschluss* is the base: you choose it for its meaning. The verb *fassen* is the collocator: it is selected by the noun, and that is what you have to learn.

Collocations sit on a scale between free combinations and idioms:

| Type | Example | Meaning from the parts? | Words replaceable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| free combination | *ein Buch lesen, einen Brief schreiben* | yes | yes (*ein Buch kaufen, verschenken …*) |
| collocation | *Zähne putzen, Bilanz ziehen, Zweifel hegen* | yes | the collocator only within narrow limits |
| Funktionsverbgefüge (C1) | *zur Sprache bringen, in Kraft treten* | mostly; the verb is almost empty | no |
| idiom (lesson 16) | *den Bogen überspannen* | no | no |

The boundaries are disputed. Some grammars count *eine Entscheidung treffen* and *Verantwortung übernehmen* as Funktionsverbgefüge, because they can be replaced by a simple verb (*entscheiden*). Others reserve the term for combinations with a preposition and an aspect (*in Gang kommen*, *zum Abschluss bringen*). For your writing the label matters less than the combination itself.

## Register, not error: Zweifel haben and Zweifel hegen

Many nouns have several standard collocators of different register. Learners who discover the elegant one sometimes start treating the plain one as wrong. It isn't.

| Neutral | Formal or gehoben | Note |
|---|---|---|
| *Zweifel haben* | *Zweifel hegen* | *hegen* is gehoben; both are standard |
| *einen Verdacht haben* | *einen Verdacht hegen*; *Verdacht schöpfen* (to become suspicious) | |
| *Bedenken haben* | *Bedenken äußern* (to voice), *Bedenken anmelden* (formal), *Bedenken tragen* (gehoben: to hesitate) | *die Bedenken* is plural |
| *beschließen* | *einen Beschluss fassen* | the noun version is typical of minutes and press releases |
| *sich verabschieden* | *Abschied nehmen* | *Abschied nehmen* is more solemn, often about death |
| *Kritik üben* (C1) | *Kritik äußern* | both standard; *Kritik machen* is not |
| *eine Wette abschließen* | *eine Wette eingehen* | both standard; *Ich gehe jede Wette ein* is a fixed phrase |

In the press release, *Ich hege keinen Zweifel daran* fits a theatre director speaking to the press. In a chat, *Ich hab da echt Zweifel* is the natural choice; *hegen* would sound ironic.

## Types of collocation

### Noun + verb

The largest group, and the one that matters most for writing. The noun is usually the object, sometimes the subject (*die Frist läuft ab, der Verdacht erhärtet sich, Zweifel kommen auf*). Learn nouns with their typical verbs in both directions: what you do with the thing and what the thing does.

| Noun | Typical verbs |
|---|---|
| *die Frist* | *setzen, einräumen, einhalten, verlängern, versäumen; die Frist läuft ab* |
| *der Vorwurf* | *erheben, zurückweisen, entkräften; jemandem Vorwürfe machen* |
| *die Rücksicht* | *nehmen (auf), üben (gehoben); aus Rücksicht auf* |
| *das Risiko* | *eingehen, tragen, abwägen, minimieren, scheuen* |
| *die Verantwortung* | *übernehmen, tragen, ablehnen, abschieben; sich der Verantwortung entziehen* |
| *das Gespräch* | *führen, suchen, aufnehmen, abbrechen* |

Several collocations take a fixed preposition: *Wert legen auf* (acc.), *Rücksicht nehmen auf* (acc.), *Anstoß nehmen an* (dat.), *Zweifel hegen an* (dat.), *Bedenken äußern gegen*, *Partei ergreifen für / gegen*, *Einspruch erheben gegen*.

### Adjective + noun

Here the noun is the base and the adjective is selected by it, often with a meaning it has nowhere else:

- *blinder Alarm* (false alarm): *blind* here means "without cause", not "unable to see".
- *ein eingefleischter Junggeselle / Fan / Vegetarier* (die-hard): the adjective is almost never used without such a noun.
- *starker Raucher, starker Verkehr, starker Regen* but *schwerer Fehler, schwerer Unfall*; *großer Andrang, großes Interesse*; *dichter Nebel*.
- *ein heiß umkämpfter Markt, ein heiß ersehnter Urlaub*: *heiß* intensifies a participle.

### Intensifier + adjective or participle

German has a small set of intensifiers, each with its own partners. They are not interchangeable:

| Intensifier | Typical partners | Not |
|---|---|---|
| *bitter* | *nötig, kalt, arm, enttäuscht, ernst* | ~~*bitter schön*~~ |
| *heiß* | *umkämpft, ersehnt, geliebt, diskutiert* | ~~*heiß nötig*~~ |
| *schwer* | *verletzt, krank, beschädigt, bewaffnet, enttäuscht* | ~~*schwer müde*~~ |
| *hell-* (compound) | *hellwach, hellhörig* | |
| *hochgradig* | *giftig, gefährdet, nervös, kurzsichtig, korrupt* | rarely with positive adjectives |
| *tief* | *betroffen, enttäuscht, religiös, verwurzelt* | |
| *heillos* | *überfordert, zerstritten, verschuldet* | |

*schwer verletzt* can be written apart or together (Duden allows *schwer verletzt* and *schwerverletzt*); the noun is always together: *der Schwerverletzte*. The opposite is *leicht verletzt*, not ~~*wenig verletzt*~~. German C1 lesson 19 covered intensifying compounds (*stockdunkel, todmüde, brandneu*); these are their two-word relatives.

### Verb + adverb

Verbs, too, select their intensifiers: *fest schlafen*, *heftig kritisieren*, *scharf verurteilen* (also *aufs Schärfste verurteilen*), *inständig bitten*, *fest versprechen*, *ausdrücklich betonen*, *eindringlich warnen*. ~~*stark kritisieren*~~ is understood but less idiomatic than *heftig* or *scharf*.

## English interference

English collocations are the most common source of almost-right German. The verb in English is often *make, take, have* or *give*; German usually wants a more specific verb.

| English | German | Not |
|---|---|---|
| to make a decision | *eine Entscheidung treffen* | ~~*eine Entscheidung machen*~~ |
| to take a risk | *ein Risiko eingehen* | ~~*ein Risiko nehmen*~~ |
| to take responsibility | *Verantwortung übernehmen* | ~~*Verantwortung nehmen*~~ |
| to pass a resolution | *einen Beschluss fassen* | ~~*einen Beschluss passieren*~~ |
| to raise an objection | *Einspruch erheben* | ~~*einen Einspruch heben*~~ |
| to hold a conversation | *ein Gespräch führen* | ~~*ein Gespräch halten*~~ |
| to give a speech / lecture | *eine Rede / einen Vortrag halten* | ~~*eine Rede geben*~~ |
| to ask a question | *eine Frage stellen* | ~~*eine Frage fragen*~~ |
| to make an effort | *sich Mühe geben* | ~~*eine Anstrengung machen*~~ (understood, but rare) |
| to take sides | *Partei ergreifen* | ~~*Seiten nehmen*~~ |
| to take offence | *Anstoß nehmen* (an), *sich gekränkt fühlen* | ~~*Beleidigung nehmen*~~ |
| a heavy smoker | *ein starker Raucher* | ~~*ein schwerer Raucher*~~ |
| a false alarm | *ein blinder Alarm* (also *Fehlalarm*) | *falscher Alarm* is heard but less idiomatic |

Not every English verb is wrong in German: *einen Fehler machen*, *einen Vorschlag machen* and *ein Foto machen* are standard. The lesson is not "never use *machen*", but "check".

## Collocation or Funktionsverbgefüge?

C1 lesson 07 taught Funktionsverbgefüge (FVG): *zur Sprache bringen, in Betracht ziehen, unter Druck setzen*. The difference from a collocation, in its clearest form:

- In an FVG the verb is nearly empty, the noun carries the meaning, and the whole can usually be replaced by a simple verb: *zur Sprache bringen* = *ansprechen*. The verb often adds aspect: *in Gang kommen* (start) / *in Gang setzen* (cause to start) / *in Gang halten* (continue).
- In a collocation the verb keeps some of its own meaning and the noun is a normal object: *Wurzeln schlagen* still pictures roots going into the ground; *einen Kompromiss schließen* is like *einen Vertrag schließen*.

Many combinations sit in between (*eine Entscheidung treffen, Anklang finden*). Two tests help: Can you replace it with one verb (*entscheiden*)? Can you add an article or adjective to the noun freely (*eine schwere Entscheidung treffen*: yes, so it behaves like a collocation)? FVGs with a preposition usually refuse adjectives: ~~*zur deutlichen Sprache bringen*~~.

## Finding collocations

Don't guess the collocator; look it up.

- **DWDS-Wortprofil** (dwds.de): enter the noun and see the verbs it is most strongly associated with, sorted by grammatical relation (as object, as subject, with which adjectives). The list is ranked by a statistical association measure over large corpora, so the top entries are the typical partners, not merely frequent words.
- **Duden online** shows a computer-generated list of typical combinations ("Typische Verbindungen") on many entries.
- **A corpus search** for the noun with a wildcard verb shows real sentences, which tells you the register.

Use the tools in both directions: to find the verb you are missing, and to check whether the combination you wrote exists at all. If a combination returns almost nothing in a large corpus, it is not a collocation, however logical it seems.

## Editing almost-right German

Here is a paragraph a learner might write. Every sentence is understandable; none is quite right.

> ~~Der Vorstand hat letzte Woche eine Entscheidung gemacht. Er hat das Risiko genommen, den Standort zu schließen, und will dafür die Verantwortung nehmen. Viele Mitarbeiter haben starke Bedenken gesagt, aber ihre Kritik hat kein Ohr gefunden.~~

The repaired version, with the collocations a native writer would choose:

> *Der Vorstand hat letzte Woche eine Entscheidung getroffen. Er ist das Risiko eingegangen, den Standort zu schließen, und will dafür die Verantwortung übernehmen. Viele Mitarbeiter haben erhebliche Bedenken geäußert, doch ihre Kritik fand kein Gehör.*

Notice *ist … eingegangen* (perfect with *sein*), *erhebliche Bedenken* (*erheblich* is a typical intensifier of *Bedenken*; *starke Bedenken* is possible but weaker as a collocation) and *Gehör finden* (the noun is *Gehör*, not *Ohr*; *ein offenes Ohr finden* exists too, with a friendlier tone).

## The words of this lesson

Most items are collocations listed as phrases. Learn the preposition where there is one (*Wert legen auf*, *Anstoß nehmen an*) and the perfect auxiliary of the verb: *ein Risiko / eine Wette eingehen* takes *sein* although it has an object (*Ich bin das Risiko eingegangen*). *ein Exempel statuieren* (bildungssprachlich) is one of the few uses of *statuieren* at all. Three adjectives stand alone: *eingefleischt* (die-hard, almost only before *Fan, Junggeselle, Vegetarier, Optimist*), *hochgradig* and *hellwach*. *die Kollokation* is the linguist's term.

## Common mistakes

- *machen* for everything: ~~*eine Entscheidung machen*~~, ~~*Abschied machen*~~, ~~*einen Beschluss machen*~~.
- Calques of *take*: ~~*ein Risiko nehmen*~~, ~~*Verantwortung nehmen*~~ (correct: *eingehen*, *übernehmen*).
- The wrong intensifier: ~~*heiß nötig*~~, ~~*bitter umkämpft*~~, ~~*wenig verletzt*~~.
- Wrong preposition: ~~*Wert legen für*~~, ~~*Anstoß nehmen über*~~.
- Treating the neutral collocation as wrong: *Zweifel haben* and *Bedenken haben* are standard German. *hegen* and *äußern* are a register choice.
- Over-formality: *Zweifel hegen* in a text message, *einen Beschluss fassen* about where to go for pizza. That is a Stilbruch in the other direction.
- Forgetting *sein* in the perfect of *eingehen*: ~~*Er hat ein Risiko eingegangen*~~.
- Inventing a combination because it seems logical. If the DWDS-Wortprofil doesn't show it, rephrase.

## Key points

- A **[[collocation]]** is a conventional combination whose meaning is transparent but whose form you can't predict: the base (usually the noun) selects the collocator.
- Collocations lie between free combinations and Funktionsverbgefüge/idioms; the boundaries are disputed.
- Many nouns have neutral and formal collocators: *Zweifel haben / hegen*, *Bedenken haben / äußern / anmelden*. Both are correct; choose by register.
- The main types: noun + verb (with fixed prepositions), adjective + noun (*blinder Alarm, eingefleischter Fan*), intensifier + adjective (*bitter nötig, heiß umkämpft, schwer verletzt, hellwach, hochgradig giftig*), verb + adverb (*scharf verurteilen*).
- English *make/take/give* calques are the biggest source of error: *eine Entscheidung treffen, ein Risiko eingehen, Verantwortung übernehmen, eine Rede halten*.
- Check collocations in the DWDS-Wortprofil or Duden's typical combinations instead of guessing.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Kalauer, Ironie, Understatement: humour and wordplay
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Understanding a joke is one of the last things a learner masters, and making one in German is harder still. Humour depends on everything at once: double meanings, sound, register, shared knowledge and the precise moment when the expectation is broken. This lesson takes German humour apart linguistically (without, it is hoped, killing it): the **[[pun]]** (*Wortspiel*) and its cheaper cousin the Kalauer, the Schüttelreim, **[[irony]]** and its signals, **[[sarcasm]]**, **[[understatement]]**, black humour and Galgenhumor, comedy of situation, and the difference between Persiflage and Parodie.

German B2 honors covered satire and Kabarett, and B2 taught the basic words (*die Ironie, ironisch, der Sarkasmus, die Pointe, die Anspielung*). Here you learn to see how a joke is built, why it works in German and not in translation, and how to recognize irony that isn't marked at all.

## An interview on German humour

Read this interview from the (invented) weekend supplement of a newspaper. The interviewee is a linguist who studies humour.

> **„Der Kalauer ist ehrlicher, als man denkt“**
>
> *Frau Dr. Brandt, die Deutschen gelten im Ausland als humorlos. Zu Recht?*
>
> Das ist selbst ein guter Witz. Fragen Sie mal in Köln während des Karnevals oder in einer Berliner Eckkneipe nach. Was stimmt: Im Beruf trennt man in Deutschland Ernst und Spaß strenger als etwa in Großbritannien. Wer in einer Sitzung witzelt, gilt schnell als unseriös.
>
> *Sie forschen über den Kalauer. Warum ausgerechnet über den schlechtesten aller Witze?*
>
> Weil er ehrlicher ist, als man denkt. Ein Kalauer gibt gar nicht vor, geistreich zu sein. „Sagt der Anlageberater im Stadtpark: Ich setze voll auf diese Bank.“ Darüber stöhnt man, und genau das ist die Pointe. Der Kalauer lebt von der Doppeldeutigkeit eines Wortes, und er zwinkert dabei mit beiden Augen.
>
> *Und die Ironie?*
>
> Die ist anspruchsvoller. Ironie heißt, etwas zu sagen und das Gegenteil zu meinen, und darauf zu vertrauen, dass der andere es merkt. Wenn mein Zug zum dritten Mal ausfällt und ich sage: „Na, das läuft ja wieder prima“, dann brauche ich Ironiesignale: das „ja“, den Tonfall, vielleicht ein Augenrollen. Schriftlich fehlen die oft. Deshalb setzen viele heute ein Zwinker-Emoji, und deshalb gehen so viele ironische Beiträge im Netz schief.
>
> *Gibt es einen typisch deutschen Humor?*
>
> Es gibt Klischees, und die sind selbst ein Stück Humor: die Berliner Schnauze, der trockene Norden, der Schwabe, der angeblich jeden Cent zweimal umdreht. Interessanter finde ich den Galgenhumor. Als in meiner Heimatstadt das Hochwasser kam, hing an einem überfluteten Café ein Schild: „Heute nur Wasser aus dem Hahn – und aus dem Keller.“ Das ist schwarzer Humor ohne Bosheit. Man lacht, um nicht zu verzweifeln.
>
> *Und das Understatement, das man den Briten nachsagt?*
>
> Gibt es hier auch, nur seltener. Mein Großvater hat den Bombenangriff auf seine Stadt immer als „eine etwas unruhige Nacht“ bezeichnet. Das war nicht komisch gemeint. Aber es war die einzige Art, wie er darüber reden konnte.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**"The groaner is more honest than you think"**

*Dr Brandt, abroad the Germans are considered humourless. Rightly?*

That's a good joke in itself. Go and ask in Cologne during carnival or in a Berlin corner pub. What is true is that in Germany work and fun are kept apart more strictly than, say, in Britain. Anyone who cracks jokes in a meeting is quickly seen as unprofessional.

*You research the groaner, the corny pun. Why the worst of all jokes, of all things?*

Because it's more honest than you think. A groaner doesn't even pretend to be witty. "The investment adviser in the park says: I'm putting everything on this bench" (*Bank*: bank or bench). People groan at it, and that's exactly the punchline. The groaner lives off the double meaning of a word, and it winks with both eyes as it does so.

*And irony?*

That's more demanding. Irony means saying something, meaning the opposite and trusting that the other person will notice. When my train is cancelled for the third time and I say "Well, this is going splendidly again", I need irony markers: the *ja*, the tone of voice, perhaps an eye-roll. In writing these are often missing. That's why many people now add a winking emoji, and why so many ironic posts online go wrong.

*Is there a typically German humour?*

There are clichés, and they are a piece of humour themselves: the Berlin lip, the dry north, the Swabian who supposedly turns every cent over twice. I find gallows humour more interesting. When the flood came to my home town, a sign hung on a flooded café: "Today only water from the tap – and from the cellar." That is black humour without malice. You laugh so as not to despair.

*And the understatement people attribute to the British?*

It exists here too, just more rarely. My grandfather always called the bombing raid on his city "a somewhat restless night". It wasn't meant to be funny. But it was the only way he could talk about it.

</details>

## Wordplay: Wortspiel, Kalauer, Teekesselchen

A **[[pun]]** (*das Wortspiel*) exploits a word or phrase that has two meanings, or two words that sound alike. German offers three main sources.

**Homonyms and polysemous words.** *die Bank* (bank / bench), *das Schloss* (castle / lock), *die Kiefer* (pine) and *der Kiefer* (jaw), *der Strauß* (ostrich / bouquet), *die Mutter* (mother / nut for a bolt), *umfahren* (to knock down / to drive round, lesson 10). The children's game *Teekesselchen* is built on them: one player describes "my Teekesselchen" (a green tree), the other "my Teekesselchen" (a part of the face), and the rest guess *Kiefer*.

**Re-segmenting compounds.** German writes compounds as one word, so a long word can sometimes be split in two ways: *Staubecken* is *Stau|becken* (reservoir) or *Staub|ecken* (dusty corners); *Urinstinkt* is *Ur|instinkt* (primal instinct) or, as schoolchildren love to point out, *Urin|stinkt*. Advertising plays with word boundaries deliberately: a hair salon called *Haarmonie* blends *Haar* and *Harmonie*, a pun that only works in writing.
