lessons.title: Das große Lalula: nonsense poetry and Dada
lessons.body:
## Words that mean nothing, and sound German

Lesson 19 ended with the Schüttelreim, a game that produces absurd sense from swapped sounds. This honors lesson goes to the edge where sense disappears altogether: **[[nonsense poetry]]** (*Unsinnspoesie*) and the **[[sound poem]]** (*Lautgedicht*). The texts are from Christian Morgenstern (1871–1914), Hugo Ball (1886–1927) and Kurt Schwitters (1887–1948), all in the public domain. They are fun, but they also make a serious point for a C2 learner: even when German stops meaning anything, it doesn't stop being German. Nonsense obeys the sound rules, the word formation and the grammar of the language, and you can only enjoy it fully if you know those rules well.

Contemporary nonsense poets such as Ernst Jandl and Robert Gernhardt are not quoted here: their work is still under copyright.

## Morgenstern's Galgenlieder

Christian Morgenstern's *Galgenlieder* ("gallows songs", first published 1905) are sung, in the fiction of the book, by a band of hanged men on a gallows hill. They are the classic of German nonsense poetry, and many of their coinages (*das Nasobēm*, *das Mondschaf*) have become part of the language of educated jokes. The quotations below follow the 22nd edition (Bruno Cassirer, Berlin 1917) as transcribed in Project Gutenberg eBook 33541 (*Galgenlieder nebst dem 'Gingganz'*), with its original spelling (*daß*, *mußte*, *Wißt*) and its special characters.

### Pure sound: Das große Lalula

The first stanza of *Das große Lalula*:

> Kroklokwafzi? Seṁemeṁi!
> Seiokrontro – prafriplo:
> Bifzi, bafzi; hulaleṁi:
> quasti basti bo ...
> Lalu lalu lalu lalu la!

There is not one German word in it, and yet it sounds German, not Italian, Finnish or English. Why?

- **The consonant clusters are German.** *kr, kl, pr, fr, pl, qu* [kv] begin syllables exactly as in *Krone, klein, Preis, frei, Platz, Quelle*. A cluster that German doesn't allow at the start of a syllable, such as *tl* or *ng*, never appears.
- **The stress is German.** Read aloud, the words fall into trochees, stressed–unstressed: *KROK-lok-WAF-zi*, *BIF-zi, BAF-zi*. That is the rhythm of *Kinder, Wagen, Fenster*.
- **The punctuation is German syntax.** The question mark, colon, semicolon and dash make you hear questions, announcements and pauses, so the stanza sounds like a dialogue in a language you almost understand.
- **The refrain** *Lalu lalu lalu lalu la!* is a children's singing syllable, and it ties the poem to the lullaby and the nursery rhyme.

The dots over some letters (*ṁ*) and the other signs in later stanzas are part of the joke: they look like the diacritics of a scholarly transcription, as if the poem had to be pronounced exactly right.

### Grammar as a joke: Der Werwolf

*Der Werwolf* is a poem about German grammar. A werewolf goes to the grave of a village schoolteacher and asks to be declined ("Bitte, beuge mich!"). The first, third, fourth and fifth stanzas:

> Ein Werwolf eines Nachts entwich
> von Weib und Kind und sich begab
> an eines Dorfschullehrers Grab
> und bat ihn: Bitte, beuge mich!
>
> ›Der Werwolf‹ – sprach der gute Mann,
> ›des Weswolfs, Genitiv sodann,
> ›dem Wemwolf, Dativ, wie man's nennt,
> ›den Wenwolf, – damit hat's ein End'.‹
>
> Dem Werwolf schmeichelten die Fälle,
> er rollte seine Augenbälle.
> Indessen, bat er, füge doch
> zur Einzahl auch die Mehrzahl noch!
>
> Der Dorfschulmeister aber mußte
> gestehn, daß er von ihr nichts wußte.
> Zwar Wölfe gäb's in großer Schar,
> doch ›Wer‹ gäb's nur im Singular.

The joke works only if you know two things. First, the teacher treats *Wer-* as the interrogative pronoun *wer* and declines it: *wer, wes* (the old genitive, still in *Wes Brot ich ess, des Lied ich sing*; today *wessen*), *wem, wen*. Second, *wer* really has no plural, so the teacher is grammatically right: there is no plural of *Wer*. The real word *Werwolf* has nothing to do with the pronoun; its first part is usually explained as an old word for "man" (Old High German *wer*). The poem turns a fact of morphology into a tragedy: the wolf goes home without his plural.

Notice also the old-fashioned syntax that makes the poem sound like a ballad: *Ein Werwolf eines Nachts entwich* (the verb at the end of a main clause, a poetic licence), *gestehn* (syncopated for *gestehen*), *gäb's* (Konjunktiv II with an apocopated *es*, for reported speech), and the adverbial genitive *eines Nachts* (one night; note the *-s* on a feminine noun, by analogy with *eines Tages*).

### Rhyme forcing sense: Das ästhetische Wiesel

The whole poem:

> Ein Wiesel
> saß auf einem Kiesel
> inmitten Bachgeriesel.
>
> Wißt ihr
> weshalb?
>
> Das Mondkalb
> verriet es mir
> im Stillen:
>
> Das raffinier-
> te Tier
> tat's um des Reimes willen.

The title in the edition is spelled *Das æsthetische Wiesel*. The poem's answer to its own question is the joke: the weasel sits on the pebble only because *Wiesel* rhymes with *Kiesel* and *Bachgeriesel* (a coinage of the Ge-…-e type, lesson 09, from *rieseln*, lesson 20). The rhyme dictates the content. German has a word for this: *der Reimzwang*, the constraint of rhyme that makes a poet choose a word for its sound. The poem even breaks *raffinierte* across a line (*raffinier- / te*) so that *Tier* can rhyme with *mir*. Morgenstern makes the poet's dirty secret into the subject of the poem.

### A poem without words: Fisches Nachtgesang

*Fisches Nachtgesang* consists only of metrical signs, the marks for stressed and unstressed syllables used in verse analysis (C1 lesson 27), arranged in the shape of a fish. It can't be reproduced in plain text, and the Project Gutenberg transcription gives it only as an image. It is a silent poem: a fish can't sing, so its song is pure metre. Visual poems like this are described, not quoted, in this course.

## Ringelnatz

Joachim Ringelnatz (1883–1934) belongs to the same tradition but is earthier: his sailor Kuttel Daddeldu drinks, swears and philosophizes in a mixture of nonsense, slang and sentiment, and his *Turngedichte* (1920) make the language of gymnastics absurd. Where Morgenstern's nonsense is learned and exact, Ringelnatz's is that of the harbour bar. Both are good examples of how a register can be played against its content.

## Dada and the sound poem

Dada began in Zurich during the First World War. In February 1916 Hugo Ball and Emmy Hennings opened the Cabaret Voltaire, where artists from several countries performed provocations against a culture that, in their eyes, had produced the war. *Der Dadaismus* rejected sense, art and logic as such. Its German adjective is *dadaistisch*.

In the summer of 1916 Ball recited his first sound poems at the Cabaret Voltaire, dressed in a cardboard costume, and later described them as "Verse ohne Worte". The best known, *Karawane*, is usually dated 1917 and was first printed in Richard Huelsenbeck's *Dada Almanach* (Berlin: Erich Reiss, 1920, p. 53), each line in a different typeface. It begins (as Reinhard Döhl transcribes the Almanach print; simplified reprints write plain *o*):

> jolifanto bambla ô falli bambla

A sound poem (*Lautgedicht*; the genre is *die Lautpoesie*) goes further than Morgenstern: it doesn't play with German, it leaves it. And still the listener hears something. *Karawane* is the title, and the sounds that follow (heavy *b, m, bl*, open vowels) are heard as the trudging of elephants and the rhythm of a caravan. A sound poem means through sound symbolism and through its title, not through words.

## Grammar played with: Schwitters's Anna Blume

Kurt Schwitters, a Dada artist from Hanover, published *An Anna Blume* in 1919. It is a love poem that breaks every rule of the genre, starting with grammar. Short passages, quoted from the first book edition (*Anna Blume. Dichtungen*, Hannover: Paul Steegemann, 1919, as transcribed on Wikisource; the line breaks there fall differently):

> O du, Geliebte meiner siebenundzwanzig Sinne, ich liebe dir!

*ich liebe dir* uses the dative where German requires the accusative (*ich liebe dich*). The mistake is deliberate: in Berlin and parts of northern Germany, mixing up *mir/mich* and *dir/dich* was a well-known feature of popular speech, and the poem's lover sounds both clumsy and sincere. A few lines later the speaker runs through the pronoun's forms (*Du deiner dich dir, ich dir, du mir*) as if declining the beloved, a game very close to Morgenstern's werewolf. And Anna's name is celebrated as a palindrome, spelled out as *a-n-n-a*: *Man kann dich auch von hinten lesen*. *Blau ist die Farbe deines gelben Haares* is the most quoted line: a contradiction that sounds like a compliment.

The poem was attacked and parodied when it appeared, and it made Schwitters famous. Read today, it shows how much a C2 reader takes for granted: you only find *ich liebe dir* funny or touching if the accusative is automatic for you.

## Writing your own

Nonsense is a good exercise in German phonotactics and morphology. Try these:

- **A Lautgedicht of four lines** that sounds German: use only syllable onsets German allows (*schl, kn, pfl, str, zw*), put the stress on the first syllable of each "word", and give it a title that tells the listener what to hear (*Gewitter*, *Bahnhof*).
- **A Morgenstern-style declension joke**: find a word whose first part looks like a pronoun or article (*der Dermatologe, das Dasein, die Diebin*) and decline the false part.
- **A Schüttelreim** (lesson 19): find two words whose initial consonants can swap into two other words (*Rasen Hosen – Hasen Rosen*).

## The words of this lesson

*die Unsinnspoesie* and *der Nonsens* (lesson 19) overlap, but the first is the literary genre. *das Sprachspiel* is any game with language (in philosophy also Wittgenstein's "language-game"); *die Sprachspielerei* is more casual and can sound dismissive. *die Wortneuschöpfung* is a newly invented word, like *Mondschaf*. *verballhornen* (to garble, distort a word or text) is usually traced to Johann Balhorn, a 16th-century Lübeck printer whose edition was said to have made a text worse; the story is told in many versions. *der Unfug* (nonsense, mischief) and *der Ulk* (a lark, a harmless joke) are everyday words; *sinnfrei* (meaningless) is mostly colloquial and ironic (*eine völlig sinnfreie Diskussion*), but critics also use it descriptively for Dada.

## Key points

- **[[Nonsense poetry]]** (*Unsinnspoesie*) still obeys German phonotactics, stress and syntax: *Kroklokwafzi* sounds German because its clusters and trochees are German.
- Morgenstern's *Galgenlieder* (1905) play with grammar (*Der Werwolf*: *wer* has no plural), rhyme (*Das ästhetische Wiesel*: Reimzwang) and the page (*Fisches Nachtgesang*: metrical signs only).
- Dada began at the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in 1916; Hugo Ball's **[[sound poems]]** (*Lautgedichte*) leave words behind and mean through sound and title.
- Schwitters's *An Anna Blume* (1919) breaks grammar on purpose (*ich liebe dir*) and declines the pronoun as a love game.
- Quote these texts from a named edition with their original spelling; describe visual poems rather than reproducing them.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Der Rabe und der Fuchs: fables, parables and Lessing
lessons.body:
## Stories that teach

A **[[fable]]** (*die Fabel*) is the oldest form of figurative storytelling: animals act like people, and the reader is meant to recognize himself. A **[[parable]]** (*die Parabel*) does the same with human figures, and leaves more to the reader. Both connect to the rest of this module: like a proverb (lesson 17) they end in a general truth, like a metaphor (lesson 20) they say one thing and mean another, and they rely on fixed images: the cunning fox, the vain raven, the strong lion.

This honors lesson looks at the fable as a form, at Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (1729–1781), who rewrote the old fables for the Enlightenment, and at the most famous German parable, the Ringparabel from his play *Nathan der Weise* (1779). At the end you write an original fable yourself.

## The fable as a form

A classic fable has four parts:

| Part | What happens | In the raven and the fox |
|---|---|---|
| situation | two animals meet, one has something the other wants | a raven sits in a tree with a piece of food; a fox below |
| action | one tries a trick or uses force | the fox flatters the raven |
| reaction and turn | the other reacts, and the result is the opposite of what he hoped | the raven, pleased, lets the food fall |
| moral (*die Lehre*, *die Moral*) | a general truth, stated or implied | beware of flatterers |

The animals are types, not individuals. The fox is *listig*, the raven *eitel*, the lion powerful, the lamb innocent, the wolf greedy. This is why fables are short: the reader knows the characters before the story begins.

The language of a German fable is just as typical. It is told in the Präteritum (*Ein Rabe saß auf einem Baum*), with an indefinite article for the characters at the start (*ein Fuchs*) and the definite article afterwards (*der Fuchs*), short sentences, and the decisive moment in direct speech: the trick is spoken, not reported. The moral may stand before the story (rhetoric calls it the *promythium*) or after it (*epimythium*); in many modern fables it is left out, and the reader must draw it.

The tradition runs from the Greek Aesop (to whom the old fables are attributed; whether he existed is uncertain) through the Latin Phaedrus to Jean de La Fontaine (1621–1695), whose verse fables are the version most Europeans know. Martin Luther began a German collection of Aesop's fables in 1530, in a sober prose meant for teaching; it was printed only after his death.

## The traditional raven and fox

In the version most people know, the fox praises the raven's beauty and asks to hear his voice, which must surely be just as beautiful. The raven opens his beak to sing, the cheese (or meat) falls, and the fox takes it and leaves with the remark that flatterers live off those who listen to them. The moral is clear and comfortable: the reader identifies with the clever fox, laughs at the vain raven and resolves not to be flattered.

## Lessing's version: the flatterer punished

Lessing published *Fabeln. Drei Bücher* in 1759, together with essays on the theory of the fable (*Abhandlungen über die Fabel*). He rejected the elaborate verse fables of his time: a fable, he argued, should be short, in prose, and should make the general truth visible in one particular case. Many of his fables take an old story and turn it.

His *Der Rabe und der Fuchs* (in the second book) is the famous example. Retold in modern German:

> *Ein Rabe trug ein Stück Fleisch in seinen Krallen davon. Was er nicht wusste: Ein wütender Gärtner hatte es vergiftet und für die Katzen des Nachbarn ausgelegt. Als der Rabe es auf einer Eiche verzehren wollte, schlich ein Fuchs heran und begrüßte ihn als den Adler des Göttervaters, der ihm Armen täglich Nahrung bringe. Der Rabe war geschmeichelt, für einen Adler gehalten zu werden, und ließ das Fleisch großzügig fallen. Der Fuchs fraß es lachend – und starb kurz darauf an dem Gift.*

Lessing ends with an apostrophe to all flatterers, wishing them nothing but poison as their reward: *„Möchtet ihr euch nie etwas anders als Gift erloben, verdammte Schmeichler!“* (Book II, No. 15; text as in Lessing, *Werke und Briefe*, ed. Wilfried Barner, vol. 4, Deutscher Klassiker Verlag, 1997, p. 321 f.)

Three things have changed compared with the traditional version:

1. **The trick is more refined.** The fox doesn't praise the raven's voice but mistakes him, on purpose, for an eagle. The raven's vanity is not about singing but about rank.
2. **The winner loses.** The fox gets the meat and dies of it. The reader who identified with the clever fox is caught out.
3. **The moral is an attack, not a rule of prudence.** The traditional version says "don't listen to flatterers"; Lessing says "flatterers deserve poison". The *Möchtet ihr …* is an optative, the old wish form with the Konjunktiv II of *mögen* (lesson 03 in module 1 covers optative formulas): a curse, not a piece of advice.

*erloben* is an old verb: to obtain by praising. Lessing needs it because the flatterer "earns" his reward by praise. It is a typical Enlightenment technique: an old form, a sharper point, and the reader is made to think instead of nodding along.

## The parable

A parable tells a story with human characters that stands for something else, and the reader has to transfer it. German has two words:

- *das Gleichnis* is mostly used for the parables of the Bible (*das Gleichnis vom verlorenen Sohn*, Luke 15) and for extended comparisons in rhetoric. The adjective is *gleichnishaft*.
- *die Parabel* is the literary term for a parable as a genre, from the Enlightenment to the 20th century. The adjective is *parabelhaft*. (In mathematics *die Parabel* is also the parabola.)

The difference from the fable: a fable states or strongly implies its moral, and its animals are types. A parable is more open, its figures are human, and the transfer from the story to its meaning (*die Übertragung*) is the reader's work. A parable can be read in several ways, which is why it suits questions that have no simple answer.

## The Ringparabel

In *Nathan der Weise* (1779), set in Jerusalem at the time of the Crusades, the sultan Saladin asks the Jewish merchant Nathan a dangerous question: which of the three religions, Judaism, Christianity or Islam, is the true one? Nathan, who suspects a trap, answers with a story (Act III, Scene 7).

Long ago a man in the East owned a ring with a stone that made its wearer pleasing to God and to people, if he wore it with confidence in its power. The play begins the tale with (quoted, here and below, in modernized spelling from Projekt Gutenberg-DE, after a Reclam edition of 1995):

> Vor grauen Jahren lebt' ein Mann in Osten,

The ring passed from father to the favourite son for generations, until a father loved his three sons equally and had two perfect copies made. After his death each son claimed to own the true ring, and they went to court. The judge's answer is the heart of the parable: the true ring cannot be identified. Perhaps the father had lost the original. Each son should act as if his ring were the true one, and prove it by his conduct:

> Es eifre jeder seiner unbestochnen
> Von Vorurteilen freien Liebe nach!

*Es eifre jeder … nach* is a hortative subjunctive: Konjunktiv I in a main clause as an appeal (lesson 03 in module 1): "Let each one strive to emulate …". *unbestochen* (unbribed) and *von Vorurteilen frei* describe the father's love, which each son should imitate. The judge then postpones the final verdict to a wiser judge in the distant future.

**The form.** *Nathan der Weise* is written in blank verse (*Blankvers*): unrhymed lines of five iambs, x x́ x x́ x x́ x x́ x x́, the metre that Lessing helped to establish in German drama (C1 lesson 27 introduced metre). *lebt'* (for *lebte*) and *unbestochnen* (for *unbestochenen*) are shortened to fit it: apocope and syncope (lesson 26 in module 6 covers them).

**How the moral works.** The Ringparabel doesn't answer Saladin's question; it replaces it. Instead of "which religion is true?" it asks "how should one live if no one can prove it?". The moral is stated by the judge, but its application is left to the listeners, and that is what makes it a parable and not a fable.

## Stating the moral or leaving it

Fables and parables differ in how much they say. In German writing you will meet the full range:

- **The moral stated after the story** (traditional fables): *Die Lehre aus der Geschichte: Wer Schmeichlern glaubt, verliert.*
- **The moral as an attack** (Lessing): *verdammte Schmeichler!*
- **The moral in a character's mouth** (the judge in the Ringparabel).
- **No moral at all** (modern fables and parables): the reader has to work it out, and different readers may draw different lessons.

The more the moral is spelled out, the more *belehrend* the text sounds. That is not always a fault: a children's book may want *Belehrung*. But at C2, a fable whose moral is too obvious reads as preachy, and modern writers prefer to stop one sentence early.

## An original modern fable

Here is a short fable written for this course. Notice the Präteritum, the articles, the direct speech at the turning point and the missing moral.

> *Eine Elster hatte im Park einen glänzenden Schlüssel gefunden und trug ihn stolz von Ast zu Ast. „Was schließt er auf?“, fragte die Amsel. „Das ist doch egal“, antwortete die Elster. „Er glänzt.“ Am Abend kam ein Mann in den Park, suchte lange im Gras und setzte sich schließlich auf eine Bank. Er konnte nicht nach Hause. Die Elster sah ihm eine Weile zu. Dann legte sie den Schlüssel in ihr Nest, zu den anderen.*

*A magpie had found a shiny key in the park and carried it proudly from branch to branch. "What does it open?" asked the blackbird. "That doesn't matter," answered the magpie. "It shines." In the evening a man came into the park, searched the grass for a long time and finally sat down on a bench. He couldn't get home. The magpie watched him for a while. Then she put the key in her nest, with the others.*

The reader draws the moral (about collecting things for their shine, or about not caring what our pleasures cost others), and *zu den anderen* adds a last, darker detail: this happens every day. Try it yourself: choose two animals with known traits, a conflict over one object, a turn in direct speech, and stop before the moral.

## The words of this lesson

*die Fabel* is also the technical term for the plot of a play or novel in literary analysis (*die Fabel des Stücks*). *der Fabeldichter / die Fabeldichterin* writes fables. *die Lehre* is the lesson to be drawn (*eine Lehre aus etwas ziehen*), also doctrine (*die Lehre Luthers*) and apprenticeship (*eine Lehre machen*). *die List* is a trick or ruse and *listig* the adjective; the plural *die Listen* looks the same as that of *die Liste*. *die Belehrung* and *belehrend* are about teaching, usually with a critical undertone (*ein belehrender Ton*). *das Tierepos* (plural *die Tierepen*) is a long verse tale with animals, like Goethe's *Reineke Fuchs* (1794), in hexameters. *der Rabe* is a weak noun: *des Raben, dem Raben, den Raben*.

## Key points

- A **[[fable]]** has animals as fixed types (the cunning fox, the vain raven), a conflict, a turn and a moral; it is told in the Präteritum with the decisive moment in direct speech.
- The tradition runs from Aesop and Phaedrus to La Fontaine; Luther began a German Aesop in 1530; Lessing's *Fabeln* (1759) are short, in prose and pointed.
- Lessing's *Der Rabe und der Fuchs* turns the old story: the meat is poisoned, the flattering fox dies, and the moral is a curse on flatterers in the optative.
- A **[[parable]]** (*Parabel*; biblical *Gleichnis*) uses human figures and leaves the transfer to the reader; it can be read in several ways.
- The Ringparabel (*Nathan der Weise*, 1779, III, 7) answers the question of the true religion by replacing it with the question of how to live; the judge's appeal *Es eifre jeder …* is a hortative Konjunktiv I in blank verse.
- The more explicit the moral, the more *belehrend* the text; modern fables often leave it out.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Fraglich ist, ob …: judgments, Gutachtenstil and contracts
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 5 is about **[[specialist language]]** (*Fachsprache*): the German of lawyers, doctors, accountants, scientists and civil servants. The Goethe C2 exam doesn't test specialist vocabulary, but a C2 reader meets these texts every week (a court letter, a contract, a hospital leaflet, an annual report, a Bescheid), so this module teaches you to read them accurately and to recognize their register.

C1 lesson 21 taught you to read a statute (Tatbestand and Rechtsfolge, conditions without *wenn*, Legaldefinitionen). This lesson goes on to the texts in which lawyers *apply* statutes: the legal opinion written in **[[Gutachtenstil]]**, the judgment written in **[[Urteilsstil]]**, and the contract. The law is checked against gesetze-im-internet.de (November 2026); the case is invented; nothing here is legal advice.

## Two ways to write a legal argument

### Gutachtenstil: the question first

The **[[Gutachtenstil]]** (the style of a legal opinion) starts from an open question and works towards the answer. It has four steps:

| step | what it does | typical German |
|---|---|---|
| Obersatz | states the question as a possibility | *A könnte gegen B einen Anspruch auf … aus § … haben.* / *Fraglich ist, ob …* |
| Definition | says what a legal term requires | *Dies setzt voraus, dass …* / *Ein … liegt vor, wenn …* / *Darunter versteht man …* |
| Subsumtion | compares the facts with the definition | *Hier …* / *Vorliegend …* / *Im vorliegenden Fall …* / *Dafür spricht …, dagegen …* |
| Ergebnis | gives the answer to the Obersatz | *Mithin …* / *Somit …* / *Folglich …* / *Also ist … gegeben.* |

The third step is called **[[subsumption]]** (*die Subsumtion*): placing the facts of a case under a legal rule (*den Sachverhalt unter eine Norm subsumieren*). It is the heart of legal reasoning, and in an exam it is where the marks are.

The Obersatz is always open. That is why it uses the Konjunktiv II: *könnte … haben, müsste … sein, dürfte … zustehen*. Here the KII is not a polite or an unreal form but a hypothetical one: the writer doesn't yet know whether the answer is yes. A short example, from the case you are about to read:

> *K könnte gegen V einen Anspruch auf Übereignung der Kamera aus § 433 Abs. 1 Satz 1 BGB haben. Dann müsste zwischen ihnen ein wirksamer Kaufvertrag bestehen. Ein Vertrag kommt durch zwei übereinstimmende Willenserklärungen zustande, Angebot und Annahme. Hier hat V die Kamera auf einer Plattform zum Sofortkauf angeboten, und K hat das Angebot angenommen. Mithin ist ein Kaufvertrag zustande gekommen. Er könnte jedoch nach § 142 Abs. 1 BGB von Anfang an nichtig sein, wenn V ihn wirksam angefochten hat …*

*Die Willenserklärung* (declaration of intent) is the basic unit of contract law: an offer, an acceptance, a notice of termination. Notice also *mithin* (C1), the classic connector of the Ergebnis, and *dann müsste*, which turns the requirements into a chain.

### Urteilsstil: the answer first

The **[[Urteilsstil]]** (judgment style) turns the order round: the result first, then the reasons, introduced with *denn, da, weil* or a plain explanation. Judges write it because they owe the parties an answer, not a search:

> *Der Kläger hat keinen Anspruch auf Übereignung der Kamera. Denn der Kaufvertrag ist infolge der Anfechtung durch die Beklagte von Anfang an nichtig (§ 142 Abs. 1 BGB).*

A Bescheid from an authority is written in Urteilsstil too (lesson 25); internal memos often use the Gutachtenstil for the one difficult point and the Urteilsstil for everything obvious. Writing an easy point in full Gutachtenstil (*Fraglich ist, ob K ein Mensch ist …*) is a classic fault that examiners mark down.

## The parts of a civil judgment

A judgment of a German civil court (*ein Zivilurteil*) has four parts:

1. **Rubrum**: the heading, with the court, the *Aktenzeichen*, the parties and their lawyers, and *Im Namen des Volkes* (§ 311 Abs. 1 ZPO). The parties are *der Kläger / die Klägerin* (plaintiff, who brings the *Klage*, B2) and *der Beklagte / die Beklagte* (defendant), together *die Parteien*.
2. **Tenor**: the operative part, in numbered sentences (C1 taught *der Tenor* as "gist"). Present tense or passive, no reasons:
   - *Die Klage wird abgewiesen.* — The action is dismissed.
   - *Der Beklagte wird verurteilt, an die Klägerin 2.400 Euro zu zahlen.* — The defendant is ordered to pay the plaintiff 2,400 euros.
   - *Der Kläger trägt die Kosten des Rechtsstreits.* — The plaintiff bears the costs of the proceedings.
   - *Das Urteil ist vorläufig vollstreckbar.* — The judgment is provisionally enforceable.
3. **Tatbestand**: the facts and what each party claims. This is a second sense of the word (in a statute, the situation the rule describes). The parties' claims are reported in Konjunktiv I: *Der Kläger behauptet, er habe den Irrtum nicht bemerkt.*
4. **Entscheidungsgründe**: the reasons, in Urteilsstil. Together with the Tatbestand they are the *Urteilsbegründung*.

A party who loses can appeal. *Das Rechtsmittel* is the general word for a remedy that takes the case to a higher court. In civil cases the first is *die Berufung* (B2), heard by the *Berufungsgericht* (the Landgericht for judgments of an Amtsgericht, the Oberlandesgericht for judgments of a Landgericht); it reviews facts and law, within limits. The next is *die Revision* to the Bundesgerichtshof, which reviews only errors of law and usually has to be admitted (*zugelassen*). Each level is an *Instanz*: *in erster Instanz, in letzter Instanz, durch alle Instanzen*. There are five branches of courts (*Gerichtsbarkeiten*): ordinary (civil and criminal), administrative, labour, social and finance.

*Die Rechtsprechung* means both "the administration of justice" (one of the three powers: *Gesetzgebung, Verwaltung, Rechtsprechung*) and "case law": *nach ständiger Rechtsprechung des Bundesgerichtshofs* (according to the settled case law of the BGH).

## The text: a judgment excerpt

The case: on an online marketplace, a private seller (V, the defendant) offered a used camera for immediate purchase. She meant to type 1.290 Euro and typed 129 Euro. The buyer (K, the plaintiff) clicked "buy" within minutes. That evening she wrote to him that she had made a typing mistake and challenged the sale. He sued for the camera. Here is the court's reasoning (an invented judgment, written for this course in the style of an Amtsgericht).

> **Entscheidungsgründe**
>
> Die zulässige Klage ist unbegründet. Dem Kläger steht gegen die Beklagte kein Anspruch auf Übergabe und Übereignung der Kamera Zug um Zug gegen Zahlung von 129 Euro aus § 433 Abs. 1 Satz 1 BGB zu.
>
> 1\. Zwar ist zwischen den Parteien zunächst ein Kaufvertrag zustande gekommen. Die Beklagte hat die Kamera auf der Plattform zum Sofortkauf angeboten; der Kläger hat dieses Angebot durch Betätigen der Schaltfläche „Sofort-Kaufen“ angenommen. Dass der Kaufpreis nur einen Bruchteil des Marktwerts betrug, steht dem Vertragsschluss nicht entgegen.
>
> 2\. Der Vertrag ist jedoch infolge der Anfechtung durch die Beklagte gemäß § 142 Abs. 1 BGB als von Anfang an nichtig anzusehen. Die Beklagte war zur Anfechtung berechtigt, denn sie befand sich bei Abgabe ihrer Willenserklärung in einem Erklärungsirrtum im Sinne des § 119 Abs. 1 Alt. 2 BGB. Sie wollte einen Preis von 1.290 Euro eingeben und hat sich lediglich vertippt; eine Erklärung dieses Inhalts wollte sie überhaupt nicht abgeben. Das Gericht hat keinen Anlass, an dieser Darstellung zu zweifeln. Sie wird durch die als Anlage B 2 vorgelegte frühere Anzeige gestützt, in der die Beklagte dieselbe Kamera eine Woche zuvor für 1.290 Euro angeboten hatte. Es ist auch anzunehmen, dass sie die Erklärung bei Kenntnis der Sachlage nicht abgegeben hätte.
>
> 3\. Die Anfechtung ist rechtzeitig erfolgt. Die Beklagte hat sie noch am Abend des Kaufs und damit unverzüglich im Sinne des § 121 Abs. 1 Satz 1 BGB erklärt. Ob der Kläger den Irrtum erkannt hat, wofür angesichts des krassen Missverhältnisses zwischen Preis und Wert einiges spricht, kann dahinstehen.
>
> 4\. Ob dem Kläger ein Anspruch auf Ersatz seines Vertrauensschadens nach § 122 Abs. 1 BGB zusteht, hatte das Gericht nicht zu entscheiden, da er einen solchen Anspruch nicht geltend gemacht hat. Die Schadensersatzpflicht der Beklagten entfiele im Übrigen, wenn der Kläger den Irrtum kannte oder kennen musste (§ 122 Abs. 2 BGB).
>
> Die Kostenentscheidung beruht auf § 91 Abs. 1 Satz 1 ZPO.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Reasons for the decision.** The action is admissible but unfounded. The plaintiff has no claim against the defendant under § 433(1), first sentence, BGB to delivery and transfer of ownership of the camera in exchange for payment of 129 euros.

1\. It is true that a contract of sale was initially concluded between the parties. The defendant offered the camera for immediate purchase on the platform; the plaintiff accepted this offer by clicking the "Buy now" button. The fact that the purchase price was only a fraction of the market value does not prevent the contract from being concluded.

2\. However, as a result of the defendant's avoidance, the contract is to be regarded as void from the outset under § 142(1) BGB. The defendant was entitled to avoid it, because when she made her declaration of intent she was in error as to the declaration within the meaning of § 119(1), second alternative, BGB. She meant to enter a price of 1,290 euros and merely made a typing error; she did not intend to make a declaration with this content at all. The court has no reason to doubt this account. It is supported by the earlier listing submitted as exhibit B 2, in which the defendant had offered the same camera for 1,290 euros a week before. It must also be assumed that she would not have made the declaration had she known the true situation.

3\. The avoidance was declared in time. The defendant declared it on the evening of the purchase and thus without undue delay within the meaning of § 121(1), first sentence, BGB. Whether the plaintiff recognized the error, for which there is much to be said given the glaring disproportion between price and value, can be left open.

4\. Whether the plaintiff has a claim to compensation for his reliance damage under § 122(1) BGB was not for the court to decide, since he has not asserted such a claim. Incidentally, the defendant's liability to pay damages would not arise if the plaintiff knew of the error or ought to have known of it (§ 122(2) BGB).

The decision on costs is based on § 91(1), first sentence, ZPO.

</details>

### How the text works

- **Result first.** *Die zulässige Klage ist unbegründet*: the action is admissible (right court, proper form) but unfounded (the plaintiff isn't entitled to what he asks). Each numbered point then gives a reason.
- ***Zwar …, jedoch …*** is the concession of legal reasoning: point 1 grants something (a contract was concluded), point 2 takes it away (it is void). *Zwar* (B1) prepares the reader for *jedoch* or *aber*.
- **Nominal style**: *infolge der Anfechtung, bei Abgabe ihrer Willenserklärung, bei Kenntnis der Sachlage, angesichts des krassen Missverhältnisses*. Each could be a clause (*weil sie angefochten hat; als sie … abgab; wenn sie … gekannt hätte*); the nouns fit into one sentence with a citation.
- ***ist … als nichtig anzusehen*** is the wording of § 142 Abs. 1 itself: *sein + zu*-infinitive, "is to be regarded as". Courts quote the statute's verbs back, so the Subsumtion is visible.
- ***kann dahinstehen*** ("can be left open"; also *Es kann dahingestellt bleiben, ob …*): this point doesn't change the result. If K recognized the typing error, the declaration is interpreted by its real meaning (§ 133 BGB, below): V offered 1.290 Euro, and there is no contract at 129 Euro either.
- **Konjunktiv II for a hypothetical consequence**: *entfiele* (would not arise) in point 4. Note *kannte oder kennen musste*, the standard legal pair for "knew or ought to have known".
- **Abbreviations**: *Alt.* (Alternative: one of the cases a sentence names), *Anlage B 2* (the defendant's exhibit 2; the plaintiff's are *K 1, K 2 …*), *ZPO* (Zivilprozessordnung, Code of Civil Procedure).

§ 119 Abs. 1 BGB names two errors: about the content of a declaration (*über deren Inhalt im Irrtum*), and the *Erklärungsirrtum*, when someone *eine Erklärung dieses Inhalts überhaupt nicht abgeben wollte* (wording of the statute): you type or say something you didn't mean. That is the court's *Alt. 2*. The time limit is a famous Legaldefinition in § 121 Abs. 1 Satz 1 BGB: the avoidance must come *ohne schuldhaftes Zögern (unverzüglich)*, "without culpable delay". So *unverzüglich* in law is not "immediately" (*sofort*): a short time to think or to get advice is allowed.

## Generalklauseln and two basic rules

A few rules of the BGB are deliberately open: they use undefined concepts that courts fill case by case. These are the *Generalklauseln* (general clauses), above all § 242 and § 138. With them, two basic rules that the judgment relied on, all quoted verbatim from gesetze-im-internet.de (November 2026; statutes are free to quote, § 5 UrhG):

> **§ 242 Leistung nach Treu und Glauben**
>
> Der Schuldner ist verpflichtet, die Leistung so zu bewirken, wie Treu und Glauben mit Rücksicht auf die Verkehrssitte es erfordern.
>
> **§ 138 Abs. 1** (Sittenwidriges Rechtsgeschäft; Wucher)
>
> Ein Rechtsgeschäft, das gegen die guten Sitten verstößt, ist nichtig.
>
> **§ 133 Auslegung einer Willenserklärung**
>
> Bei der Auslegung einer Willenserklärung ist der wirkliche Wille zu erforschen und nicht an dem buchstäblichen Sinne des Ausdrucks zu haften.
>
> **§ 142 Abs. 1** (Wirkung der Anfechtung)
>
> Wird ein anfechtbares Rechtsgeschäft angefochten, so ist es als von Anfang an nichtig anzusehen.

In English (working translations, not official ones): § 242: The obligor must perform in the way that good faith requires, taking customary practice into consideration. § 138(1): A legal transaction that is contrary to public policy (literally "offends against good morals") is void. § 133: When a declaration of intent is interpreted, the true intention must be sought, rather than adhering to the literal meaning of the words. § 142(1): If a voidable legal transaction is avoided, it is to be regarded as void from the outset.

What to notice:

- ***Treu und Glauben*** ("good faith") is a pair formula with a frozen old form: *Treu* is an old form of *die Treue* that survives only here, and the pair takes a plural verb (*erfordern*). It is used without article: *gegen Treu und Glauben verstoßen, nach Treu und Glauben*. Out of § 242 the courts have built whole doctrines, for instance that no one may exercise a right in bad faith or contradict their own earlier conduct (*venire contra factum proprium*).
- ***die guten Sitten*** is the old phrase behind *sittenwidrig* and *die Sittenwidrigkeit*. Courts define it with a formula of their own (roughly: what offends the sense of decency of all who think fairly and justly) and group the cases; § 138 Abs. 2 names *Wucher* (usury) as a special case.
- **Old forms in § 133**: *dem buchstäblichen Sinne* keeps the dative *-e* of 1900, and *haften an* is the old literal sense "to cling to": not to cling to the literal meaning. In modern legal German *haften (für)* means "to be liable (for)", and *die Haftung* is liability; reading § 133 that way produces nonsense.
- ***nichtig, anfechtbar, unwirksam***: *nichtig* (void) has no effect from the start, by force of law (§ 138). *Anfechtbar* (voidable) is valid until the person entitled challenges it (*anfechten*: *ficht an, focht an, hat angefochten*; *die Anfechtung*); then § 142 makes it void retroactively. *Unwirksam* (ineffective) is the broad term that covers void and avoided transactions and more, such as an unfair clause in standard terms. They are not free synonyms.

*Die Auslegung* is interpretation: *die Auslegung eines Vertrags*; *etwas weit / eng auslegen*. *Die Rechtsnorm* is any legal rule, from the Grundgesetz to a municipal by-law.

## Contract language

Contracts (*Verträge*) use a small set of formulas. Learn to recognize them; most are good formal German outside contracts too.

| formula | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *sich verpflichten, … zu …* | to undertake to | *Der Mieter verpflichtet sich, die Wohnung bei Auszug in vertragsgemäßem Zustand zurückzugeben.* |
| *sofern nichts anderes vereinbart ist* | unless otherwise agreed | *Sofern nichts anderes vereinbart ist, gelten die gesetzlichen Bestimmungen.* |
| *unbeschadet* + gen. | without prejudice to | *Unbeschadet des § 8 kann jede Partei den Vertrag aus wichtigem Grund kündigen.* |
| *haften für* | to be liable for | *Der Vermieter haftet nicht für Schäden, die der Mieter selbst verursacht hat.* |
| *ist … verwirkt* / *ist … zu zahlen* | (a penalty) is incurred / payable | *Für jeden Fall der Zuwiderhandlung ist eine Vertragsstrafe von 5.000 Euro zu zahlen.* |
| *Sollte …, so …* | should …, then … | *Sollten einzelne Bestimmungen dieses Vertrags unwirksam sein oder werden, so bleibt die Wirksamkeit der übrigen Bestimmungen unberührt.* |

Notes:

- *Die Vertragsklausel* is any clause of a contract. The last one in the table is the *salvatorische Klausel* (severability clause), found in almost every German contract; its *Sollten …, so …* is a verb-first condition ("should it happen that", not "ought to").
- *Die Vertragsstrafe* is a contractual penalty, agreed in advance for a breach. Between businesses it is common; in standard terms used against consumers several kinds are unwirksam (§ 309 Nr. 6 BGB).
- *Die Gewährleistung* is the usual word for the statutory liability for defects (the BGB speaks of the buyer's *Rechte bei Mängeln*); *die Garantie* (A2) is a voluntary extra promise. The buyer first asks for *Nacherfüllung* (§ 439 BGB): a replacement or *die Nachbesserung*, the repair. Figuratively, *nachbessern* is "to improve on": *Die Regierung muss beim Gesetz nachbessern.*
- *Der Schadensersatz* is compensation for damage (*Schadensersatz leisten, auf Schadensersatz verklagen*); who owes it is *schadensersatzpflichtig*, and the duty is *die Schadensersatzpflicht*, as in point 4 of the judgment. Spelling: Duden gives *Schadensersatz* and *Schadenersatz*; the BGB uses *Schadensersatz*.
- *Die Klageschrift* is the document that starts a lawsuit: the plaintiff's statement of claim.

## Common mistakes

- **Gutachtenstil where the reader wants an answer.** A letter to a client, an e-mail to a colleague, a summary for the press: all start with the result. *Fraglich ist, ob Sie die Miete mindern können* is the opening of an exam paper, not of advice. Conversely, *Die Klage ist begründet* at the start of a law-school opinion skips the reasoning the examiner wants to see.
- **False precision with *nichtig* and *unwirksam*.** *Der Vertrag ist nichtig* is a strong legal statement (void from the start). If you only mean that a clause doesn't apply, *unwirksam* is the safer word, and in everyday German *ungültig* (B1).
- **Mixing up the people.** *Der Beklagte* is the defendant in a civil or administrative case, *der Angeklagte* (B2) the accused in a criminal trial; *der Kläger* sues.
- **Translating *unverzüglich* as "immediately".** In law it is "without culpable delay" (§ 121 BGB): prompt, not instantaneous.
- **Calling every appeal *Revision*.** Revision is the appeal on points of law only, usually to a federal court; the appeal that re-examines the facts is *die Berufung*. *Das Rechtsmittel* covers both.

## Key points

- **[[Gutachtenstil]]**: Obersatz (*könnte … haben; Fraglich ist, ob …*) → Definition (*… liegt vor, wenn …*) → **[[subsumption]]** (*Hier …; Vorliegend …*) → Ergebnis (*Mithin …; Somit …*). The KII of the Obersatz marks an open hypothesis.
- **[[Urteilsstil]]**: result first, then *denn, da, weil*. Judgments and Bescheide use it; *Zwar …, jedoch …* concedes and turns.
- A civil judgment: Rubrum, Tenor (*Die Klage wird abgewiesen*), Tatbestand (facts; KI for the parties' claims), Entscheidungsgründe. Berufung reviews facts and law, Revision only law.
- Generalklauseln: § 242 (*Treu und Glauben*), § 138 (*die guten Sitten*); § 133 (*der wirkliche Wille*). *nichtig* ≠ *anfechtbar* ≠ *unwirksam*.
- Contract formulas: *sich verpflichten, sofern nichts anderes vereinbart ist, unbeschadet* + gen., *haften für*, *Sollten …, so …* (salvatorische Klausel).
- Judges' phrases: *kann dahinstehen; im Sinne des …; ist als … anzusehen; geltend machen; kannte oder kennen musste*. The reference sheet "Gutachtenstil and Bescheide" collects them.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Inzidenz und Prävalenz: medical German from the clinic to the public
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Medical German has two faces. Between doctors it is a Latin- and Greek-based **[[specialist language]]**, written in clipped nominal style. With patients it has to be plain, verbal and careful, and the law requires that: under § 630e BGB the doctor must explain an operation orally, in good time and in a way the patient can understand. Health reporting adds a third layer, the numbers of epidemiology, where *Inzidenz* and *Prävalenz* are confused in newspapers every week.

This lesson builds on the hedging of lesson 04 (*legt nahe, dürfte, nach allem, was wir wissen*) and on the risk language of C1 (relative and absolute risk). It is about language, not medicine: the facts are general, the numbers in the examples are invented, and nothing here is medical advice.

## Greek and Latin terms, German equivalents

Most clinical **[[technical terms]]** have a German everyday equivalent. Doctors use the international term with colleagues and should use the German one with patients; a C2 reader needs both.

| term | everyday German | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *die Ätiologie* | *die Ursache* | the cause of a disease (and the study of causes) |
| *die Pathogenese* | *die Entstehung* | how a disease develops, its mechanism |
| *die Komorbidität* | *die Begleiterkrankung* | another disease present at the same time |
| *die Indikation* | *der Grund für eine Behandlung* | the medical reason that justifies a treatment |
| *die Kontraindikation* | *die Gegenanzeige* | a reason against a treatment |
| *die Remission* | *die Rückbildung* | the (temporary or lasting) retreat of a disease |
| *das Rezidiv* | *der Rückfall* | the return of a disease after treatment |
| *die Metastase* | *die Tochtergeschwulst* | a secondary tumour, spread from the first one |
| *die Biopsie* | *die Gewebeprobe* | taking a sample of tissue to examine it |
| *die Bildgebung* | *(Ultraschall, Röntgen, CT, MRT)* | imaging |

Some details that matter:

- *Die Indikation* comes with a collocation: a doctor *stellt die Indikation* (decides that a treatment is justified). The adjective is *indiziert*: *Eine Operation ist nicht zwingend indiziert.* Its opposite, *kontraindiziert*, means a treatment must not be used: *Bei Schwangeren ist das Medikament kontraindiziert.* Package leaflets and the specialists' *Fachinformation* traditionally list *Gegenanzeigen* (C1).
- *Gutartig* (benign) and *bösartig* (malignant) are the everyday words; doctors also say *benigne* and *maligne*. *Der Tumor* (plural *die Tumoren*; Duden also gives *Tumore*, more colloquial) is any growth, benign or malignant. Telling a patient "Sie haben einen Tumor" without saying which kind is a classic communication error.
- *Die Begleiterkrankung* and *die Komorbidität* are near-synonyms; *Komorbidität* is the term of research and statistics (*Patienten mit hoher Komorbidität*), *Begleiterkrankung* of the clinic and the patient letter.
- *Die Differenzialdiagnose* is a disease that could explain the same symptoms and has to be ruled out (*differenzialdiagnostisch kommt auch … infrage*). Duden's main spelling is *Differenzial-*; *Differential-* is also correct.
- *Palliativ* describes treatment that relieves symptoms when cure is no longer the aim; *die Palliativmedizin* is the specialty, not "giving up": *palliativ behandelt werden*, *eine Palliativstation*.

### Prefixes and suffixes

Clinical terms are built from a small set of parts. Knowing them lets you parse words you have never seen:

| part | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *-itis* | inflammation | *die Appendizitis* (*Blinddarmentzündung*), *die Arthritis* |
| *-ose* | condition, often degenerative | *die Arthrose* (joint wear, not inflammation) |
| *-om* | swelling, usually a tumour | *das Lipom* (benign fatty tumour), *das Karzinom* (malignant) |
| *-ektomie* | surgical removal | *die Cholezystektomie* (removal of the gallbladder) |
| *-skopie* | looking inside | *die Laparoskopie* (of the abdomen), *die Endoskopie* |
| *-logie* | study of | *die Onkologie* (cancer), *die Epidemiologie* |
| *kontra-* | against | *kontraindiziert* |
| *minimal-* | minimal | *minimalinvasiv* (through small incisions) |
| *prä- / post-* | before / after | *präoperativ, postoperativ* |

Don't over-apply them. *-om* usually means a tumour, but *das Hämatom* is a bruise, a swelling of blood. *Arthritis* (inflammation) and *Arthrose* (wear) are different diseases that patients constantly confuse.

## The text: an Aufklärungsgespräch

Before an operation the doctor must inform the patient (*das Aufklärungsgespräch*, from *aufklären*, "to inform, to explain"). This transcript was written for this course. Herr Brandt has had several attacks of biliary colic; a surgeon explains the planned operation. Read it for the language: how she makes technical content plain, how she hedges, and how she checks understanding.

> **Ärztin:** Herr Brandt, Sie hatten jetzt drei Koliken in zwei Monaten, und im Ultraschall sieht man mehrere Gallensteine. Wir empfehlen deshalb, die Gallenblase zu entfernen. Medizinisch sagen wir: Die Operation ist indiziert. Zwingend ist sie nicht, aber die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass die Koliken wiederkommen, ist hoch.
>
> **Patient:** Und das wird ein großer Schnitt?
>
> **Ärztin:** Nein, wir operieren minimalinvasiv, also durch drei, vier kleine Schnitte. Durch einen davon führen wir eine Kamera ein. In seltenen Fällen müssen wir während der Operation doch auf einen größeren Bauchschnitt umsteigen, etwa wenn die Gallenblase stark entzündet ist. Das sage ich Ihnen vorher, damit Sie nicht erschrecken, falls es passiert.
>
> **Patient:** Bekomme ich eine Vollnarkose?
>
> **Ärztin:** Ja. Eine örtliche Betäubung reicht für diesen Eingriff nicht. Die Narkoseärztin spricht mit Ihnen noch gesondert, auch wegen Ihres Diabetes. Begleiterkrankungen wie Ihre sind kein Grund, nicht zu operieren, wir müssen sie aber einplanen.
>
> **Patient:** Was ist mit Risiken?
>
> **Ärztin:** Es kann, wie bei jeder Operation, zu Blutungen oder einer Wundinfektion kommen. Selten wird ein Gallengang verletzt; das wäre dann eine ernste Komplikation, die meist eine weitere Behandlung nötig macht. Ich will Ihnen das nicht verschweigen, aber ich möchte es auch einordnen: Die allermeisten Patienten gehen nach zwei, drei Tagen nach Hause.
>
> **Patient:** Und wenn das doch ein Tumor ist?
>
> **Ärztin:** Nach allem, was wir im Ultraschall sehen, spricht nichts dafür. Die entfernte Gallenblase wird routinemäßig feingeweblich untersucht, und in aller Regel ist der Befund gutartig. Sicher sagen können wir es erst, wenn das Ergebnis da ist. Darf ich Sie bitten, mir kurz mit Ihren eigenen Worten zu sagen, was wir vorhaben? Dann sehe ich, ob ich etwas unklar erklärt habe.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Doctor:** Mr Brandt, you've now had three attacks of colic in two months, and the ultrasound shows several gallstones. So we recommend removing the gallbladder. In medical terms we say the operation is indicated. It isn't absolutely necessary, but the probability that the colic comes back is high.

**Patient:** And will that be a big incision?

**Doctor:** No, we operate minimally invasively, through three or four small incisions. Through one of them we insert a camera. In rare cases we have to switch to a larger abdominal incision during the operation, for instance if the gallbladder is badly inflamed. I'm telling you this beforehand so that you aren't alarmed if it happens.

**Patient:** Will I get a general anaesthetic?

**Doctor:** Yes. A local anaesthetic isn't enough for this procedure. The anaesthetist will talk to you separately, also because of your diabetes. Accompanying conditions like yours are no reason not to operate, but we have to plan for them.

**Patient:** What about risks?

**Doctor:** As with any operation, there can be bleeding or a wound infection. Rarely, a bile duct is injured; that would be a serious complication, which usually needs further treatment. I don't want to keep that from you, but I'd also like to put it in perspective: the vast majority of patients go home after two or three days.

**Patient:** And what if it is a tumour after all?

**Doctor:** From everything we can see on the ultrasound, nothing suggests that. The removed gallbladder is examined under the microscope as a matter of routine, and as a rule the finding is benign. We can only say for certain once the result is in. May I ask you to tell me briefly, in your own words, what we're planning to do? Then I'll see whether I've explained anything unclearly.

</details>

### How the doctor talks

- **Term, then translation.** *Medizinisch sagen wir: Die Operation ist indiziert* introduces the technical word and has already explained it (*Wir empfehlen …*). *Minimalinvasiv, also durch drei, vier kleine Schnitte* glosses with *also*. *Begleiterkrankungen* is the patient-friendly word; in the file it will say *Komorbidität Diabetes mellitus*.
- **Verbs, not nouns.** *die Gallenblase zu entfernen* rather than *Entfernung der Gallenblase*; *wenn die Gallenblase stark entzündet ist* rather than *bei ausgeprägter Entzündung*. Each fact gets its own short sentence.
- **Graded certainty.** *Zwingend ist sie nicht* (fronted predicate: the restriction is made prominent), *die Wahrscheinlichkeit … ist hoch, selten, in seltenen Fällen, die allermeisten, in aller Regel, nach allem, was wir sehen, spricht nichts dafür, Sicher sagen können wir es erst, wenn …*. No absolute promises, and no false precision: she doesn't invent a percentage she can't defend.
- **Konjunktiv II for the unwelcome case**: *das wäre dann eine ernste Komplikation*. The KII keeps the event hypothetical while naming it honestly.
- **Framing**: *Ich will Ihnen das nicht verschweigen, aber ich möchte es auch einordnen* announces bad news and its weight in one sentence. *einordnen* (to put in context) is a useful word for every C2 speaker.
- **Checking understanding** ("teach-back"): *Darf ich Sie bitten, mir kurz mit Ihren eigenen Worten zu sagen …* The polite *Darf ich Sie bitten* takes the pressure off the patient: the doctor checks her explanation, not his intelligence.

### The same facts in clinical style

The surgeon's note in the patient file says the same thing in a quite different register:

> *Z. n. rezidivierenden Gallenkoliken. Sonografisch Cholezystolithiasis, kein Anhalt für Malignität. Indikation zur laparoskopischen Cholezystektomie gestellt. Komorbidität: Diabetes mellitus Typ 2. Pat. über Vorgehen, Risiken (u. a. Blutung, Infektion, Gallengangsverletzung) und mögliche Konversion aufgeklärt; Einwilligung liegt vor.*

*Z. n.* is *Zustand nach* (status after, history of); *rezidivierend* (recurring) is the adjective of *das Rezidiv*; *sonografisch* means "on ultrasound"; *kein Anhalt für* means "no sign of"; *Malignität* is malignancy; *Konversion* is the switch to open surgery. There are hardly any finite verbs: participles (*gestellt, aufgeklärt*) and nouns carry everything. That is efficient for a colleague and opaque for a patient, which is why the same doctor needs both registers.

## Epidemiology: counting illness

Epidemiology (*die Epidemiologie*; *epidemiologisch*) studies how often diseases occur in a population. Its basic terms are precise, and the press often blurs them.

- *Die Inzidenz* counts **new** cases in a period: *Neuerkrankungen pro 100.000 Einwohner und Jahr*. During the COVID-19 pandemic the *Sieben-Tage-Inzidenz* (new cases per 100,000 in seven days) became an everyday word.
- *Die Prävalenz* counts **all** existing cases at a point or in a period: how many people *have* the disease, new or old.
- *Die Sterblichkeit* (*Mortalität*) is the number of deaths from a disease in the whole population; *die Letalität* is the share of the **sick** who die of it.

An invented example shows the difference:

> In einer Stadt mit 200.000 Einwohnern erkranken in einem Jahr 60 Menschen neu an einer chronischen Krankheit: Die Inzidenz beträgt 30 pro 100.000 Einwohner und Jahr. Am Stichtag leben in der Stadt 1.000 Menschen mit dieser Krankheit: Die Prävalenz liegt bei 0,5 Prozent, also 500 pro 100.000. Von den 60 Neuerkrankten sterben im selben Jahr drei: Die Letalität beträgt in diesem Zeitraum fünf Prozent, die Sterblichkeit in der Bevölkerung 1,5 pro 100.000.

A chronic disease has a low incidence and a high prevalence (people live with it for years); a short infection can have a high incidence and a low prevalence. *Die Inzidenz steigt* and *Immer mehr Menschen leben mit der Krankheit* are two different statements.

For infections (*Infektionskrankheiten*), two more words: *die Ansteckung* (infection, passing on: *Die Ansteckung erfolgt über Tröpfchen*) and *die Inkubationszeit*, the time between infection and the first symptoms. In Germany, the *Infektionsschutzgesetz* makes many infections notifiable (*meldepflichtig*), and the Robert Koch-Institut publishes the figures; if you quote one, give its date, since they change weekly.

### Relative and absolute risk (recap)

A headline says *Neues Medikament senkt das Risiko um 25 Prozent.* The study behind it: the risk falls from 4 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000. That is a *relative* reduction of 25 percent, but an *absolute* reduction of 0.1 percentage points: 1,000 people must take the drug for one of them to benefit. Both numbers are true; a careful text gives both: *Das Risiko sank von 0,4 auf 0,3 Prozent; relativ entspricht das einem Rückgang um ein Viertel.*

## Treatment and after

The rest of this lesson's words follow the path of a patient:

- *die Vollnarkose* (general anaesthesia) vs *die örtliche Betäubung* (local anaesthesia). *betäuben* is to anaesthetize or to stun; *die Betäubung* covers both and is also figurative (*wie betäubt*, as if stunned). *Die Narkose* (B2) is the general word.
- *die Nachsorge*: follow-up care after treatment, especially after cancer (*Nachsorgeuntersuchungen*). *die Rehabilitation*, usually *die Reha*: rehabilitation after an illness or operation (*in die Reha gehen*, *eine Reha beantragen*).
- In oncology: a tumour may *metastasieren* (form *Metastasen*); after therapy the disease may go into *Remission* (*eine vollständige Remission*); if it returns, that is *ein Rezidiv*. Doctors avoid the word *geheilt* (cured) for years after a cancer treatment and speak of *Remission* or *rezidivfrei*: hedging again, for good reasons.

## Common mistakes

- **Inzidenz for Prävalenz.** *Die Inzidenz von Diabetes liegt bei acht Prozent* is almost always wrong: a share of the population with a disease is a prevalence. Incidence is a rate of new cases per period.
- **Sterblichkeit for Letalität.** *Die Krankheit hat eine Sterblichkeit von 20 Prozent* usually means that 20 percent of the *sick* die: that is the Letalität.
- **Tumor = Krebs.** *Tumor* is neutral; only a malignant tumour is cancer (*Krebs*). Saying *Tumor* to a patient without *gutartig/bösartig* causes needless fear.
- **The clinical register in the wrong place.** *Bei Ihnen besteht eine Indikation zur Cholezystektomie* is correct and useless for most patients. Translate, then use the term if it helps.
- **False certainty.** *Das ist garantiert gutartig* promises what no one can know before the histology. *In aller Regel …, sicher wissen wir es, wenn …* is honest and still reassuring.
- **-itis and -ose.** *Arthrose* is not an inflammation; *Arthritis* is.

## Key points

- Clinical terms have everyday equivalents: *Ätiologie / Ursache, Pathogenese / Entstehung, Komorbidität / Begleiterkrankung, Rezidiv / Rückfall, Metastase / Tochtergeschwulst*. *eine Indikation stellen; indiziert, kontraindiziert*.
- Word parts: *-itis* (inflammation), *-ose* (condition), *-om* (usually a tumour), *-ektomie* (removal), *-skopie* (looking inside), *-logie*, *kontra-, minimal-, prä-/post-*.
- With patients: verbs, short sentences, term plus gloss (*also …*), graded certainty, KII for the unwelcome case, teach-back. In the file: nominal, abbreviated (*Z. n., kein Anhalt für, Pat.*).
- *Inzidenz* = new cases per period; *Prävalenz* = all cases; *Sterblichkeit* = deaths in the population; *Letalität* = deaths among the sick. Give relative and absolute risk together.
- *gutartig / bösartig*; *der Tumor, die Tumoren*; *Remission, Rezidiv, Nachsorge, Reha, palliativ*.

lessons.title: Bilanz und Lagebericht: the language of company finance
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Every listed German company publishes a *Geschäftsbericht* (annual report) once a year, and every business page summarizes it. Its core is the *Jahresabschluss* (annual financial statements: balance sheet, income statement, notes), audited by a *Wirtschaftsprüfer*, and the *Lagebericht* (management report), in which the board explains how the year went and what it expects. The *Lagebericht* is a text type of its own: formal, nominal, full of numbers, and written with great care to sound neither too gloomy nor too confident.

This lesson teaches you to read it: the structure of a balance sheet, numbers in prose (*um* vs *auf*, *Prozent* vs *Prozentpunkte*), the modal language of forecasts (lesson 04), and the polished euphemisms of reporting. C1 lesson 22 covered central banks and monetary policy; this one is about companies. All figures belong to an invented company; nothing here is investment advice.

## The balance sheet: Aktiva and Passiva

*Die Bilanz* (B2) shows, on a given date, what a company has and where the money for it came from. The two sides always add up to the same total, the *Bilanzsumme*.

| *Aktiva* (assets: what the money is used for) | *Passiva* (equity and liabilities: where it comes from) |
|---|---|
| *Anlagevermögen*: buildings, machines, patents, holdings | *Eigenkapital* (B2): share capital, reserves (*Rücklagen*), profit carried forward |
| *Umlaufvermögen*: stocks (*Vorräte*), receivables (*Forderungen*), cash (*flüssige Mittel*) | *Fremdkapital*: provisions (*Rückstellungen*) and liabilities (*Verbindlichkeiten*) |

- *Die Aktiva* and *die Passiva* are plural nouns (Latin plurals; the singular *Aktivum* is rare): *Die Aktiva übersteigen …*. They have nothing to do with "active" and "passive" in grammar.
- *Die Forderung* here is a receivable, money that others owe the company (*Forderungen aus Lieferungen und Leistungen*). In everyday German *eine Forderung* is a demand (*Forderungen stellen*). Its mirror is *die Verbindlichkeit*, money the company owes: *Verbindlichkeiten gegenüber Kreditinstituten* (bank debt). In everyday German *die Verbindlichkeit* is also "binding force" or "friendliness" (*mit großer Verbindlichkeit*): context decides.
- Whoever is owed money is *der Gläubiger / die Gläubigerin* (creditor), whoever owes it *der Schuldner*. Don't confuse *der Gläubiger* (creditor) with *der Gläubige* (believer, C1), a nominalized adjective. The two meet in *ein Gläubiger*, which can be either (a creditor, or a believer after *ein*); the plurals differ: *die Gläubiger* (creditors), *die Gläubigen* (the faithful).
- *Die Rückstellung* is a provision: money set aside for an obligation whose amount or date is uncertain (pensions, lawsuits, restructuring). It is borrowed money in the sense of the balance sheet, so it belongs to *Fremdkapital*. *Die Rücklage* (B2) is a reserve, part of the company's own equity. The two words differ by one syllable and are confused constantly.
- *Die Eigenkapitalquote* is equity as a share of the Bilanzsumme. A high quota means a cushion against losses; it is one of the figures a *Ratingagentur* looks at when it judges a company's *Bonität* (creditworthiness).

The income statement is *die Gewinn-und-Verlust-Rechnung* (*GuV*). From the revenue (*Umsatzerlöse*) it subtracts the expenses (*Aufwendungen*) step by step: the operating result (*das Betriebsergebnis*, in reports often equated with the English *EBIT*), the financial result, taxes, and at the bottom the net profit for the year (*der Jahresüberschuss*) or net loss (*der Jahresfehlbetrag*). The Commercial Code (HGB) prescribes these statements and the *Lagebericht* (§ 289 HGB for its content); listed groups prepare their consolidated statements under international standards (IFRS), but the German words stay.

## The text: from a Lagebericht

The extract below was written for this course in the style of a German annual report. The company and every number are invented.

> **Nordwerk Antriebstechnik AG, Konzernlagebericht 2025 (Auszug)**
>
> **Geschäftsverlauf**
>
> Das Geschäftsjahr 2025 war von einem anhaltend herausfordernden Marktumfeld geprägt. Die Nachfrage im Maschinenbau blieb insbesondere in Europa verhalten, während sich das Geschäft in Nordamerika erfreulich entwickelte. Vor diesem Hintergrund steigerte der Konzern seinen Umsatz um 2,8 Prozent auf 1,84 Milliarden Euro (Vorjahr: 1,79 Milliarden Euro). Bereinigt um Währungseffekte lag das Wachstum bei 3,5 Prozent.
>
> Das Betriebsergebnis (EBIT) ging dagegen um 11,6 Prozent auf 99 Millionen Euro zurück (Vorjahr: 112 Millionen Euro). Belastend wirkten vor allem gestiegene Material- und Personalkosten sowie Rückstellungen in Höhe von 14 Millionen Euro für die Neuausrichtung des Standorts Bremen. Die EBIT-Marge verringerte sich entsprechend von 6,3 auf 5,4 Prozent. Der Jahresüberschuss belief sich auf 61 Millionen Euro nach 72 Millionen Euro im Vorjahr.
>
> **Vermögens- und Finanzlage**
>
> Die Bilanzsumme erhöhte sich zum 31. Dezember 2025 auf 1,62 Milliarden Euro (Vorjahr: 1,58 Milliarden Euro). Da das Eigenkapital stärker wuchs als die Bilanzsumme, stieg die Eigenkapitalquote um 1,4 Prozentpunkte auf 41,2 Prozent. Die Verbindlichkeiten gegenüber Kreditinstituten konnten planmäßig um 38 Millionen Euro zurückgeführt werden.
>
> **Prognosebericht**
>
> Für das Geschäftsjahr 2026 rechnet der Vorstand mit einem Umsatz auf Vorjahresniveau; die EBIT-Marge dürfte zwischen 5,0 und 6,0 Prozent liegen. Sollte sich die Nachfrage in Europa im Jahresverlauf spürbar beleben, halten wir ein moderates Umsatzwachstum für möglich. Risiken sehen wir vor allem in handelspolitischen Spannungen und in der Entwicklung der Energiepreise. Der Vorstand wird der Hauptversammlung vorschlagen, eine Dividende von 1,10 Euro je Aktie (Vorjahr: 1,30 Euro) auszuschütten.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Nordwerk Antriebstechnik AG, group management report 2025 (extract)**

**Business performance.** The 2025 financial year was shaped by a persistently challenging market environment. Demand in mechanical engineering remained subdued, particularly in Europe, while business in North America developed pleasingly. Against this background the group increased its revenue by 2.8 percent to 1.84 billion euros (previous year: 1.79 billion euros). Adjusted for currency effects, growth was 3.5 percent.

Operating profit (EBIT), by contrast, fell by 11.6 percent to 99 million euros (previous year: 112 million euros). The main burdens were higher material and personnel costs and provisions of 14 million euros for the realignment of the Bremen site. The EBIT margin accordingly decreased from 6.3 to 5.4 percent. Net profit for the year amounted to 61 million euros, after 72 million euros in the previous year.

**Assets and financial position.** Total assets increased to 1.62 billion euros as of 31 December 2025 (previous year: 1.58 billion euros). Since equity grew faster than total assets, the equity ratio rose by 1.4 percentage points to 41.2 percent. Liabilities to banks were reduced by 38 million euros as planned.

**Forecast report.** For the 2026 financial year the executive board expects revenue at the previous year's level; the EBIT margin is likely to be between 5.0 and 6.0 percent. Should demand in Europe pick up noticeably in the course of the year, we consider moderate revenue growth possible. We see risks above all in trade-policy tensions and in the development of energy prices. The executive board will propose to the annual general meeting a dividend of 1.10 euros per share (previous year: 1.30 euros).

</details>

## Numbers in prose

The Lagebericht is a lesson in German number syntax. Each pattern has a fixed preposition:

| pattern | meaning | from the text |
|---|---|---|
| *um* + amount | by (the difference) | *steigerte … seinen Umsatz um 2,8 Prozent* |
| *auf* + amount | to (the new level) | *… auf 1,84 Milliarden Euro* |
| *von … auf …* | from … to … | *verringerte sich von 6,3 auf 5,4 Prozent* |
| *(Vorjahr: …)* | previous year's figure | *(Vorjahr: 112 Millionen Euro)* |
| *nach … im Vorjahr* | compared with … before | *61 Millionen Euro nach 72 Millionen Euro im Vorjahr* |
| *sich belaufen auf* | to amount to | *Der Jahresüberschuss belief sich auf …* |
| *in Höhe von* | in the amount of | *Rückstellungen in Höhe von 14 Millionen Euro* |
| *bei … liegen* | to be at | *lag das Wachstum bei 3,5 Prozent* |

Leaving out *um* or *auf* changes the meaning: *Der Umsatz stieg 2,8 Prozent* is colloquial and ambiguous; *um* is standard. *um … zurückgehen* (to fall by) and *auf … zurückgehen* (to fall to) are both in the text.

**Prozent and Prozentpunkte.** When a quota changes, the difference is in percentage points: from 39.8 to 41.2 percent is *ein Anstieg um 1,4 Prozentpunkte*, not "um 1,4 Prozent". Relative to the old value it would be an increase of about 3.5 percent, a different statement. Business journalists who mix them up get letters.

**Reading aloud.** *1,84 Mrd. €* is *eins Komma acht vier Milliarden Euro*; after the comma, digits are read one by one. *1,10 Euro* is usually *ein Euro zehn*. *Mio.* and *Mrd.* are the abbreviations of *Million(en)* and *Milliarde(n)*; English "billion" is German *Milliarde*, and German *Billion* is a million millions. *Das Geschäftsjahr 2025* is read *zweitausendfünfundzwanzig*.

## How the text manages tone

- **Euphemism and cautious adjectives.** *Herausfordernd* (challenging) means "difficult" or "bad"; *verhalten* (restrained) means "weak"; *die Neuausrichtung des Standorts Bremen* almost certainly means job cuts or closing parts of the plant: the Rückstellung of 14 Millionen Euro is the clue. *Zurückgeführt* (literally "led back") is the polite word for "repaid". *Erfreulich* is as enthusiastic as a Lagebericht gets. Read these words as signals, not as information.
- **The bad news is subordinate.** The fall in profit comes after the rise in revenue and is introduced with *dagegen*; the cause is put in a nominal Vorfeld, *Belastend wirkten vor allem …*, which names factors and no one who decided anything.
- **Nominal and passive style.** *Bereinigt um Währungseffekte* (a participle phrase), *in Höhe von, vor diesem Hintergrund, planmäßig*; *konnten … zurückgeführt werden* (a modal passive that also sounds like an achievement).
- **Forecasting with modal language.** *rechnet … mit* (expects), *dürfte* (is likely to: lesson 04), *Sollte sich … beleben, halten wir … für möglich* (a verb-first condition with *sollte*, then a cautious *für möglich halten*), *Risiken sehen wir in …*. No forecast uses *wird* about the market. The only plain future is about what the board itself will do: *Der Vorstand wird … vorschlagen*.
- **Ranges.** *zwischen 5,0 und 6,0 Prozent* gives a corridor rather than a point. Forecasts in Lageberichte are typically stated as ranges or as *leicht steigend, stabil, deutlich rückläufig*.

## The people and events of the financial year

- *Der Wirtschaftsprüfer / die Wirtschaftsprüferin* (auditor) checks the Jahresabschluss and, if all is in order, *testiert* it: issues an unqualified audit opinion (*den Jahresabschluss mit einem uneingeschränkten Bestätigungsvermerk testieren*). In law, *testieren* also means "to make a will" (Duden: *Rechtssprache*); DWDS gives the auditing sense first, labelled *Betriebswirtschaft*. In financial texts it is the auditor's verb.
- *Die Hauptversammlung* (annual general meeting) of the shareholders decides on the dividend, among other things; *eine Dividende ausschütten* (to pay out a dividend).
- *Der Börsengang* (IPO), *die Kapitalerhöhung* (capital increase, issuing new shares), *die Übernahme* (takeover: *ein feindliches Übernahmeangebot*; in other contexts *die Übernahme* is "taking over" a task or costs).
- On the markets: *die Volatilität* (volatility; *volatil*, Duden: *Finanzwesen* for this sense, *Chemie* for "evaporating"), *der Leerverkauf* (short sale, Duden: *Börsenwesen*), *das Portfolio* (a set of investments, also of products), *diversifizieren* (to diversify: *ein breit diversifiziertes Portfolio*).
- Interest and debt: *die Verzinsung* (the rate of interest an investment earns: *eine Verzinsung von drei Prozent*), *der Zinseszins* (compound interest), *die Tilgung* (repayment of a loan; *tilgen* is B2).
- Crisis: *zahlungsunfähig* (unable to pay debts as they fall due) and *die Zahlungsunfähigkeit*, the classic ground for insolvency (§ 17 InsO; for legal entities such as a GmbH or an AG, *Überschuldung*, over-indebtedness, is a further ground, § 19 InsO). *Die Insolvenz* (B2) is the procedure that follows.
- The economy as a whole: *das Bruttoinlandsprodukt* (*BIP*, gross domestic product) is the figure Lageberichte cite for their markets: *Das BIP dürfte im Euroraum nur leicht wachsen.*

## Ad-hoc-Mitteilungen

Listed companies must publish inside information that directly concerns them *unverzüglich* (Art. 17 Abs. 1 of the EU Market Abuse Regulation, MAR, in its German version; English "as soon as possible"). These short announcements are called *Ad-hoc-Mitteilungen* and are a text type of their own: a factual headline, the news in the first sentence, the figures, and no adjectives. An invented example:

> *Nordwerk Antriebstechnik AG senkt Prognose für das Geschäftsjahr 2026. Der Vorstand rechnet aufgrund eines unerwartet starken Auftragsrückgangs in Europa nunmehr mit einem Umsatzrückgang von fünf bis acht Prozent und einer EBIT-Marge von 3,5 bis 4,5 Prozent (bisher: Umsatz auf Vorjahresniveau, EBIT-Marge 5,0 bis 6,0 Prozent).*

*nunmehr* (now, from now on: formal) and *bisher* in brackets mark the change; the reason comes as a nominal *aufgrund*-phrase. Since 5 June 2026, the EU Listing Act has changed Art. 17 so that, for processes that run over a long time (a merger, say), intermediate steps generally no longer have to be announced, only the final event (as of November 2026; the details are set in delegated EU rules).

## Common mistakes

- **Prozent for Prozentpunkte.** A quota rising from 40 to 42 percent rises by two percentage points (by five percent of its old value).
- **Rückstellung for Rücklage.** A provision is a debt-like obligation (*Fremdkapital*); a reserve is the company's own money (*Eigenkapital*).
- **Gläubiger for Schuldner.** The creditor is owed; the debtor owes. And *die Gläubiger* (creditors) are not *die Gläubigen* (the faithful).
- **Billion for billion.** English "1.8 billion" is German *1,8 Milliarden*.
- **Reading euphemisms literally.** A *herausforderndes Umfeld* is a bad market; *Neuausrichtung* usually costs jobs. In a summary for a reader, translate them into plain German, but attribute: *Nach Angaben des Vorstands …*.
- **Taking *wird* into the forecast.** *Der Umsatz wird 2026 steigen* sounds like a promise; reports write *dürfte, rechnen mit, gehen von … aus*.

## Key points

- Bilanz: *Aktiva* (Anlage- und Umlaufvermögen) = *Passiva* (Eigenkapital + Fremdkapital); total *die Bilanzsumme*; *Eigenkapitalquote*. *Forderungen* (receivables) vs *Verbindlichkeiten* (liabilities); *Rückstellung* (provision, Fremdkapital) vs *Rücklage* (reserve, Eigenkapital).
- GuV: revenue → *Betriebsergebnis* → *Jahresüberschuss / Jahresfehlbetrag*. Audited and *testiert* by the *Wirtschaftsprüfer*; dividend decided by the *Hauptversammlung*.
- Number syntax: *um* (by), *auf* (to), *von … auf …*, *(Vorjahr: …)*, *sich belaufen auf, in Höhe von, bei … liegen*; quota changes in *Prozentpunkten*; *Milliarde* = billion.
- Tone: euphemism (*herausfordernd, verhalten, Neuausrichtung, zurückführen*), bad news after *dagegen*, forecasts with *dürfte, rechnen mit, Sollte …, halten wir … für möglich*, ranges.
- Ad-hoc-Mitteilung: inside information *unverzüglich* (Art. 17 MAR); headline, facts, *nunmehr … (bisher: …)*.
