lessons.title: Es ist alles eitel: reading older German, 1600–1800
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 6 is about literature, about the way German is changing today, about mediation and about the C2 exam. It begins with the oldest texts in this course: poems and prose written between about 1600 and 1800, in the spelling of their time.

Older German is not a museum piece: hymns still sung (*Der Mond ist aufgegangen*), inscriptions, quotations in essays and the playful archaisms of the Feuilleton (*Es ward Licht*, *ehedem*, *voller Gram*) all come from it, and an old word dropped into a modern text is exactly the kind of fine stylistic difference a C2 reader is expected to notice. This lesson reads a Baroque sonnet, an 18th-century poem and two letters from Goethe's *Werther*, shows which forms have changed, and how to modernize a passage without flattening it.

## Before standard German

German had no single standard spelling or grammar in 1600; printers, chancelleries and regions each had their habits. Historians call the period up to about 1650 *Frühneuhochdeutsch* (Early New High German) and what follows *Neuhochdeutsch*; a *Sprachstufe* (stage of a language) never ends on a particular day. Spelling became uniform only after the orthographic conference of 1901, whose rules came into force in 1902–03.

So in a text from 1650 or 1770, expect spelling that varies even within one text (*sey/sei, Thaten/Taten*), forms that are old-fashioned or gone (*ward, frug, hülfe, mich dünkt*), and common words whose meaning has shifted (*schlecht* meant "plain, simple").

A word or form that is no longer current and is used to sound old is an **[[archaism]]** (*der Archaismus*). Duden's labels help you tell how far gone a word is: *veraltend* (going out of use), *veraltet* (out of use), *gehoben* (elevated), *dichterisch* (poetic).

## A review: Alles eitel?

The text below is an exhibition review of the kind a regional newspaper's Feuilleton prints (the museum and the exhibition are invented). Notice how the critic uses older words for effect.

> **Alles eitel? Eine Ausstellung über die Vergänglichkeit**
>
> Wer die neue Sonderausstellung im Landesmuseum betritt, wird zunächst von einem Totenkopf empfangen. Er liegt, halb verdeckt von einer welkenden Tulpe, auf einem Tisch neben einer erloschenen Kerze und einer umgestürzten Sanduhr – ein Memento mori, wie es die Maler des Barock zu Hunderten geschaffen haben. „Alles eitel?“ heißt die Schau, und das Fragezeichen ist Programm. Denn die Kuratorin will zeigen, dass die Stillleben des 17. Jahrhunderts mehr sind als fromme Ermahnungen.
>
> Gewiss: Die Vergänglichkeit alles Irdischen war das große Thema einer Epoche, die den Dreißigjährigen Krieg erlebt hatte. Andreas Gryphius, dessen Sonett „Es ist alles eitel“ in großen Lettern die Stirnwand des ersten Saals ziert, hatte früh beide Eltern verloren und Brände und Seuchen gesehen. Doch wer genauer hinsieht, entdeckt in den Bildern eine eigentümliche Doppelbödigkeit. Dieselben Maler, die den Betrachter zur Andacht mahnen, schwelgen in Seidenglanz, venezianischem Glas und Früchten von geradezu unanständiger Frische. Die Eitelkeit, die das Bild verurteilt, stellt es zugleich mit größter Wonne zur Schau – und es verkaufte sich damit vortrefflich an wohlhabende Bürger, die es sich leisten konnten, über die Nichtigkeit ihres Reichtums nachzusinnen.
>
> Klug ist, dass die Ausstellung nicht beim Barock stehen bleibt. Ein zweiter Raum führt ins 18. Jahrhundert, in die Zeit der Empfindsamkeit, als man die Schwermut nicht mehr als Sünde, sondern als Zeichen eines zarten Gemüts verstand. Neben Stammbuchblättern liegt dort eine Erstausgabe von Goethes „Werther“, jenem Briefroman, der nach seinem Erscheinen 1774 ein Skandalerfolg war.
>
> Ein wenig ratlos lässt einen allein der letzte Saal zurück, in dem Selfies und Fitness-Apps als „Vanitas von heute“ präsentiert werden. Der Vergleich liegt nahe, gewiss; ehedem hätte man von einem Gemeinplatz gesprochen. Nach zwei Sälen voller Schädel und Sanduhren hätte man dem Publikum zutrauen dürfen, ihn selbst zu ziehen.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**All vanity? An exhibition on transience**

Anyone entering the new special exhibition at the Landesmuseum is first greeted by a skull. It lies, half hidden by a wilting tulip, on a table next to a snuffed-out candle and an overturned hourglass: a memento mori of the kind the painters of the Baroque produced by the hundred. "All vanity?" is the show's title, and the question mark is its programme. For the curator wants to show that the still lifes of the 17th century are more than pious admonitions.

Certainly, the transience of all earthly things was the great theme of an age that had lived through the Thirty Years' War. Andreas Gryphius, whose sonnet "All is vanity" adorns the end wall of the first room in large letters, had lost both parents early and seen fires and epidemics. But anyone who looks more closely discovers a peculiar double meaning in the pictures. The same painters who urge the viewer to devotion revel in the sheen of silk, Venetian glass and fruit of almost indecent freshness. The vanity the picture condemns, it displays at the same time with the greatest delight, and so it sold splendidly to wealthy burghers who could afford to meditate on the worthlessness of their riches.

It is a clever move that the exhibition doesn't stop at the Baroque. A second room leads into the 18th century, the age of sensibility, when melancholy was understood no longer as a sin but as the sign of a tender soul. Next to leaves from friendship albums lies a first edition of Goethe's "Werther", the epistolary novel that was a succès de scandale after it appeared in 1774.

Only the last room leaves one a little at a loss: there, selfies and fitness apps are presented as "the vanitas of today". The comparison is obvious, certainly; in days of old one would have called it a commonplace. After two rooms full of skulls and hourglasses, the public might have been trusted to draw it for themselves.

</details>

The review is modern German, but three things in it point back to the period it describes.

- **Period vocabulary used as terms**: *das Memento mori* ("remember that you must die", Latin) is any object or picture that reminds the viewer of death; *die Vanitas* (Latin "emptiness") is the theme and the type of still life. *eitel* in the title is the old sense, "empty, futile", not today's "vain about one's looks".
- **Old words for colour**: *Wonne* (delight) and *ehedem* (in days of old; both *gehoben* in Duden) sound deliberately old. The critic uses *ehedem* ironically, as stylistic colouring (lesson 02): the comparison is old hat.
- *fromm* in *fromme Ermahnungen* means "pious"; in older texts it also meant "good, upright", a sense that survives in *fromm wie ein Lamm* (meek as a lamb).

## Gryphius: Es ist alles eitel

Andreas Gryphius (1616–1664) is one of the best-known German poets of the Baroque. His sonnet on vanity first appeared, in a version that differs in many words, in a collection of sonnets printed in Lissa (Leszno) in 1637; he revised it for later editions. The text below is his later revision, as in the Breslau collected edition *Freuden und Trauer-Spiele auch Oden und Sonnette* (1658), transcribed by Projekt Gutenberg-DE after a Rowohlt edition of 1968. It is not the Leiden print of 1643 (*Was dieser heute bawt*).

> **Es ist alles Eitel**
>
> Du sihst / wohin du sihst nur Eitelkeit auff Erden.
> Was diser heute baut / reist jener morgen ein:
> Wo itzund Städte stehn / wird eine Wisen seyn /
> Auff der ein Schäfers-Kind wird spilen mit den Herden:
>
> Was itzund prächtig blüht / sol bald zutretten werden
> Was itzt so pocht und trotzt ist Morgen Asch und Bein /
> Nichts ist / das ewig sey / kein Ertz / kein Marmorstein.
> Itzt lacht das Glück uns an / bald donnern die Beschwerden.
>
> Der hohen Thaten Ruhm muß wie ein Traum vergehn.
> Soll denn das Spil der Zeit / der leichte Mensch bestehn?
> Ach! was ist alles diß / was wir vor köstlich achten /
>
> Als schlechte Nichtikeit / als Schatten/ Staub und Wind;
> Als eine Wisen-Blum / die man nicht wider find't.
> Noch will was Ewig ist kein einig Mensch betrachten!

In plain English: Wherever you look, you see only vanity on earth. What one man builds today, another tears down tomorrow; where cities stand now there will be a meadow on which a shepherd's child will play with the flocks. What blooms splendidly now will soon be trampled; what struts and defies today is ashes and bones tomorrow. Nothing is eternal, neither bronze nor marble. Now fortune smiles on us, soon troubles thunder. The fame of great deeds must pass like a dream. Shall man, the plaything of time, light as he is, endure? Ah, what is all this that we think precious but mere nothingness, shadow, dust and wind, a meadow flower that cannot be found again? And yet not a single person will consider what is eternal!

### How to read it

| in the poem | today | note |
|---|---|---|
| *sihst, diser, Wisen, spilen* | *siehst, dieser, Wiese, spielen* | long *i* written without *e* |
| *seyn, sey* | *sein, sei* | *y* for *i* |
| *Thaten* | *Taten* | *th* for *t*, common until 1901 |
| *auff, sol, will* | *auf, soll, will* | doubled and single consonants vary |
| *reist ... ein* | *reißt ... ein* | no fixed *ß* |
| *itzund, itzt* | *jetzt* | old forms of *jetzt* |
| *zutretten* | *zertreten* | *zu-* as an older form of *zer-* |
| *vor köstlich achten* | *für köstlich halten* | *vor* and *für* were not yet kept apart |
| *schlechte Nichtikeit* | *bloße Nichtigkeit* | *schlecht* = "plain, mere" (cf. *schlecht und recht*) |
| *wider find't* | *wiederfindet* | *wider/wieder* not yet distinguished |
| *kein einig Mensch* | *kein einziger Mensch* | *einig* = "single" |
| *Asch und Bein* | *Asche und Knochen* | *Bein* = "bone" (as in *Gebeine*) |
| *Beschwerden* | *Beschwernisse, Mühen* | troubles, not complaints |

Two changes recur. **[[Apocope]]** (*die Apokope*) is the loss of a final unstressed *-e*: *Asch, Wisen-Blum*. **[[Syncope]]** (*die Synkope*) is the loss of an unstressed vowel inside a word: *stehn, vergehn, bestehn* for *stehen, vergehen, bestehen*, and *find't* for *findet*. Both fit the metre, and both survive in speech and song (*Ich hab's*, *unsre*).

The virgule (*/*) does the work of a comma. Here it often also marks the caesura, the pause in mid-line: the lines are alexandrines, six iambs with a break after the third (*Du sihst / wohin du sihst // nur Eitelkeit auff Erden*). Capitals are not yet regular either: *Morgen* (tomorrow) and *Ewig* have them, *morgen* in line 2 does not.

### Word order

Baroque word order is freer than today's, mostly for rhyme and metre:

- *wird spilen mit den Herden*: a prepositional phrase after the infinitive, today *mit den Herden spielen wird*.
- *Der hohen Thaten Ruhm*: the genitive before its noun (*der Ruhm der hohen Taten*), still possible today in elevated style (*des Kaisers neue Kleider*).
- *Soll denn das Spil der Zeit / der leichte Mensch bestehn?*: the subject is *der leichte Mensch*, and *das Spil der Zeit* is an apposition placed before it.
- *Noch will was Ewig ist kein einig Mensch betrachten!*: the object clause *was ewig ist* stands between the verb and the subject. Today: *Und doch will kein einziger Mensch betrachten, was ewig ist.*

The theme is the Baroque's own: the *Vergänglichkeit* of everything earthly, the vanitas of Ecclesiastes 1:2 ("Vanity of vanities"), and the turn to the eternal in the last line. The two quatrains rhyme abba abba, the tercets ccd eed. The *Schäferdichtung* (pastoral poetry) of the same century imagined shepherds in an ideal countryside; here the shepherd's child playing on the site of a city is the image of ruin.

## Older forms you will meet

| form | modern | where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| *er ward* | *er wurde* | Bible, fairy tales, ironic journalism: *Und es ward Licht.* |
| *er frug* | *er fragte* | 18th and 19th century; now regional or old-fashioned |
| *er hülfe, stürbe, stünde* | *er würde helfen* | the old Konjunktiv II formed from the old preterite plural (*sie hulfen*); *stürbe* and *stünde* are still standard, *hülfe* rare |
| *mich dünkt, mir deucht* | *ich finde, mir scheint* | *gehoben*, or ironic today |
| *sich des Lebens freuen* | *sich über das Leben freuen* | genitive objects (lesson 05) |
| *im Hause, dem Manne* | *im Haus, dem Mann* | the dative *-e*, now only in fixed phrases (*zu Hause, im Grunde*) |
| *-et* in verse: *schweiget, steiget* | *schweigt, steigt* | an extra syllable for the metre |

*dünken* is impersonal, with the accusative or, less often, the dative: *Mich dünkt, er hat recht* (it seems to me he's right). Duden: *gehoben veraltend*; *dünkte* (veraltet *deuchte*), *gedünkt*; older texts also have *deucht, gedeucht*. Today it is mostly mock-solemn.

## Empfindsamkeit and Sturm und Drang

A hundred years after Gryphius, the tone has changed. The *Empfindsamkeit* (age of sensibility, roughly the middle decades of the 18th century) valued tender feeling, friendship and private piety. *Der Sturm und Drang* (about 1765–1785) went further: genius, nature, revolt against rules. The dates overlap, and both are labels given later.

Matthias Claudius (1740–1815) first printed his "Abendlied" in the *Poetische Blumenlese für das Jahr 1779*, a poetry almanac edited by Johann Heinrich Voß. Here are its first and third stanzas from the *Asmus* edition, Part IV (1782), as transcribed by LiederNet and schubertsong.uk (LiederNet notes no variants from 1779 here):

> Der Mond ist aufgegangen,
> Die goldnen Sternlein prangen
> Am Himmel hell und klar.
> Der Wald steht schwarz und schweiget,
> Und aus den Wiesen steiget
> Der weiße Nebel wunderbar.
>
> Seht ihr den Mond dort stehen? –
> Er ist nur halb zu sehen,
> Und ist doch rund und schön!
> So sind wohl manche Sachen,
> Die wir getrost belachen,
> Weil unsre Augen sie nicht sehn.

(The moon has risen, the little golden stars shine bright and clear in the sky. The wood stands black and silent, and from the meadows rises the white mist, wonderfully. Do you see the moon standing there? Only half of it can be seen, and yet it is round and beautiful! So, no doubt, are many things that we confidently laugh at because our eyes don't see them.)

The language is almost modern; the old features are small: syncope (*goldnen, unsre, sehn*), the metrical *-et* (*schweiget*), *-lein* (*Sternlein*), *prangen* (to be resplendent). What dates it is the piety: the half-visible moon becomes a lesson about what reason cannot see.

Goethe's *Die Leiden des jungen Werthers* (1774) is a *Briefroman*, a novel in letters. Werther writes mostly to his friend Wilhelm, whose replies we never read; near the end a fictional editor takes over. Its first letter opens:

> *Wie froh bin ich, daß ich weg bin! Bester Freund, was ist das Herz des Menschen!*

and the second:

> *Eine wunderbare Heiterkeit hat meine ganze Seele eingenommen, gleich den süßen Frühlingsmorgen, die ich mit ganzem Herzen genieße. Ich bin allein und freue mich meines Lebens in dieser Gegend, die für solche Seelen geschaffen ist wie die meine.*

(quoted from Projekt Gutenberg-DE, which names no source; its title *Werther* is the form of the 1787 revision. The 1774 edition has *Ich bin allein, und freue mich meines Lebens in dieser Gegend die für …*)

(How glad I am to be away! Dearest friend, what a thing is the heart of man! A wonderful serenity has taken possession of my whole soul, like the sweet spring mornings that I enjoy with all my heart. I am alone and rejoice in my life in this place, which was made for souls like mine.)

Notice *daß* (spelling before 1996), the genitive object *freue mich meines Lebens*, *gleich* + dative ("like"), and *wie die meine* placed after the verb. The exclamations, *Herz* and *Seele* are the vocabulary of feeling that the Sturm und Drang made fashionable. Grimmelshausen's *Simplicissimus*, a picaresque novel of the Thirty Years' War, belongs a century earlier (usually dated 1668/69); the epochs reference sheet lists it.

## Modernizing without flattening

Sometimes you need to put an old passage into today's German: for a programme note, a school handout, a summary. Compare three versions of Gryphius's second quatrain:

1. **Normalized spelling only**: *Was jetzund prächtig blüht, soll bald zertreten werden; was jetzt so pocht und trotzt, ist morgen Asch und Bein.* Rhythm and old words stay.
2. **Modern prose, same tone**: *Was heute in voller Pracht blüht, wird bald zertreten sein; was jetzt noch prahlt und trotzt, ist morgen Asche und Gebein.* *Gebein* keeps the solemn sound; the sentence is still elevated.
3. **Flat paraphrase**: *Schöne Dinge gehen schnell kaputt, und starke Menschen sterben auch.* Correct in content, but the register has collapsed; *kaputtgehen* is colloquial, and the images are gone.

At C2 you should be able to write version 2: choose modern grammar, but keep an elevated word where the original is elevated (*Gebein, vergehen, die Pracht*), and keep the images.

## The words of this lesson

- *eitel* in the old sense can stand uninflected before a noun and mean "nothing but": *Es herrschte eitel Freude* (ironic today). *die Eitelkeit* covers both the Baroque emptiness and today's vanity about appearance.
- *die Schwermut* is heavy, lasting melancholy; *der Gram* gnawing grief (*gehoben*), *sich grämen* to grieve or fret (*Gräm dich nicht!*). The gentler, nostalgic *Wehmut* comes in 30h1.
- *das Gemüt* is heart and mind, temperament (*ein heiteres Gemüt*); *sich etwas zu Gemüte führen* is now jocular for "to treat oneself to something". *die Andacht* is devotion, and also a short service.
- *frohlocken* (to exult) is often ironic today, for open gloating; *die Huld* (gracious favour) survives mainly in irony; *gülden* only in poetry and old names.
- *ehedem* (formerly) and *alsbald* (straight away) are the old adverbs you will meet most; *darben* (to go without) is *gehoben*.
- *barock* also means "ornate, extravagant" (*ein barocker Lebensstil*).

## Common mistakes

- Reading old *eitel* as "vain (about one's looks)". In *Es ist alles eitel* and *eitel Sonnenschein* it means "empty, futile" or "nothing but".
- Taking *schlecht, Beschwerden, vor* in their modern sense. In older texts, check the meaning of common words before the rare ones: they are the real traps.
- "Correcting" the spelling of a quotation. An older text is quoted as printed, with *seyn, daß, Thaten*; a modernized quotation must say so.
- Using archaisms as decoration. *Mich dünkt* in a cover letter is a Stilbruch; use old words for irony or in quotations.
- Reading *ward* as *war*: it is the old preterite of *werden* (*es ward Licht* = *es wurde Licht*).
- Treating *der Barock* and *das Barock* as a mistake: both genders are standard.

## Key points

- Before 1901, German spelling varied: *y* for *i*, *th*, *v* for *u*, virgules for commas, no rule for capitals. Quote older texts as printed and name the edition.
- Apocope drops a final *-e* (*Blum, hab*); syncope drops a vowel inside the word (*gehn, unsre, find't*). Both are metrical tools and survive in speech.
- Older forms: *ward, frug*, Konjunktiv II with *ü* (*hülfe, stürbe*), *mich dünkt*, genitive objects, the dative *-e*.
- Common words with an older meaning (*schlecht, eitel, fromm, Bein*) cause more misreadings than rare words.
- Baroque: vanitas, memento mori, the Thirty Years' War, the alexandrine sonnet. Empfindsamkeit and Sturm und Drang: feeling, friendship, genius; Claudius and the young Goethe.
- Modernize by changing grammar and spelling while keeping the register and the images.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Erzählhaltung und Zwischentöne: reading literary prose, 1850–1930
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 26 read older German at the level of the word and the sentence. This lesson reads narrative prose from the age of Realism to early Modernism (about 1850–1930) at the level of the whole text: who tells the story, from where, how fast, and what is left unsaid. At C2 you don't only follow the plot; you notice the *Zwischentöne*, the shades of meaning between the lines, and you can say in German how a passage produces them.

You will read an original short passage written for this lesson, then the opening of Storm's *Der Schimmelreiter*, the last line of Fontane's *Effi Briest* and the first paragraph of Musil's *Der Mann ohne Eigenschaften*. The last section shows how to write a short interpretation. Thomas Mann and Schnitzler follow in the honors lessons 30h1 and 30h2.

## Narrative stance

German literary studies describe a narrator's *Erzählhaltung* (**[[narrative stance]]**): the position from which the story is told, and the narrator's attitude to it. Three types are usually distinguished, following the scholar Franz K. Stanzel's model of *Erzählsituationen*; real texts mix them.

| type | who tells | typical signs |
|---|---|---|
| *auktorial* (authorial) | a narrator outside the story who knows more than the characters and may comment | *unser Held*, judgements, looks ahead (*Er ahnte nicht, dass …*), summaries of years |
| *personal* (figural) | the story is filtered through one character's perception; the narrator seems to disappear | only what the character sees and thinks; free indirect speech; no comments |
| *Ich-Form* (first person) | a character tells his or her own story | *ich*; the older self judges the younger (*Damals wusste ich noch nicht, …*) |

**[[Figural narration]]** (*personales Erzählen*) is the hardest to read for a learner, because the text never says "she thought". Its main tool is free indirect speech (*erlebte Rede*): the character's thoughts in the third person and the narrative past, but with the character's own words, questions and exclamations: *Morgen würde er es ihr sagen. Morgen, ganz bestimmt!* Go one step further, drop the narrator altogether and record thoughts in the present tense as they come, and you have the interior monologue, which Schnitzler's *Leutnant Gustl* (30h2) uses from first line to last. The **[[stream of consciousness]]** (*der Bewusstseinsstrom*) is the wider term for such writing that imitates the unordered flow of thought, associations included.

## A passage: Die Abreise

The passage below was written for this lesson in the manner of a novel set around 1910. Read it once for what happens, then again for how it is told.

> **Die Abreise**
>
> Als Marie Lindner an jenem Oktobermorgen den Bahnsteig betrat, hatte es bereits zu regnen aufgehört. Der Zug nach Hamburg stand noch nicht da. Sie stellte den Koffer ab, zog die Handschuhe aus und gleich wieder an. Vierzehn Jahre hatte sie in dieser Stadt gelebt, und nun genügten zehn Minuten, um alles hinter sich zu lassen. Zehn Minuten! War das nicht beinahe lächerlich?
>
> Ihr Bruder hatte darauf bestanden, sie zu begleiten. Er stand neben ihr, rauchte und sprach vom Wetter, von den Preisen in Hamburg, von einem Kollegen, der sich dort „sehr verbessert“ habe. Marie hörte zu und nickte. Dass er die Sache mit Robert mit keinem Wort erwähnte, rechnete sie ihm hoch an; dass er sie so beharrlich nicht erwähnte, kränkte sie ein wenig.
>
> Dann kam der Zug. Er kam langsam, mit einem Seufzen der Bremsen, das ihr unverhältnismäßig laut vorkam, und hielt so, dass ihr Wagen genau vor ihr stand, als hätte man es eigens für sie so eingerichtet. Ein Schaffner öffnete die Tür. Sie sah den Griff, das nasse Trittbrett, den schmalen Gang dahinter, und für einen Augenblick, der ihr später sehr lang erscheinen sollte, war ihr, als könne sie den Fuß nicht heben.
>
> „Na, dann“, sagte der Bruder.
>
> „Ja“, sagte sie, „dann.“
>
> Er half ihr mit dem Koffer, küsste sie auf die Stirn, wie er es als Junge getan hatte, und trat zurück. Durch das Fenster sah sie ihn noch eine Weile stehen, den Hut in der Hand, ein wenig zu gerade, wie jemand, der fotografiert wird. Dann setzte sich der Zug in Bewegung, und die Stadt glitt vorüber, Fabriken, Gärten, die Kirche, in der sie getauft worden war. Sie dachte, sie werde weinen. Sie weinte nicht. Erst hinter Uelzen, als eine Mitreisende ihr ungefragt ein Butterbrot anbot, musste sie sich abwenden.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**The Departure**

When Marie Lindner stepped onto the platform that October morning, it had already stopped raining. The train to Hamburg wasn't in yet. She put down her suitcase, took off her gloves and put them straight back on. She had lived in this town for fourteen years, and now ten minutes were enough to leave it all behind. Ten minutes! Wasn't that almost ridiculous?

Her brother had insisted on coming with her. He stood beside her, smoking, and talked about the weather, about prices in Hamburg, about a colleague who had "done very well for himself" there. Marie listened and nodded. That he didn't say a word about the business with Robert, she gave him much credit for; that he so doggedly didn't mention it hurt her a little.

Then the train came. It came slowly, with a sigh of its brakes that seemed to her out of all proportion, and stopped so that her carriage stood exactly in front of her, as if it had been arranged that way especially for her. A guard opened the door. She saw the handle, the wet step, the narrow corridor behind it, and for a moment that would later seem very long to her, she felt as if she couldn't lift her foot.

"Well, then," said her brother.

"Yes," she said, "then."

He helped her with the suitcase, kissed her on the forehead as he used to as a boy, and stepped back. Through the window she saw him standing there for a while, hat in hand, a little too upright, like someone having his photograph taken. Then the train started, and the town slid past: factories, gardens, the church in which she had been baptized. She thought she would cry. She didn't cry. Only after Uelzen, when a fellow passenger offered her a sandwich without being asked, did she have to turn away.

</details>

### How the passage is told

- **[[Erzählhaltung]]**: personal. We see only what Marie sees and know only what she thinks. Nobody tells us who Robert is.
- **Erlebte Rede**: *Zehn Minuten! War das nicht beinahe lächerlich?* is Marie's thought, in the third person and the past, but with her exclamation and her question. The narrator doesn't say *dachte sie*.
- **Figurenrede** (the characters' own speech) is reduced to almost nothing: *Na, dann. – Ja, dann.* The brother's talk is summarized as reported speech, with the Konjunktiv I *habe* and the quotation marks around *sehr verbessert* marking his phrase, not Marie's.
- ***Das Unausgesprochene*** (what is left unsaid): *die Sache mit Robert* is the centre of the passage and is never explained. The reader infers a broken engagement or a scandal from the departure, the brother's silence and Marie's reaction.
- ***Zwischentöne***: the parallel *Dass er … erwähnte, rechnete sie ihm hoch an; dass er sie so beharrlich nicht erwähnte, kränkte sie ein wenig* shows mixed feelings in one sentence; *beharrlich nicht erwähnen* is a deliberately paradoxical phrase.
- **Tempo**: fourteen years in one clause (*Vierzehn Jahre hatte sie in dieser Stadt gelebt*), then a few seconds at the carriage door in a long sentence. More on this below.
- **One authorial touch**: *für einen Augenblick, der ihr später sehr lang erscheinen sollte* looks into the future. *sollte* + infinitive here is the "future in the past" of narration, not obligation. Such a look ahead is a *Vorausdeutung*.
- **Understatement at the end**: *Sie dachte, sie werde weinen. Sie weinte nicht.* The emotion breaks through only over a trivial kindness (a sandwich), and even then the text says only that she turned away.

## Time: Erzählzeit and erzählte Zeit

**[[Narrative time]]** has two sides. *Die Erzählzeit* is the time it takes to read a passage; *die erzählte Zeit* is the time that passes in the story. When the story moves faster than reading, that is *Zeitraffung* (summary: *Vierzehn Jahre hatte sie … gelebt*); when the reading takes longer than the event, that is *Zeitdehnung* (the moment at the door, slowed down by a list of what she sees). Dialogue comes closest to equality (*Zeitdeckung*, a scene). Skipping time altogether is an ellipsis: between the farewell and *hinter Uelzen* an hour or more passes in a single word.

Tense helps. The Präteritum is the ordinary narrative tense and carries no sense of pastness for the reader; the Plusquamperfekt (*hatte aufgehört, hatte bestanden*) marks what happened before the story's "now"; Konjunktiv I (*habe, werde*) reports speech and thought from a slight distance.

## Storm: the frame

Theodor Storm (1817–1888) published *Der Schimmelreiter* in the year of his death. It is the classic German **[[frame narrative]]** (*die Rahmenerzählung*): an outer story, the *Rahmenhandlung*, frames one or more inner stories, *Binnenerzählungen*. Here there are even three levels. It begins:

> *Was ich zu berichten beabsichtige, ist mir vor reichlich einem halben Jahrhundert im Hause meiner Urgroßmutter, der alten Frau Senator Feddersen, kundgeworden, während ich, an ihrem Lehnstuhl sitzend, mich mit dem Lesen eines in blaue Pappe eingebundenen Zeitschriftenheftes beschäftigte; …*

(What I intend to relate came to my knowledge more than half a century ago in the house of my great-grandmother, old Frau Senator Feddersen, while I, sitting by her armchair, was occupied with reading a magazine bound in blue cardboard; quoted from Projekt Gutenberg-DE, after an Ullstein edition of 1994.)

The first narrator remembers reading a story; that story's narrator, a traveller, rides along a North Frisian dike in a storm and stops at an inn, where a schoolmaster tells him the inner story of the dike-reeve Hauke Haien. Each frame puts the legend at a further distance, and each narrator reminds us that he only reports what he heard. Notice the style of the first sentence: the long participle attribute (*eines in blaue Pappe eingebundenen Zeitschriftenheftes*), the inserted participle clause (*an ihrem Lehnstuhl sitzend*), the dative *-e* (*im Hause*) and *kundwerden* (to become known, now old-fashioned). This is the measured, slightly formal *Erzählstil* of Poetic Realism.

## Fontane: Plauderton and what is not said

Theodor Fontane (1819–1898) is the great *Gesellschaftsroman* writer of German Realism: novels of society that are also *gesellschaftskritisch*, critical of society, without ever preaching. His *Plauderton* (chatty tone) is famous: much of *Effi Briest* (serialized 1894–95, the book dated 1896) consists of conversation, letters and small talk, and the decisive events happen off stage. Effi's affair with Major von Crampas is never shown; the reader infers it from a sleigh ride, a few evasions and, years later, a bundle of letters. The novel ends with her parents in the garden after her death. Her mother asks whether they are not to blame after all, whether Effi was not too young; her father answers:

> *»Ach, Luise, laß … das ist ein zu weites Feld.«*

(Oh, Luise, leave it … that is too wide a field. Quoted from Projekt Gutenberg-DE.)

Briest's refrain, heard earlier in the novel (Innstetten even quotes it to Effi: *wie dein Papa immer sagte: „Das ist ein zu weites Feld.“*), refuses an answer, and that refusal is the answer. The phrase is still quoted for a question too big to settle.

## Musil: irony from the first sentence

Robert Musil (1880–1942) published the first volume of *Der Mann ohne Eigenschaften* in 1930. The first chapter, headed *Woraus bemerkenswerter Weise nichts hervorgeht* (from which, remarkably, nothing follows), opens like a weather report:

> *Über dem Atlantik befand sich ein barometrisches Minimum; es wanderte ostwärts, einem über Rußland lagernden Maximum zu, und verriet noch nicht die Neigung, diesem nördlich auszuweichen.*

After several more sentences of meteorology, it concludes:

> *Mit einem Wort, das das Tatsächliche recht gut bezeichnet, wenn es auch etwas altmodisch ist: Es war ein schöner Augusttag des Jahres 1913.*

(Over the Atlantic there was a barometric low; it was moving eastward, towards a high lying over Russia, and showed no inclination yet to bypass it to the north. … In a word that describes the facts quite well, even if it is a little old-fashioned: it was a fine August day in the year 1913. Quoted from Adolf Frisé's edition, Rowohlt.)

The irony works on two levels. A traditional novel opens with *Es war ein schöner Tag*; Musil first parodies scientific precision and then offers the cliché as the "old-fashioned" word for the same facts. And the date carries a *Vorausdeutung* that the narrator doesn't spell out: every reader in 1930 knew what followed August 1913. This is authorial narration at its most ironic: a narrator who comments on his own way of telling.

## Writing a short interpretation

An interpretation of a *Textstelle* (passage) answers three questions: what happens, how it is told, and what this achieves. A paragraph of 120–150 words is enough for practice. Useful phrases:

| purpose | phrases |
|---|---|
| place the passage | *Die Textstelle stammt aus …; Sie bildet den Wendepunkt der Handlung / die Exposition des Romans.* |
| describe the telling | *Erzählt wird aus personaler Perspektive; Die Erzählhaltung ist auktorial; In erlebter Rede gibt der Erzähler Maries Gedanken wieder; Die Zeit wird gedehnt / gerafft.* |
| interpret | *Dadurch entsteht der Eindruck, dass …; Die Auslassung lenkt den Blick auf …; Was unausgesprochen bleibt, ist …; Diese Lesart wird durch … gestützt.* |
| characterize | *Die Figur wird indirekt charakterisiert: durch ihr Verhalten, nicht durch Erzählerkommentare.* |

A model for *Die Abreise*:

> *Die Szene am Bahnsteig wird aus Maries Perspektive erzählt; ein Erzählerkommentar fehlt fast ganz. Gerade dadurch gewinnt das Unausgesprochene Gewicht: Was „die Sache mit Robert“ war, erfährt der Leser nicht, er erschließt es aus dem Schweigen des Bruders und aus Maries Zögern an der Wagentür. Dieser Augenblick ist der Höhepunkt der Szene und wird stark gedehnt, während vierzehn Jahre in einem Nebensatz vergehen. Die einzige Vorausdeutung („der ihr später sehr lang erscheinen sollte“) deutet an, dass die Abreise einen Einschnitt in Maries Leben bedeutet. Der knappe Schluss bestätigt diese Lesart: Die Figur wird nicht durch große Gefühlsäußerungen charakterisiert, sondern durch eine kleine, abgewandte Geste.*

Keep the interpretation in the present tense, quote briefly, and tie every claim to a place in the text.

## The words of this lesson

- *auktorial* and *personal* are terms of literary studies; *personal* in this sense is not *persönlich* (personal, private). *das Personal* (staff) is a different word.
- *die Exposition* (the opening that introduces characters and situation), *der Höhepunkt* (climax) and *der Wendepunkt* (turning point) describe structure; *novellistisch* means "in the manner of a novella" (concentrated, with a turning point).
- *die Figurenkonstellation* is the arrangement of characters and their relations; *die Nebenfigur* a minor character; *der Schauplatz* the setting; *die Schlüsselszene* a key scene.
- *der Entwicklungsroman* follows a hero's development (the *Bildungsroman* is its best-known type); *das Sittenbild* is a picture of the manners of a society.
- *charakterisieren* and *die Charakterisierung* (direct: by the narrator; indirect: by behaviour and speech).
- *die Lesart* is one reading or interpretation of a text (also a textual variant in an edition).

## Common mistakes

- Confusing the narrator with the author: *Fontane sagt, Effi …* → *Der Erzähler / Briest sagt …*. Even in an Ich-Form, the narrator is a figure.
- Calling every third-person text *auktorial*. A third-person text without comments and limited to one character's view is *personal*.
- Reading *sollte* + infinitive in narration as obligation: *der ihr später sehr lang erscheinen sollte* = "which would later seem very long".
- Treating the Präteritum as a sign of pastness for the reader. In narration it is the normal tense; the Plusquamperfekt marks the time before.
- Retelling the plot instead of interpreting. Every sentence of an interpretation should say how the text works, not only what happens.
- False precision: "Fontane uses erlebte Rede 23 times" says nothing. Name the effect.

## Key points

- *Erzählhaltung*: auktorial (comments, knows more), personal (filtered through a character, erlebte Rede), Ich-Form. Real texts mix them.
- Erlebte Rede = third person + past + the character's own words and questions; interior monologue drops the narrator; stream of consciousness imitates the flow of thought.
- *Erzählzeit* vs *erzählte Zeit*: *Zeitraffung* (summary), *Zeitdehnung* (slowing down), scene, ellipsis.
- Storm's *Schimmelreiter* (1888): a frame narrative with three levels. Fontane's *Effi Briest*: Plauderton, decisive events left unsaid, *Das ist ein zu weites Feld*. Musil (1930): irony and a silent *Vorausdeutung* in *August 1913*.
- An interpretation says what, how and to what effect, in the present tense, with short quotations.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Weil das ist so: language change and variation today
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 26 and 27 looked back. This one looks at German as it is changing now: constructions that spread in speech and are argued about in letters to the editor, new words from English and from the internet, the multiethnic youth language of big cities, the debate about gender-fair language, and the minority languages spoken in Germany. German C1 lesson 26 covered regional German and the *am*-Progressiv (*Ich bin am Arbeiten*); here they come back only in passing.

At C2 you need two skills for this. First, recognize a form and place it: is it standard, colloquial, regional, group-specific, or simply new? Second, talk about change in neutral, precise German, without repeating the complaint that the language is falling apart, and without pretending that norms don't matter in an exam or an application.

## An interview: Sprachverfall?

Read this interview from the weekend supplement of a newspaper (invented; the linguist is fictional).

> **„Die Klage über den Sprachverfall ist so alt wie die Schrift“**
>
> *Jugendliche sagen „weil das ist so“, Firmen werben auf Englisch, Behörden gendern oder verbieten es. Geht das Deutsche vor die Hunde? Fragen an die Sprachwissenschaftlerin Anna Bergmann.*
>
> **Frau Bergmann, viele Leserinnen und Leser schreiben uns, das Deutsche verfalle. Haben sie recht?**
>
> Sie haben recht damit, dass es sich verändert. Das tut es seit jeher. Von Verfall würde ich nicht sprechen. Schon im 17. Jahrhundert klagten Gelehrte, das Deutsche werde vom Französischen verdorben, und im 19. Jahrhundert schimpfte Schopenhauer über das Deutsch der Zeitungsschreiber. Die Sprache hat beides überlebt.
>
> **Aber „weil“ mit Verbzweitstellung ist doch schlicht falsch.**
>
> In der geschriebenen Standardsprache ja, da gehört das Verb ans Ende. Im Gespräch ist „weil“ mit Hauptsatzstellung aber längst verbreitet, und zwar nicht zufällig. Man sagt: „Er ist bestimmt zu Hause – weil, das Licht brennt.“ Da begründe ich nicht, warum er zu Hause ist, sondern warum ich das glaube. Mit Verbletztstellung ginge das kaum. Das ist kein Fehler, sondern eine neue Funktion.
>
> **Und die Anglizismen?**
>
> Die meisten verschwinden so schnell, wie sie gekommen sind. Andere werden eingedeutscht, bis niemand sie mehr bemerkt: Wer denkt bei „Streik“ noch an Englisch? Interessanter finde ich Wörter wie „Handy“ oder „Beamer“, die es im Englischen in dieser Bedeutung gar nicht gibt.
>
> **Kritiker sprechen beim Kiezdeutsch von gebrochenem Deutsch.**
>
> Das ist es nicht. „Lassma Kino gehen“ folgt Regeln, die Sprecherinnen und Sprecher sehr genau beherrschen, und dieselben Jugendlichen schreiben im Deutschaufsatz ganz anders. Wer zwischen Varietäten wechseln kann, beherrscht mehr, nicht weniger.
>
> **Und das Gendern?**
>
> Da halte ich mich als Wissenschaftlerin mit Ratschlägen zurück. Beschreiben kann ich: Es gibt mehrere Formen, keine hat sich allgemein durchgesetzt, und die Regeln für Schulen und Behörden unterscheiden sich von Land zu Land. Wer schreibt, muss wissen, für wen.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**"Complaints about the decline of language are as old as writing"**

*Young people say "weil das ist so", companies advertise in English, authorities use gender-fair language or ban it. Is German going to the dogs? Questions for the linguist Anna Bergmann.*

**Ms Bergmann, many readers write to tell us that German is in decline. Are they right?**

They are right that it is changing. It always has. I wouldn't speak of decline. As early as the 17th century scholars complained that German was being corrupted by French, and in the 19th century Schopenhauer railed against the German of newspaper writers. The language survived both.

**But "weil" with the verb in second position is simply wrong.**

In written standard German, yes: there the verb goes at the end. In conversation, though, "weil" with main-clause order has long been widespread, and not by chance. People say: "He's definitely at home – because, the light's on." There I'm not giving the reason why he is at home but why I think so. With the verb at the end that would hardly work. It isn't a mistake but a new function.

**And Anglicisms?**

Most of them disappear as quickly as they came. Others are naturalized until nobody notices them any more: who thinks of English when they hear "Streik"? I find words like "Handy" (mobile phone) or "Beamer" (projector) more interesting, because they don't exist in English with that meaning at all.

**Critics call Kiezdeutsch broken German.**

It isn't. "Lassma Kino gehen" (let's go to the cinema) follows rules that its speakers master very precisely, and the same young people write quite differently in a German essay at school. Someone who can switch between varieties has command of more, not less.

**And gender-fair language?**

There, as a scholar, I hold back with advice. What I can describe is this: there are several forms, none has become generally accepted, and the rules for schools and authorities differ from one Land to the next. Anyone who writes has to know who they are writing for.

</details>

The interview is a good model of neutral talk about change: *Das ist kein Fehler, sondern eine neue Funktion*; *keine hat sich allgemein durchgesetzt*; *In der geschriebenen Standardsprache ja, …*. Notice also that the journalist's questions are phrased as challenges (*doch schlicht falsch*), and the linguist answers each by distinguishing: written vs spoken, standard vs variety, describing vs prescribing.

## Change in progress

### weil, obwohl, wobei + verb second

In speech, *weil, obwohl* and *wobei* are increasingly followed by main-clause order, usually after a short pause:

- *Ich nehm den Schirm mit – weil, die haben Regen angesagt.* (I'll take the umbrella, because they've forecast rain.)
- *Das Restaurant ist gut. Obwohl, teuer ist es schon.* (The restaurant's good. Mind you, it is expensive.)

Studies of spoken German find the verb-second variant mostly where the clause gives a reason for saying something or corrects what came before, as in the interview: *obwohl* + V2 nearly always takes back part of a previous statement, which *obwohl* with the verb at the end can't do. In writing, this order belongs only to transcribed speech, chats and deliberately informal texts. In the Goethe C2 Schreiben, use the verb at the end.

### wegen + dative, and the genitive in retreat

Standard written German uses *wegen* with the genitive (*wegen des Wetters*). The dative (*wegen dem Wetter*) is, in Duden's words, standard in speech but colloquial in writing; it is standard where a genitive can't be recognized (*wegen Geschäften*, plural without article). *wegen mir* is colloquial for *meinetwegen*. The genitive is retreating in speech more generally: *das Auto von meinem Bruder* instead of *das Auto meines Bruders*, and regionally *meinem Bruder sein Auto* (C1 26). Lesson 05 showed the other direction: in elevated writing the genitive object is alive and is a mark of style.

### Anglicisms and loan formations

German takes words from English in several ways:

| type | example | what happens |
|---|---|---|
| *Lehnwort* (loanword) | *der Streik, das Meeting, liken* | taken over, often adapted (*gestreikt, geliked*) |
| *Lehnbildung* (loan formation) | *Wolkenkratzer* (skyscraper), *Mausklick* | a foreign model built from German parts; loan translations are one kind |
| pseudo-Anglicism | *das Handy, der Beamer, das Public Viewing* | English-looking, but not used so in English |
| *Denglisch* | *Wir müssen das upgraden, damit es mehr performt.* | heavy mixing, usually meant critically |

*Denglisch* is an evaluative word: people use it for mixing they dislike. Verbs show how the grammar absorbs the loan; participles are often unstable (*gedownloadet* and *downgeloadet* both occur), and dictionaries list one form first without banning the other.

## Kiezdeutsch: a variety with rules

In multilingual neighbourhoods of German cities a way of speaking has developed among young people that the linguist Heike Wiese calls *Kiezdeutsch* (*Kiez* = neighbourhood, Berlin). In her book *Kiezdeutsch. Ein neuer Dialekt entsteht* (C. H. Beck, 2012) she argues that it is a new dialect of German, used by young people of many backgrounds, including those whose only language is German. Other researchers prefer the term **[[ethnolect]]** or *Multiethnolekt* (a way of speaking shaped by language contact in a multiethnic setting), and some reject the comparison with dialects; the book also set off a heated public debate.

Features she describes include:

- **Bare local phrases** after verbs of motion: *Gehst du heute auch Kino?* (standard *ins Kino*).
- **Contracted particles**: *lassma* (*lass uns mal*), *musstu* (*musst du*).
- **New word order** with an adverb and the subject before the verb: *Morgen ich geh Kino.*
- **Loanwords** from Turkish and Arabic used as particles: *lan* (roughly "man, dude"), *wallah* (I swear).
- ***so* before new information**, marking what follows as the point: *Meine Schwester arbeitet jetzt so bei einer Bank.*

Media parodies (*Isch mach disch Messer*) are stereotypes, not the variety itself. And speakers use these forms in particular situations, with friends; the same speakers switch to standard German at school or at a job interview. Switching between languages or varieties within one conversation, or even within one sentence, is **[[code-switching]]** (*das Code-Switching*): *Ich hab's ihm gesagt, aber er meinte so: "Whatever."*

Three more terms describe variation by speaker rather than place. A **[[sociolect]]** (*der Soziolekt*) is the speech of a social group (students, a profession, a class); an **[[idiolect]]** (*der Idiolekt*) is one person's own way of speaking, with its favourite words and habits; an ethnolect is shaped by the languages of a group of speakers with migrant backgrounds.

## Language on the internet

*Netzsprache* (internet language) is written but close to speech. Its typical features are:

- **Acronyms** (*das Akronym*): *lol, omg, imho*; German ones too (*mfg* = *mit freundlichen Grüßen*, *vlt* = *vielleicht*).
- **Inflectives**, bare verb stems used as action words: *\*grins\*, \*seufz\**, from comic strips.
- **Lower case** throughout and missing punctuation, which in a chat sounds relaxed rather than careless; a full stop after a short answer (*Ok.*) can sound cold.
- **Emoji** as punctuation and as a signal of tone: a smiley after a criticism softens it, like a modal particle in speech.

None of this "replaces" standard writing; it is another register, and switching register is the C2 skill (lesson 02).

## Gender-fair language: the forms and the positions

This is a politically charged topic. What follows describes the forms and the state of the rules as of November 2026, and the main arguments on each side; it takes no position.

| form | example | note |
|---|---|---|
| generic masculine (*das generische Maskulinum*) | *die Lehrer* (meaning all) | traditional; criticized as making women less visible |
| *Paarform* (both forms) | *Lehrerinnen und Lehrer* | long accepted in official texts; makes texts longer |
| participle or neutral noun | *die Lehrenden, die Lehrkräfte* | avoids the question; not every word has one |
| *Binnen-I* | *LehrerInnen* | from the 1980s; less used now |
| *Genderstern*, colon, underscore | *Lehrer\*innen, Lehrer:innen, Lehrer_innen* | include people who are neither men nor women; spoken with a glottal stop |

**The Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung** (Council for German Orthography), whose rules bind schools and public administration once the states approve them, has repeatedly said that everyone should be addressed in gender-fair language but that word-internal signs such as the star, colon and underscore are not part of the core of German orthography. In July 2023 it adopted a passage on such *Sonderzeichen im Wortinnern* for its rulebook; the updated Amtliches Regelwerk, in force for schools and administration since 1 July 2024, contains it. It describes the signs without making them part of correct spelling and says the development will be watched. (The grammatical problems are easy to see: *Ärzt\*innen* contains no readable masculine form.)

**The Länder** decide what that means in school. A CORRECTIV report of 18 September 2024 found that some states mark gender signs as errors and count them (for example Hesse and Saxony), while others mark them without counting them (Brandenburg); in March 2024 Bavaria banned them in its schools, universities and authorities. Rules are changing; check the current ones for the state where you write.

**The arguments.** Supporters say that the generic masculine makes people think first of men, citing psycholinguistic experiments, and that language should include everyone. Opponents say that the signs harm readability and grammar, that they are not used by most speakers, and that the generic masculine is a grammatical, not a biological, category. In German you report such a debate with distance: *Befürworter verweisen auf …; Kritiker halten dagegen, dass …; Umstritten ist vor allem …*

## Minority and regional languages

Germany has ratified the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages (ECRML). Under it, *Niederdeutsch* (Low German) is protected as a regional language (C1 26), and the following as minority languages:

- **Danish** in Schleswig-Holstein, spoken by the Danish minority in Südschleswig;
- **Upper and Lower Sorbian** (*das Sorbische*), West Slavic languages of Lusatia in Saxony and Brandenburg;
- **North Frisian** in Schleswig-Holstein and **Saterland Frisian** in Lower Saxony (*das Friesische*);
- **Romani**, the language of the German Sinti and Roma.

Bilingual place-name signs (*Bautzen / Budyšin*, *Niebüll / Naibel*) are the most visible sign of protection. A *Sprachgrenze* (language border) runs not only between states but through regions where *Sprachkontakt* (language contact) has shaped both languages for centuries.

## Purism and "decline": an old genre

*Der Sprachpurismus*, the effort to keep a language "pure" of foreign words, has a long history in German. In the 17th century the *Fruchtbringende Gesellschaft* (founded 1617) and writers such as Philipp von Zesen proposed German words for foreign ones; *Anschrift* (for *Adresse*) and *Leidenschaft* (for *Passion*) are usually credited to Zesen, while many of his proposals failed. Around 1800 Joachim Heinrich Campe did the same in his dictionaries. Some coinages stayed; the foreign words often stayed too, with a different shade of meaning. Today associations campaign against Anglicisms, and others defend them; the argument itself is the old one.

The *Sprachverfall* (decline) claim follows a pattern you can recognize: each generation thinks the language was correct when it learned it. Linguists prefer neutral words: *Sprachwandel, Sprachveränderung, Sprachentwicklung*. *Sprachkritik* covers both the reflection on language use (the critique of political phrases, for example) and complaints about change.

## The words of this lesson

- *das Jugendwort* is any word typical of young people, and *das Jugendwort des Jahres* the one chosen each year by a publisher's poll (2025: *das crazy*; 2026: *Ragebait*). Such words are often already old-fashioned when they win.
- *die Wortneubildung* is a newly formed word (wider than *der Neologismus*, B2, which may also be a new meaning); *die Sprachmischung* is mixing of languages.
- *gendergerecht* is a common alternative to *geschlechtergerecht* (earlier); *puristisch* describes a purist attitude; *die Sprachreinheit* is the purists' ideal.
- *das Sprachbewusstsein* is awareness of language: how consciously speakers notice and judge it.

## Common mistakes

- Writing *weil* + verb second in an exam essay. It is normal in speech, but not in standard written German.
- Calling Kiezdeutsch "bad German" in a neutral text. Describe it: *eine Varietät, die …*, *ein Multiethnolekt*.
- Presenting your opinion on gender-fair language as a fact in a mediation or summary. Report positions with *Befürworter, Kritiker, umstritten*.
- Using pseudo-Anglicisms in English: a *Handy* is a mobile (phone) or cell phone, a *Beamer* a projector.
- Saying "the Rat banned the Genderstern". It said the signs are not part of the core orthography; bans and grading are decided by the Länder.
- False precision about frequency (*Jeder dritte Jugendliche sagt …*) without a source.

## Key points

- Change in progress: *weil/obwohl/wobei* + V2 in speech (with new functions), *wegen* + dative, the genitive retreating in speech, the *am*-Progressiv.
- Loans: *Lehnwort, Lehnbildung*, pseudo-Anglicisms (*Handy*), *Denglisch* (evaluative).
- Kiezdeutsch (Wiese 2012) and *Multiethnolekt*: a variety with its own rules; code-switching between varieties is a skill. Sociolect, idiolect, ethnolect: variation by speaker.
- *Netzsprache*: acronyms, inflectives, emoji as tone markers; a register of its own.
- Gender-fair forms: generic masculine, Paarform, participles, Binnen-I, star/colon/underscore. The Rat (2023/2024): not core orthography; the Länder set school rules (check current ones).
- ECRML in Germany: Low German; Danish, Sorbian, North and Saterland Frisian, Romani.
- Complaints about decline and purism are an old genre; describe change in neutral words.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Synthesizing sources: mediation and summary at C2
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

German C1 lesson 29 taught mediation from one source: you read a text and passed its content on to someone else, in the register that person needs. At C2 the CEFR asks for more: you summarize information from *several* sources, reconstruct their arguments and present them coherently, and you convey finer shades of meaning, including tone and what a source only implies. That is what a policy adviser, a journalist, a translator, an academic and anyone writing a briefing does every day.

This lesson uses three short sources on the same question that disagree with each other: a study, a position paper by an interest group and a newspaper commentary. You will learn to write a neutral **[[synopsis]]** (*die Synopse*), a side-by-side summary of positions; to report each source's stance precisely; to keep its hedges and its tone; to notice what it leaves out; and to explain a technical point to a lay person and between two people who disagree. Throughout, you add no view of your own.

The theme is the energy transition. Prices, laws and targets in this field change quickly; the sources below are invented, and the few facts in the lesson are dated "as of November 2026".

## Three sources

The question: when many households have solar panels, who should pay for the electricity grid? Background: in Germany, the price of electricity includes *Netzentgelte*, fees for using the grid, which are charged mostly per kilowatt-hour. A household that produces much of its own electricity with *Photovoltaik* (solar power) buys fewer kilowatt-hours and so pays less towards the grid, although it still uses the grid when the sun doesn't shine.

> **Quelle A: Kurzfassung einer Studie (Forschungsinstitut)**
>
> Die Simulation legt nahe, dass die Netzentgelte für Haushalte ohne eigene Solaranlage bis 2035 deutlich steigen könnten, sofern die Entgelte weiterhin überwiegend nach verbrauchten Kilowattstunden berechnet werden. Unter den getroffenen Annahmen trügen Haushalte mit Photovoltaik und Stromspeicher einen geringeren Anteil an den Netzkosten, obwohl sie das Netz in sonnenarmen Monaten in ähnlichem Umfang beanspruchen. Ein höherer Grundpreis würde diese Verschiebung verringern, belastete aber Haushalte mit niedrigem Verbrauch überproportional. Die Ergebnisse hängen stark von der künftigen Speicherkapazität ab und sind daher mit Vorsicht zu interpretieren.
>
> **Quelle B: Positionspapier eines Solarverbands**
>
> Wer heute in eine Solaranlage investiert, entlastet das Netz und treibt die Dekarbonisierung voran. Eine zusätzliche Netzgebühr für Eigenverbrauch wäre nichts anderes als eine Strafgebühr für Engagement. Statt neue Bürokratiemonster zu schaffen, müssen Netzbetreiber endlich digitalisieren und den Netzausbau beschleunigen. Wir fordern eine verlässliche Einspeisevergütung und eine Abschaffung aller Hemmnisse für Speicher. Nur so bleibt die Akzeptanz der Energiewende erhalten.
>
> **Quelle C: Kommentar (Tageszeitung)**
>
> Man kann es den Hausbesitzern nicht verdenken: Wer Sonne vom eigenen Dach erntet, freut sich über jede Kilowattstunde, die er nicht kaufen muss. Nur zahlt das Netz, über das er im Januar trotzdem Strom bezieht, am Ende jemand anderes – gern der Mieter im dritten Stock. Dass ausgerechnet die Branche, die vom Ausbau lebt, jede Debatte über eine faire Verteilung der Netzkosten als „Strafgebühr“ abtut, ist bemerkenswert. Dass die Politik sich vor dieser Debatte drückt, ist es allerdings auch. Wer die Energiewende will, wird über die Rechnung reden müssen.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Source A: summary of a study (research institute)**

The simulation suggests that grid fees for households without their own solar installation could rise considerably by 2035, provided that fees continue to be calculated mainly per kilowatt-hour consumed. Under the assumptions made, households with photovoltaics and battery storage would bear a smaller share of grid costs, although they use the grid to a similar extent in months with little sun. A higher standing charge would reduce this shift but would place a disproportionate burden on households with low consumption. The results depend heavily on future storage capacity and should therefore be interpreted with caution.

**Source B: position paper of a solar industry association**

Anyone who invests in a solar installation today relieves the grid and drives decarbonization forward. An additional grid fee for self-consumption would be nothing other than a penalty fee for commitment. Instead of creating new bureaucratic monsters, grid operators must finally digitalize and speed up grid expansion. We demand a reliable feed-in tariff and the removal of all obstacles to storage. Only in this way will public acceptance of the energy transition be preserved.

**Source C: commentary (daily newspaper)**

You can't blame the homeowners: anyone who harvests sunshine from their own roof is glad of every kilowatt-hour they don't have to buy. Only, the grid from which they still draw electricity in January is paid for in the end by someone else, quite possibly the tenant on the third floor. That the very industry that lives off the expansion dismisses any debate about a fair distribution of grid costs as a "penalty fee" is remarkable. That politicians are dodging this debate is remarkable too, mind you. Anyone who wants the energy transition will have to talk about the bill.

</details>

## Reading the sources as a mediator

Before you summarize, note for each source three things: its claim, its status (how certain, how interested) and its tone.

| | claim | status and hedging | tone and loaded words |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | per-kWh fees shift grid costs to households without PV; a higher standing charge would reduce the shift but hit low consumers | a model: *legt nahe, könnten, unter den getroffenen Annahmen, mit Vorsicht zu interpretieren*; KII *trügen, belastete* = hypothetical | neutral, technical |
| B | PV relieves the grid; no extra fee; grid operators should digitalize; demands feed-in tariff and fewer obstacles | an interest group's demands; no figures | polemical: *Strafgebühr, Bürokratiemonster, endlich*; *nur so* |
| C | PV owners still use the grid in winter, others pay; both industry and politics avoid the debate | opinion | ironic and pointed: *Man kann es … nicht verdenken*, *gern der Mieter*, *ausgerechnet*, *bemerkenswert* (twice) |

Three observations matter for the summary:

1. **A and B contradict each other on a fact** (does PV relieve the grid?), but not exactly: A speaks of winter months and cost shares; B of *entlasten* in general. A mediator shows this difference rather than declaring a winner.
2. **B leaves something out.** It doesn't mention who pays if PV owners pay less. Saying what a source doesn't address is legitimate (*Auf die Frage, wer …, geht das Papier nicht ein*), as long as you don't speculate why.
3. **C's irony must survive.** *Man kann es den Hausbesitzern nicht verdenken* sounds like sympathy but prepares a criticism. *bemerkenswert* is understatement for "astonishing, objectionable". Summarizing C as "C supports homeowners" would be wrong.

## Writing the synopsis

A **[[synopsis]]** sets out the positions side by side, usually by question rather than by source. It is not the same as a *Zusammenfassung* (a summary of one text), an *Abstract* (the author's own summary of a paper) or an *Exzerpt* (notes from a text, lesson 13). For three sources, two structures work:

- **by source**: A, then B, then C, then a short *Zusammenschau* (overall view) of where they agree and differ. Good for short texts and lay readers.
- **by question**: first the facts in dispute, then the proposals, then the arguments about fairness, each with all three sources. Good for decision-makers. This is the *Gegenüberstellung* (juxtaposition) in its strict form.

Here is a synopsis by question, about 170 words:

> *Umstritten ist zunächst, ob Haushalte mit Solaranlage das Netz entlasten. Der Solarverband bejaht dies uneingeschränkt. Die Studie kommt zu einem differenzierteren Ergebnis: In sonnenarmen Monaten beanspruchten solche Haushalte das Netz in ähnlichem Umfang wie andere, trügen aber bei verbrauchsabhängigen Entgelten einen geringeren Anteil an den Kosten. Sie weist allerdings darauf hin, dass ihre Ergebnisse stark von der künftigen Speicherkapazität abhängen.*
>
> *Unterschiedlich fallen auch die Vorschläge aus. Während die Studie einen höheren Grundpreis als mögliche, aber für Geringverbraucher nachteilige Lösung prüft, lehnt der Verband jede zusätzliche Gebühr ab, die er als „Strafgebühr“ bezeichnet, und fordert stattdessen eine schnellere Digitalisierung der Netze sowie eine verlässliche Einspeisevergütung. Auf die Frage, wer die Netzkosten andernfalls trägt, geht das Papier nicht ein.*
>
> *Der Kommentar stellt genau diese Frage in den Mittelpunkt: Den Hausbesitzern sei ihr Verhalten nicht vorzuwerfen, die Kosten trügen aber andere, etwa Mieter. Kritisch sieht der Kommentator sowohl die Haltung der Branche als auch die Zurückhaltung der Politik.*

What makes this C2:

- **Stance is reported precisely**: *bejaht uneingeschränkt* (B), *kommt zu einem differenzierteren Ergebnis* (A), *prüft … als mögliche Lösung* (A doesn't recommend), *lehnt ab, fordert* (B), *sieht kritisch* (C).
- **Hedges survive**: the study's *könnten* and its caution appear (*weist darauf hin, dass …*); the synopsis doesn't say "the study proves".
- **Loaded words are quoted, not adopted**: *die er als „Strafgebühr“ bezeichnet*. Writing *die Strafgebühr* without quotation marks would take B's side.
- **Konjunktiv I and II for reported content**: *beanspruchten, trügen* (KII replacing KI forms that look like the indicative), *sei … vorzuwerfen* (KI).
- **Irony is translated into stance**: C's mock sympathy becomes *Den Hausbesitzern sei ihr Verhalten nicht vorzuwerfen, …*: the concession, then the point.
- **Nothing is added**: no *meines Erachtens*, no *zu Recht*, no *leider*. Even *bemerkenswerterweise* would be a judgement.

### Words for weighting and attributing

| function | phrases |
|---|---|
| attribute | *der Studie zufolge* (dative, usually after the noun), *laut Verband*, *nach Angaben des Instituts*, *wie der Kommentator schreibt* |
| contrast | *Während X betont, …, gibt Y zu bedenken, dass …*; *X hingegen …*; *Anders als A …* |
| agreement | *In einem Punkt stimmen alle drei überein: …*; *Ähnlich argumentiert …* |
| weighting | *Im Mittelpunkt steht …*; *Nur am Rande erwähnt …*; *Ausführlich begründet A …, B dagegen nennt keine Zahlen.* |
| reporting omissions | *Offen lässt der Text, …*; *Nicht berücksichtigt wird …*; *Auf … geht das Papier nicht ein.* |
| reporting tone | *spöttisch merkt der Kommentator an, …*; *in polemischem Ton*; *in zurückhaltender Formulierung* |

*zufolge* follows its noun and takes the dative (*der Studie zufolge*); *laut* takes the genitive or, without an article, often the dative or no visible case (*laut Verband*). *nach Angaben* is the most neutral and fits figures.

## Oral mediation: explaining to a lay person

C2 mediation is not only written. Imagine your neighbour, who doesn't follow energy politics, asks why her electricity bill shows *Netzentgelte* and whether she should be angry at people with solar roofs. You explain the point, not the sources:

> *Also, das Netzentgelt ist sozusagen die Miete für die Stromleitungen. Die zahlt jeder mit, der Strom aus dem Netz bezieht, und zwar bisher vor allem pro Kilowattstunde. Wer viel Strom selbst auf dem Dach erzeugt, kauft weniger und zahlt deshalb auch weniger für die Leitungen – obwohl er sie im Winter genauso braucht. Eine Studie meint, dass dadurch für alle anderen die Kosten steigen könnten. Die Solarbranche sieht das anders und sagt, die Anlagen entlasten das Netz. Wer recht hat, hängt unter anderem davon ab, wie viele Stromspeicher es in Zukunft gibt. Ob man sich ärgern sollte – na ja, das müssen Sie selbst entscheiden.*

Notice: an image (*Miete für die Stromleitungen*), *sozusagen* to mark it as an image, colloquial *Also* and *na ja*, the indicative in reported speech where speech allows it (*die Anlagen entlasten das Netz*), and a polite refusal to decide for her. For a technical term, give a paraphrase rather than a definition: *Abregelung* (curtailment) is *wenn man Windräder abschaltet, weil das Netz den Strom gerade nicht aufnehmen kann*.

## Mediating between two people who disagree

At a residents' meeting, Herr Kaya (who has a solar roof) and Frau Brandt (a tenant) argue. Your role is to make each understand the other, not to judge:

> **Kaya:** Ich hab zwanzigtausend Euro investiert, damit wir vom Gas wegkommen, und jetzt soll ich auch noch draufzahlen?
>
> **Brandt:** Und ich soll Ihre Leitungen bezahlen, nur weil ich kein Dach habe?
>
> **Sie:** Darf ich kurz zusammenfassen, wie ich Sie beide verstehe? Herr Kaya, Ihnen geht es darum, dass Ihre Investition anerkannt wird und sich nicht nachträglich verteuert. Frau Brandt, Sie haben den Eindruck, dass Sie Kosten tragen, die andere verursachen. Eigentlich streiten Sie beide gar nicht darüber, ob Solaranlagen gut sind, sondern darüber, wie die Netzkosten verteilt werden sollen. Wäre das ein Punkt, über den man an einem Abend sprechen könnte?

The moves: reformulate each position in a fairer form than the speaker's (*draufzahlen* becomes *nachträglich verteuert*; *Ihre Leitungen* becomes *Kosten, die andere verursachen*), name the shared ground, and turn a quarrel into a question. Avoid *Sie haben beide recht* (empty) and *Eigentlich hat Frau Brandt recht* (a verdict).

## Facts in the background (as of November 2026)

- Germany shut down its last three nuclear power stations on 15 April 2023 (*der Atomausstieg*; *die Kernkraft* is the technical word, *die Atomkraft* the everyday one).
- The coal phase-out law (Kohleverstromungsbeendigungsgesetz, 2020) sets the end of coal-fired power at 2038 at the latest; earlier dates have been agreed for some regions.
- How grid fees are calculated is under review, and rules for feed-in tariffs (*die Einspeisevergütung*) for new small installations have changed several times. Check current figures before you quote any.

## The words of this lesson

- **Generation and storage**: *die Solaranlage* (general, also solar thermal), *die Photovoltaik* (electricity from sunlight; also spelled *Fotovoltaik*), *die Windkraftanlage* (the technical word for *das Windrad*), *der Windpark*, *das Gaskraftwerk*, *der Stromspeicher*, *die Speicherkapazität*, *der Wasserstoff* and *der Elektrolyseur* (the device that splits water into hydrogen and oxygen).
- **Grid and market**: *der Netzbetreiber*, *das Netzentgelt*, *die Stromtrasse* (a long-distance power line, often controversial), *die Grundlast* (base load), *der Strommix*, *einspeisen* (to feed into the grid), *die Abregelung* (curtailment).
- **Policy**: *die Dekarbonisierung* and *dekarbonisieren*, *der Emissionshandel* and *das Emissionszertifikat*, *die Sektorkopplung* (linking electricity, heat and transport), *die Energieeffizienz* and *energieeffizient*, *die Akzeptanz* (public acceptance).
- **Mediation**: *die Synopse*, *die Synthese* and *synthetisieren*, *die Gegenüberstellung* and *gegenüberstellen*, *die Zusammenschau*, *das Positionspapier*.

## Common mistakes

- Adopting a source's loaded word: *die Strafgebühr* instead of *eine zusätzliche Gebühr, die der Verband als „Strafgebühr“ bezeichnet*.
- Turning a hedge into a fact: *Die Studie beweist, dass …* when it says *legt nahe*. False precision is a C2 mistake: don't round "could rise considerably" into a percentage.
- Missing irony: *Man kann es den Hausbesitzern nicht verdenken* is the start of a criticism.
- Summarizing source by source without saying where they meet. A synopsis needs at least one sentence of *Zusammenschau*.
- Letting your view slip in through adverbs: *zu Recht, leider, bezeichnenderweise, immerhin*.
- *zufolge* before the noun: *zufolge der Studie* (with the genitive) is not wrong, but Duden gives it only as less common, Swiss and legal usage; write *der Studie zufolge*.

## Key points

- C2 mediation synthesizes several sources, keeps their stance, hedges and tone, notes what they leave out and adds nothing.
- A synopsis sets positions side by side, by source or by question, and ends with a *Zusammenschau*.
- Report stance precisely (*bejaht, räumt ein, lehnt ab, prüft, gibt zu bedenken*), quote loaded words, use KI/KII and *zufolge, laut, nach Angaben*.
- Explaining to a lay person: an image, a paraphrase, the indicative of speech, no verdict. Between two people: reformulate fairly, name the shared ground, turn a quarrel into a question.
- Energy facts change fast; date them.
