lessons.title: The Goethe-Zertifikat C2: GDS and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last core lesson of German C2, and of the whole German series. It says in plain words what C2 means, describes the exam at this level, the Goethe-Zertifikat C2: Großes Deutsches Sprachdiplom (GDS), with a strategy for each part and an original practice task, reviews the course with a table that points back to the lessons, and ends with how to keep your German at this level.

You don't need a certificate to have reached C2. But the *Großes Deutsches Sprachdiplom* is the most demanding general German exam the Goethe-Institut offers, and some employers, universities and authorities ask for it. Requirements, fees and rules change; check with the institution that asks for the certificate and with the exam centre.

## What C2 means

C2 is the top of the six CEFR levels, the upper of the two "proficient user" levels. In plain words, at C2 you:

- understand practically everything you hear or read, including long and stylistically complex texts, what they imply and how they are meant;
- summarize information from several spoken and written sources and present the arguments coherently in your own words;
- express yourself spontaneously, fluently and precisely, with fine shades of meaning, even in complex situations;
- choose the register that fits the reader and purpose, and shift it on purpose.

"C2" doesn't mean "like a native speaker". Many native speakers can't write a neutral synopsis of three sources or explain the difference between *scheinbar* and *anscheinend*. What C2 adds over C1 is precision, range and control: the right near-synonym (01), the register shift as a tool (02), the Konjunktiv formula (03), the hedge that fits (04), the reformulation that keeps the meaning (06), and reading older and literary texts (26, 27).

## The Goethe-Zertifikat C2: GDS

The facts below come from the Modellsatz ("Stand März 2026"), the *Durchführungsbestimmungen* (implementing regulations, "Stand: 1. September 2025", for exams after 1 September 2025) and the exam pages of goethe.de, all read in November 2026.

The exam has four modules, which can be taken separately or in combination. According to the Goethe-Institut's exam page, four module certificates together are equivalent to a full certificate. The Goethe-Institut recommends it for candidates aged 18 and over, and estimates that reaching C2 takes at least 1,000 teaching units of 45 minutes.

| module | time | parts and items | what you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lesen | 80 minutes | 4 parts, 30 items | Teil 1 (25 min): a commentary, 10 multiple-choice items with 4 options. Teil 2 (20 min): an article in sections; statements a–h to match to six sections (11–16), two statements fit none. Teil 3 (25 min): a reportage with gaps; seven paragraphs a–g for six gaps (17–22), one fits none. Teil 4 (10 min): four short ads and eight statements (23–30); several statements can fit the same ad. |
| Hören | about 35 minutes | 3 parts, 30 items | Teil 1 (about 12 min): five radio excerpts, three Ja/Nein statements each, heard once. Teil 2 (about 5 min): a conversation between two people; for five opinions, decide whether they come from Person 1, Person 2 or both (*beide*); heard once. Teil 3 (about 18 min): an expert interview, 10 multiple-choice items with 3 options, heard twice. |
| Schreiben | 80 minutes | 2 parts | Teil 1 (20 min): revise marked passages of a short presentation (*Kurzreferat*) using given words, which may not be changed; 10 items. Teil 2 (60 min): about 350 words on one of four topics: two general topics (in the Modellsatz a reader's letter and an e-mail) and two on the books of the *Literaturliste*. |
| Sprechen | about 15 minutes, individual | 2 parts, 15 min preparation for both | Teil 1, *Produktion* (about 10 min): a talk of about 5 minutes on a topic, then questions. Teil 2, *Interaktion* (about 5 min): a discussion with an examiner in which you defend a position. |

A few details that matter on the day:

- **Lesen, Teil 2**: the instruction says *Sieben der folgenden Aussagen entsprechen dem Inhalt des Artikels*. The seventh is the example (*Beispiel 0*), which is printed separately; of the eight lettered statements, six fit and two don't.
- **Lesen and Hören**: you mark answers on the task sheets first and transfer them to the answer sheet at the end. For Hören there are three minutes; for Lesen the regulations plan about five minutes. Points are entered on the answer sheet, so transfer every answer.
- **The written modules** together take about 195 minutes without breaks; the regulations require breaks of at least 15 minutes between them. The recommended order is Lesen, Hören, Schreiben; Sprechen usually comes after the written modules.
- **Sprechen** is an individual exam with two examiners: one leads the conversation, the other is your partner in the discussion. Your short introduction at the start isn't scored. You may use the notes you made during preparation.
- **The Literaturliste** names the books for the literature topics of the current calendar year and is published online; the literature tasks are developed with the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. If you want to choose a literature topic, read the books on the current list, and check it again before the exam: it changes.

### Points and grades

Each module is scored out of 100 points and passed with at least 60. In Lesen and Hören, each item is right or wrong, and the parts are weighted: on the Modellsatz answer sheet, Lesen Teil 1 counts ×4 and Teile 2–4 ×3; Hören Teil 1 ×2, Teil 2 ×4, Teil 3 ×5.

In Schreiben, Teil 1 gives 2, 1 or 0 points per item (maximum 20); Teil 2 is rated on five criteria (*Aufgabenerfüllung, Textaufbau, Kohärenz, Wortschatz, Strukturen*), 0–4 points each, multiplied by four (maximum 80). Two raters mark independently and the mean counts. In Sprechen, each part is rated on five criteria (*Erfüllung der Aufgabenstellung, Kohärenz, Wortschatz, Strukturen, Aussprache und Intonation*), 0–4 points each; the total (maximum 40) is multiplied by 2.5, and the mean of the two examiners counts.

| points | grade |
|---|---|
| 90–100 | sehr gut |
| 80–89 | gut |
| 70–79 | befriedigend |
| 60–69 | ausreichend |
| 0–59 | nicht bestanden |

Modules can be repeated as often as the exam centre's schedule allows. The free official materials are on goethe.de: the [Modellsatz (PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/pro/relaunch/prf/materialien/C2/c2_modellsatz.pdf) with answers, transcripts and marking criteria, and the practice page for the exam with a second practice test and audio. Do the whole Modellsatz once under exam conditions about four weeks before the exam; the strategies below tell you what to practise in between.

## Strategies

### Lesen

| part | what helps | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| Teil 1: commentary, 4 options | The items test implicit meaning and attitude. The right option paraphrases; an option that repeats the text's words often distorts them. Watch irony, concession (*zwar … aber*) and modal words (*schwerlich, mitunter*). | 04, 11, 14, 19 |
| Teil 2: article, statements to sections | Read the statements first, mark their key idea, then skim each section for it. Two statements fit nowhere: often they mention a topic of the text but claim something it doesn't say. | 07, 13 |
| Teil 3: reportage, paragraphs into gaps | Paragraphs fit by cohesion: pronouns, *dies, Letzteres*, connectors, time sequence, a name introduced before it is used. Cross out each paragraph as you use it. | 07, 08, 14 |
| Teil 4: ads, statements to ads | Ten minutes for eight items: scan, don't read. Several statements can fit one ad, so don't rule an ad out because you've used it. | 01, 06 |

### Hören

| part | what helps | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| Teil 1: radio excerpts, Ja/Nein, once | Statements paraphrase and often target attitude: *Die Sprecherin hält … für übertrieben.* Listen for evaluating words, particles and stress. KI and KII look-alikes (*hätte/hatte, wäre/war*) decide what really happened. | 03, 04, 16 |
| Teil 2: two people, Person 1 / Person 2 / beide, once | Keep two columns. *beide* needs agreement, not just the same topic: *Da gebe ich dir recht* or a parallel opinion. A concession (*Das mag sein, aber …*) is not agreement. | 11, 12 |
| Teil 3: expert interview, 3 options, twice | First hearing: the structure and the expert's position; second: the details. Experts hedge (*gewisse Hinweise, nach derzeitigem Stand*); an option that sounds more certain than the expert is usually wrong. | 04, 13, 22, 24 |

### Schreiben

- **Teil 1, Umformulierung.** For each marked passage, identify the transformation the given word forces (clause → nominal phrase, connector → preposition, modal verb → *sich lassen* or *es gilt*, active → passive substitute). Then check that the rest of the sentence still fits: case after a new preposition, word order after a new connector, nothing lost (*seit Jahren*). Lesson 06 and the reference sheet on reformulation have every type; the practice task below shows six.
- **Teil 2.** Cover all three content points of the task, in a structure the reader can follow (Textaufbau, Kohärenz). For a Leserbrief, refer to the article and take a position (15); for a Buchbesprechung, summarize briefly, then evaluate with reasons and examples, not adjectives (15). Use register on purpose, and save ten minutes to check verb positions, endings, commas (§ 73, § 72) and your own typical mistakes.

### Sprechen

- **Teil 1, talk.** In the 15 minutes' preparation, choose the topic on which you have examples, and note a structure: an opening, three points with an example each, a conclusion. Speak from key words. Answer questions by first acknowledging them (*Das ist eine berechtigte Frage …*), then answering (12).
- **Teil 2, discussion.** You argue a position, weigh the other side and try to persuade. Take up the examiner's arguments, concede part of them and limit the concession (*Das ist sicher richtig, nur …*), and bring a new argument rather than repeating the old one (11, 12).
- **Aussprache und Intonation** is a criterion: stress carries meaning in German (*'umfahren* vs *um'fahren*, 10; stressed particles, 16).

## Practice: a Kurzreferat to revise

This is an original practice task of the Schreiben Teil 1 type. Rewrite each marked passage using the word given, without changing that word and without changing the meaning.

> **Öffentliche Bibliotheken im Wandel**
>
> Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, in meinem Kurzreferat geht es um die Frage, welche Rolle öffentliche Bibliotheken heute noch spielen. **(1) Obwohl die Ausleihzahlen gedruckter Bücher seit Jahren sinken,** verzeichnen viele Bibliotheken mehr Besucher als früher. Wie lässt sich das erklären?
>
> Zunächst haben sich die Bibliotheken neu erfunden. **(2) Man kann dort heute Nähmaschinen und 3D-Drucker ausleihen.** Außerdem gibt es Sprachcafés und Lesungen. Viele Städte haben ihre Bibliotheken umgebaut, **(3) damit sie als Treffpunkt dienen können.** Fachleute sprechen von einem „dritten Ort“ zwischen Wohnung und Arbeitsplatz.
>
> Zweitens profitieren besonders Menschen von diesem Angebot, **(4) die zu Hause keinen ruhigen Arbeitsplatz haben.** Schülerinnen und Schüler etwa nutzen die Lesesäle zur Prüfungsvorbereitung.
>
> Allerdings ist die Finanzierung vielerorts unsicher. **(5) Wenn die Kommunen sparen müssen,** wird häufig zuerst bei den Bibliotheken gekürzt. **(6) Es ist deshalb wichtig, dass man den gesellschaftlichen Wert dieser Einrichtungen sichtbar macht.**

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Public libraries in transition**

Ladies and gentlemen, my short presentation is about the question of what role public libraries still play today. (1) Although loans of printed books have been falling for years, many libraries record more visitors than before. How can this be explained?

First, libraries have reinvented themselves. (2) Today you can borrow sewing machines and 3D printers there. There are also language cafés and readings. Many towns have rebuilt their libraries (3) so that they can serve as meeting places. Experts speak of a "third place" between home and work.

Second, the people who benefit most from this offer are those (4) who don't have a quiet place to work at home. School students, for example, use the reading rooms to prepare for exams.

However, funding is uncertain in many places. (5) When local authorities have to save money, libraries are often the first to be cut. (6) It is therefore important to make the social value of these institutions visible.

</details>

| | given word | a correct rewriting | transformation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | *trotz* | *Trotz seit Jahren sinkender Ausleihzahlen gedruckter Bücher* | concessive clause → preposition + participle attribute |
| 2 | *lassen* | *Dort lassen sich heute Nähmaschinen und 3D-Drucker ausleihen.* | modal verb + *man* → *sich lassen* |
| 3 | *Ziel* | *mit dem Ziel, dass sie als Treffpunkt dienen (können)* | purpose clause → noun + clause |
| 4 | *verfügen* | *die zu Hause über keinen ruhigen Arbeitsplatz verfügen* | simple verb → verb with fixed preposition, higher register |
| 5 | *Sparzwang* | *Stehen die Kommunen unter Sparzwang,* / *Wenn die Kommunen unter Sparzwang stehen,* | verb → noun in a fixed phrase |
| 6 | *gilt* | *Es gilt deshalb, den gesellschaftlichen Wert dieser Einrichtungen sichtbar zu machen.* | *es ist wichtig, dass man* → *es gilt zu* |

Typical lost points: in (1), dropping *seit Jahren* (the meaning changes) or writing *trotz den …* in a written exam (the genitive is expected); in (2), keeping *man* (*Man lässt sich dort … ausleihen* is not a rewording of *man kann*); in (6), keeping *man* after *es gilt*.

## Exam language

The words of this lesson come from instructions, descriptions of the exam and marking criteria.

- *das Sprachdiplom* (as in *Großes Deutsches Sprachdiplom*), *die Literaturliste*, *die Einzelprüfung* (an exam taken alone), *das Aufgabenblatt* (task sheet, where you first mark answers), *die Bestehensgrenze* (pass mark: *Die Bestehensgrenze liegt bei 60 Punkten*), *der Hörbeitrag* (an item of audio, a radio piece).
- For speaking: *die Interaktion* (the discussion part), *die Intonation*, *die Gegenposition* (the opposing position you argue against), *die Diskussionsführung* (how you conduct a discussion), *die Spontaneität*.
- For quality, the words of descriptors and examiners' comments: *die Sprachbeherrschung* (command of the language), *die Sprachgewandtheit* and *sprachgewandt* (verbal skill, eloquence), *die Ausdruckskraft* (expressiveness), *die Ausdrucksvielfalt* (range of expression), *die Treffsicherheit* and *treffsicher* (accuracy in hitting the right word), *die Stilsicherheit* and *stilsicher* (sure sense of style), *die Nuancierung* and *nuancenreich* (shading, rich in nuance), *fehlerfrei* (error-free), *nahezu* (almost; no Duden label, but typical of written German: *nahezu fehlerfrei*).

Note how examiners hedge: *nahezu fehlerfrei* means a few slips are allowed; *weitgehend* (largely) allows more. "Error-free" is not the C2 standard; precision and appropriateness are.

## Course review: where to look again

| topic | lessons |
|---|---|
| Near-synonyms and Wortfelder; register shift; Konjunktiv formulas; modality beyond modal verbs; genitive objects | 01–05 |
| Umformulierung in both directions; complex periods; Mittelfeld and Vorfeld; word formation; verb prefixes | 06–10 |
| Argument and fallacies; rhetoric and the C2 Sprechen tasks; academic German; journalism; writing at C2 | 11–15 |
| Idioms; proverbs and geflügelte Worte; collocations; humour and irony; metaphor | 16–20 |
| Legal, medical, financial, scientific and administrative German | 21–25 |
| Older German; literary prose; language change; mediation and synthesis | 26–29 |

A useful method: after each Modellsatz part, list your mistakes and sort them into vocabulary, grammar, strategy and time. Grammar and vocabulary mistakes send you back to the table above; strategy mistakes to this lesson; time mistakes to timed practice.

## After C2

C2 is the end of the scale, not of learning. At this level progress comes from reading and listening widely and from noticing.

- **Read** in different registers every week: a quality newspaper's Feuilleton and its commentary pages, a specialist magazine in your field, and literature. Public-domain texts from lessons 26–27 and 30h1–30h2 are free online; the course reading list suggests podcasts, newspapers and books to go on with.
- **Check** words and constructions in the DWDS (free; the *Wortprofil* shows typical collocations) and in Duden online. When two words seem interchangeable, compare their corpus examples (01).
- **Collect** what surprises you: an unusual collocation, a particle you wouldn't have used, a sentence you would have built differently. Rewrite it in another register (02).
- **Write and speak** for real readers and listeners: letters to the editor, reviews, comments, conversations. Ask native speakers not "Is this correct?" but "Would you say it like that?"

## Common mistakes

- Preparing the Modellsatz topics. The exam has new topics each time; practise the task types.
- In Lesen Teil 4, ruling out an ad because it already has a statement. Several statements can fit the same ad.
- In Hören Teil 2, choosing *beide* because both speakers talk about the same thing. *beide* means they share the opinion.
- In Schreiben Teil 1, changing the given word (*Ziele* for *Ziel*, *galt* for *gilt*) or losing part of the meaning.
- In Schreiben Teil 2, forgetting one of the three content points, or reviewing a book that isn't on the current Literaturliste.
- In Sprechen Teil 2, agreeing too soon. The task is to defend a position and weigh the other side.
- Not transferring answers in Lesen and Hören.

## Key points

- Goethe-Zertifikat C2: GDS, four modules, separately or together: Lesen 80 min (4 parts, 30 items), Hören about 35 min (3 parts, 30 items), Schreiben 80 min (Umformulierung 20 min; about 350 words on one of four topics, 60 min), Sprechen about 15 min, individual, 15 min preparation (talk about 5 min with questions; discussion about 5 min).
- 100 points per module, pass at 60; sehr gut 90, gut 80, befriedigend 70, ausreichend 60. Two raters in Schreiben and Sprechen; the mean counts.
- Lesen Teil 2: of eight statements, six fit; the "seventh" in the instruction is the example. Teil 4: several statements per ad.
- Hören: Ja/Nein once; Person 1 / Person 2 / beide once; interview twice.
- Schreiben Teil 1: find the transformation the given word forces, keep every part of the meaning, never change the given word.
- After C2: read widely, check with DWDS and Duden, rewrite in other registers, and ask native speakers how they would say it.

lessons.title: Thomas Mann, Tonio Kröger: irony and the artist
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Thomas Mann (1875–1955) is the German novelist whose sentences C2 learners most often meet in quotations, and the one they most often find hard: long, balanced, ironic, full of qualifications. Since 1 January 2026 his works are in the public domain in the EU (70 years after his death), so they can now be quoted freely.

*Tonio Kröger*, published in 1903, two years after *Buddenbrooks*, is a novella and the best way in. It is about a writer who belongs neither to the world of ordinary, healthy, unreflecting people (*die Bürger*) nor fully to the world of art, and it is told with the ironic distance that became Mann's trademark. This lesson reads a few short passages, looks at how Mann builds his sentences, follows the leitmotifs and the argument with the painter Lisaweta, and paraphrases Mann in modern German.

Quotations are from Project Gutenberg ebook 23313, which reproduces an S. Fischer school edition of 1964 (text copyright 1922), in its spelling (*daß*).

## The story

Tonio Kröger grows up in a narrow north German merchant town (it is never named; Mann's own was Lübeck). His father, the consul, is correct and northern and *immer eine Feldblume im Knopfloch trug*; his mother, *die Consuelo mit Vornamen*, is dark and southern. As a schoolboy Tonio loves his friend Hans Hansen, blond, blue-eyed, good at sport, who prefers horse books to the literature Tonio cares about; a little later he loves Ingeborg Holm, blonde and laughing, who doesn't notice him at the dancing lesson. Both belong to the "others": the healthy, the unproblematic, the people who live instead of observing life.

Tonio leaves, becomes a successful writer in the south and lives as an artist. In the long central chapter (IV) he visits the Russian painter Lisaweta Iwanowna in her studio *in München, in einem Rückgebäude der Schellingstraße*, and pours out his doubts about art. Then he travels north, through his home town, where the police almost take him for a wanted swindler, to a Danish seaside hotel at Aalsgaard. There, at a dance, he sees a couple who look like Hans and Inge, and watches them without speaking to them. The last chapter is his letter to Lisaweta.

## The conversation with Lisaweta: an argument

Chapter IV is almost all Tonio's monologue, with Lisaweta's short replies. It is built like an argument (lesson 11): a thesis, provocations, examples, a counter-thesis.

**Thesis.** Art cuts the artist off from life:

> *Die Literatur ist überhaupt kein Beruf, sondern ein Fluch, – damit Sie's wissen.*

(Literature isn't a profession at all, but a curse – just so you know.)

**The cost of knowing.** The writer sees through everything, and seeing through it spoils it:

> *Es gibt etwas, was ich Erkenntnisekel nenne, Lisaweta. Der Zustand, in dem es dem Menschen genügt, eine Sache zu durchschauen, um sich bereits zum Sterben angewidert (und durchaus nicht versöhnlich gestimmt) zu fühlen, – der Fall Hamlets, des Dänen, dieses typischen Literaten.*

(There is something I call nausea of knowledge, Lisaweta: the state in which it is enough for a person to see through a thing to feel sick to death of it (and by no means reconciled) – the case of Hamlet, the Dane, that typical literary man.)

*Erkenntnisekel* is Mann's own coinage: *die Erkenntnis* (knowledge, insight) + *der Ekel* (disgust). Notice the construction *es genügt, … zu durchschauen, um … zu fühlen*: to see through something is already enough to feel disgust. And the dash before *der Fall Hamlets* is typical of Mann: after a long definition, an apposition that names an example from literature, with a learned wink.

**Confession.** He still loves what he can't belong to:

> *Ich sage Ihnen, daß ich es oft sterbensmüde bin, das Menschliche darzustellen, ohne am Menschlichen teilzuhaben...*

(I tell you that I am often sick to death of portraying what is human without having any part in it …)

*etwas müde sein* (to be tired of something) is used here with *es* pointing ahead to the infinitive; it sounds *gehoben* today, where *etwas leid sein* or *es satthaben* are commoner.

**Counter-thesis.** Lisaweta listens, then gives her verdict in one sentence:

> *Sie sind ein Bürger auf Irrwegen, Tonio Kröger, – ein verirrter Bürger.*

(You are a bourgeois gone astray, Tonio Kröger – a bourgeois who has lost his way.)

This is the turning point of the novella. Tonio's long speech is answered by a short definition that he accepts (*Ich bin erledigt*, he says at the end of the chapter: "I'm done for"). Note the rhetorical form: the second half repeats the first with a variation (*auf Irrwegen → verirrt*), and the name in the middle gives it the weight of a judgement.

## The letter: understatement and balance

In the final letter Tonio summarizes his position:

> *Ich stehe zwischen zwei Welten, bin in keiner daheim und habe es infolgedessen ein wenig schwer.*

(I stand between two worlds, am at home in neither and consequently have a rather hard time of it.)

The sentence is a model of Mann's understatement. Three verbs with one subject: a grand image (*zwischen zwei Welten*), a plain statement (*in keiner daheim*) and an anticlimax in officialese (*infolgedessen*) and a shrug (*ein wenig schwer*). The irony is directed at the speaker himself: he presents his existential problem as a minor inconvenience.

Later in the letter:

> *Aber meine tiefste und verstohlenste Liebe gehört den Blonden und Blauäugigen, den hellen Lebendigen, den Glücklichen, Liebenswürdigen und Gewöhnlichen.*

(But my deepest and most secret love belongs to the blond and blue-eyed, the bright and living, the happy, the lovable and the ordinary.)

The list climbs and then drops: after *glücklich* and *liebenswürdig* comes *gewöhnlich*, which a reader expects to be negative. Tonio loves them *because* they are ordinary. This is the irony of the whole novella in one adjective.

And the last sentence of the story:

> *Sehnsucht ist darin und schwermütiger Neid und ein klein wenig Verachtung und eine ganze keusche Seligkeit.*

(There is longing in it, and melancholy envy, and a tiny bit of contempt, and a whole chaste bliss.)

Count the *und*: a polysyndeton that slows the reading. And notice the balance of *ein klein wenig* (a tiny bit) against *eine ganze* (a whole): contempt is admitted, but measured, and bliss outweighs it. Even the feeling is weighed.

## How Mann builds a sentence

Mann's sentences are long, but they are not chaotic like the sentences of a careless writer. Take the first sentence of the story:

> *Die Wintersonne stand nur als armer Schein, milchig und matt hinter Wolkenschichten über der engen Stadt.*

(The winter sun stood only as a poor glimmer, milky and dull, behind layers of cloud above the narrow town.)

Even in this short opening, the method is visible: a main clause, then the qualifications stacked after it (*nur als armer Schein*, *milchig und matt*, *hinter Wolkenschichten*, *über der engen Stadt*), each narrowing the picture. In longer sentences Mann adds participle groups, parentheses and appositions in the same way. The reading strategy from lesson 07 works: find the finite verbs, bracket the insertions, and read the frame first.

The contrast with Kleist (C1 honors), whose periods hold back the decisive word until the end and create suspense, is instructive: Mann's periods state the main point early and then qualify it. Kleist builds tension, Mann distance.

## Leitmotifs and irony

A leitmotif (lesson 15) is a phrase or image that returns and gathers meaning. In *Tonio Kröger* the main ones are:

- **Blond and blue-eyed** (Hans and Inge, later the Danish couple): life, health, the *Bürger*.
- **The father's wildflower in his buttonhole**: the correct burgher with a hidden touch of feeling.
- **The mother's southern darkness**: the artist's inheritance.
- **"Bürger" and "Künstler"**: the two words come back so often that by the end they are almost names.

Mann's irony is not sarcasm. It is a double perspective: the narrator, and Tonio himself, see both sides of each world and take neither quite seriously, and yet both are loved. Critics often speak of a "loving" irony; use the label carefully: it describes an effect, not a technique you can point to in one sentence.

## Paraphrasing Mann in modern German

At C2 you should be able to put a Mann sentence into today's German without losing its sense, and to say what is lost. Lisaweta's verdict, paraphrased:

> *Eigentlich sind Sie ein ganz normaler Bürger, Tonio, der nur vom Weg abgekommen ist.*

The content is there; lost are the repetition with variation, the formal address in the middle and the solemnity of a verdict. Tonio's sentence from the letter:

> *Ich gehöre weder zu der einen noch zu der anderen Welt, und deshalb habe ich es nicht ganz leicht.*

Lost is the anticlimax of *infolgedessen*, the officialese word that makes the confession ironic. A good paraphrase can keep it: *… und habe es folglich ein wenig schwer*.

## The words of this lesson

- *das Künstlertum* (being an artist, the artist's nature), *die Künstlernatur* (an artistic temperament, or a person who has one), *der Literat* and *die Literatin* (a man or woman of letters; often slightly ironic or dismissive, as in Tonio's *dieses typischen Literaten*).
- *bürgerlich, die Bürgerlichkeit, das Bürgertum*: in Mann, the solid middle-class world of merchants and officials, with its values (order, duty, respectability). Today *bürgerlich* also means "civil" (*das bürgerliche Recht*) and, in politics, "centre-right".
- *der Außenseiter* and *die Außenseiterin*: the outsider; Tonio is one in his town and among artists.
- *die Zerrissenheit* and *zerrissen*: inner conflict, being torn between two sides.
- *die Wehmut* and *wehmütig*: wistful, nostalgic sadness, gentler than *die Schwermut* (26).
- *die Verachtung, verachten*: contempt, to despise.
- *die Lebensferne*: remoteness from life, the artist's distance that Tonio suffers from.
- *der Erkenntnisekel*: Mann's coinage, used today in essays and reviews as a quotation.

## Common mistakes

- Reading Tonio's view as Mann's verdict. The novella is ironic about Tonio too; Lisaweta's sentence is a counterweight, and the narrator never simply agrees.
- Translating *Bürger* as "citizen" here. In this context it is "bourgeois" or "burgher", the opposite of the artist.
- Reading *gewöhnlich* in the letter as an insult. In context it is the climax of a declaration of love.
- Quoting from a modern-spelling edition and calling it Mann's text. Name the edition and keep *daß*.
- Calling Mann's irony "sarcasm". It is distance with sympathy, not mockery.

## Key points

- *Tonio Kröger* (1903): the writer between *Bürger* and *Künstler*; Hans Hansen, Ingeborg Holm, Lisaweta; the journey north; the final letter. Mann's works are public domain in the EU since 1 January 2026.
- Chapter IV is an argument: thesis (*Die Literatur ist … ein Fluch*), the *Erkenntnisekel*, confession, Lisaweta's verdict *ein verirrter Bürger*.
- Mann's sentences state the main point, then qualify it; his irony works through anticlimax (*infolgedessen*), balance (*ein klein wenig … eine ganze*) and unexpected words (*gewöhnlich*).
- Leitmotifs: blond and blue-eyed, the wildflower, the southern mother, Bürger and Künstler.
- A paraphrase keeps the content; say what it loses.

lessons.title: Schnitzler, Leutnant Gustl: the interior monologue and Vienna 1900
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 27 described a scale of narrative techniques, from the commenting narrator to free indirect speech, where the narrator almost disappears. Arthur Schnitzler's novella *Lieutenant Gustl* goes to the end of that scale: there is no narrator at all. For the whole story we are inside the head of a young officer, hearing his thoughts as they come, in the present tense, from a boring concert in the evening to breakfast the next morning. It is usually named as one of the first German-language narratives told entirely as interior monologue.

The novella is also a document of Vienna around 1900: of its army, its idea of honour, its class barriers and its nerves. It caused a scandal and cost its author his rank as a reserve officer. This lesson reads short passages, looks at the language of the interior monologue (ellipsis, fragments, particles, Austrian forms), explains the code of honour behind the plot, and places the text in the *Wiener Moderne*. At the end you write a short interior monologue yourself.

## Author, text and title

Arthur Schnitzler (1862–1931) was a Viennese doctor and one of the central writers of the *Wiener Moderne* (Viennese Modernism). The novella first appeared in the Christmas supplement of the Vienna daily *Neue Freie Presse* (25 December 1900) and as a book in 1901 (S. Fischer, Berlin). The original title is *Lieutenant Gustl*, in the French-derived spelling of the time; many later editions modernize it to *Leutnant Gustl*.

The quotations below are from the Reclam XL edition (*Text und Kontext* no. 19128, edited by Sabine Wolf, 2013). Its text is page- and line-identical with Reclam's Universal-Bibliothek no. 18156, cautiously modernized in spelling (*muss* for *muß*), with typographic apostrophes. The public-domain transcription on Projekt Gutenberg-DE (after a Fischer Taschenbuch edition of 1998) has the same wording in these passages, but older spelling (*muß*), *Wie lang'* in the first line and *Leutnant* for *Lieutenant*. Schnitzler died in 1931, so the text is in the public domain.

## The first lines

> *Wie lang wird denn das noch dauern? Ich muss auf die Uhr schauen … schickt sich wahrscheinlich nicht in einem so ernsten Konzert.*

(How much longer is this going to go on? I have to look at my watch … probably isn't done at such a serious concert.)

A few lines later:

> *Erst viertel auf zehn? … Mir kommt vor, ich sitz’ schon drei Stunden in dem Konzert. Ich bin’s halt nicht gewohnt …*

(Not even ten yet? … I feel as if I've been sitting in this concert for three hours already. I'm just not used to it …)

and:

> *Was ist es denn eigentlich? Ich muss das Programm anschauen … Ja, richtig: Oratorium! Ich hab’ gemeint: Messe.*

(What is it actually? I must look at the programme … Yes, right: an oratorio! I thought it was a mass.)

There is no *dachte er*, no description of the hall, no information about who Gustl is. We learn everything indirectly: he is bored, he isn't used to concerts, he doesn't know what is being performed, and he worries what others think (*schickt sich … nicht*). Within three sentences, Schnitzler has characterized him by his thoughts alone.

### The language of thought

| feature | example | effect |
|---|---|---|
| present tense, first person | *Ich muss auf die Uhr schauen* | we follow the thoughts in real time |
| ellipsis, missing subject | *… schickt sich wahrscheinlich nicht* | thought skips what is obvious to the thinker |
| the ellipsis mark *…* | throughout | pauses, jumps, unfinished thoughts |
| questions to himself | *Wie lang wird denn das noch dauern?* | inner dialogue |
| modal particles | *denn, halt, eigentlich, ja* | spoken, emotional tone (C1 16) |
| apocope and contractions | *sitz’, hab’, bin’s* | spoken Viennese rhythm (lesson 26) |
| Austrian and regional forms | *viertel auf zehn* (a regional way of telling the time), *mir kommt vor* (it seems to me) | place and class |

*viertel auf zehn* is one of the regional ways of telling the time with quarters (C1 26); editions explain the exact time in a footnote. *Mir kommt vor, …* without *es* is typical of Austrian German; in Germany you'd hear *Mir kommt es so vor, als ob …*

Further Austrian words in the text, glossed in the Reclam edition, include *nachtmahlen* (to have supper), *das Beisl* (a simple pub), *stad* (quiet) and *der Pflanz* (a lie, a hoax: *jemandem einen Pflanz vormachen*). They mark the novella as Viennese without making it hard to read.

### Interior monologue, erlebte Rede and stream of consciousness

Compare the techniques of lesson 27:

- **Erlebte Rede**: *Wie lange würde das noch dauern? Er musste auf die Uhr sehen.* Third person, past tense, the narrator still present.
- **Interior monologue**: *Wie lang wird denn das noch dauern? Ich muss auf die Uhr schauen …* First person, present tense, no narrator.
- **[[Stream of consciousness]]**: the wider term for writing that imitates the flow of thought, with associations, perceptions and memories mixed. Gustl's monologue becomes more like a stream later in the night, when memories, fears and fragments of conversations run together.

Schnitzler is usually said to have been inspired by Édouard Dujardin's French novel *Les lauriers sont coupés* (1887–88), an early experiment with the technique.

## The insult and the code of honour

At the cloakroom after the concert, Gustl quarrels with a master baker he knows from his café, who is pushing to get his coat. Gustl is rude; the baker grips the hilt of Gustl's sabre and says quietly:

> *Herr Lieutenant, wenn Sie das geringste Aufsehen machen, so zieh’ ich den Säbel aus der Scheide, zerbrech’ ihn und schick’ die Stück’ an Ihr Regimentskommando.*

(Lieutenant, if you make the slightest fuss, I'll pull the sabre out of its scabbard, break it and send the pieces to your regimental command.)

and calls him a stupid boy. No one else hears it. Gustl's thoughts circle around the words for the rest of the night: *Dummer Bub – dummer Bub …*

Why is this a catastrophe? Because of the military code of honour (*der Ehrbegriff* of the officer corps, a *Standesehre*, the honour of a social estate). An officer who was insulted had to demand *Satisfaktion*, usually in a duel (*das Duell*). But only men of a certain standing were *satisfaktionsfähig*, entitled to fight a duel; a baker was not, and an officer could not fight him. An insult that could not be avenged left the officer without honour, unable to give satisfaction himself, as Gustl puts it: *ich bin satisfaktionsunfähig*. In his mind, the only way out is to shoot himself, even though nobody saw the scene.

The irony is that Gustl already has a duel arranged for the next afternoon, at four o'clock, with a *Doktor* who had suggested, at a social evening, that not every officer had joined the army out of patriotism. He is ready to fight over a remark about the army in general, and ready to die over an insult no one witnessed.

### The ending

Gustl wanders through the city all night, through the Prater, thinks of his family and of Steffi, his lover, and decides to shoot himself in the morning. In the morning he goes for a last coffee to his usual café, where the waiter tells him that the baker suffered a stroke around midnight and is dead. Nobody knows of the insult. Gustl is overjoyed, and his last thoughts are already back on the duel that afternoon. Nothing in him has changed. The novella ends without a narrator's comment; the reader draws the conclusion.

## The scandal

The novella was read as an attack on the army's honour. Nationalist and conservative newspapers attacked Schnitzler, and in 1901 a military court of honour stripped him of his rank as a reserve officer (he had served as an army doctor). The case showed precisely the code of honour the novella describes: the court did not argue with the text; it judged its author's standing.

## Vienna 1900: the Wiener Moderne

Around 1900 Vienna was the capital of a multinational empire, a city of rapid growth, poverty and luxury, and the scene of a remarkable cultural flowering. The group of young writers known as *Jung-Wien* met in coffee houses: Hermann Bahr, Hugo von Hofmannsthal, Richard Beer-Hofmann and Schnitzler. The painters around Gustav Klimt founded the Secession in 1897; Sigmund Freud published *Die Traumdeutung* in 1899 (dated 1900). The French term *Fin de Siècle* (end of the century) is used for the mood of the time: refinement, decadence, a sense of an ending, and a new interest in the psyche, in *Nervosität* (nervousness, a fashionable diagnosis) and in the *Seelenzustand* (state of mind) of the individual.

Schnitzler and Freud knew of each other's work; in a letter of 1922 Freud wrote to Schnitzler that he had long regarded him as a kind of double, who had reached by intuition what Freud had found by laborious research. *Lieutenant Gustl* is a good illustration: a whole mind exposed from the inside, without a word of psychological theory.

## Writing an interior monologue

To practise the technique, write 120–150 words of interior monologue in German. Choose a small, everyday situation with an inner conflict: waiting for an exam result, sitting in a meeting after a mistake, standing in a queue after an argument. Rules:

- first person, present tense, no narrator, no *dachte ich*;
- perceptions mixed with thoughts (*Die Uhr da drüben geht vor …*);
- questions to yourself, particles, short fragments and the ellipsis mark;
- one thought that keeps coming back, like Gustl's *dummer Bub*;
- a register that fits the person: colloquial forms are fine, but keep them consistent.

A short model:

> *Elf Uhr zwölf. Die schreiben doch immer erst nachmittags … Oder? Letztes Jahr kam die Mail um elf, hat die Jana gesagt. Die Jana weiß ja immer alles. Nicht auf das Handy schauen. Nicht. Dieser Kaffee schmeckt nach gar nichts. Und wenn ich durchgefallen bin? Dann halt nächstes Jahr, ist ja keine Katastrophe … doch, ist es. Die Mama hat schon allen erzählt, dass ich … Elf Uhr dreizehn.*

## The words of this lesson

- *die Ehre* (honour) and *der Ehrbegriff* (a concept or code of honour); *die Standesehre*: the honour of a profession or social estate, here the officer corps.
- *das Duell, sich duellieren* (*sich mit jemandem duellieren*), *die Satisfaktion* (satisfaction demanded for an insult; historical in this sense), *die Beleidigung* (insult; also the legal offence of insult, § 185 StGB).
- *der Leutnant* (plural *Leutnants*), *der Offizier*, *die Uniform*.
- *der innere Monolog*, *die Wiener Moderne*, *das Fin de Siècle* (pronounced as in French), *die Nervosität*, *der Seelenzustand*.

## Common mistakes

- Calling *Lieutenant Gustl* erlebte Rede. There is no third person and no narrator: it is interior monologue.
- Correcting the title. *Lieutenant* is Schnitzler's spelling; *Leutnant* is the modernized one. Say which edition you quote.
- Reading Gustl's thoughts as Schnitzler's views. The novella exposes Gustl; it doesn't share his opinions.
- Explaining the plot without the code of honour. Without *satisfaktionsfähig*, Gustl's despair over an unseen insult makes no sense.
- Using Austrian forms like *mir kommt vor* in a standard German text without meaning to. In a quotation or a character's speech they are right; in your essay, write *mir kommt es vor*.

## Key points

- *Lieutenant Gustl* (Neue Freie Presse, 25 December 1900; book 1901): told entirely as interior monologue, usually named among the first in German.
- Interior monologue: first person, present tense, no narrator, ellipsis, fragments, particles, self-questions; Austrian forms (*viertel auf zehn, mir kommt vor, nachtmahlen, Beisl*).
- The plot depends on the officers' code of honour: *Satisfaktion*, *satisfaktionsfähig*, the duel. A baker can't be challenged, so the insult seems to leave only suicide.
- The ending: the baker dies of a stroke; Gustl is relieved and unchanged.
- The scandal cost Schnitzler his reserve officer's rank (1901). Vienna 1900: Jung-Wien, Freud, Klimt, the Fin de Siècle.

lessons.title: Die blaue Blume: German Romanticism (Novalis, Schlegel, Hoffmann)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This honors module follows German thought and style from 1798 to 1942: the Romantics, who discovered the inner life and its night side; Nietzsche, who doubted that language can tell the truth; Freud, who gave the unconscious a plain German vocabulary; and Stefan Zweig, who wrote the memoir of a world that ended. Quotations come from public-domain works and follow the edition named; everything else was written for this course.

This lesson goes to the beginning of Romanticism (*die Romantik*, C1): Friedrich Schlegel's programme of 1798, Novalis and the blue flower, and E. T. A. Hoffmann's *Der Sandmann*, the story that made the uncanny a German speciality. You'll also practise reading prose from around 1800 and writing about it in modern German.

## Jena, 1798: a programme in a fragment

In 1798 the brothers August Wilhelm and Friedrich Schlegel founded a journal, the *Athenaeum* (1798–1800). Its circle in Jena and Berlin, which included Novalis and Schleiermacher, is now called the *Frühromantik* (early Romanticism). Instead of treatises they published hundreds of short, numbered texts: the *Athenäums-Fragmente*.

A **[[fragment]]** in their sense is not a broken piece of a lost whole but a deliberate form: a short prose text that throws out an idea without working it through, so that the reader has to continue the thought. One fragment (usually numbered 206) compares the ideal fragment to a hedgehog, complete in itself and closed off from the world. A *fragmentarisch* text in the everyday sense is unfinished; the Romantic fragment is open on purpose.

The most quoted of them, number 116, defines Romantic poetry. It begins:

> „Die romantische Poesie ist eine progressive Universalpoesie. Ihre Bestimmung ist nicht bloß, alle getrennten Gattungen der Poesie wieder zu vereinigen und die Poesie mit der Philosophie, und Rhetorik in Berührung zu setzen.“

and later says:

> „Die romantische Dichtart ist noch im Werden; ja das ist ihr eigentliches Wesen, daß sie ewig nur werden, nie vollendet sey kann. Sie kann durch keine Theorie erschöpft werden, […]“

> „Sie allein ist unendlich, wie sie allein frey ist, und das als ihr erstes Gesetz anerkennt, daß die Willkühr des Dichters kein Gesetz über sich leide.“

(Quoted from the first printing, *Athenaeum*, vol. 1, no. 2, 1798, as transcribed by German History in Documents and Images, GHDI. The spelling *daß, sey, frey, Willkühr* and the comma before *und Rhetorik* are the original's.)

"Romantic poetry is a progressive universal poetry. Its purpose is not merely to reunite all the separate genres of poetry and to bring poetry into contact with philosophy and rhetoric." … "The Romantic kind of poetry is still in the process of becoming; indeed, that is its very essence, that it can forever only become and never be completed. It cannot be exhausted by any theory." … "It alone is infinite, just as it alone is free and recognizes as its first law that the poet's free will shall suffer no law above itself."

*Universalpoesie* is one poetry that mixes everything the classical tradition kept apart (verse and prose, poetry and philosophy, art and criticism) and is *progressiv*, always moving and never finished: a novel containing poems, letters, essays and comments on itself would be its model.

Notes on the German:

- *noch im Werden sein*: still in the making (*eine Demokratie im Werden*). In *daß sie ewig nur werden … kann*, *werden* is a full verb, "to become".
- *ja das ist ihr eigentliches Wesen, daß …*: *ja* is not a modal particle here but an intensifier correcting upwards, "indeed". *das* points forward to the *daß*-clause as a correlate.
- *daß die Willkühr des Dichters kein Gesetz über sich leide*: *leide* is Konjunktiv I of *leiden* in its old sense "to tolerate" (still in *Ich kann ihn nicht leiden*). The Konjunktiv I states a rule: "shall suffer no law". Today: *dass … kein Gesetz über sich duldet*.
- *Willkühr* (today *Willkür*) is positive here: the poet's free choice. Today *die Willkür* means arbitrariness (*staatliche Willkür*). Watch for such shifts in texts from 1800.

### Romantic irony

The fragments also coined **[[romantic irony]]**: not a figure of speech (saying the opposite of what one means) but an attitude of the artist, who creates a world and at the same time steps outside it, shows that it is made and comments on it. The work reflects on itself. You'll see it below in Hoffmann, whose narrator interrupts the story to discuss with the reader how to begin it.

## Novalis and the blue flower

Novalis is the pen name of Friedrich von Hardenberg (1772–1801), who trained in law and mining and worked as an official of the Saxon salt works. He died of tuberculosis at 28. The early death of his young fiancée Sophie von Kühn in 1797 lies behind the *Hymnen an die Nacht*, which appeared in 1800 in the last volume of the *Athenaeum*: hymns in rhythmic prose (a verse version survives in manuscript) that praise the night over the day, death over the visible world, and a love that reaches beyond the grave. The "night side" of human life (*die Nachtseite*), with dreams, death, longing and the irrational, becomes a Romantic theme from here on.

His novel *Heinrich von Ofterdingen* remained unfinished and was published after his death, in 1802, by his friends Ludwig Tieck and Friedrich Schlegel. It opens with a young man lying awake at night:

> „Die Eltern lagen schon und schliefen, die Wanduhr schlug ihren einförmigen Takt, vor den klappernden Fenstern sauste der Wind; […]“

A stranger has told him about a blue flower, and Heinrich can't stop thinking about it. He says to himself:

> „Nicht die Schätze sind es, die ein so unaussprechliches Verlangen in mir geweckt haben […] fern ab liegt mir alle Habsucht: aber die blaue Blume sehn' ich mich zu erblicken. Sie liegt mir unaufhörlich im Sinn, und ich kann nichts anderes dichten und denken.“

(Quoted from Projekt Gutenberg-DE, based on an Insel edition of 1982.)

"My parents were already lying asleep, the wall clock beat its monotonous time, the wind whistled outside the rattling windows; …" — "It is not the treasures that have awakened such an inexpressible longing in me … all greed is far from me: but I long to see the blue flower. It is always on my mind, and I can write and think of nothing else."

Notes:

- *Nicht die Schätze sind es, die …*: a cleft sentence with *es*: "It is not the treasures that …". The contrastive *nicht* takes the front position.
- *fern ab liegt mir alle Habsucht*: the predicate *fern ab* (today *fernab*) is fronted for emphasis; *mir* is a dative of the person concerned: "greed is far from me".
- *die blaue Blume sehn' ich mich zu erblicken*: *sich sehnen* with a *zu*-infinitive (today usually *Ich sehne mich danach, die blaue Blume zu sehen*), the object of the infinitive fronted, and the apocope *sehn'* (the *-e* dropped and marked by an apostrophe, as in poetry).

The book follows Heinrich on a journey, a *Wanderschaft*, towards becoming a poet. The blue flower became the symbol of Romantic longing (*die Sehnsucht*): for something infinite that is never reached. Typical too is the turn inward, *die Innerlichkeit*, a word used both as praise (depth of feeling) and as criticism (withdrawal from politics into private feeling).

*romantisch* goes back to *Roman* in its old sense of a tale of adventure and love. Today it has three uses: *die romantische Dichtung* (of Romanticism), *ein romantisches Tal* (picturesque) and *ein romantischer Abend* (amorous).

## E. T. A. Hoffmann and the night side

Ernst Theodor Amadeus Hoffmann (1776–1822) was a Prussian jurist and also a composer, music critic, caricaturist and author. He wrote *Kunstmärchen* (literary fairy tales, such as *Der goldne Topf*, 1814) and tales of the supernatural and of madness that literary history files under *Schauerromantik*, the German counterpart of the English Gothic novel. His characters meet their *Doppelgänger*, a word usually credited to the novelist Jean Paul (1796) and borrowed by English.

*Der Sandmann* appeared in 1816 as the first of Hoffmann's *Nachtstücke* ("night pieces"). The student Nathanael believes that the barometer seller Coppola is Coppelius, the sinister lawyer who visited his father at night and whom he blames for his father's death. Through a telescope bought from Coppola he falls in love with Olimpia, supposedly the daughter of his professor Spalanzani, who turns out to be an automaton. His fiancée Clara tells him that the dark powers are in his own mind. The story ends in madness and death, and never says whether Coppelius is a demon or just an unpleasant old man.

As a child, Nathanael asks his little sister's nurse who the Sandman is:

> „Das ist ein böser Mann, der kommt zu den Kindern, wenn sie nicht zu Bett gehen wollen und wirft ihnen Händevoll Sand in die Augen, daß sie blutig zum Kopf herausspringen, […]“

"He's a wicked man who comes to children when they won't go to bed and throws handfuls of sand in their eyes, so that they jump out of their heads all bloody, …"

The nurse speaks like a nurse: *der kommt …* has main-clause word order after *der*, as in spoken German (*Das ist einer, der kommt immer zu spät*). *daß* introduces a result, today *sodass*. And modern rules would need a comma to close the *wenn*-clause before *und*; the quotation keeps its edition's punctuation.

Then, after Nathanael's letters, a narrator steps in and addresses the reader directly:

> „Seltsamer und wunderlicher kann nichts erfunden werden, als dasjenige ist, was sich mit meinem armen Freunde, dem jungen Studenten Nathanael, zugetragen, und was ich dir, günstiger Leser! zu erzählen unternommen.“

"Nothing stranger or more wondrous can be invented than what happened to my poor friend, the young student Nathanael, and what I have undertaken to tell you, kind reader!"

He discusses how best to begin a story, and suggests:

> „Vielleicht wirst du, o mein Leser! dann glauben, daß nichts wunderlicher und toller sei, als das wirkliche Leben“

"Perhaps you will then believe, o my reader, that nothing is more wondrous and crazier than real life"

Here is romantic irony at work: the story stops to show that it is a story, and the narrator plays with the reader's expectations. Note the dropped auxiliaries (*zugetragen [hat]*, *unternommen [habe]*: C1 honors called this the dropped auxiliary), *günstiger Leser* ("kind, well-disposed reader": the old sense of *günstig*), and Konjunktiv I *sei* after *glauben*.

When the truth about Olimpia comes out, Hoffmann satirizes the town's reaction: a professor declares the whole affair an allegory, but many respectable gentlemen are not reassured: *„[…] die Geschichte mit dem Automat hatte tief in ihrer Seele Wurzel gefaßt“* ("the story of the automaton had taken deep root in their souls"), and they begin to distrust their own sweethearts. Note *dem Automat*: today *der Automat* is a weak noun (*dem Automaten*), but older texts often leave the ending off. (Hoffmann quotations from Project Gutenberg no. 6341, *Nachtstücke*, prepared from Projekt Gutenberg-DE files.)

### Das Unheimliche

In 1919 Sigmund Freud published an essay, *Das Unheimliche*, whose central example is *Der Sandmann* (lesson 92). He notes that *heimlich* once meant "homely, familiar" as well as "secret", and argues that *das Unheimliche* is the familiar become strange and frightening: the father turned monster, the doll that seems alive. *unheimlich* (uncanny, eerie) and *das Unheimliche* have been key words of criticism ever since; in everyday speech *unheimlich* is also an intensifier (*unheimlich nett*).

A *Spukgeschichte* (ghost story, from *der Spuk*, haunting) is the simpler relative of such tales. Hoffmann's stories are rarely just that, because the reader can't be sure whether the ghost is real or in the hero's head: the hesitation that later theory calls *das Fantastische* (*fantastisch*, also *phantastisch*).

## Reading prose from around 1800

| You read | Today | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| *daß, bloß, gefaßt* | *dass, bloß, gefasst* | *ß* after a short vowel before the 1996 reform (*bloß* has a long vowel and keeps it) |
| *andre, goldne, sehn'* | *andere, goldene, sehe* | syncope and apocope: vowels dropped for rhythm |
| *zugetragen, und was ich … zu erzählen unternommen* | *zugetragen hat … unternommen habe* | dropped auxiliary at the end of a subordinate clause |
| *dem Automat, dem Freunde* | *dem Automaten, dem Freund* | weak ending missing; old dative *-e* |
| *günstiger Leser, Willkür* | *geneigter Leser, freie Wahl* | words whose meaning has shifted |

Commas, too, often follow rhythm rather than today's rules. Editions differ in how far they modernize (the Insel *Ofterdingen* has *anderes*, the Gutenberg *Sandmann* keeps *daß*): quote the spelling of the edition you name.

## A modern text: *Olimpia antwortet immer*

Romanticism is a favourite reference of the German Feuilleton, the arts and ideas pages of the newspaper. Read this commentary, written for this course.

> **Olimpia antwortet immer**
>
> Wer heute E. T. A. Hoffmanns Erzählung „Der Sandmann“ liest, bleibt an einer Episode hängen, die vor zweihundert Jahren vor allem schaurig-komisch gewirkt haben dürfte. Der Student Nathanael verliebt sich in Olimpia, die Tochter seines Professors, und bemerkt nicht, dass er einen Automaten anbetet. Sie sagt kaum mehr als „Ach“, doch gerade das genügt ihm: Endlich hört ihm jemand zu, ohne zu widersprechen. Clara dagegen, seine Verlobte, die seine Ängste nüchtern als Hirngespinste deutet, erscheint ihm plötzlich kalt.
>
> Man muss kein Kulturpessimist sein, um darin eine Vorahnung zu erkennen. Chatprogramme, die uns rund um die Uhr bestätigen, sind die Olimpias unserer Tage: Sie widersprechen selten, ermüden nie und spiegeln uns, was wir ohnehin denken. Unheimlich ist daran nicht die Maschine, sondern die Bereitwilligkeit, mit der wir ihr Leben einhauchen.
>
> Freilich sollte man Hoffmann nicht zum Propheten der Digitalisierung verklären. Seine Erzählung handelt ebenso sehr von Kindheitsangst, Wahn und dem Riss, der durch das bürgerliche Ich geht. Und sie weigert sich, eine eindeutige Erklärung zu liefern: Ob Coppelius ein Dämon ist oder nur ein unsympathischer Advokat, bleibt in der Schwebe. Gerade diese Unentscheidbarkeit macht den Text so modern.
>
> Die Romantiker haben die Nachtseite des Menschen nicht erfunden, aber sie haben ihr eine Sprache gegeben. Novalis suchte die blaue Blume, Schlegel eine Poesie, die nie fertig wird, Hoffmann die Stelle, an der das Vertraute fremd wird. Vielleicht liegt darin ihre eigentliche Aktualität: Sie misstrauten der Vernunft nicht, weil sie sie verachteten, sondern weil sie wussten, wie leicht man sich mit ihr selbst betrügt.
>
> Wer also beim nächsten Gespräch mit einer Software das wohlige Gefühl hat, endlich verstanden zu werden, darf ruhig an Nathanael denken. Es muss ja nicht gleich so enden wie bei ihm.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Olimpia always answers**

Anyone who reads E. T. A. Hoffmann's story "The Sandman" today gets stuck on an episode that two hundred years ago probably struck readers above all as grotesquely comic. The student Nathanael falls in love with Olimpia, his professor's daughter, and doesn't notice that he is worshipping an automaton. She says little more than "Ah", but that is exactly what's enough for him: at last someone listens to him without contradicting. Clara, by contrast, his fiancée, who soberly interprets his fears as figments of his imagination, suddenly seems cold to him.

You don't have to be a cultural pessimist to see a premonition in this. Chat programs that affirm us around the clock are the Olimpias of our day: they rarely contradict, never tire, and reflect back to us what we think anyway. What is uncanny about it is not the machine but the readiness with which we breathe life into it.

Admittedly, one shouldn't glorify Hoffmann into a prophet of digitalization. His story is just as much about childhood fear, delusion and the crack that runs through the bourgeois self. And it refuses to provide an unambiguous explanation: whether Coppelius is a demon or just an unpleasant lawyer remains undecided. It is precisely this undecidability that makes the text so modern.

The Romantics didn't invent the night side of humanity, but they gave it a language. Novalis looked for the blue flower, Schlegel for a poetry that is never finished, Hoffmann for the point at which the familiar becomes strange. Perhaps that is where their real relevance lies: they distrusted reason not because they despised it, but because they knew how easily one deceives oneself with it.

So anyone who, in their next conversation with a piece of software, has the cosy feeling of finally being understood is welcome to think of Nathanael. It needn't end the way it did for him.

</details>

Things to notice:

- *gewirkt haben dürfte*: *dürfte* + perfect infinitive, a cautious guess about the past ("probably struck readers").
- *Unheimlich ist daran nicht die Maschine, sondern …*: the predicative adjective in the Vorfeld, then *nicht … sondern*: the classic way to correct an expected view.
- *Freilich sollte man … nicht … verklären*: the concession before the conclusion; *freilich* (admittedly) is more literary than *allerdings*.
- *Novalis suchte die blaue Blume, Schlegel eine Poesie, …, Hoffmann die Stelle, …*: the verb is given once and understood three times (ellipsis).

## Writing about a Romantic text

A short interpretation names the text, places it, says what it does and how, and supports each claim with a brief quotation or a precise paraphrase:

> In seiner Erzählung „Der Sandmann“ (1816) lässt E. T. A. Hoffmann offen, ob die unheimlichen Ereignisse übernatürlich sind oder nur in Nathanaels Kopf stattfinden. Die Erzählung beginnt mit drei Briefen; erst danach meldet sich ein Erzähler zu Wort, der den „günstigen Leser“ direkt anspricht und über den richtigen Anfang seiner Geschichte nachdenkt. Damit zeigt der Text, dass er gemacht ist: ein Beispiel romantischer Ironie. Zugleich verweigert er dem Leser einen sicheren Standpunkt, denn weder Nathanaels Angst noch Claras nüchterne Erklärung wird eindeutig bestätigt.

Notice *lässt offen, ob …*, *meldet sich … zu Wort*, *verweigert … einen sicheren Standpunkt* and *weder … noch … wird bestätigt* (after *weder … noch* with singular subjects, singular and plural verbs are both in use). Write about the text in the present tense; use the past only for its history (*erschien 1816*).

## Common mistakes

- Reading *Fragment* as "a broken piece". In Romantic theory a fragment is a complete short text that is open on purpose; the Athenaeum fragments are finished works.
- Equating romantic irony with sarcasm. It is the author's self-reflection inside the work: the story shows it is a story, even when nothing is meant the opposite way.
- Reading *Willkür* or *günstig* in texts from 1800 with today's meanings: Schlegel's *Willkür* is the poet's freedom, Hoffmann's *günstiger Leser* the kind reader.
- Correcting old punctuation and spelling inside a quotation. Quote the edition exactly (*daß*, no comma before *und*) and modernize only in your paraphrase.
- Writing *dem Automat* in modern German. It's a weak noun: *des Automaten, dem Automaten, die Automaten*.

## Key points

- The *Athenaeum* (1798–1800) made the **[[fragment]]** a deliberate form. Fragment 116 defines Romantic poetry as *eine progressive Universalpoesie* that *ewig nur werden, nie vollendet sey kann*.
- **[[Romantic irony]]** is the artist's self-reflection in the work: creating an illusion and stepping out of it.
- Novalis: *Hymnen an die Nacht* (1800) and the unfinished *Heinrich von Ofterdingen* (1802), whose blue flower is the symbol of Romantic longing.
- Hoffmann's *Der Sandmann* (1816): the automaton Olimpia, Clara's reason against Nathanael's fear, a narrator who addresses the reader, an ending that explains nothing; Freud's *Das Unheimliche* (1919) made it the model of the uncanny.
- Prose from around 1800 shows *daß*, apocope and syncope, dropped auxiliaries, missing weak endings, rhythmic commas and shifted meanings (*Willkür, günstig*). Quote it as printed; paraphrase it in modern German.
