lessons.title: Ein bewegliches Heer von Metaphern: Nietzsche's German
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) is the German philosopher most quoted out of context: his prose is short, sharp and musical, easy to lift and hard to understand. This lesson reads an early essay on truth and metaphor (building on lesson 20), two aphorisms, the parable of the madman and the biblical voice of *Zarathustra*. You'll learn his key terms with their actual meaning, see how his work was distorted after his death, and look at his rhythm: the dash, the exclamation mark, the question.

## A short life

Nietzsche became professor of classical philology in Basel in 1869, at 24, and gave up the post for health reasons ten years later. He then moved between Switzerland, Italy and the south of France, writing a book almost every year, until he collapsed in Turin in January 1889. He spent his last eleven years mentally ill and died in Weimar in 1900.

His sister, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche, took control of his papers (the *Nachlass*) and set up a Nietzsche Archive. She published a selection of his notes as *Der Wille zur Macht*, as if it were his main work, edited his letters to suit her picture of him, and presented him as a forerunner of the nationalism and antisemitism he had attacked; she later welcomed the Nazis to the archive. The critical edition of Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari (from 1967) showed how much of that picture was her construction. So check what a claim rests on: the books he published, or notes his sister arranged.

## Truth as metaphor (1873)

In 1873 Nietzsche wrote an essay he never published: *Über Wahrheit und Lüge im außermoralischen Sinne* ("On Truth and Lying in an Extra-Moral Sense"). It appeared from his papers after his breakdown. *außermoralisch* means "outside morality": Nietzsche is not asking whether lying is wrong, but what truth is, if we leave moral judgment aside.

The essay begins like a fable:

> „In irgend einem abgelegenen Winkel des in zahllosen Sonnensystemen flimmernd ausgegossenen Weltalls gab es einmal ein Gestirn, auf dem kluge Tiere das Erkennen erfanden. Es war die hochmütigste und verlogenste Minute der "Weltgeschichte": aber doch nur eine Minute. Nach wenigen Atemzügen der Natur erstarrte das Gestirn, und die klugen Tiere mußten sterben.“

"In some remote corner of the universe, poured out and glittering in countless solar systems, there was once a star on which clever animals invented knowing. It was the most arrogant and most mendacious minute of 'world history': but only a minute. After nature had drawn a few breaths the star froze, and the clever animals had to die."

How it works:

- *gab es einmal*: the fairy-tale opening (*Es war einmal*) applied to the universe; the tone is ironic from the first line.
- *des in zahllosen Sonnensystemen flimmernd ausgegossenen Weltalls*: a long participle attribute between article and noun, nominal style used for poetic effect.
- *kluge Tiere*: humans are never named, the first of many demotions; the scare quotes make "world history" a minute.

Then comes the passage everyone quotes:

> „Was ist also Wahrheit? Ein bewegliches Heer von Metaphern, Metonymien, Anthropomorphismen, kurz eine Summe von menschlichen Relationen, die, poetisch und rhetorisch gesteigert, übertragen, geschmückt wurden, und die nach langem Gebrauch einem Volke fest, kanonisch und verbindlich dünken: die Wahrheiten sind Illusionen, von denen man vergessen hat, daß sie welche sind, Metaphern, die abgenutzt und sinnlich kraftlos geworden sind, Münzen, die ihr Bild verloren haben und nun als Metall, nicht mehr als Münzen, in Betracht kommen.“

(Both passages from Projekt Gutenberg-DE; the page names no print edition and gives the date "1873, aus dem Nachlaß". It has *Tiere* and *kanonisch* in modern spelling but keeps *daß*.)

"What, then, is truth? A mobile army of metaphors, metonymies, anthropomorphisms, in short a sum of human relations that were poetically and rhetorically heightened, transferred and embellished, and that after long use seem fixed, canonical and binding to a people: truths are illusions of which one has forgotten that they are illusions, metaphors that have become worn out and drained of sensuous force, coins that have lost their image and now count only as metal, no longer as coins."

Read it with lesson 20 in mind: a metaphor transfers a word to something it doesn't literally mean, metonymy replaces a thing by something connected with it, and an *Anthropomorphismus* describes the non-human in human terms (*die Natur will*). Nietzsche claims that all our concepts began as such transfers and that we have forgotten it, as we no longer see the face on a worn coin. "Truth" is then what a community has agreed to treat as fixed. The grammar carries the argument:

- *Was ist also Wahrheit?* The question, then an answer without a verb (*Ein bewegliches Heer …*): an elliptical definition.
- *ein bewegliches Heer*: an army is the opposite of what we expect truth to be, and *beweglich* (mobile) the opposite of fixed. The image is itself a metaphor about metaphors.
- *die … einem Volke … dünken*: *dünken* (to seem; lesson 26) with a dative, here plural: they seem binding *to a people*. The dative *-e* in *Volke* is old.
- *daß sie welche sind*: *welche* as an indefinite pronoun, "that they are (illusions)", as in *Hast du Brot? – Ja, ich habe welches*: an everyday form in the middle of high style.
- The colon turns the whole first half into a premise; after it come three appositions (*Illusionen*, *Metaphern*, *Münzen*), each more concrete.

This early text is often read as the beginning of what is called Nietzsche's **[[perspectivism]]**: the view that there is no knowledge from nowhere, only knowledge from a standpoint, and that the more perspectives we have on a thing, the more complete (never final) our view of it becomes. *perspektivisch* (from a particular point of view) and *der Perspektivismus* are now standard words in philosophy; the doctrine is developed in his later books, especially *Zur Genealogie der Moral* (1887).

## The aphorism

From 1878 on Nietzsche wrote mostly in aphorisms: numbered sections from one line to several pages. *Menschliches, Allzumenschliches* (1878) is subtitled *Ein Buch für freie Geister*: a *Freigeist* is someone who thinks independently of tradition and religion. In *Götzen-Dämmerung* (1889), "Sprüche und Pfeile" (sayings and arrows), he writes:

> „Aus der Kriegsschule des Lebens. – Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker.“

> „Ich mißtraue allen Systematikern und gehe ihnen aus dem Weg. Der Wille zum System ist ein Mangel an Rechtschaffenheit.“

(Projekt Gutenberg-DE, Kröner edition, Leipzig 1922; numbers 8 and 26.)

"From the military school of life. – What does not kill me makes me stronger." — "I distrust all systematizers and avoid them. The will to a system is a lack of integrity."

The first is his most famous sentence, usually quoted without its heading, which gives it an ironic frame: a lesson from a hard school, not a recipe for success. The second explains the form: a system pretends to be complete, an aphorism admits that it isn't (compare the Romantic fragment, lesson 90).

## The madman (1882)

*Die fröhliche Wissenschaft* (1882; a fifth book was added in 1887) contains section 125, *Der tolle Mensch* (the madman):

> „Habt ihr nicht von jenem tollen Menschen gehört, der am hellen Vormittage eine Laterne anzündete, auf den Markt lief und unaufhörlich schrie: "ich suche Gott! Ich suche Gott!"“

The people in the market are those who don't believe in God, and they laugh at him. Then he turns on them:

> „Wohin ist Gott? rief er, ich will es euch sagen! Wir haben ihn getödtet, – ihr und ich! Wir Alle sind seine Mörder!“

> „Gott ist todt! Gott bleibt todt! Und wir haben ihn getödtet!“

> „Ist nicht die Grösse dieser That zu gross für uns?“

and at the end, when they fall silent and stare at him:

> „Ich komme zu früh, sagte er dann, ich bin noch nicht an der Zeit.“

(Projekt Gutenberg-DE; the page names no print edition. It keeps the spelling of Nietzsche's time: *todt, getödtet, That, gross, Grösse, Alle*.)

"Haven't you heard of that madman who lit a lantern in the bright morning, ran to the market place and cried incessantly: I am looking for God! I am looking for God!" — "Where has God gone? he cried, I will tell you! We have killed him, – you and I! We are all his murderers!" — "God is dead! God remains dead! And we have killed him!" — "Is not the greatness of this deed too great for us?" — "I have come too early, he said then, my time has not yet come."

In context, the famous sentence is no atheist's cheer. The madman speaks to unbelievers who don't see what they have done: if the belief that held European values together is gone, those values have lost their foundation. Nietzsche calls the consequence *der Nihilismus*, the state in which the highest values devalue themselves and nothing seems to matter. His later project is a *Umwertung aller Werte*, a revaluation of all values, and an attitude he calls *Lebensbejahung* (affirmation of life) instead of despair.

Notes on the language:

- *am hellen Vormittage*: a lantern in daylight, as the Greek philosopher Diogenes is said to have looked for a human being with a lamp; old dative *-e*.
- *Wohin ist Gott?*: *wohin* with *sein* and no verb of motion, "where has God gone?"; *rief er* stands inside the open quotation.
- *getödtet, – ihr und ich!*: the comma plus dash makes a pause before the accusation lands on the listeners.

## Zarathustra's voice (1883–85)

*Also sprach Zarathustra*, written in four parts between 1883 and 1885, is a philosophical poem in prose. Its hero, named after the Persian prophet, comes down from the mountains to teach. The style parodies Luther's Bible: short verses, parallel clauses, parables, the address *meine Brüder*, and the refrain *Also sprach Zarathustra* that ends the speeches like *So spricht der Herr*. In the prologue he speaks to the crowd in a market place:

> „Ich lehre euch den Übermenschen. Der Mensch ist Etwas, das überwunden werden soll. Was habt ihr gethan, ihn zu überwinden?“

> „Der Mensch ist ein Seil, geknüpft zwischen Thier und Übermensch, – ein Seil über einem Abgrunde.“

> „Ich beschwöre euch, meine Brüder, bleibt der Erde treu […]“

(Projekt Gutenberg-DE, after the C. G. Naumann edition, Leipzig 1901.)

"I teach you the overman. Man is something that shall be overcome. What have you done to overcome him?" — "Man is a rope, tied between animal and overman, – a rope over an abyss." — "I implore you, my brothers, remain true to the earth …"

Zarathustra is the *Verkünder* (herald, proclaimer) of two ideas: the *Übermensch* and the *ewige Wiederkehr*.

## The key terms, accurately

| Term | What Nietzsche means | What it does not mean |
|---|---|---|
| *der Übermensch* | a goal beyond present humanity: a human being who has overcome himself and creates his own values | a biologically or racially superior type; a comic-book superhero |
| *der Wille zur Macht* | in his published books, a basic drive of life to grow, master and shape, also in art and thought | simply the wish for political power |
| *die ewige Wiederkehr* (des Gleichen) | the thought that everything returns eternally in the same way; above all a test: could you will your life again, exactly as it was? | a theory of reincarnation |
| *die Umwertung aller Werte* | the critical re-examination of inherited values, especially Christian morality | abolishing all values |
| *das Ressentiment* | in *Zur Genealogie der Moral* (1887): the resentment of the powerless, which Nietzsche thinks created a morality that calls weakness good | any personal grudge (in everyday German *Ressentiments* are prejudices or grudges) |
| *die Genealogie* | tracing a value back to its origins, to show that it has a history and is not eternal | family history (the word's ordinary sense) |
| *die Moralkritik* | critique of morality as such: asking what moral judgments do and whom they serve | criticizing someone's behaviour |

Scholars still argue about how these ideas fit together; the table gives the core most readers of the published works agree on.

## Dash, exclamation mark, question

Nietzsche is a writer for the ear. Look at the punctuation in the quotations above:

- the dash (*der Gedankenstrich*) as a pause before the point: *– ihr und ich!*; *– ein Seil über einem Abgrunde*; between heading and saying in the aphorism. He often uses it where a modern editor would put nothing or a comma.
- the exclamation mark in series: *Gott ist todt! Gott bleibt todt!* Repetition with variation (*ist / bleibt*), then the turn (*Und wir haben ihn getödtet!*).
- the question that answers itself or refuses an answer: *Was ist also Wahrheit?*; *Ist nicht die Grösse dieser That zu gross für uns?* (a negative question that expects "yes").
- scare quotes and italics (in his books, letter-spaced print) for words he distrusts or stresses.

In an interpretation, describe this rather than imitate it: *Nietzsche setzt Gedankenstriche als Atempausen ein; die Ausrufe steigern sich, bis die Anklage die Zuhörer selbst trifft.*

## A modern text: *Nietzsche auf der Kaffeetasse*

Read this commentary, written for this course in the style of a newspaper's arts pages.

> **Nietzsche auf der Kaffeetasse**
>
> Kaum ein Philosoph wird so oft zitiert und so selten gelesen wie Friedrich Nietzsche. „Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker“ steht auf Kaffeetassen, in Fitnessstudios und in Motivationsvorträgen für Führungskräfte. Dass der Satz aus der „Götzen-Dämmerung“ stammt, einem Buch, das „mit dem Hammer“ philosophieren will, und dass ihm dort die ironische Überschrift „Aus der Kriegsschule des Lebens“ vorangeht, erfährt man auf der Tasse nicht.
>
> Das ist kein Zufall. Nietzsches Aphorismen sind so gebaut, dass sie sich herauslösen lassen: kurz, zugespitzt, ohne Herleitung. Wer sie zitiert, nimmt sich die Pointe und lässt den Zweifel zurück. Gerade dieser Zweifel aber ist der Kern seines Denkens. Ein Autor, der Wahrheiten für abgenutzte Metaphern hält, taugt schlecht zum Lieferanten von Lebensweisheiten.
>
> Schwerer wiegt der politische Missbrauch. Nietzsches Schwester, die nach seinem Zusammenbruch über den Nachlass verfügte, stellte aus nachgelassenen Notizen ein Buch mit dem Titel „Der Wille zur Macht“ zusammen, das es in dieser Form nie gegeben hatte, und rückte den Bruder in die Nähe eines Nationalismus, den er verachtet hatte. Die Nationalsozialisten machten ihn bereitwillig zu ihrem Hausphilosophen. Die kritische Ausgabe von Colli und Montinari hat diese Legende Jahrzehnte später zerlegt; in der Fachwelt ist das Bild seither korrigiert, in der Öffentlichkeit nur zum Teil.
>
> Was folgt daraus? Gewiss nicht, dass man Nietzsche nur noch mit Fußnoten lesen dürfte. Wer ihn liest, sollte aber wissen, dass dieser Autor selten belehrt, sondern fragt, provoziert und sich selbst widerspricht. Seine Gedankenstriche sind Atempausen, seine Ausrufezeichen oft Masken. Man muss ihn nicht mögen, um zu merken, dass er seine Leser zu etwas zwingt, was keine Kaffeetasse leistet: zum Weiterdenken.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Nietzsche on a coffee mug**

Hardly any philosopher is quoted as often and read as rarely as Friedrich Nietzsche. "What does not kill me makes me stronger" is printed on coffee mugs, hangs in gyms and turns up in motivational talks for managers. That the sentence comes from "Twilight of the Idols", a book that sets out to philosophize "with a hammer", and that it is preceded there by the ironic heading "From the military school of life" is something the mug doesn't tell you.

That is no accident. Nietzsche's aphorisms are built so that they can be lifted out: short, pointed, with no derivation. Whoever quotes them takes the punchline and leaves the doubt behind. But it is precisely this doubt that is the core of his thinking. An author who considers truths to be worn-out metaphors makes a poor supplier of life wisdom.

The political misuse weighs more heavily. Nietzsche's sister, who controlled his papers after his breakdown, put together from his unpublished notes a book entitled "The Will to Power" that had never existed in that form, and moved her brother close to a nationalism he had despised. The National Socialists readily made him their house philosopher. Decades later, the critical edition by Colli and Montinari took this legend apart; among specialists the picture has been corrected since then, in public only in part.

What follows from this? Certainly not that Nietzsche may only be read with footnotes. But anyone who reads him should know that this author rarely lectures; instead he asks, provokes and contradicts himself. His dashes are pauses for breath, his exclamation marks often masks. You don't have to like him to notice that he forces his readers into something no coffee mug achieves: thinking further.

</details>

Things to notice:

- *Dass der Satz …, und dass ihm dort … vorangeht, erfährt man auf der Tasse nicht.*: two subject clauses in the Vorfeld, the main verb only at the end of a long period, and the short main clause as a punchline.
- *Nietzsches Aphorismen sind so gebaut, dass sie sich herauslösen lassen*: *so …, dass* (result) with *sich lassen* (possibility).
- *Schwerer wiegt der politische Missbrauch.*: the comparative in the Vorfeld ranks the second argument higher.

## Summarizing a philosophical passage

Name the text, report with Konjunktiv I and keep his images in quotation marks:

> In seinem 1873 verfassten, aber erst aus dem Nachlass veröffentlichten Aufsatz „Über Wahrheit und Lüge im außermoralischen Sinne“ vertritt Nietzsche die These, dass Wahrheit keine Übereinstimmung mit der Wirklichkeit sei, sondern eine Übereinkunft. Begriffe seien ursprünglich Metaphern gewesen, deren bildlichen Ursprung man vergessen habe; Wahrheiten seien daher „Illusionen, von denen man vergessen hat, daß sie welche sind“.

## Common mistakes

- Reading *Gott ist todt* as a triumphant atheist slogan. In § 125 a madman says it to unbelievers who laugh at him; the point is the loss of a foundation of values, which they haven't grasped.
- Translating *Übermensch* as "superman" in an academic text. Use "overman" or keep *Übermensch*, and don't give it a racial meaning: that is the misuse the lesson warns against.
- Quoting *Der Wille zur Macht* as a book by Nietzsche without comment. It is a compilation from his notes made after his collapse; say so.
- Confusing *außermoralisch* (outside morality, beyond moral judgment) with *unmoralisch* (immoral) or *amoralisch* (without morals).
- Using *Ressentiment* in Nietzsche's technical sense in everyday German. *Er hat Ressentiments gegen Fremde* means he has prejudices or grudges, not a theory of morality.
- Modernizing *todt, getödtet, That* when quoting. Quote the edition; modernize only in your own sentences (*tot, getötet, Tat*).

## Key points

- *Über Wahrheit und Lüge im außermoralischen Sinne* (1873, published from the Nachlass): truth is *ein bewegliches Heer von Metaphern, Metonymien, Anthropomorphismen*; truths are worn coins whose image is forgotten. A starting point for **[[perspectivism]]**.
- Nietzsche wrote in aphorisms from 1878 on (*Ein Buch für freie Geister*); *Was mich nicht umbringt, macht mich stärker* has the heading *Aus der Kriegsschule des Lebens* (*Götzen-Dämmerung*).
- *Die fröhliche Wissenschaft* § 125 (1882): the madman's *Gott ist todt!* diagnoses the loss of a foundation of values (*Nihilismus*); Nietzsche answers with the *Umwertung aller Werte* and *Lebensbejahung*.
- *Also sprach Zarathustra* (1883–85) parodies Luther's Bible; its hero is the *Verkünder* of the *Übermensch* and the *ewige Wiederkehr*. These terms have precise meanings; interpretations differ in detail.
- His sister's compilations and the Nazi reception distorted his work; the Colli–Montinari edition corrected the record.
- His rhythm comes from dashes, exclamations, self-answering questions and scare quotes: describe it, quote it as printed.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Das Ich und das Es: Freud's German and its translation
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) wrote some of the most influential German prose of the twentieth century, and most of the world reads it in translation. In German his key terms are ordinary words: *das Ich* (the I), *das Es* (the it), *das Über-Ich* (the over-I), *die Fehlleistung* (a faulty performance). In the standard English translation they became *ego*, *id*, *super-ego* and *parapraxis*. This lesson reads short passages from *Die Traumdeutung*, Freud's lectures on slips of the tongue and *Das Ich und das Es*, looks at his essayistic style, and asks what is gained and lost when plain German turns into Latinized English. It takes no position on the scientific status of psychoanalysis, which remains disputed; it is about language.

Lesson 04 gave you *die Psychoanalyse* and lesson 90 Freud's essay on the uncanny. Two words you know take on a special sense here: *die Verdrängung*, which you met as "displacement", is Freud's "repression", and *die Übertragung* (lesson 05h1: "translation, rendering") is his "transference".

## Freud and his readers

Freud trained as a doctor in Vienna and worked there for almost his whole life. After the annexation of Austria in March 1938 he emigrated to London, where he died in September 1939; he is therefore in the public domain. His books were among those burned in Germany in May 1933 (lesson 93).

He wrote for an educated general public, not only for doctors. In 1930 the city of Frankfurt gave him its Goethe Prize, an award for cultural achievement that has often gone to writers, and German critics have praised his prose ever since: clear, ironic, full of everyday comparisons, and constantly in dialogue with the reader. You'll see why below.

## The essayist: the first sentence of *Die Traumdeutung*

*Die Traumdeutung* (The Interpretation of Dreams) appeared in November 1899 with the date 1900 on its title page. It opens:

> „Auf den folgenden Blättern werde ich den Nachweis erbringen, daß es eine psychologische Technik gibt, welche gestattet, Träume zu deuten, und daß bei Anwendung dieses Verfahrens jeder Traum sich als ein sinnvolles psychisches Gebilde herausstellt, welches an angebbarer Stelle in das seelische Treiben des Wachens einzureihen ist.“

(From Project Gutenberg no. 40739, which reproduces the fourth, enlarged edition, Franz Deuticke, Leipzig and Vienna 1914.)

"In the following pages I shall prove that there is a psychological technique which makes it possible to interpret dreams, and that, if this procedure is applied, every dream turns out to be a meaningful psychical structure which can be assigned a specific place in the mental activity of waking life."

This is a classic German scholarly period, and still easy to follow:

- *ich* in the first sentence: Freud takes personal responsibility for the claim, as essayists do. (Compare the impersonal academic style of lesson 13: *Im Folgenden wird gezeigt, dass …*)
- *den Nachweis erbringen*: a function-verb phrase for *nachweisen* (to prove), formal and confident.
- Two parallel *daß*-clauses joined by *und*: the method exists, and it works. Each ends in a relative clause with *welche/welches*, the more formal alternative to *die/das*.
- *bei Anwendung dieses Verfahrens*: a nominal condition (= *wenn man dieses Verfahren anwendet*), C1 lesson 21.
- *an angebbarer Stelle … einzureihen ist*: *sein* + *zu*-infinitive (can/must be), and *angebbar* (that can be stated) with *-bar*.

Freud keeps this voice throughout: he anticipates objections (*Man wird mir einwenden …*), admits difficulties, and argues with the reader like a lawyer with a jury.

## Fehlleistungen: the Freudian slip

In *Zur Psychopathologie des Alltagslebens* (1901 in a journal, 1904 as a book) Freud collected *Fehlleistungen* (**[[parapraxis]]** in the English of the Standard Edition): everyday mistakes that seem accidental. German has a family of verbs with *ver-* in the sense "wrongly", and the book's subtitle uses them: *Über Vergessen, Versprechen, Vergreifen, Aberglaube und Irrtum*.

| Fehlleistung | verb | example |
|---|---|---|
| *der Versprecher* | *sich versprechen* (to misspeak) | *Entschuldigung, ich habe mich versprochen.* |
| *der Verleser* | *sich verlesen* (to misread) | *Ich habe mich verlesen: Es heißt „Mittwoch“, nicht „Montag“.* |
| *der Verschreiber* | *sich verschreiben* (to make a slip of the pen) | *In der Mail hat sie sich verschrieben.* |
| *das Verhören* | *sich verhören* (to mishear) | *Hast du „Hund“ gesagt? Dann habe ich mich verhört.* |
| *das Vergreifen* | *sich vergreifen* (to pick the wrong thing) | (Freud's term for slips of action) |

Note the reflexive: *versprechen* means "to promise", *sich versprechen* "to make a slip of the tongue". *Er hat mir das versprochen* and *Er hat sich versprochen* are different verbs in practice.

In his *Vorlesungen zur Einführung in die Psychoanalyse* (lectures given in Vienna in 1915–17), Freud's best-known example is this:

> „Ein Präsident unseres Abgeordnetenhauses eröffnete einmal die Sitzung mit den Worten:“

> „Meine Herren, ich konstatiere die Anwesenheit von ... Mitgliedern und erkläre somit die Sitzung für geschlossen.“

and his explanation:

> „Er erwartet sich nichts Gutes von der Sitzung und wäre froh, sie sofort wieder abbrechen zu können.“

(From Projekt Gutenberg-DE, after the S. Fischer edition of 1969, second lecture, *Die Fehlleistungen*. The dots stand for the number, as in the source.)

"A president of our Chamber of Deputies once opened the session with the words: 'Gentlemen, I note the presence of … members and hereby declare the session closed.'" — "He expects nothing good of the session and would be glad to be able to break it off at once."

For Freud such a slip is not noise but a compromise: an intention the speaker has pushed away (*geschlossen*) breaks through the intended one (*eröffnet*). Everyday German has kept the idea: *Das war ein freudscher Versprecher* (also spelled *Freud'scher*), said with a grin when a slip seems to reveal what someone really thinks.

Language notes: *unseres Abgeordnetenhauses* is the Austrian Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of the Reichsrat in Freud's Vienna. *konstatieren* (to state, to note formally) is formal and a little old-fashioned. *sich (Dativ) etwas von etwas erwarten*: to expect something of something for oneself.

## The structure of the mind: *Das Ich und das Es* (1923)

In 1923 Freud described the mind as three agencies. *Das Es* (the it) holds the drives (*die Triebe*); *das Über-Ich* (the over-I) is conscience and the internalized demands of parents and society; *das Ich* (the I) mediates between them and the outside world. Freud took the word *Es* from the physician Georg Groddeck, who, Freud suggests in a footnote, probably followed Nietzsche's usage: we are "lived" by forces we do not control.

> „Das Ich repräsentiert, was man Vernunft und Besonnenheit nennen kann, im Gegensatz zum Es, welches die Leidenschaften enthält.“

> „Es gleicht so im Verhältnis zum Es dem Reiter, der die überlegene Kraft des Pferdes zügeln soll, mit dem Unterschied, daß der Reiter dies mit eigenen Kräften versucht, das Ich mit geborgten.“

(From Projekt Gutenberg-DE, after the S. Fischer edition of 1975, chapter II.)

"The ego represents what may be called reason and good sense, in contrast to the id, which contains the passions." — "In its relation to the id it is thus like a rider who is meant to hold in check the superior strength of the horse, with the difference that the rider tries to do so with his own strength, the ego with borrowed strength."

Read the second sentence slowly, because German grammar sets a trap here:

- The first *Es* is the pronoun *es*, capitalized because it begins the sentence, and refers to *das Ich* (neuter). The second *Es* (*zum Es*) is the noun, the id. "It (the I) is like a rider in relation to the it." Freud's terms are so ordinary that they collide with the grammar.
- *einer Sache gleichen*: to resemble, with a dative (*dem Reiter*).
- *mit eigenen Kräften …, das Ich mit geborgten*: an ellipsis: *das Ich [versucht es] mit geborgten [Kräften]*. The adjective *geborgt* (borrowed) stands alone and agrees with the missing noun.

Why are *Ich* and *Es* neuter nouns with *das*? German nominalizes pronouns freely: *das Ich*, *das Du*, *das Wir-Gefühl*. In philosophy *das Ich* already meant "the self" (Fichte). Freud's move was to keep the everyday word.

Ten years later, in his *Neue Folge der Vorlesungen* (1933), Freud summed up the aim of analysis in five words and an image:

> „Wo Es war, soll Ich werden. Es ist Kulturarbeit etwa wie die Trockenlegung der Zuydersee.“

(Projekt Gutenberg-DE, after the S. Fischer edition of 1969, lecture *Die Zerlegung der psychischen Persönlichkeit*.)

"Where id was, there ego shall be. It is a work of culture, like the draining of the Zuyder Zee."

Without articles, *Es* and *Ich* sound like names or places; *soll* is the "ought" of a goal; *Kulturarbeit* compares therapy to the great Dutch land reclamation of Freud's time. Translators have argued about this sentence for decades.

## Words of psychoanalysis

- *der Trieb* (drive), *triebhaft* (driven by urges, often critical: *triebhaftes Verhalten*), *die Triebregung* (an instinctual impulse).
- *das Unbewusste* (the unconscious): a nominalized adjective, so *des Unbewussten*, *im Unbewussten*. Not the same as *das Unterbewusstsein* (lesson 04), which Freud avoided as a term.
- *die Verdrängung* (repression): keeping an unacceptable wish out of consciousness. *verdrängen* in this sense: *Sie hat die Erinnerung verdrängt*.
- *die Abwehr* and *der Abwehrmechanismus* (defence, defence mechanism): Anna Freud's *Das Ich und die Abwehrmechanismen* (1936) made the term standard.
- *die Sublimierung*, *sublimieren*: **[[sublimation]]**, redirecting a drive towards a goal society values, such as art or research. In chemistry *die Sublimation* is the passage from solid to gas; Freud's metaphor comes from there.
- *die Übertragung* (transference): the patient transfers feelings about earlier figures, often the parents, onto the analyst.
- *der Ödipuskomplex*: the child's desire for one parent and rivalry with the other, named after Sophocles' Oedipus.
- *die Couch*: the analyst's couch, on which the patient lies while the analyst sits out of sight (plural *Couchs* or *Couches*; Duden also gives *Couchen*).
- *die Traumdeutung*: both Freud's book and the activity.

Some of these are contested as science. In Germany psychoanalytically based therapy is one of the procedures covered by statutory health insurance (G-BA Psychotherapie-Richtlinie, § 15, as of November 2026), while many psychologists regard parts of Freud's theory as unproven. When you write about it, keep the two levels apart: *Nach Freud entsteht …* reports a theory; *Studien zeigen …* needs a source.

## Translating Freud

James Strachey's *Standard Edition* of Freud's psychological works (24 volumes, 1953–1974) made Freud's English what it is. Some of its choices:

| Freud | Standard Edition | literal | today's alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| *das Ich* | the ego | the I | the I, the self |
| *das Es* | the id | the it | the it |
| *das Über-Ich* | the super-ego | the over-I | — |
| *die Fehlleistung* | parapraxis | faulty act | slip, Freudian slip |
| *der Trieb* | instinct | drive | drive |
| *die Besetzung* | cathexis | occupation, investment | investment |

Latin *ego* and *id* had already appeared in English translations in Freud's lifetime; Strachey made them standard. In *Freud and Man's Soul* (first published as an essay in *The New Yorker* in 1982, then as a book), the psychoanalyst Bruno Bettelheim argued that these choices turned a humane, personal language into a cold, pseudo-medical one: *das Ich* is what I call myself, *the ego* is an object I observe. Defenders of Strachey answer that a consistent technical vocabulary was needed for an international science, and that *the it* would hardly have worked in English.

This is a C2 lesson about translation as much as about Freud: a term carries not only a meaning but a register and a relationship with the reader.

## A modern text: *Wie aus dem Ich ein Ego wurde*

Read this column, written for this course. Its second paragraph paraphrases Bettelheim's argument in reported speech; it is not a quotation.

> **Wie aus dem Ich ein Ego wurde**
>
> Wer Freud auf Deutsch liest, ist oft überrascht, wie wenig Fachjargon er braucht. Er spricht vom Ich, vom Es und vom Über-Ich, von Fehlleistungen und Trieben – Wörtern, die jedes Schulkind versteht oder zumindest zu verstehen glaubt. In der maßgeblichen englischen Ausgabe, der sogenannten Standard Edition, klingt derselbe Autor wie ein Mediziner des 19. Jahrhunderts: Aus dem Ich wird das „ego“, aus dem Es das „id“, aus der Fehlleistung die „parapraxis“.
>
> Der Psychoanalytiker Bruno Bettelheim hat dieser Übersetzung vorgeworfen, sie habe Freuds Menschenbild verfälscht. Wer „das Ich“ sage, meine sich selbst; wer „the ego“ sage, rede über einen Gegenstand. Ein Leser, der Freud nur auf Englisch kenne, halte die Psychoanalyse deshalb für kühler und technischer, als sie gemeint gewesen sei.
>
> Ganz von der Hand zu weisen ist der Einwand nicht. Allerdings hatten die Übersetzer gute Gründe. Sie wollten die Psychoanalyse als Wissenschaft etablieren, und die Medizin sprach damals Latein und Griechisch. Zudem lässt sich das deutsche „Es“ im Englischen kaum nachbilden: „the it“ wäre schlicht unverständlich gewesen. Und die lateinischen Begriffe waren schon zu Freuds Lebzeiten in englischen Übersetzungen üblich.
>
> Lehrreich ist der Streit trotzdem, und zwar weit über die Psychoanalyse hinaus. Er zeigt, dass Übersetzen nie nur Wörter austauscht, sondern auch einen Ton, eine Haltung, ein Verhältnis zwischen Autor und Leser. Freud schrieb für ein gebildetes Publikum, nicht nur für Ärzte; er argumentierte, räumte Einwände ein und zog Vergleiche aus dem Alltag. Wer ihn auf Deutsch liest, hört einen Essayisten. Wer ihn in Fachbegriffen liest, begegnet einem Theoretiker. Beides ist Freud – nur nicht in derselben Mischung.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**How the I became an ego**

Anyone who reads Freud in German is often surprised by how little jargon he needs. He speaks of the I, the it and the over-I, of faulty acts and drives – words every schoolchild understands, or at least thinks they understand. In the authoritative English edition, the so-called Standard Edition, the same author sounds like a 19th-century physician: the I becomes the "ego", the it the "id", the faulty act "parapraxis".

The psychoanalyst Bruno Bettelheim accused this translation of having distorted Freud's view of human beings. Anyone who says "das Ich", he argued, means himself; anyone who says "the ego" is talking about an object. A reader who knows Freud only in English therefore takes psychoanalysis to be colder and more technical than it was meant to be.

The objection can't be dismissed out of hand. But the translators had good reasons. They wanted to establish psychoanalysis as a science, and medicine at the time spoke Latin and Greek. Besides, the German "Es" can hardly be reproduced in English: "the it" would simply have been incomprehensible. And the Latin terms were already common in English translations during Freud's lifetime.

All the same, the dispute is instructive, and far beyond psychoanalysis. It shows that translating never just exchanges words, but also a tone, an attitude, a relationship between author and reader. Freud wrote for an educated public, not only for doctors; he argued, conceded objections and drew comparisons from everyday life. Whoever reads him in German hears an essayist. Whoever reads him in technical terms meets a theorist. Both are Freud – just not in the same mixture.

</details>

Things to notice:

- *Bettelheim hat … vorgeworfen, sie habe … verfälscht. Wer „das Ich“ sage, meine sich selbst; …*: after one introducing verb, the whole paragraph continues in Konjunktiv I (*sage, meine, rede, kenne, halte, sei*), the standard way to report an argument at length without repeating *er sagt*.
- *als sie gemeint gewesen sei*: Konjunktiv I past in a comparison clause.
- *Ganz von der Hand zu weisen ist der Einwand nicht.*: the idiom *etwas von der Hand weisen* (to dismiss), fronted with *zu* (*sein* + *zu*: can be), and the negation at the very end: a careful concession.
- *Wer ihn auf Deutsch liest, hört einen Essayisten. Wer ihn in Fachbegriffen liest, begegnet einem Theoretiker.*: two parallel *wer*-sentences, a contrast built by repetition.
- *Beides ist Freud*: *beides* (neuter singular) for two different things taken together.

## Common mistakes

- Confusing *sich versprechen* (to make a slip of the tongue) with *versprechen* (to promise). *Ich habe mich versprochen* doesn't promise anything.
- Translating *das Es* as "it" in an English essay without explanation. In English writing about Freud, use *the id* and give the German once, or explain your choice.
- Reading the first *Es* in *Es gleicht so im Verhältnis zum Es dem Reiter* as the id. It's the pronoun for *das Ich*.
- Using *das Unterbewusstsein* when you mean Freud's *das Unbewusste*. The everyday word is fine in conversation; in writing about Freud, use his term.
- Giving *die Verdrängung* only the sense "displacement" (of residents, of competitors). In psychology it is "repression".
- Presenting Freud's claims as established fact or dismissing them in a sentence. Report them (*Nach Freud …; Freud zufolge …*) and keep evaluation separate and sourced.
- Writing *Freudscher Versprecher* (capital, no apostrophe). The spelling rules allow *freudscher* (lower case) or *Freud'scher* (capital with apostrophe).

## Key points

- Freud's terms are plain German: *das Ich, das Es, das Über-Ich, die Fehlleistung, der Trieb*; Strachey's *Standard Edition* (1953–1974) Latinized them as *ego, id, super-ego, parapraxis, instinct*. Bettelheim (*Freud and Man's Soul*) criticized the loss of tone; defenders point to the need for a technical vocabulary.
- *Die Traumdeutung* (November 1899, dated 1900) opens with a confident first-person period: *Auf den folgenden Blättern werde ich den Nachweis erbringen, daß …*
- **[[Parapraxis]]** (*Fehlleistungen*): *sich versprechen, verlesen, verschreiben, verhören, vergreifen*; the president who declares the session closed instead of open.
- *Das Ich und das Es* (1923): the ego as a rider on the horse of the id, *mit geborgten* (strength); *Wo Es war, soll Ich werden* (1933).
- Special senses: *Verdrängung* = repression, *Übertragung* = transference, **[[sublimation]]** (*Sublimierung*) = redirecting a drive towards valued goals; *Abwehrmechanismus, Ödipuskomplex, das Unbewusste*.
- Report psychoanalytic claims neutrally; the scientific status of psychoanalysis is disputed.

lessons.title: Stefan Zweig, Die Welt von Gestern: memory, Europe and exile
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The module ends with a book written at the end of the world it describes. Stefan Zweig wrote *Die Welt von Gestern. Erinnerungen eines Europäers* in exile, during the last years of his life, and it was published in 1942 in Stockholm, after his death. It is one of the most widely read German memoirs of the twentieth century and a key text of **[[exile literature]]**. This lesson reads the preface and the famous opening of the first chapter, looks at the memoir as a genre and at the question every reader of this book faces: how far can nostalgia be trusted? It also gives the historical context of German-language exile after 1933 and practises summarizing and commenting (lessons 29 and 11).

## Stefan Zweig (1881–1942)

Zweig was born in Vienna into a wealthy Jewish family. Before 1933 he was one of the most successful and most translated German-language authors: novellas, historical biographies (*Joseph Fouché*, *Marie Antoinette*) and the miniatures of *Sternstunden der Menschheit*. He lived in Salzburg from 1919. In 1934, after the police searched his house for weapons he had never owned, he left Austria for England, first London, later Bath. He moved on to New York in 1940 and then to Brazil, and in February 1942 he and his wife Lotte took their own lives in Petrópolis, near Rio de Janeiro. He died in 1942, so his work has been in the public domain since 2013.

## The preface: who is speaking

The book's first sentence announces modesty:

> „Ich habe meiner Person niemals so viel Wichtigkeit beigemessen, daß es mich verlockt hätte, anderen die Geschichten meines Lebens zu erzählen.“

Zweig says he writes not because his life is important but because his generation lived through more upheaval than any before it. He describes the circumstances of writing:

> „Ich schreibe sie mitten im Kriege, ich schreibe sie in der Fremde und ohne den mindesten Gedächtnisbehelf.“

> „Kein Exemplar meiner Bücher, keine Aufzeichnungen, keine Freundesbriefe sind mir in meinem Hotelzimmer zur Hand.“

and then turns the lack of sources into a theory of memory:

> „Denn ich betrachte unser Gedächtnis nicht als ein das eine bloß zufällig behaltendes und das andere zufällig verlierendes Element, sondern als eine wissend ordnende und weise ausschaltende Kraft.“

He calls himself a witness, *Zeuge*, against his will:

> „Wider meinen Willen bin ich Zeuge geworden der furchtbarsten Niederlage der Vernunft und des wildesten Triumphes der Brutalität innerhalb der Chronik der Zeiten; […]“

and, having lost his country, finds a strange freedom in it:

> „[…] gerade der Heimatlose wird in einem neuen Sinne frei, und nur der mit nichts mehr Verbundene braucht auf nichts mehr Rücksicht zu nehmen.“

(All quotations from Projekt Gutenberg-DE, after an edition of the Deutscher Bücherbund, 1981. The spelling *daß, bloß* is that edition's.)

"I have never attached so much importance to my own person that I was tempted to tell others the stories of my life." — "I am writing them in the middle of the war, I am writing them abroad and without the slightest aid to my memory." — "Not a single copy of my books, no notes, no letters from friends are at hand in my hotel room." — "For I regard our memory not as an element that keeps one thing merely by chance and loses another by chance, but as a force that knowingly orders and wisely excludes." — "Against my will I have become a witness of the most terrible defeat of reason and the wildest triumph of brutality in the chronicle of the ages; …" — "… it is precisely the homeless man who becomes free in a new sense, and only the man who is bound to nothing need have regard for nothing."

Notes on the German:

- *Wichtigkeit beimessen* (+ dative): to attach importance to. *so viel …, daß es mich verlockt hätte*: a result clause in Konjunktiv II past, because the result never happened.
- *Ich schreibe sie …, ich schreibe sie …*: anaphora, the rhetoric of a speech rather than a diary.
- *der Gedächtnisbehelf*: an aid to memory (*der Behelf*, makeshift aid, is rare today; everyday German says *die Gedächtnisstütze*).
- *ein das eine bloß zufällig behaltendes und das andere zufällig verlierendes Element*: two extended participle attributes, each with its own object (*das eine*, *das andere*), between *ein* and *Element*. Unpack them: *ein Element, das das eine bloß zufällig behält und das andere zufällig verliert*. The second half answers with two short participles: *wissend ordnend*, *weise ausschaltend*.
- *Wider meinen Willen*: *wider* + accusative (gehoben) = *gegen*. *bin ich Zeuge geworden der furchtbarsten Niederlage …*: the genitive attribute of *Zeuge* is placed after the participle, in the Nachfeld, so the sentence can grow long without losing its frame. Modern standard order would be *bin ich Zeuge der furchtbarsten Niederlage … geworden*.
- *der Heimatlose*, *der mit nichts mehr Verbundene*: nominalized adjective and participle, the second extended (*mit nichts mehr*). The freedom is bitter: *Heimatlosigkeit* as liberation is a paradox.

## "Das goldene Zeitalter der Sicherheit"

The first chapter, *Die Welt der Sicherheit*, opens with the formula that made the book famous:

> „Wenn ich versuche, für die Zeit vor dem Ersten Weltkriege, in der ich aufgewachsen bin, eine handliche Formel zu finden, so hoffe ich am prägnantesten zu sein, wenn ich sage: es war das goldene Zeitalter der Sicherheit. Alles in unserer fast tausendjährigen österreichischen Monarchie schien auf Dauer gegründet und der Staat selbst der oberste Garant dieser Beständigkeit.“

> „Dieses Gefühl der Sicherheit war der erstrebenswerteste Besitz von Millionen, das gemeinsame Lebensideal. Nur wer sorglos in die Zukunft blicken konnte, genoß mit gutem Gefühl die Gegenwart.“

A little later comes a pun: *„das Jahrhundert der Sicherheit wurde das goldene Zeitalter des Versicherungswesens“*.

"If I try to find a handy formula for the time before the First World War in which I grew up, I hope to be most concise if I say: it was the golden age of security. Everything in our almost thousand-year-old Austrian monarchy seemed founded to last, and the state itself the supreme guarantor of this permanence." — "This feeling of security was the most desirable possession of millions, the common ideal of life. Only those who could look into the future without worry enjoyed the present with a good conscience." — "the century of security became the golden age of insurance".

How it works:

- *Wenn ich versuche …, so hoffe ich …, wenn ich sage: …*: a conditional resumed by *so* (formal, older), then a second *wenn*-clause, then the colon: the long approach makes the short formula land.
- *vor dem Ersten Weltkriege*: old dative *-e*.
- *es war* after the colon in lower case: older practice. Today's rule capitalizes after a colon when a complete sentence follows (*… wenn ich sage: Es war …*).
- *schien auf Dauer gegründet und der Staat selbst der oberste Garant*: coordination ellipsis: *schien* serves both halves (*und der Staat selbst [schien] der oberste Garant*).
- *erstrebenswerteste*: superlative of *erstrebenswert* (worth striving for).
- *Sicherheit → Versicherungswesen*: the wordplay is the critique. A world that insures everything believes everything can be calculated.
- The tense is the narrative Präteritum, but the stance is evaluative from the first line: *hoffe ich am prägnantesten zu sein* is the present of the writer in 1941, not the past.

## Memoir, autobiography, memory

German distinguishes, loosely:

- *die Autobiografie* (also *Autobiographie*): the account of one's own life, centred on the self and its development.
- *die Memoiren* (plural only): recollections of a public figure, centred on events and people they witnessed.
- *die Erinnerungen* (plural): the neutral word, as in Zweig's subtitle.

*Die Welt von Gestern* is closer to *Memoiren*: Zweig tells the story of a generation and of Europe, and leaves out a great deal about himself. Critics have long noted that his two marriages hardly appear and that the "security" he describes was the security of the prosperous middle class of Vienna. The book is also a work of art: carefully composed chapters, a few unforgettable formulas, and the knowledge of the ending shaping every page about the beginning. Reading it as a source means reading it as one person's ordered memory, which is exactly what Zweig says it is.

## Exile after 1933

In 1933 the Nazi regime brought the federal states, associations, the press and cultural life into line, a process called *die Gleichschaltung*. On 10 May 1933, students burned books by Jewish, left-wing, pacifist and other unwanted authors in Berlin and many university towns: *die Bücherverbrennung*. Zweig's books were among them. In *Die Welt von Gestern* he records how they were *„auf großen Scheiterhaufen unter Rezitierung patriotischer Sprüche zu Asche verbrannt“* (burned to ashes on great pyres while patriotic slogans were recited), and how printing and selling them became a crime.

Hundreds of writers left: some *emigrierten* early, others fled at the last moment. The regime answered with *Ausbürgerung*, stripping emigrants of their citizenship; Thomas Mann, for example, was *ausgebürgert* in December 1936. From October 1940 to 1945 he spoke to German listeners through the BBC in a series of radio addresses that began *Deutsche Hörer!* What these writers produced in Prague, Amsterdam, Paris, Moscow, Los Angeles or Rio is called *die Exilliteratur*. For Zweig, an Austrian, the turning point was the annexation of Austria in 1938, which made his Austrian passport worthless. The last chapter, *Die Agonie des Friedens*, describes the humiliation of waiting for papers; he recalls the words of an exiled Russian:

> „Früher hatte der Mensch nur einen Körper und eine Seele. Heute braucht er noch einen Paß dazu, sonst wird er nicht wie ein Mensch behandelt.“

"In the past a person had only a body and a soul. Today he needs a passport as well, or he is not treated like a human being."

Words for people who leave:

| Word | Nuance |
|---|---|
| *der Emigrant, die Emigrantin* | someone who has left their country, often for political reasons; the usual word for the émigrés of 1933–45 |
| *der Exilant, die Exilantin* | someone living in exile; stresses that return is impossible |
| *der Flüchtling* (B1) | someone who flees danger; today also the legal and political term |
| *der Auswanderer* (from *auswandern*, B1) | someone who emigrates by choice, for work or a new life |

Many exiles disliked the word *Emigranten*, because it suggested they had left of their own free will. Zweig's own ideal was the *Weltbürger*, the citizen of the world: the subtitle *Erinnerungen eines Europäers* makes Europe, not a nation, his homeland. The book shows what it costs when that idea has no passport.

## A modern text: *Die Sicherheit der anderen*

Read this review essay, written for this course.

> **Die Sicherheit der anderen**
>
> Kaum ein Buch über das alte Europa wird so gern verschenkt wie Stefan Zweigs „Die Welt von Gestern“. Das hat Gründe. Zweig erzählt elegant, er beherrscht die Pointe wie das Panorama, und die Formel vom „goldenen Zeitalter der Sicherheit“ hat sich so tief ins Gedächtnis eingegraben, dass man sie für eine historische Tatsache halten könnte.
>
> Genau darin liegt das Problem. Die Sicherheit, die Zweig beschreibt, war die Sicherheit eines wohlhabenden Wiener Bürgersohns. Wer um 1900 in einer Hinterhofwohnung in Ottakring lebte, zwölf Stunden in der Fabrik stand oder in Galizien hungerte, hätte das Jahrhundert kaum golden genannt. Auch der Antisemitismus, mit dem in Wien lange vor 1914 Wahlen gewonnen wurden, klingt bei Zweig erstaunlich gedämpft.
>
> Das macht das Buch nicht wertlos. Man muss es nur als das lesen, was es ist: nicht als Geschichtsschreibung, sondern als Erinnerung, und zwar als Erinnerung eines Menschen, der im Exil schreibt, ohne Bücher und Aufzeichnungen, und der weiß, dass die Welt, von der er erzählt, unwiederbringlich verloren ist. Zweig selbst hat das Gedächtnis eine „wissend ordnende“ Kraft genannt. Wer so offen erklärt, dass er auswählt, kann schwerlich der Verfälschung bezichtigt werden.
>
> Bleibt die Frage, warum uns diese Nostalgie noch heute berührt. Vielleicht, weil Zweig den Verlust der Sicherheit nicht als Theorie beschreibt, sondern als Erfahrung: den Pass, der plötzlich mehr zählt als der Mensch, die Bücher, die öffentlich verbrannt werden, das Land, das einen nicht mehr haben will. Diese Kapitel sind keine Verklärung. Sie sind das Zeugnis eines Weltbürgers, der zusehen musste, wie seine Welt zerfiel, und der am Ende nicht mehr die Kraft hatte, auf eine neue zu warten.

<details><summary>Translation</summary>

**Other people's security**

Hardly any book about old Europe is given as a present as often as Stefan Zweig's "The World of Yesterday". There are reasons for that. Zweig writes elegantly, he commands the punchline as well as the panorama, and the formula of the "golden age of security" has dug itself so deeply into our memory that one could take it for a historical fact.

That is precisely the problem. The security Zweig describes was the security of a wealthy Viennese bourgeois son. Anyone who around 1900 lived in a back-courtyard flat in Ottakring, stood twelve hours in a factory or went hungry in Galicia would hardly have called the century golden. The antisemitism with which elections were won in Vienna long before 1914 also sounds surprisingly muted in Zweig.

That doesn't make the book worthless. One just has to read it as what it is: not as historiography but as memory, and the memory of a man writing in exile, without books or notes, who knows that the world he is telling of is irretrievably lost. Zweig himself called memory a force that "knowingly orders". Someone who declares so openly that he is selecting can hardly be accused of falsification.

That leaves the question why this nostalgia still moves us today. Perhaps because Zweig describes the loss of security not as a theory but as an experience: the passport that suddenly counts for more than the person, the books burned in public, the country that no longer wants you. These chapters are no glorification. They are the testimony of a citizen of the world who had to watch his world fall apart, and who in the end no longer had the strength to wait for a new one.

</details>

Things to notice:

- *Genau darin liegt das Problem.*: the turn of a review after the praise; *darin* points back to the whole previous sentence.
- *Wer um 1900 … lebte, …, hätte das Jahrhundert kaum golden genannt.*: a free relative clause with three verbs, then Konjunktiv II past for a counterfactual judgment.
- *mit dem in Wien … Wahlen gewonnen wurden*: a passive in a relative clause, so no agent needs to be named.
- *Wer so offen erklärt, dass er auswählt, kann schwerlich der Verfälschung bezichtigt werden.*: *bezichtigen* with a genitive (lesson 05) and the modal word *schwerlich* (lesson 04).
- *Bleibt die Frage, warum …*: verb-first with the subject after it, a fixed opening for the last point (*Bleibt die Frage* = *Es bleibt die Frage*).
- The end returns to Zweig's death without naming it: *nicht mehr die Kraft hatte, auf eine neue zu warten*. A review may allude where a biography must state.

## Summarizing and commenting

A summary of the preface reports and keeps its distance (lesson 29):

> In seinem Vorwort zu „Die Welt von Gestern“ erklärt Stefan Zweig, er schreibe nicht aus Eitelkeit, sondern weil seine Generation mehr Umbrüche erlebt habe als jede vor ihr. Er verfasse das Buch im Krieg und im Exil, ohne Bücher, Notizen oder Briefe. Das Gedächtnis sei für ihn kein zufälliger Speicher, sondern eine Kraft, die bewusst ordne und auswähle.

A comment then takes a position, with a concession and a reason (lesson 11): *Zweigs Offenheit über die Grenzen seiner Quellen spricht für ihn; dennoch sollte man …*; *Was er als Weisheit des Gedächtnisses bezeichnet, kann man auch als Verklärung lesen.*; *Gerade weil das Buch so meisterhaft erzählt ist, …*

## Common mistakes

- Treating "das goldene Zeitalter der Sicherheit" as a historian's finding. It's a memoirist's formula, and Zweig himself says he selects.
- Using *Emigrant* and *Flüchtling* as exact synonyms. For the exiles of 1933–45 *Emigrant* or *Exilant* is usual; *Flüchtling* is the general and legal word for someone who flees danger; *Auswanderer* left by choice.
- Writing *die Memoiren* in the singular. It's plural only: *Seine Memoiren erschienen 1942.* (The singular *Memoire* is a different, rare word for a memorandum.)
- Confusing *ausbürgern* (to strip someone of citizenship; separable: *Er wurde 1936 ausgebürgert*) with *auswandern* (to emigrate) or *abschieben* (to deport).
- Copying *es war* in lower case after a colon in your own text. Modern rules capitalize a complete sentence after a colon.

## Key points

- *Die Welt von Gestern. Erinnerungen eines Europäers* was written in exile and published in Stockholm in 1942, after Zweig's death in Petrópolis in February 1942. It is a central work of **[[exile literature]]**.
- The preface: written *mitten im Kriege, … in der Fremde und ohne den mindesten Gedächtnisbehelf*; memory as *eine wissend ordnende und weise ausschaltende Kraft*; *gerade der Heimatlose wird in einem neuen Sinne frei*.
- The first chapter's formula: *es war das goldene Zeitalter der Sicherheit*, with the pun on *Versicherungswesen*.
- The book is closer to *Memoiren* than to an *Autobiografie*: a generation's story, selective and nostalgic, to be read as ordered memory, not as history.
- Context: *Gleichschaltung* and *Bücherverbrennung* (10 May 1933), *Ausbürgerung* (Thomas Mann, December 1936), *Deutsche Hörer!* (BBC, from 1940), the passport as the exile's fate.
- Style: long periods resumed by *so*, extended participle attributes, genitive in the Nachfeld (*bin ich Zeuge geworden der …*), anaphora, ellipsis, older spelling and capitalization in the edition quoted.
